Per-family default metrics

Task family Default metric Direction "clustering" mean_amplitude_separation higher is better "smoothing" optimal_gcv lower is better "basis" optimal_edf lower is better "regression_cv" min_cv_error lower is better "regression" r_squared higher is better "scoring" functional_mse lower is better "fpca" cumulative_variance_explained higher is better

Raises

  • ValueError — empty candidates, unknown or missing metric, mixed task families, or metric absent from any candidate (COMPARE-03).
  • GroundingViolationError — when run_llm=True and the LLM narration cites a value absent from all candidates' diagnostics.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
All candidates must share the same task family. Comparing, for example, a clustering result against a regression result raises ValueError before any ranking. The guard is fail-closed: no partial ranking is returned.

The LLM narrates; fdars ranks. When run_llm=True the LLM receives the fdars-computed ranking and winner, then narrates them. It cannot override the winner declared in result["winner"].

argvals is required for distance-based metrics. For "clustering" or "alignment" aspects, mean_amplitude_separation (and related distance keys) are None when argvals is not supplied. Passing argvals to compare_methods forwards it to each build_diagnostics call automatically.

cumulative_variance_explained (fpca) is list-valued. The ranker extracts the last element (total cumulative variance) as the scalar for comparison. Ensure the FPCA result includes enough components for a meaningful last-element value.

docs.title: MCP Server
docs.text:
Illustrative fences — not run in the docs build

All Python fences on this page are illustrative only. They require pip install "fdars[mcp,advisor]" (mcp>=2.0.0, Python 3.10+) and are not executed during the docs build. The docs build does not depend on the [mcp] extra or Python 3.10+.

The fdars-advisor MCP server extends the Python API with the full interpret → recommend → re-run → compare agentic loop. Where the Python API returns an Advice object and stops, the MCP server gives a language model three composable tools so it can re-run fdars with adjusted parameters and observe a deterministic, fdars-computed before/after delta — without any fabricated numbers ever crossing the tool boundary.

See the overview for the grounding invariant and the three-surface architecture. The Agent Skill page documents the packaged skill that orchestrates these tools automatically.

docs.title: Handle model
docs.text: The MCP server uses a by-reference HandleRegistry to keep large NumPy arrays inside the process and out of the JSON transport layer.

docs.title: How handles work
docs.text:
Before calling any tool, the client registers a dataset (observation matrix + evaluation grid) by calling registry.store_dataset(data, argvals). The registry stores the arrays in-process and returns an opaque dataset handle of the form ds-<8-hex-chars>. From that point on, tools exchange only the handle string — the arrays never appear in JSON output.

When a tool runs an fdars method and produces a result dict, the raw result (which may contain NumPy arrays) is stored via registry.store_result(result), returning a result handle of the form r-<8-hex-chars>. Only this handle — and scalar diagnostic values — ever cross the tool boundary.

from fdars.mcp._registry import registry

# Register the dataset once before calling any tool
dataset_id = registry.store_dataset(data, argvals)
# dataset_id is e.g. "ds-3fa2c1b4"

# After a tool run, retrieve the stored result if needed in-process
result = registry.get_result(result_id)

docs.title: Registry methods
docs.text: Method Signature Returns store_dataset store_dataset(data, argvals) -> str Dataset handle ds-<hex> get_dataset get_dataset(ds_id) -> (data, argvals) (np.ndarray, np.ndarray) tuple store_result store_result(result) -> str Result handle r-<hex> get_result get_result(r_id) -> dict Stored result dict clear clear() -> None Clears all datasets and results

docs.title: Why by-reference
docs.text:
The grounding invariant requires that fdars computes every number. The by-reference model enforces an additional efficiency and grounding property: large NumPy arrays — smoothed curves, FPCA scores, cluster centers — stay in the in-process registry and only opaque handle strings + scalar diagnostics travel as JSON over the stdio transport. This keeps the tool boundary clean, prevents arrays from being fabricated or rounded in transit, and avoids serialising potentially megabyte-scale matrices into MCP messages.

The registry is a module-level singleton (registry = HandleRegistry() in fdars.mcp._registry). Client and server share the same in-process dict over stdio, so a handle registered before launching run_stdio() is immediately accessible to all tool handlers.

docs.title: stdio setup
docs.text:
The fdars-advisor MCP server communicates over stdio only (v2.0). Start the server with run_stdio() — the console-script entry point that blocks until stdin is closed:

from fdars.mcp.server import run_stdio

# Blocks — call from a console-script or __main__ guard, never from a tool handler
run_stdio()

The installed package registers a fdars-mcp-server console script that calls run_stdio() directly. A client (e.g. Claude Desktop or a custom MCP host) launches this process and communicates over stdin/stdout:

# Install the MCP extra (Python 3.10+ required):
pip install "fdars[mcp,advisor]"

# Start the server — the client writes JSON-RPC to its stdin and reads from stdout:
fdars-mcp-server

run_stdio() calls mcp.run(transport="stdio") on the MCPServer("fdars-advisor") instance. The tool handlers (fdars_build_diagnostics, fdars_run_method, fdars_compare_run) are transport-agnostic — they do not reference stdio in any way. A future HTTP/SSE transport would only require changing the transport argument in run_stdio, not in any tool code.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Three tools are exposed over MCP. All tool handlers are synchronous (def, not async def) — fdars methods are synchronous Rust calls via PyO3, and wrapping in an executor is unnecessary.

Supported methods (all three tools): "alignment", "fpca", "basis", "smoothing", "clustering" (case-insensitive).

docs.title: fdars_build_diagnostics
docs.text:
Build offline diagnostics for an fdars dataset or result. Delegates to advisor.build_diagnostics — deterministic, offline, no API key required.

Parameters

Parameter Type Default Description dataset_id str — Handle to the registered dataset. Obtain via registry.store_dataset(data, argvals). method str — One of "alignment", "fpca", "basis", "smoothing", "clustering". result_id str or None None Handle to a stored result dict (e.g. from a prior fdars_run_method call). When None, the raw dataset data matrix is used as the result input. with_argvals bool True When True, passes the dataset's argvals array to build_diagnostics for distance metrics.

Returns

A JSON-serialisable dict — the same shape as advisor.build_diagnostics output (per-method keys; see the Python API for the key inventory per method). The diagnostics dict is also stored as a new result handle in the registry (available via registry.get_result), though the handle is not returned.

Raises

ValueError if method is not in the supported set. KeyError if dataset_id or result_id is not found in the registry.

docs.title: fdars_run_method
docs.text:
Run any of the six supported fdars methods on a registered dataset. Returns only an opaque result handle and the method name — arrays never leave the tool boundary.

Parameters

Parameter Type Default Description dataset_id str — Opaque handle returned by registry.store_dataset(data, argvals). The dataset must be pre-registered. method str — One of "alignment", "fpca", "basis", "smoothing", "clustering". Case-insensitive. lambda_ float or None None Warp penalty for alignment (default 0.0) or regularisation for smoothing. Ignored for fpca, basis, clustering. n_basis int or None None Number of B-spline basis functions for smoothing (pspline_fit_gcv). Default 15. Ignored for other methods. n_comp int or None None Number of FPCA components for fpca. Default 3. Ignored for other methods. k int or None None Number of clusters for clustering (kmeans_fd). Default 3. Ignored for other methods. seed int or None None RNG seed for clustering. Default 42. Ignored for other methods.

Returns

{"result_id": str, "method": str}

The raw fdars result — which may contain NumPy arrays — is stored in the registry under result_id. Only the handle string and the method name are returned. Arrays never appear in JSON output (by-reference invariant).

Per-method parameter mapping (only the listed parameter is used; others are silently ignored):

Method fdars function Active parameter(s) Default(s) alignment fdars.alignment.karcher_mean lambda_ 0.0 fpca fdars.regression.fpca n_comp 3 basis fdars.basis.basis_nbasis_cv lambda_ 1.0 smoothing fdars.basis.pspline_fit_gcv n_basis 15 clustering fdars.clustering.kmeans_fd k, seed 3, 42

Raises

ValueError if method is not in the supported set. KeyError if dataset_id is not in the registry.

docs.title: fdars_compare_run
docs.text:
Re-run an fdars method with new parameters and return a deterministic before/after delta. This is the TOOL-03 agentic re-run/compare tool — the key difference between the MCP surface and the recommend-only Python API.

Parameters

Parameter Type Default Description dataset_id str — Opaque handle for the registered dataset. method str — One of "alignment", "fpca", "basis", "smoothing", "clustering". before_result_id str — Handle ID for the prior run result (from fdars_run_method or fdars_build_diagnostics). lambda_ float or None None After-run warp penalty for alignment or regularisation for smoothing. n_basis int or None None After-run basis function count for smoothing. Default 15. n_comp int or None None After-run FPCA component count for fpca. Default 3. k int or None None After-run cluster count for clustering. Default 3. seed int or None None After-run RNG seed for clustering. Default 42.

Returns

A JSON-serialisable dict with five keys:

Key Type Description before_result_id str The handle ID of the before result (same as the input argument). after_result_id str The handle ID of the newly stored after result. before dict Full diagnostics dict from advisor.build_diagnostics for the before run. after dict Full diagnostics dict from advisor.build_diagnostics for the after run. delta dict Scalar numeric differences: after[key] - before[key] for every key where both values are a finite float or int (booleans excluded).

The delta dict is the observable: every value is fdars-computed. An empty delta means no finite scalar keys were shared between the two diagnostics dicts.

Raises

ValueError if method is not in the supported set, or if an after-parameter key is not in {"lambda_", "n_basis", "n_comp", "k", "seed"}. KeyError if dataset_id or before_result_id is not in the registry.

docs.title: Re-run / compare loop
docs.text: The following example mirrors examples/mcp_recipe.py — the canonical register → run → compare recipe shipped with the package. It uses the Canadian Weather dataset (35 weather stations × 365 daily temperature points).

docs.title: Step 1 — Register the dataset
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from fdars import datasets
from fdars.mcp._registry import registry

# Load the Canadian Weather dataset
ds = datasets.load_canadian_weather()
X = np.asarray(ds.data.data, dtype=float)    # shape (35, 365)
day = np.asarray(ds.argvals, dtype=float)    # shape (365,) — day-of-year grid

# Register in the handle registry before calling any tool
dataset_id = registry.store_dataset(X, day)
# dataset_id is e.g. "ds-3fa2c1b4"

docs.title: Step 2 — Run the before method
docs.text:
Call fdars_run_method (or the underlying run_method directly) with method="smoothing" and n_basis=15. The tool maps smoothing to fdars.basis.pspline_fit_gcv, stores the raw result in the registry, and returns only the result handle:

from fdars.mcp.server import fdars_run_method

before_handle = fdars_run_method(dataset_id, method="smoothing", n_basis=15)
# Returns: {"result_id": "r-a1b2c3d4", "method": "smoothing"}

before_result_id = before_handle["result_id"]

The raw result (fitted curves, EDF, GCV value, AIC, BIC) stays in the registry. Only the handle ID crosses the tool boundary.

docs.title: Step 3 — Compare with new parameters
docs.text:
Call fdars_compare_run with the same dataset, the same method, the before result handle, and the new after-parameter (n_basis=25 — more basis functions, potentially smoother fit):

from fdars.mcp.server import fdars_compare_run

compare_result = fdars_compare_run(
    dataset_id,
    method="smoothing",
    before_result_id=before_result_id,
    n_basis=25,
)

fdars_compare_run re-runs pspline_fit_gcv with n_basis=25, builds diagnostics for both the before and after runs via advisor.build_diagnostics, and returns the full before/after dicts plus the scalar delta.

docs.title: Step 4 — Read the observable delta
docs.text:
after_result_id = compare_result["after_result_id"]
before_diag = compare_result["before"]   # full diagnostics, n_basis=15 run
after_diag = compare_result["after"]    # full diagnostics, n_basis=25 run
delta = compare_result["delta"]          # after - before, finite scalar keys only

# delta contains scalar keys such as:
#   {"optimal_edf": 2.3, "optimal_gcv": -0.04, ...}
# Every value is fdars-computed — no fabricated numbers.

print(f"Delta [{len(delta)} scalar keys]:")
for key, change in delta.items():
    sign = "+" if change >= 0 else ""
    print(f"  {key}: {sign}{change:.6f}")

The delta covers every key present in both the before and after diagnostics where both values are a finite scalar float or int (booleans and non-scalar values are excluded). For smoothing via pspline_fit_gcv, the scalar diagnostic keys typically include optimal_edf, optimal_gcv, rss, aic, and bic — all fdars-computed, none fabricated.

docs.title: The closed loop
docs.text: After reading the delta, a language model can feed the updated after diagnostics back into fdars_build_diagnostics (for a fresh interpretation pass) or call fdars_compare_run again with another parameter change — forming the full interpret → recommend → re-run → compare loop described in the overview.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Python API — the recommend-only surface (build_diagnostics + advise)
  • Overview — grounding invariant and three-surface architecture
  • Agent Skill — the packaged skill that orchestrates these tools automatically

docs.title: Pipeline Diagnostic Report
docs.text:
A typical FDA workflow is a multi-stage pipeline: represent the raw data, smooth or align curves, decompose with FPCA, then cluster or regress. Diagnostics from each stage provide complementary information — and issues upstream (high missingness, many outliers, low cumulative variance) propagate silently into downstream results unless they are surfaced explicitly.

The pipeline diagnostic report aggregates per-stage diagnostics into an ordered, labeled report. Cross-stage caveats are computed by deterministic Python rules before any LLM call — the LLM narrates them but never invents them.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
build_pipeline_report accepts an ordered list of stage entries, runs build_diagnostics per stage (or accepts pre-built diagnostics dicts), and returns per-stage labeled blocks.

Aggregation invariant: Each stage's diagnostics live in their own labeled block — {"stage": str, "aspect": str, "diagnostics": dict}. They are never flat-merged. Two stages that share a key (e.g. n_obs) both survive with their individual values. A plain dict.update or {**a, **b} would silently overwrite earlier values; this is prevented by the list structure.

Python-computed cross-stage caveats (PIPE-03): Three deterministic rules fire before the LLM call:

Rule Trigger Caveat R1 represent stage: imputed_fraction > 0.20 High imputation rate may bias FPCA and clustering R2 outliers stage: derived outlier fraction > 0.15 Substantial outlier rate distorts downstream FPCA, clustering, regression R3 fpca stage: last cumulative_variance_explained < 0.80 Subspace captures too little variance for reliable clustering

These caveats are authoritative — the LLM only narrates them; it cannot invent additional caveats beyond these Python-computed ones.

Union grounding: Grounding is checked once against the union of all stages' diagnostics ({"_stages": [<diag>, ...]}). A cited value is grounded when it appears in any stage's diagnostics, allowing legitimate cross-stage narration (e.g. citing FPCA cumulative variance in the context of a clustering caveat) without false rejection.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The fence below builds a synthetic three-stage pipeline (represent → fpca → clustering) and runs the offline pipeline report. No ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is needed — the fence runs fully offline in the docs build.

import numpy as np
from fdars.advisor import build_diagnostics, build_pipeline_report

# Small synthetic data (n=12 observations, m=50 grid points)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n, m = 12, 50
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
X = np.array([np.sin(2 * np.pi * t + rng.uniform(-0.3, 0.3)) for _ in range(n)])

# Stage 1: represent diagnostics (pre-built)
diag_represent = {
    "method": "represent",
    "n_obs": n,
    "n_points": m,
    "argvals_min": 0.0,
    "argvals_max": 1.0,
    "argvals_spacing_mean": 1.0 / (m - 1),
    "argvals_spacing_std": 0.0,
    "is_uniform_grid": True,
    "data_range_min": float(X.min()),
    "data_range_max": float(X.max()),
    "data_range_mean": float(X.mean()),
    "nan_frac": None,
    "has_boundary_nans": None,
    "imputation_method": None,
    "imputed_fraction": None,
}

# Stage 2: FPCA diagnostics (pre-built)
from fdars import regression
fp = regression.fpca(X, t, n_comp=3)
diag_fpca = build_diagnostics(fp, method="fpca")

# Stage 3: clustering diagnostics (pre-built)
from fdars.clustering import kmeans_fd
cl = kmeans_fd(X, t, k=3, seed=0)
diag_cluster = build_diagnostics(cl, method="clustering", argvals=t)

stages = [
    {"stage_name": "represent", "aspect": "represent", "diagnostics": diag_represent},
    {"stage_name": "fpca",      "aspect": "fpca",      "diagnostics": diag_fpca},
    {"stage_name": "cluster",   "aspect": "clustering", "diagnostics": diag_cluster},
]

report = build_pipeline_report(stages, run_llm=False)

for block in report["stages"]:
    stage = block["stage"]
    aspect = block["aspect"]
    diag = block["diagnostics"]
    if aspect == "fpca":
        cv = diag["cumulative_variance_explained"]
        print(f"Stage '{stage}': cumulative_variance_explained[-1]={cv[-1]:.4f}")
    elif aspect == "clustering":
        amp = diag["mean_amplitude_separation"]
        print(f"Stage '{stage}': mean_amplitude_separation={amp:.4f}")
    else:
        print(f"Stage '{stage}': n_obs={diag['n_obs']}, is_uniform_grid={diag['is_uniform_grid']}")

print("cross_stage_caveats:", len(report.get("caveats", [])))
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")
Stage 'represent': n_obs=12, is_uniform_grid=True Stage 'fpca': cumulative_variance_explained[-1]=1.0000 Stage 'cluster': mean_amplitude_separation=0.2066 cross_stage_caveats: 0 FDARS_FENCE_OK

docs.title: build_pipeline_report
docs.text:
build_pipeline_report(stages, *, argvals=None, run_llm=True,
                      domain_context="", model="claude-opus-4-8",
                      provider=None, **kwargs) -> dict

Aggregate per-stage diagnostics into an offline pipeline diagnostic report.

Stage entry schema: each entry in stages must be a dict with:

Key Type Description "stage_name" str Human-readable label (e.g. "represent", "smooth", "fpca", "cluster") "aspect" str build_diagnostics aspect key for this stage "diagnostics" / "result" / "value" dict Pre-built diagnostics dict (has "method" key) or raw fdars result dict

When the stage value is a pre-built diagnostics dict (has a "method" key), it is passed through without re-running build_diagnostics. When it is a raw fdars result dict, build_diagnostics(value, aspect, argvals=argvals, **kwargs) is called.

Parameters

Parameter Type Default Description stages list — Ordered list of stage entry dicts argvals array_like None Shared evaluation grid forwarded to build_diagnostics (required for clustering/alignment aspects) run_llm bool True When False, return the raw aggregated dict of per-stage blocks offline domain_context str "" Free-text domain description forwarded to LLM narration (run_llm=True only) model str "claude-opus-4-8" LLM model identifier provider str or Provider or None None LLM provider

Returns (offline, run_llm=False)

{
    "stages": [
        {"stage": <str>, "aspect": <str>, "diagnostics": <dict>},
        ...  # one labeled block per input stage, in caller order
    ]
}

Returns (LLM path, run_llm=True)

PipelineReport — schema-validated object with:

Field Type Description stages list[str] Per-stage narrative sections (one per input stage) narrative str Overall pipeline health summary caveats list[dict] Python-computed cross-stage caveats (authoritative)

Raises

  • ValueError — stages is empty, or a stage entry is missing "stage_name" or "aspect".
  • GroundingViolationError — when run_llm=True and the narration cites a value absent from all stages' diagnostics.

docs.title: pipeline_report
docs.text:
pipeline_report(stages, *, argvals=None, domain_context="",
                model="claude-opus-4-8", provider=None,
                thresholds=None, **kwargs) -> PipelineReport

LLM narrative entry point — called automatically by build_pipeline_report(run_llm=True). Direct access is useful when you need custom caveat thresholds.

thresholds parameter: override any of the three Python caveat rule constants for this call only:

Key Default Rule "imputed_fraction" 0.20 R1 threshold "outlier_fraction" 0.15 R2 threshold "cumulative_variance" 0.80 R3 threshold

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
Per-stage blocks are never merged. If two stages both report n_obs, both values survive independently in their own list elements. A caller that flat-merges blocks (e.g. {**a, **b}) risks silently dropping earlier values; use the labeled list structure instead.

Python caveats are authoritative; LLM caveats are not. The caveats field in the returned PipelineReport always reflects the Python-computed R1/R2/R3 rules — even if the LLM emitted different caveats. The LLM narrates what Python found; it cannot override.

argvals propagation. A shared argvals grid passed to build_pipeline_report is forwarded to every build_diagnostics call for raw result dicts. For pre-built diagnostics dicts it is ignored (they already carry the computed values). Distance-based metrics (clustering, alignment) require argvals — pass it at the build_pipeline_report level rather than per stage.

Ordering matters. Stages are processed in caller order; the LLM is told the stages represent a pipeline in sequence. Reordering stages changes the caveat computation (R1 and R3 can interact: a high imputation rate preceding a low-variance FPCA compounds the downstream clustering reliability concern).

docs.title: Provider Setup
docs.text:
The fdars advisor routes every LLM call through a uniform Provider protocol. advise(provider=, model=) is the only entry point for provider selection — the MCP tools (fdars_build_diagnostics, fdars_run_method, fdars_compare_run) are compute-only and never call advise().

Four backends are supported: Anthropic (default), OpenAI (and OpenAI-compatible endpoints), Google Gemini, and local Ollama. The backend is selected at call time via explicit parameters or environment variables; no configuration file is required.

docs.title: Anthropic (default)
docs.text:
Property Value Provider name "anthropic" Install extra pip install "fdars[advisor]" Required credential ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Default model claude-opus-4-8

Anthropic is the default backend. When provider=None (the default), the advisor resolves to "anthropic" and reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment. This is the same behavior as the pre-v3.0 API — existing code that does not pass provider= is unaffected.

The [advisor] extra installs anthropic>=0.72.0 and pydantic>=2.0. These are the only dependencies required for build_diagnostics (no LLM, fully offline) and for advise() with the Anthropic backend.

docs.title: OpenAI and OpenAI-compatible endpoints
docs.text:
Property Value Provider name "openai" Install extra pip install "fdars[openai]" Required credential OPENAI_API_KEY Default model gpt-4o

The OpenAI adapter calls the OpenAI Chat Completions API for structured output. The same adapter works with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint — vLLM, LM Studio, LocalAI, or any service that exposes the /v1/chat/completions API. For compatible endpoints, set FDARS_ADVISOR_BASE_URL (or pass base_url= to resolve_provider directly) to the custom base URL; the adapter forwards it to the SDK.

The [openai] extra installs openai>=1.40.0,<2.0.

docs.title: Google Gemini
docs.text:
Property Value Provider name "gemini" Install extra pip install "fdars[gemini]" SDK package google-genai>=1.0 Required credential GEMINI_API_KEY Default model gemini-2.0-flash Python requirement Python 3.10+

The Gemini adapter uses google-genai's native structured-output support (response_json_schema). The google-genai SDK requires Python 3.10 or later; attempting to use this backend on Python 3.9 raises a clear ImportError pointing to the [openai] or [ollama] alternatives.

The [gemini] extra installs google-genai>=1.0.

docs.title: Local Ollama
docs.text:
Property Value Provider name "ollama" Install extra pip install "fdars[ollama]" Required credential None — no API key required Default model llama3.2 Default endpoint http://localhost:11434

Ollama runs entirely locally and requires no API key. The Ollama daemon must be running before advise() is called. Endpoint can be customised via FDARS_ADVISOR_BASE_URL.

The [ollama] extra installs ollama>=0.6.2.

docs.title: All providers
docs.text:
pip install "fdars[all-providers]"

The [all-providers] umbrella extra pulls every provider adapter at once: anthropic>=0.72.0, openai>=1.40.0,<2.0, google-genai>=1.0, and ollama>=0.6.2. Use this to avoid repeated installs when switching between backends during development.

docs.title: Selection and precedence
docs.text:
resolve_provider() (called internally by advise()) applies a strict precedence order:

  1. Explicit advise(provider=, model=) parameters — highest priority; override everything else.
  2. Environment variables — used when no explicit argument is given.
  3. Anthropic default — provider=None resolves to "anthropic", reproducing the pre-v3.0 behavior exactly.

Model resolution follows the same layering: explicit model= argument → FDARS_ADVISOR_MODEL env var → provider default (e.g. "claude-opus-4-8" for Anthropic, "gpt-4o" for OpenAI, "gemini-2.0-flash" for Gemini, "llama3.2" for Ollama).

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Variable Purpose Example values FDARS_ADVISOR_PROVIDER Provider name anthropic, openai, ollama, gemini FDARS_ADVISOR_MODEL Model identifier claude-opus-4-8, gpt-4o, llama3.2 FDARS_ADVISOR_BASE_URL Custom API endpoint http://localhost:11434

Each provider also reads its own API-key variable from the environment when no explicit api_key= is passed:

Provider API-key variable anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY openai OPENAI_API_KEY gemini GEMINI_API_KEY ollama (no key required)

docs.title: Install extras reference
docs.text:
Provider Extra API-key variable Notes anthropic fdars[advisor] ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Default; also installs pydantic>=2.0 openai fdars[openai] OPENAI_API_KEY Also covers OpenAI-compatible endpoints gemini fdars[gemini] GEMINI_API_KEY Python 3.10+ required ollama fdars[ollama] (none) Requires running Ollama daemon (all) fdars[all-providers] (per provider) Installs all four adapter packages

Offline core with no extra installed

build_diagnostics and the run_llm=False escape hatch of describe_cluster_differences work fully offline with no provider extra installed — they import only NumPy and fdars itself. A missing extra raises a clear ImportError with the install hint only when advise() is called.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Requires a provider SDK and API key — not run in the docs build

The examples below are illustrative only. Each requires the corresponding provider extra and API credential to be available. They are plain (unexecuted) fences and do not run during the docs build.

docs.title: Explicit parameters
docs.text:
from fdars.advisor import build_diagnostics, advise

# build diagnostics offline first (no provider needed)
diag = build_diagnostics(result, method="clustering", argvals=day)

# call advise with an explicit provider and model
advice = advise(
    diag,
    task="interpretation",
    domain_context="35 Canadian weather stations, 4 climate-region groups.",
    provider="openai",
    model="gpt-4o",
)

docs.title: Local / offline path — Ollama
docs.text:
Requires a running Ollama daemon — not run in the docs build

Pull the model once with ollama pull llama3.2 before running your script. No API key is needed.

# Start the Ollama daemon first: https://ollama.com
ollama pull llama3.2

FDARS_ADVISOR_PROVIDER=ollama \
FDARS_ADVISOR_MODEL=llama3.2 \
python my_analysis.py

docs.title: OpenAI-compatible endpoint (vLLM, LM Studio, LocalAI)
docs.text:
Requires an OpenAI-compatible server — not run in the docs build

Point FDARS_ADVISOR_BASE_URL at any endpoint that exposes the /v1/chat/completions API. OPENAI_API_KEY can be set to any non-empty string for key-free local servers.

FDARS_ADVISOR_PROVIDER=openai \
FDARS_ADVISOR_MODEL=meta-llama/Llama-3-8B-Instruct \
FDARS_ADVISOR_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000/v1 \
python my_analysis.py

docs.title: Python API
docs.text: The Python advisor surface is recommend-only: call build_diagnostics to compute a deterministic, offline diagnostics report from your fdars result, then call advise (or the describe_cluster_differences convenience wrapper) to get a schema-validated Advice object with interpretation, recommendations, and caveats. The API returns Advice and stops — it does not re-run fdars or compute a before/after delta. See the overview for the full picture.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The fence below loads the Canadian Weather dataset, clusters the 35 daily temperature curves into four groups with kmeans_fd, and builds the offline cluster diagnostics with build_diagnostics. No ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is required — the fence runs fully offline in the docs build.

from docs_data import load_canadian_weather
from fdars.clustering import kmeans_fd
from fdars.advisor import build_diagnostics

day, X, meta = load_canadian_weather("temperature")
result = kmeans_fd(X, day, k=4, seed=42)
diag = build_diagnostics(result, method="clustering", argvals=day)

print(f"k (clusters):              {diag['k']}")
print(f"cluster sizes:             {diag['cluster_sizes']}")
print(f"mean amplitude separation: {diag['mean_amplitude_separation']:.4f}  FDARS_FENCE_OK")
print(f"mean phase separation:     {diag['mean_phase_separation']:.4f}")
k (clusters): 4 cluster sizes: [8, 10, 3, 14] mean amplitude separation: 5.3006 FDARS_FENCE_OK mean phase separation: 0.4158

docs.title: build_diagnostics
docs.text:
build_diagnostics(result, method, *, argvals=None, **kwargs) -> dict

Compute a deterministic, JSON-serialisable diagnostics dict from an fdars result.

Offline and deterministic — uses only NumPy and fdars submodules. No anthropic import, no network call, no RNG, no wall-clock dependency. Two calls on the same input always return an equal dict.

Parameters

Parameter Type Default Description result dict or result wrapper — Native fdars output dict, or a wrapper whose .raw attribute is the underlying dict method str — The fdars method that produced result; one of "alignment", "fpca", "basis", "smoothing", "clustering", "depth", "outliers", "classification", "represent", "regression", "regression_cv", "spm" argvals array_like None Shared evaluation grid, shape (m,). Used for amplitude/phase distance computations n_classes int None Ground-truth class count for the "classification" aspect; cannot be inferred from a result dict, so the caller supplies it. Ignored by all other methods **kwargs Reserved for future per-method options

Returns

A plain-Python dict with JSON-serialisable values (float, list, str, bool, int, None). No NumPy scalars. Keys depend on method — see Per-Aspect Coverage for the complete per-aspect key sets. A summary of the most commonly used aspects:

  • "clustering" — k, cluster_means, cluster_sizes, pairwise_amplitude_distance, pairwise_phase_distance, mean_amplitude_separation, mean_phase_separation
  • "alignment" — mean_length, mean_min, mean_max, mean_avg, n_obs, amplitude_distances, phase_distances, amplitude_mean, amplitude_max, phase_mean, phase_max, converged, n_iter
  • "fpca" — n_components, n_obs, eigenvalues, explained_variance_ratio, cumulative_variance_explained, total_variance, phase_leakage_indicator, phase_leakage_flagged
  • "basis" and "smoothing" — GCV curve, optimal value, and EDF keys
  • "depth", "outliers", "classification", "represent", "regression", "regression_cv", "spm" — see Per-Aspect Coverage for details

Raises

ValueError if method is not in the supported set.

docs.title: advise
docs.text:
advise(diagnostics, *, task, domain_context, model="claude-opus-4-8",
       provider=None, aspect="") -> Advice

Return a schema-validated Advice object by routing diagnostics through a uniform Provider protocol to any of four LLM backends with a grounding-invariant system prompt. The three task families ("interpretation", "parameter", "method") apply to every aspect. See Provider Setup for backend selection, model names, and credential precedence.

Requires the [advisor] extra (pip install fdars[advisor]) when using the Anthropic backend (default). Raises ImportError if the required SDK is not installed.

Parameters

Parameter Type Default Description diagnostics dict — Output from build_diagnostics task str — Task family: "interpretation", "parameter", or "method" domain_context str — Free-text description of the problem domain, dataset, or analysis goal model str "claude-opus-4-8" Model identifier for the selected provider (e.g. "claude-opus-4-8", "gpt-4o", "gemini-2.0-flash", "llama3.2") provider str \| Provider \| None None LLM backend. None → Anthropic (default, preserves pre-v3.0 behaviour). Pass "anthropic", "openai", "gemini", or "ollama" to select a backend explicitly. See Provider Setup. aspect str "" Selects the per-aspect FDA primer clause injected into the system prompt (e.g. "depth", "outliers", "spm"). Default "" uses no aspect clause — equivalent to pre-v3.0 behaviour.

Returns

Advice — schema-validated advice with interpretation, recommendations, and caveats.

docs.title: describe_cluster_differences
docs.text:
describe_cluster_differences(
    result,
    *,
    argvals=None,
    domain_context="",
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    run_llm=True,
    **kwargs,
)

Convenience wrapper that runs build_diagnostics(method="clustering") (Stage 1, offline) and optionally advise(task="interpretation") (Stage 2, LLM) in sequence for a clustering result.

run_llm=False offline escape hatch — when run_llm=False the function returns the raw clustering diagnostics dict with no anthropic import and no network call. This path is fully usable in CI without an API key and is how the worked example above inspects the feature report.

Parameters

Parameter Type Default Description result dict or wrapper — fdars clustering result with keys centers, cluster, k argvals array_like None Shared evaluation grid for amplitude/phase distance computation domain_context str "" Free-text domain description passed to advise model str "claude-opus-4-8" Claude model identifier run_llm bool True When False, return the raw diagnostics dict (offline); when True, call advise and return Advice **kwargs Forwarded to build_diagnostics

Returns

Advice when run_llm=True; dict (raw clustering diagnostics) when run_llm=False.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Each Advice object contains a recommendations list of Recommendation objects. Every Recommendation cites specific diagnostic values in its evidence list — the grounding invariant enforced by the Pydantic schema and the system prompt.

Field Type action str kind Literal["parameter", "method", "none"] rationale str expected_effect str evidence list[str]

docs.title: Advice
docs.text: Field Type interpretation str recommendations list[Recommendation] caveats list[str]

docs.title: Recommend-only surface
docs.text:
The Python API is the recommend-only surface of the fdars advisor. It returns an Advice object and stops. It does not re-run fdars with the recommended parameters or compute a before/after delta of diagnostic values — that is the MCP server and Agent Skill surface.

For the full interpret → recommend → re-run → compare agentic loop, see MCP Server and Agent Skill.

docs.title: Illustrative advise() call
docs.text:
Requires a provider credential — not run in the docs build

The fence below is illustrative only. It requires pip install fdars[advisor] and a provider credential (e.g. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for the default Anthropic backend — see Provider Setup for other backends). It is not an executed fence and does not run during the docs build.

from docs_data import load_canadian_weather
from fdars.clustering import kmeans_fd
from fdars.advisor import build_diagnostics, describe_cluster_differences

day, X, meta = load_canadian_weather("temperature")
result = kmeans_fd(X, day, k=4, seed=42)

# Option A: describe_cluster_differences runs both stages in sequence
advice = describe_cluster_differences(
    result,
    argvals=day,
    domain_context=(
        "35 Canadian weather stations clustered by daily temperature curve. "
        "4 climate regions expected: Arctic, Atlantic, Continental, Pacific."
    ),
    run_llm=True,
)

print(advice.interpretation)
for rec in advice.recommendations:
    print(f"[{rec.kind}] {rec.action}")
    for ev in rec.evidence:
        print(f"  evidence: {ev}")
print("caveats:", advice.caveats)

# Option B: build diagnostics first, then call advise directly
diag = build_diagnostics(result, method="clustering", argvals=day)
advice2 = advise(
    diag,
    task="interpretation",
    domain_context="35 Canadian weather stations, 4 climate-region groups.",
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
)

A representative Advice value returned by describe_cluster_differences looks like:

Advice(
    interpretation=(
        "The four clusters show clear amplitude separation "
        "(mean_amplitude_separation ≈ 15.3) driven by the temperature level "
        "difference between Arctic and Pacific stations, with moderate phase "
        "variation (mean_phase_separation ≈ 3.1) reflecting timing shifts in "
        "the seasonal peak."
    ),
    recommendations=[
        Recommendation(
            action="Inspect cluster means to confirm Arctic/Atlantic/Continental/Pacific grouping.",
            kind="none",
            rationale="Cluster sizes [3, 15, 12, 5] match the known regional counts.",
            expected_effect="Confirms that k=4 recovers the four climate regions.",
            evidence=["cluster_sizes=[3, 15, 12, 5]", "mean_amplitude_separation≈15.3"],
        )
    ],
    caveats=["Amplitude and phase distances assume a shared 365-point annual grid."],
)

docs.title: Align
docs.text:
Register and align curves to separate amplitude from phase variability.

Functional observations vary in two ways: amplitude (how tall or deep the features are) and phase (when those features occur). Methods that ignore phase blur the mean and inflate the variance. The Align module estimates a warping function per curve, so that the registered curves \(x_i(h_i(t))\) carry the amplitude and the warps \(h_i\) carry the phase. It covers rigid shifts, affine and landmark warps, smooth Ramsay–Li registration, elastic (Fisher–Rao / SRSF) alignment with several optimisers, shape spaces of curves, likelihood-based registration of non-Gaussian curves, Bayesian alignment and template-free synchronisation.

Not sure where to start? Read Choosing an Alignment Method: it matches the kind of phase variability in your data to a method, and shows on simulated data why the smallest matching warp class wins.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text: Choosing a Method Decision tree, comparison table, recommendations and pitfalls for every aligner. Comparing Methods Eight aligners on one sample with known warps and on the growth data.

docs.title: Rigid & parametric warps
docs.text: Shift Registration One time delay per curve: least-squares, iterative Newton and landmark shifts. Affine Registration Shift plus dilation of time, h(t) = a·t + b, with three criteria. Landmark Registration Pin detected features with monotone cubic warps, or elastically between them. Continuous Registration Ramsay–Li smooth monotone warps with a scale-free criterion.

docs.title: Elastic (Fisher–Rao)
docs.text: Elastic Alignment SRSF registration, Karcher mean, and amplitude/phase separation. Elastic Optimisers & Penalties DP, DP2 and RBFGS, warp penalties, the λ scale and the band. Banded Elastic Alignment A Sakoe–Chiba corridor around the diagonal for long curves. Advanced Elastic Alignment Closed curves, partial matching, multiresolution, geodesics, generative models. TSRVF Linearised elastic analysis in the tangent space at the mean. Shape Analysis (1-D) Shape quotients, shape means and elastic FPCA for real-valued curves.

docs.title: Shapes
docs.text: Shapes of Curves in R^d Outlines and trajectories modulo translation, scale, rotation, speed and start point.

docs.title: Special data
docs.text: Sparse & Irregular Curves Elastic distances and spline means from a few irregular points per curve. Non-Gaussian Registration Binary and count curves registered on the likelihood scale, with GFPCA.

docs.title: Template-free & probabilistic
docs.text: Pairwise Synchronisation Tang–Müller: each warp is the inverted average of pairwise warps. Bayesian Alignment Posterior warps and template by pCN or infHMC, with R̂, ESS and tempering.

docs.title: Time series
docs.text: Dynamic Time Warping DTW paths as discrete warps, windows, soft-DTW and DBA; when to prefer elastic alignment.

docs.title: After alignment
docs.text:
Inference after Alignment Amplitude/phase PERMANOVA, localised group differences, elastic box plots, depth, outliers, DP-means and partial-curve conformal.

Scope

  • Real-valued curves on one shared grid (argvals) are supported by every family on these pages.
  • Irregular or incomplete grids are handled by register_fpca (curves observed on their own grids, optionally cut off at the start or end) and by the sparse elastic functions sparse_elastic_align_pair / sparse_elastic_mean. elastic_partial_match matches a short curve to a sub-interval of a longer one.
  • Curves in \(\mathbb{R}^d\): the shape-space functions curve_shape_* quotient out translation, scale, rotation, reparametrisation and (for closed curves) the starting point; karcher_mean_nd_with_config and the other *_nd_with_config functions share one warp across coordinates without rotation or scale invariance.
  • Non-Gaussian values (binary, counts, positive-skewed): register_fpca(family=...).
  • Time series of different lengths for search and classification: the DTW family in fdars.metric (Dynamic Time Warping).
  • Still unsupported: manifold-valued trajectories other than the shape space (sphere-, SPD- or rotation-valued curves) and density-valued curves. Transform them to an unconstrained space first.

docs.title: Advanced Elastic Alignment
docs.text:
The baseline karcher_mean and elastic_align_pair cover the common case: curves on one interval, aligned by a warp that minimises the elastic (Fisher–Rao) distance. This page collects the variants for special situations: closed or periodic curves, a short curve that matches only part of a longer one, multiresolution alignment, alignment across two populations, geodesic paths between curves, generative models built on the amplitude/phase split, and automatic choice of \(\lambda\). Every tool works on the SRSF \(q(t)=\operatorname{sign}(\dot f(t))\sqrt{|\dot f(t)|}\), under which the Fisher–Rao metric becomes the \(L^2\) metric.

Robust centres (the Karcher median and the trimmed Karcher mean) live on the Elastic Alignment page; warp optimisers, penalties and the band on Elastic Optimisers & Penalties; elastic depth, outlier detection and shape confidence intervals on Inference after Alignment; Bayesian pairwise and group alignment on Bayesian Alignment. For which aligner to use in the first place, see Choosing an Alignment Method.

The non-executed snippets below refer to this simulated sample:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n, m = 30, 160
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
data = np.zeros((n, m))
for i in range(n):
    data[i] = rng.normal(3.0, 0.5) * np.exp(-((t - rng.normal(0.5, 0.08)) ** 2) / (2 * 0.12 ** 2))

docs.title: 1. Multiresolution alignment (long curves)
docs.text:
Dynamic programming costs \(O(m^2)\) per pair. elastic_align_pair_multires runs the DP on a grid coarsened by coarsen_factor, upsamples the warp, and then refines it on the full grid with n_refine_steps sweeps of a descent on the penalised objective

\[ \lVert q_1 - (q_2\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\rVert^2 + \lambda \sum_j \Big(\frac{\Delta\gamma_j}{\Delta t_j} - 1\Big)^2 \Delta t_j . \]

Each sweep moves the warp values one coordinate at a time with backtracking and accepts only strict decreases, so refinement never makes the coarse warp worse, and lambda_ enters both the coarse DP and the refinement. The refined warp is not restricted to the DP's quantised slopes, so it can end below the exact DP's distance, but it is a local descent from the coarse warp and is not guaranteed to.

import numpy as np
from time import perf_counter
from fdars.alignment import elastic_align_pair_multires, elastic_align_pair

m = 400
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
f1 = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 2 * t) + 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 5 * t)
f2 = np.interp(t, np.clip(t + 0.09 * np.sin(np.pi * t), 0, 1), f1)   # non-linear phase distortion

for steps in (0, 3, 10):
    t0 = perf_counter()
    r = elastic_align_pair_multires(f1, f2, t, coarsen_factor=4, n_refine_steps=steps)
    rms = np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(r["f_aligned"]) - f1) ** 2))
    print(f"multires, n_refine_steps={steps:2d}: distance {r['distance']:.3f}  RMS {rms:.4f}  {1e3 * (perf_counter() - t0):5.1f} ms")
t0 = perf_counter()
r = elastic_align_pair(f1, f2, t)
rms = np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(r["f_aligned"]) - f1) ** 2))
print(f"exact DP:                     distance {r['distance']:.3f}  RMS {rms:.4f}  {1e3 * (perf_counter() - t0):5.1f} ms")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

multires, n_refine_steps= 0: distance 0.202  RMS 0.0173    5.0 ms
multires, n_refine_steps= 3: distance 0.092  RMS 0.0107   59.2 ms
multires, n_refine_steps=10: distance 0.061  RMS 0.0054  190.2 ms
exact DP:                     distance 0.097  RMS 0.0069   76.8 ms
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The coarse DP alone (n_refine_steps=0) is an order of magnitude faster than the exact DP, at about twice its distance: that is the speed option for long curves. The refinement lowers the distance with every sweep (here below the exact DP's), but each sweep is a line search over all \(m\) warp values, so a few sweeps already cost about as much as the exact DP, and the cost grows quickly with \(m\). Use the coarse DP when speed matters, refinement when you want to improve on the coarse warp without a full-grid DP, and elastic_align_pair (or a band) as the reference. Returns f_aligned, gamma and distance.

Parameter Description coarsen_factor Grid downsampling factor for the coarse DP (default 4) n_refine_steps Refinement sweeps on the full grid (default 10; 0 = coarse DP only) step_size Initial refinement step size (default 0.01) lambda_ Warp penalty, used by the coarse DP and the refinement

docs.title: 2. Closed and periodic curves
docs.text:
A periodic signal (a gait cycle, a daily temperature cycle, a contour traced as a 1-D function) has no canonical starting point: the same cycle can start anywhere. elastic_align_pair_closed searches over a circular shift of the start index \(\theta\) in addition to the warp,

\[ d(f_1, f_2) = \min_{\theta}\;\min_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\big\lVert q_1 - (q_2^{(\theta)}\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\big\rVert_{L^2}, \]

where \(q_2^{(\theta)}\) is the SRSF of \(f_2\) rotated by \(\theta\) grid points. Two details matter:

  • The start-point search is heuristic: a coarse search over shifts, then a fine search around the best one. It is not guaranteed to find the global optimum.
  • The warp is an ordinary interval warp (\(\gamma(0)=0\), \(\gamma(1)=1\)) applied after the rotation, not a diffeomorphism of the circle.

karcher_mean_closed (and karcher_mean_closed_with_config, which takes the optimiser options) runs the Karcher iteration with this aligner and also returns the per-curve rotations.

import numpy as np
from fdars.alignment import elastic_align_pair_closed, karcher_mean_closed, karcher_mean, elastic_distance

m = 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
cycle = lambda s: np.sin(2 * np.pi * s) + 0.5 * np.cos(4 * np.pi * s)

r = elastic_align_pair_closed(cycle(t), cycle(t - 0.2), t)
print(f"pair: start shift {r['optimal_rotation']} grid points (true 20), closed distance {r['distance']:.3f}, "
      f"open distance {elastic_distance(cycle(t), cycle(t - 0.2), t):.3f}")

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = np.array([rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1) * cycle(t - rng.uniform(-0.3, 0.3)) for _ in range(8)])
ratio = lambda R: np.var(R, 0).mean() / np.var(X, 0).mean()
closed = karcher_mean_closed(X, t, max_iter=10)
opened = karcher_mean(X, t, max_iter=10)
print(f"variance after/before: closed {ratio(np.asarray(closed['aligned_data'])):.3f}, "
      f"interval-only {ratio(np.asarray(opened['aligned_data'])):.3f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

pair: start shift 20 grid points (true 20), closed distance 0.044, open distance 1.411
variance after/before: closed 0.003, interval-only 0.233
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The closed aligner recovers the 0.2-cycle start shift exactly and removes almost all the variance; the interval aligner, which must keep \(\gamma(0)=0\), cannot move features across the boundary. The start-point search costs roughly \((20 + m/10)\) ordinary alignments per pair, so the closed Karcher mean is about 40 times slower than karcher_mean at \(m = 101\). Returns f_aligned, gamma, distance, optimal_rotation (pair) and mean, aligned_data, gammas, rotations, n_iter, converged (Karcher).

For curves in the plane (outlines), where rotation and scale are also nuisance, use the shape-space functions curve_shape_*(closed=True) instead.

docs.title: 3. Partial matching (subsequence search)
docs.text:
When only a portion of a longer target matches a shorter query, full alignment is wrong. elastic_partial_match finds the best-aligned sub-interval of the target. Here a short query pattern is hidden (time-warped and buried in noise) inside a longer target, and the search recovers exactly where it sits.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import elastic_partial_match

# short query pattern on its own grid
tt = np.linspace(0, 1, 80)
template = np.exp(-((tt - 0.5) ** 2) / (2 * 0.14 ** 2)) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 2 * tt)

# longer, noisy target; the pattern is embedded (warped) on the sub-interval [0.45, 0.75]
tg = np.linspace(0, 1, 300)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
target = 0.15 * rng.standard_normal(300)
seg = (tg >= 0.45) & (tg <= 0.75); s = (tg[seg] - 0.45) / 0.30
target[seg] += 1.2 * np.interp(np.clip(s + 0.05 * np.sin(np.pi * s), 0, 1), tt, template)

pm = elastic_partial_match(template, target, tt, tg, min_span=0.25)
i0, i1 = pm["start_index"], pm["end_index"]

f, ax = fig()
ax.plot(tg, target, color="#adb5bd", lw=1, label="target (long)")
ax.plot(tg[i0:i1 + 1], target[i0:i1 + 1], color="#fd7e14", lw=2.4, label="matched sub-interval")
ax.axvspan(tg[i0], tg[i1], color="#fd7e14", alpha=0.10)
ax.axvspan(0.45, 0.75, color="#198754", alpha=0.06)     # true location (green)
ax.set(title=f"Query found in {pm['domain_fraction']:.0%} of the target  (d={pm['distance']:.2f})",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="f(t)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
print(render(f))

print(f"matched target indices {i0}..{i1}  (t = {tg[i0]:.2f}..{tg[i1]:.2f}; planted at 0.45..0.75)")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ matched target indices 140..214 (t = 0.47..0.72; planted at 0.45..0.75)

The orange sub-interval that the search selects overlaps the green planted region almost exactly, and the printed indices confirm it recovers the buried pattern despite the noise and time-warping. Crucially the match spans only a fraction of the target (see domain_fraction), which is what distinguishes partial matching from forcing a full-length alignment.

Key Description start_index / end_index Best-matching sub-interval of the target domain_fraction Fraction of the target domain that matched gamma Warp on the matched segment distance Elastic distance of the match

min_span sets the smallest fraction of the target the match may cover, guarding against trivial tiny matches. The search over windows is heuristic, and distances of matches of different lengths are not comparable (a shorter window has less curve to mismatch), so do not rank candidate matches across window lengths by distance alone.

docs.title: 4. Transfer alignment across populations
docs.text:
When curves come from two populations (two sites, two devices), transfer_alignment maps the target curves into the source population's time frame. It computes both Karcher means, a bridging warp \(\gamma_B\) that aligns the target mean to the source mean (\(\mu_T\circ\gamma_B\approx\mu_S\)), and each target curve's within-population warp \(\gamma_i\) (\(f_i\circ\gamma_i\approx\mu_T\)), and composes them as \(\gamma_i\circ\gamma_B\): first into the target mean's frame, then across the bridge, so that \(f_i\circ\gamma_i\circ\gamma_B\approx\mu_S\).

Below, both populations share a two-peak shape with individual timing variation, and the target population additionally runs on a distorted clock:

import numpy as np
from fdars.alignment import transfer_alignment

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
m = 120
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.3) ** 2 / 0.006) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.7) ** 2 / 0.006)

def population(n, clock):
    curves = []
    for _ in range(n):
        w = t + rng.uniform(-0.3, 0.3) * t * (1 - t)                     # individual timing
        curves.append(mu(np.clip(w + clock * 0.1 * np.sin(np.pi * t), 0, 1)))
    return np.array(curves)

source, target = population(15, clock=0.0), population(15, clock=1.0)
r = transfer_alignment(source, target, t)
S = np.asarray(r["source_mean"])
sup = lambda X: np.abs(np.asarray(X) - S).max(axis=1)
print(f"sup |f_i - source mean|, before: [{sup(target).min():.3f}, {sup(target).max():.3f}]")
print(f"sup |f_i - source mean|, after:  [{sup(r['aligned_data']).min():.3f}, {sup(r['aligned_data']).max():.3f}]")
print(f"bridging warp: max |gamma_B(t) - t| = {np.abs(np.asarray(r['bridging_gamma']) - t).max():.3f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

sup |f_i - source mean|, before: [0.271, 0.956]
sup |f_i - source mean|, after:  [0.016, 0.050]
bridging warp: max |gamma_B(t) - t| = 0.101
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The transferred target curves lie within about 0.05 of the source mean everywhere (against up to 0.96 before), and the bridging warp carries the population-level clock difference. Aligning the target curves straight to the source mean with align_to_target(target_data, source_mean, t) gives a similar result on data like these; the two-step transfer additionally returns the population-level warp \(\gamma_B\) separately from the individual warps, and its within-population step is anchored at the target's own mean.

transfer_alignment key Description source_mean Karcher mean of the source population aligned_data Target curves in the source frame, \(f_i\circ\gamma_i\circ\gamma_B\) gammas Composed warps \(\gamma_i\circ\gamma_B\) bridging_gamma Warp \(\gamma_B\) aligning the target mean to the source mean distances elastic_distance of each transferred curve to the source mean (which re-optimises a residual warp)

docs.title: 5. Geodesic interpolation between curves
docs.text:
A geodesic on the elastic manifold is the shortest path between two curves. curve_geodesic first aligns \(f_2\) to \(f_1\) and then interpolates the amplitude: the intermediate curves are built from a path in SRSF space between \(q_1\) and the aligned \((q_2\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\), in \(f_1\)'s time frame. The last curve is therefore the aligned \(f_2\circ\gamma\), not \(f_2\) itself, and the phase part of the path is carried by the returned warps.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.cm as cm
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import curve_geodesic

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 140)
f1 = np.exp(-((t - 0.35) ** 2) / 0.01)
f2 = 0.8 * np.exp(-((t - 0.7) ** 2) / 0.006) + 0.4 * np.exp(-((t - 0.3) ** 2) / 0.01)

geo = curve_geodesic(f1, f2, t, n_points=9)
curves = np.asarray(geo["curves"])
alphas = np.asarray(geo["parameter_values"])

f, ax = fig()
for c, a in zip(curves, alphas):
    ax.plot(t, c, color=cm.viridis(a), lw=1.4)
ax.plot(t, f1, color="#3f51b5", lw=2.4, label="$f_1$ ($\\alpha$=0)")
ax.plot(t, f2, color="#dc3545", lw=2.4, label="$f_2$ ($\\alpha$=1)")
ax.set(title="Elastic geodesic: smooth morph $f_1 \\to f_2$",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="f(t)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The viridis-graded intermediates start at \(f_1\) and end at \(f_2\) aligned to \(f_1\): features stay at \(f_1\)'s times and their heights and widths change along the path. The returned distances grow linearly in \(\alpha\), the signature of a constant-speed geodesic.

Key Description curves Interpolated curves in \(f_1\)'s time frame, shape (n_points, m) warps The intermediate warps distances Cumulative elastic distance along the path parameter_values The \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) for each curve

docs.title: 6. Gaussian generative model
docs.text:
After separating amplitude and phase, you can generate new curves by sampling from the estimated score distributions -- useful for augmentation and simulation. gauss_model fits Gaussians to the vertical (amplitude) and horizontal (phase) FPC scores and draws new samples.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import gauss_model

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n, m = 30, 120
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
base = np.exp(-((t - 0.5) ** 2) / (2 * 0.12 ** 2))
data = np.array([rng.normal(3, 0.4) * np.interp(
    t, np.clip(t + rng.normal(0, 0.06), 0, 1), base) for _ in range(n)])

gm = gauss_model(data, t, ncomp=3, n_samples=20, max_iter=15, seed=0)
synth = np.asarray(gm["samples"])

f, ax = fig()
ax.plot(t, data.T, color="#3f51b5", lw=0.8, alpha=0.35)
ax.plot(t, synth.T, color="#e8710a", lw=0.8, alpha=0.5)
ax.plot([], [], color="#3f51b5", lw=2, label="original")
ax.plot([], [], color="#e8710a", lw=2, label="generated")
ax.set(title="Gaussian generative model: original vs. synthetic",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="f(t)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The orange synthetic curves occupy the same amplitude-and-timing envelope as the blue originals: the model samples amplitude and phase scores and recombines them (each sampled amplitude is composed with the inverse of a sampled alignment warp), rather than memorising individual curves.

gauss_model samples the amplitude and the phase scores independently, so any dependence between how tall and how late a feature is in the data is lost. joint_gauss_model instead concatenates the amplitude and phase scores (the phase block weighted by balance_c) and samples the joint score vector from a Gaussian with its full sample covariance, cross-covariance included; this is equivalent in distribution to sampling the joint FPCA scores, as in fdasrsf. It keeps the amplitude–phase correlation. Below, taller peaks also come later:

import numpy as np
from fdars.alignment import gauss_model, joint_gauss_model

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n, m = 40, 120
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
z = rng.standard_normal(n)
data = np.array([(3 + 0.4 * zi) * np.exp(-((t - 0.5 - 0.06 * zi) ** 2) / (2 * 0.1 ** 2)) for zi in z])

def height_location_corr(X):
    X = np.asarray(X)
    return np.corrcoef(X.max(axis=1), t[X.argmax(axis=1)])[0, 1]

print(f"training data:     corr(height, location) = {height_location_corr(data):+.3f}")
for model in (gauss_model, joint_gauss_model):
    samples = model(data, t, ncomp=3, n_samples=200, seed=0)["samples"]
    print(f"{model.__name__:18s} corr(height, location) = {height_location_corr(samples):+.3f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

training data:     corr(height, location) = +0.999
gauss_model        corr(height, location) = -0.163
joint_gauss_model  corr(height, location) = +0.994
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Both models reproduce the spread of heights and locations, but only joint_gauss_model reproduces their coupling. Use gauss_model when amplitude and phase are plausibly independent, joint_gauss_model when they are not.

Key Description samples Synthetic curves, shape (n_samples, m) warps Sampled alignment warps (the samples use their inverses) scores Sampled FPC scores

docs.title: 7. Peak persistence for automatic \(\lambda\)
docs.text:
Choosing the regularization \(\lambda\) is usually ad hoc. Peak persistence offers a topological criterion: sweep \(\lambda\), track when peaks in the Karcher mean are born and die, and pick the \(\lambda\) where persistent (genuine) peaks survive but transient (noise) peaks have merged away.

from fdars.alignment import peak_persistence

lambdas = np.linspace(0.0, 3.0, 15)   # must be an ndarray
pers = peak_persistence(data, t, lambdas=lambdas, max_iter=8)
print(f"Optimal lambda: {float(pers['optimal_lambda']):.3f}")
print(f"Peak counts:    {list(np.asarray(pers['peak_counts'], dtype=int))}")
Key Description lambdas The swept grid peak_counts Number of Karcher-mean peaks at each \(\lambda\) optimal_lambda / optimal_index Selected regularization and its grid index

Cross-validation (next section) optimizes a reconstruction score; peak persistence optimizes topological stability. They answer slightly different questions -- use CV when you have a clear predictive target, persistence when you care about recovering the right number of features.

docs.title: 8. Choosing \(\lambda\) by cross-validation
docs.text:
lambda_cv scores a grid of regularization values by \(K\)-fold cross-validation over the whole dataset and reports the best one.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import lambda_cv

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n, m = 20, 100
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
base = np.exp(-((t - 0.35) ** 2) / 0.01) + 0.6 * np.exp(-((t - 0.7) ** 2) / 0.008)
data = np.zeros((n, m))
for i in range(n):
    warp = t ** rng.uniform(0.7, 1.5)
    warp = (warp - warp.min()) / np.ptp(warp)
    data[i] = np.interp(t, warp, base)

lambdas = np.array([0.0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5])   # must be an ndarray
cv = lambda_cv(data, t, lambdas=lambdas, n_folds=3, max_iter=10, tol=1e-3)

best = float(cv["best_lambda"])
f, ax = fig()
ax.plot(cv["lambdas"], cv["cv_scores"], "o-", color="#3f51b5", lw=1.8)
ax.axvline(best, color="#e8710a", ls="--", lw=1.5, label=f"best $\\lambda$={best:g}")
ax.set(title="Cross-validated warp regularization", xlabel="$\\lambda$",
       ylabel="CV score (lower is better)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The orange line marks the selected \(\lambda\). Treat it as a lower bound rather than an optimum: the held-out criterion of lambda_cv favours flexible warps, so it is biased toward small \(\lambda\) and often returns the smallest candidate. Combine it with peak_persistence, with the warp diagnostics on the Elastic Alignment page, and with a look at the warps. Note also that a numeric \(\lambda\) means different things on different grids and optimisers (see the λ scale).

Key Description best_lambda Regularization minimizing the CV score cv_scores Mean CV score for each candidate lambdas The candidate grid that was scored

Array arguments must be ndarray

lambda_cv, peak_persistence, and elastic_align_pair_constrained reject plain Python lists for their array arguments (lambdas, landmark_targets, landmark_sources) with a TypeError. Wrap them with np.array(...).

docs.title: Pairwise variants
docs.text:
Penalised and landmark-constrained pairwise alignment have moved:

  • Warp penalties (\(\lambda P(\gamma)\) with penalty="l2gam" | "l2psi" | "roughness" | "geodesic") are part of the objective of every *_with_config aligner and are documented on Elastic Optimisers & Penalties.
  • elastic_align_pair_penalized(penalty_type="second_order" | "combined") is deprecated: those options smooth the DP warp after the fact instead of penalising it in the objective. Use elastic_align_pair_with_config(method="rbfgs", penalty="roughness", lambda_=...) instead. Its default penalty_type="first_order" equals elastic_align_pair with the same lambda_.
  • Landmark-constrained elastic alignment (elastic_align_pair_constrained, elastic_align_pair_constrained_with_config) is on Landmark Registration.

See Elastic Alignment for the baseline aligner and the SRSF/Karcher-mean machinery, Elastic Optimisers & Penalties for DP, RBFGS and penalties, TSRVF for linearised statistics, Shape Analysis for elastic FPCA, and Choosing an Alignment Method for when to use which aligner.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Tucker, J.D., Wu, W., Srivastava, A. (2013). Generative models for functional data using phase and amplitude separation. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis 61:50-66.
  • Srivastava, A., Klassen, E. (2016). Functional and Shape Data Analysis. Springer.

docs.title: Affine Registration
docs.text:
Some phase variability is more than a delay but still simple: a movement performed at a different tempo, a growth process that runs faster in one subject, a recording sampled with a clock that drifts linearly. A single shift cannot capture a change of speed, and a fully elastic warp is far more flexible than needed. affine_registration fits the two-parameter warp in between, a shift plus a dilation of time per curve, \(h_i(t) = a_i t + b_i\), and estimates a common template at the same time. It follows R's fdacluster and reproduces its reference results.

Left: a template \(\mu\) and two copies, one dilated (\(a = 1.15\)) and one shifted (\(b = 0.12\)). Middle: the least-squares criterion over the coarse \(21 \times 21\) grid of \((a, b)\) values (darker is lower), with the best grid point refined by Nelder–Mead. Right: the two domain options; with "overlap" only the shaded part, observed by both curves, enters the criterion.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
The data model and the registration are

\[ x_i(t) = \mu(a_i t + b_i) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \tilde x_i(s) = x_i\!\left(\frac{s - b_i}{a_i}\right) = \mu(s), \]

so affine_registration returns dilations \(a_i\) and shifts \(b_i\) (in argvals units) of the data warp, and the registered curves \(\tilde x_i\). The dilation acts about \(t = 0\): on a domain like \([1, 18]\) (ages), changing \(a\) also moves features a long way, so shift and dilation become strongly coupled. Re-express time to start at 0 (pass argvals - argvals[0]) to keep the two parameters interpretable.

warp_class restricts the family:

warp_class Warp Free parameters per curve "none" identity 0 (only the template is estimated) "shift" \(t + b\) 1 "dilation" \(a\,t\) 1 "affine" (default) \(a\,t + b\) 2

The parameters are bounded: \(a \in [1 - \texttt{max\_dilation},\, 1 + \texttt{max\_dilation}]\) and \(|b| \le \texttt{max\_shift} \cdot L\) with \(L\) the domain length (both default 0.15).

docs.title: Criteria and domains
docs.text:
metric sets the distance between a registered curve and the template:

metric Distance \(d(\tilde x_i, \mu)\) Invariant to "l2" (default) \(\sqrt{\int (\tilde x_i - \mu)^2}\) — "normalized_l2" \(\sqrt{\int (\tilde x_i - \mu)^2} \,/\, (\lVert\tilde x_i\rVert + \lVert\mu\rVert)\) — (bounded by 1) "pearson" \(\tfrac12 \bigl\lVert \tilde x_i/\lVert\tilde x_i\rVert - \mu/\lVert\mu\rVert \bigr\rVert\) (uncentred) amplitude scale of \(\tilde x_i\), but not vertical offsets

domain="full" compares on the whole argvals grid, with the uncovered edge filled by extrapolation (as for shift registration); domain="overlap" interpolates both curves onto \(m\) equispaced points of the interval observed by both and compares them there (fdacluster's behaviour). Plain "l2" on the overlap is rejected for dilation and affine warps: shrinking the curve shrinks the overlap and therefore the criterion, so the optimiser could win by squeezing. Use "normalized_l2" or "pearson" there.

docs.title: The optimiser
docs.text:
For each curve and iteration:

  1. One-parameter classes ("shift", "dilation"): evaluate a grid of grid_size (default 21) values, then refine the best one by golden-section search.
  2. Affine: evaluate a grid_size × grid_size grid over \((a, b)\), then refine by Nelder–Mead projected onto the box of bounds, to relative tolerance optim_tol.

Then the template is re-estimated as the mean of the registered curves and, with center_warps=True (default), the warps are centred to mean dilation 1 and mean shift 0, so the template does not drift. The loop stops when the parameters change by less than tol or after max_iter iterations. A fixed template (an array, or a callable applied to the registered curves) skips re-estimation and centring.

docs.title: Recovering known tempo and offset
docs.text:
Twenty curves \(x_i(t) = \mu(a_i t + b_i)\) with \(a_i \in [0.9, 1.1]\) and \(b_i \in [-0.05, 0.05]\). With the true template the parameters are recovered to better than \(10^{-3}\); with the re-estimated template they are recovered up to the common frame fixed by centring (one global affine map), which shows as correlations of essentially 1.

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n, m = 20, 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.4) ** 2 / 0.008) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.65) ** 2 / 0.006)
a = rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1, n)
b = rng.uniform(-0.05, 0.05, n)
X = np.array([mu(ai * t + bi) for ai, bi in zip(a, b)])

fixed = A.affine_registration(X, t, template=mu(t))
print(f"fixed template: max |a_hat - a| = {np.abs(fixed['dilations'] - a).max():.1e}, "
      f"max |b_hat - b| = {np.abs(fixed['shifts'] - b).max():.1e}")

est = A.affine_registration(X, t)                       # template re-estimated, warps centred
print(f"estimated template: corr(a_hat, a) = {np.corrcoef(est['dilations'], a)[0, 1]:.6f}, "
      f"corr(b_hat, b) = {np.corrcoef(est['shifts'], b)[0, 1]:.6f}; "
      f"mean a_hat = {est['dilations'].mean():.3f}, mean b_hat = {est['shifts'].mean():+.1e}")

ratio = lambda R: np.var(R, 0).mean() / np.var(X, 0).mean()
for wc in ("none", "shift", "dilation", "affine"):
    R = A.affine_registration(X, t, warp_class=wc)["registered_data"]
    print(f"warp_class={wc!r:11s} variance after/before = {ratio(np.asarray(R)):.3f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

fixed template: max |a_hat - a| = 4.2e-04, max |b_hat - b| = 1.8e-04
estimated template: corr(a_hat, a) = 0.999997, corr(b_hat, b) = 0.999997; mean a_hat = 1.000, mean b_hat = -1.1e-18
warp_class='none'      variance after/before = 1.000
warp_class='shift'     variance after/before = 0.057
warp_class='dilation'  variance after/before = 0.056
warp_class='affine'    variance after/before = 0.000
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Both one-parameter classes leave about 6 % of the variance: each explains only part of a warp that has two parameters. The affine class removes it entirely.

docs.title: Amplitude differences: choose the criterion
docs.text:
If the curves also differ in overall size, the \(L^2\) criteria try to fix the size mismatch by warping. The Pearson criterion compares unit-normalised curves, so it is blind to scale and recovers the warp regardless (it is uncentred, so it is not blind to a vertical offset):

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n, m = 20, 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.4) ** 2 / 0.008) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.65) ** 2 / 0.006)
a = rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1, n)
b = rng.uniform(-0.05, 0.05, n)
scale = rng.uniform(0.5, 2.0, n)                         # amplitude varies 4-fold
Y = np.array([s * mu(ai * t + bi) for s, ai, bi in zip(scale, a, b)])

for metric in ("l2", "normalized_l2", "pearson"):
    r = A.affine_registration(Y, t, template=mu(t), metric=metric)
    print(f"metric={metric!r:16s} max |a_hat - a| = {np.abs(r['dilations'] - a).max():.4f}, "
          f"max |b_hat - b| = {np.abs(r['shifts'] - b).max():.4f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

metric='l2'             max |a_hat - a| = 0.1759, max |b_hat - b| = 0.0840
metric='normalized_l2'  max |a_hat - a| = 0.1278, max |b_hat - b| = 0.0613
metric='pearson'        max |a_hat - a| = 0.0008, max |b_hat - b| = 0.0003
FDARS_FENCE_OK

With a fixed template the two \(L^2\) criteria mis-estimate the dilation by up to 0.13–0.18 (most of the allowed range), while Pearson is exact. The same logic motivates the scale-free criterion of continuous registration.

docs.title: Clustering with affine warps
docs.text:
The same machinery powers fdars.clustering.align_cluster_fd(warp_class=...): a k-means loop in which each cluster has its own template and every curve is registered to the template of its cluster before the distances are computed. The linear-warp options are passed with an affine_ prefix (affine_metric, affine_domain, affine_grid_size, …, plus max_dilation, max_shift, center_warps).

import time
import numpy as np
from fdars.clustering import align_cluster_fd

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n, m = 24, 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
two_bumps = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.4) ** 2 / 0.008) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.65) ** 2 / 0.006)
one_bump = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.5) ** 2 / 0.02)
label = np.repeat([0, 1], n // 2)
X = np.array([(two_bumps if g == 0 else one_bump)(rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1) * t + rng.uniform(-0.05, 0.05))
              + 0.02 * rng.standard_normal(m) for g in label])

for wc in ("none", "affine", "elastic"):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    r = align_cluster_fd(X, t, k=2, warp_class=wc)
    cl = np.asarray(r["cluster"])
    acc = max((cl == label).mean(), (cl != label).mean())
    print(f"warp_class={wc!r:10s} accuracy {acc:.3f}   {time.perf_counter() - t0:6.2f} s")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

warp_class='none'     accuracy 0.875     0.00 s
warp_class='affine'   accuracy 1.000     0.13 s
warp_class='elastic'  accuracy 1.000     2.68 s
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Without alignment the tempo variation blurs the two shapes and a few curves land in the wrong cluster. Affine and elastic warps both separate the groups perfectly here, but the affine run is more than twenty times faster, and it returns interpretable per-curve dilations and shifts. Note that align_cluster_fd uses a single random start (seed); rerun with several seeds when the clusters are less clear-cut.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
from fdars import alignment as A

r = A.affine_registration(
    data, argvals,
    warp_class="affine",      # "none" | "shift" | "dilation" | "affine"
    template=None,            # None/"mean" (re-estimated), an array (m,), or callable(registered) -> (m,)
    metric="l2",              # "l2" | "normalized_l2" | "pearson"
    domain="full",            # "full" | "overlap"
    extrapolation="boundary", # "boundary" | "linear" | "periodic" | "zeros"
    max_dilation=0.15, max_shift=0.15, grid_size=21,
    max_iter=20, tol=1e-6, center_warps=True, optim_tol=1e-10,
)
X_new = A.affine_warp_curves(data, argvals, dilations, shifts, extrapolation="boundary")
Key Description registered_data \((n, m)\) registered curves \(x_i((s - b_i)/a_i)\) dilations, shifts \((n,)\) estimated \(a_i\), \(b_i\) (shifts in argvals units) template \((m,)\) final template distances \((n,)\) criterion value of each curve at the optimum n_iter, converged template iterations and convergence flag

affine_warp_curves applies known warps with the same convention: it computes \(x_i((s - b_i)/a_i)\), so passing the estimated dilations and shifts reproduces registered_data.

docs.title: When to use it, and when not
docs.text:
Use affine registration when the phase is a delay plus a uniform change of speed: tempo differences in movements or speech, linear clock drift, processes that run faster in some subjects. It is cheap (a few milliseconds for 20 curves), has two interpretable parameters per curve, and keeps the template from drifting.

Do not use it when the timing distortion varies along the domain (early in one segment, late in the next): then the residual phase stays in the registered curves. Move to continuous or elastic registration. The method chooser quantifies the trade-off: affine is best on shift and affine data and is beaten only on smooth non-linear warps.

Pitfalls:

  • Dilation about \(t = 0\) couples shift and dilation on domains far from 0.
  • Bounds. The defaults allow ±15 % tempo and ±15 % of the domain as offset; estimates at a bound mean the bound is too tight (or the model is wrong).
  • Edges. With domain="full" the extrapolated edge enters the criterion; with "overlap", pick "normalized_l2" or "pearson".
