docs.title: Comparing Alignment Methods
docs.text:
Choosing an Alignment Method argues from the assumptions of each method. This page is the evidence: eight registrations of one sample whose true warps are known, scored on how well they recover those warps, how much variance they remove, how much warping they apply and how long they take; then the same methods on the Berkeley growth velocities, where the truth is unknown but one feature (the pubertal growth spurt) is. Later sections take a closer look at elastic, landmark and constrained elastic alignment, the metrics used to score them, and the regimes where each fails.

Eight registrations of one mixed-warp sample; the lowest variance is not always the best warp.

docs.title: Bake-off on simulated data with known warps
docs.text:
Twenty-four two-bump curves, each warped by a mixture of a shift, a change of tempo and a smooth non-linear bend, \(w_i(t) = a_i t + b_i + c_i\,t(1-t)\), with ±10 % amplitude scaling and white noise. No method's warp class matches exactly: shift and affine models miss the bend, the elastic and continuous classes cannot shift the end points, landmark registration sees only the two peaks, and pairwise synchronisation uses two-knot piecewise-linear warps.

Scores (interior \(t \in [0.15, 0.85]\)):

  • warp error: mean \(\lvert\hat h_i - h_i\rvert\) against the true registering warp, after removing the common warp no method can identify (\(\times 10^{-3}\));
  • variance ratio: total pointwise variance of the registered curves over that of the raw curves;
  • complexity: mean Fisher–Rao distance of the estimated warps from the identity (warp_complexity; "—" for shift and affine warps, which are not warps of \([0,1]\) onto itself);
  • time in seconds.
import time
import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n, m = 24, 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.008) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.68) ** 2 / 0.01)
X, H = [], []
for _ in range(n):
    b, a, c = rng.uniform(-0.04, 0.04), rng.uniform(0.93, 1.07), rng.uniform(-0.4, 0.4)
    w = a * t + b + c * t * (1 - t)                          # shift + tempo + bend
    X.append(rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1) * mu(w) + 0.02 * rng.standard_normal(m))
    H.append(np.interp(t, w, t))                             # true registering warp
X, H = np.array(X), np.array(H)
inner = (t > 0.15) & (t < 0.85)

def iterative_shift():
    seed = A.least_squares_shift_registration(X, t, 0.15)["shifts"]
    r = A.iterative_shift_registration(X, t, initial=seed, max_iter=20, tol=1e-6)
    return t - r["shifts"][:, None]

def affine():
    r = A.affine_registration(X, t)
    return (t - r["shifts"][:, None]) / r["dilations"][:, None]

methods = {
    "none":               (lambda: np.tile(t, (n, 1)), True),
    "iterative shift":    (iterative_shift, False),
    "affine":             (affine, False),
    "landmark (2 peaks)": (lambda: A.landmark_detect_and_register(X, t, kind="peak", min_prominence=0.2,
                                                                  expected_count=2)["gammas"], True),
    "continuous":         (lambda: A.continuous_registration(X, t, lambda_=1e-3, max_template_iter=5)["warps"], True),
    "elastic DP":         (lambda: A.karcher_mean(X, t)["gammas"], True),
    "elastic RBFGS+l2":   (lambda: A.karcher_mean_with_config(X, t, method="rbfgs", lambda_=0.01)["gammas"], True),
    "pairwise sync":      (lambda: A.pairwise_synchronization(X, t)["warps"], True),
}
print(f"{'method':20s} {'warp error':>10s} {'var ratio':>9s} {'complexity':>10s} {'time s':>7s}")
for name, (fit, interval_warp) in methods.items():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    W = np.asarray(fit())
    dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
    R = np.array([np.interp(w, t, x) for w, x in zip(W, X)])          # registered curves x_i(h_i(t))
    err = 1000 * np.abs(((W - W.mean(0)) - (H - H.mean(0)))[:, inner]).mean()
    vr = R[:, inner].var(0).sum() / X[:, inner].var(0).sum()
    cx = f"{np.mean([A.warp_complexity(w, t) for w in W]):10.3f}" if interval_warp else f"{'—':>10s}"
    print(f"{name:20s} {err:10.2f} {vr:9.3f} {cx} {dt:7.3f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

method               warp error var ratio complexity  time s
none                      36.89     1.000      0.000   0.000
iterative shift           25.42     0.394          —   0.002
affine                     5.60     0.047          —   0.205
landmark (2 peaks)         7.34     0.076      0.055   0.000
continuous                 4.37     0.044      0.050   0.012
elastic DP                 4.17     0.028      0.225   0.609
elastic RBFGS+l2           4.50     0.035      0.084   0.449
pairwise sync             14.11     0.194      0.053   0.419
FDARS_FENCE_OK

How to read it:

  • Rigid models fall short when the phase is not rigid. A pure shift cannot follow the tempo change and the bend (error ×5 the best). The affine model gets the shift and the tempo and comes close.
  • The flexible methods recover the warps best, and they do it with very different amounts of warping. The elastic DP reaches the lowest variance ratio but applies three to four times as much warping as the other flexible methods for the same accuracy: it also "explains" part of the noise and amplitude scaling as phase. The penalised RBFGS variant warps far less and is about as accurate; penalised continuous registration is as accurate with the least warping of all.
  • Lowest variance is not best warps. Variance reduction rewards any warp that makes curves look alike, including over-registration. When the warps themselves matter (timing estimates, phase statistics), judge methods by warp plausibility, not by how flat the registered sample looks.
  • Landmark registration is competitive because the two peaks carry most of the timing here; it is the cheapest flexible method.
  • Pairwise synchronisation is limited by its two-knot warps on this smooth design; its strength is noisy data (Pairwise Synchronisation).

docs.title: Bake-off on the growth data
docs.text:
The first 30 girls of the Berkeley growth study, height velocity from age 3 to 18 (smoothing-spline derivative of the heights). There are no true warps, but one feature has a well-defined timing: the age of peak growth velocity (PGV) in the pubertal spurt. A good registration lines it up; the table reports the standard deviation of the PGV age across the registered curves (1.1 years before registration), next to the variance ratio and the warp complexity. The landmark method registers the PGV ages, detected as the maximum between ages 9 and 15, to their mean.

import time
import numpy as np
from scipy.interpolate import make_smoothing_spline
from docs_data import load_growth
from fdars import alignment as A

age, heights, meta = load_growth()
girls = heights[(meta["sex"] == "female").to_numpy()][:30]
a = np.linspace(3, 18, 101)
V = np.array([make_smoothing_spline(age, h, lam=0.5).derivative()(a) for h in girls])   # cm / year
n = len(V)
inner = (a > 4) & (a < 17)
spurt = (a > 9) & (a < 15)
u = (a - a[0]) / (a[-1] - a[0])                       # [0, 1] grid for warp_complexity

def iterative_shift():
    seed = A.least_squares_shift_registration(V, a, 2.0)["shifts"]
    r = A.iterative_shift_registration(V, a, initial=seed, max_iter=20, tol=1e-4)
    return a - r["shifts"][:, None]

def affine():
    r = A.affine_registration(V, a)
    return (a - r["shifts"][:, None]) / r["dilations"][:, None]

def landmark():
    pgv = [[a[spurt][np.argmax(v[spurt])]] for v in V]
    return A.landmark_register(V, a, pgv)["gammas"]

methods = {
    "none":             (lambda: np.tile(a, (n, 1)), True),
    "iterative shift":  (iterative_shift, False),
    "affine":           (affine, False),
    "landmark (PGV)":   (landmark, True),
    "continuous":       (lambda: A.continuous_registration(V, a, lambda_=1e-2, max_template_iter=5)["warps"], True),
    "elastic DP":       (lambda: A.karcher_mean(V, a)["gammas"], True),
    "elastic RBFGS+l2": (lambda: A.karcher_mean_with_config(V, a, method="rbfgs", lambda_=0.01)["gammas"], True),
    "pairwise sync":    (lambda: A.pairwise_synchronization(V, a)["warps"], True),
}
print(f"{'method':18s} {'sd PGV age':>10s} {'var ratio':>9s} {'complexity':>10s} {'time s':>7s}")
for name, (fit, interval_warp) in methods.items():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    W = np.asarray(fit())
    dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
    R = np.array([np.interp(w, a, v) for w, v in zip(W, V)])
    sd_pgv = np.std([a[spurt][np.argmax(r[spurt])] for r in R])
    vr = R[:, inner].var(0).sum() / V[:, inner].var(0).sum()
    cx = f"{np.mean([A.warp_complexity((w - a[0]) / (a[-1] - a[0]), u) for w in W]):10.3f}" if interval_warp else f"{'—':>10s}"
    print(f"{name:18s} {sd_pgv:10.2f} {vr:9.3f} {cx} {dt:7.3f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

method             sd PGV age var ratio complexity  time s
none                     1.12     1.000      0.000   0.000
iterative shift          0.68     0.593          —   0.003
affine                   0.43     0.386          —   0.229
landmark (PGV)           0.07     0.440      0.064   0.000
continuous               0.49     0.291      0.286   0.026
elastic DP               0.07     0.349      0.252   0.759
elastic RBFGS+l2         0.04     0.395      0.101   0.409
pairwise sync            0.58     0.463      0.153   0.603
FDARS_FENCE_OK
  • Landmark and elastic registration line up the spurt (PGV-age spread below 0.1 years); the penalised RBFGS variant does so with less than half the warping of the elastic DP.
  • Continuous registration removes the most variance but leaves the spurt spread (about half a year): its criterion is dominated by the large, steeply falling velocities of early childhood, so it spends its smooth warp there. This is the "lowest variance is not best" lesson on real data, and a reminder to check the registration on the feature you care about.
  • Shift and affine halve the PGV spread; children differ in tempo as well as timing, but not in one global linear way.
  • Pairwise synchronisation sits in between; its two-knot warps cannot follow both the infancy decline and the spurt.

docs.title: What is being compared: distances and warp metrics
docs.text:
To compare methods quantitatively rather than by eye, we need the geometry underneath elastic alignment. It rests on the square-root slope function (SRSF). For an absolutely continuous curve \(f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}\),

\[ q(t) \;=\; \operatorname{sgn}\!\big(\dot f(t)\big)\,\sqrt{\,\lvert \dot f(t)\rvert\,}. \]

The point of this transform is that the awkward, non-invariant \(\mathbb{L}^2\) distance between curves becomes the well-behaved Fisher-Rao metric, which the SRSF turns into a plain \(\mathbb{L}^2\) distance. Crucially, under a warp \(\gamma\) (a boundary-preserving diffeomorphism of \([0,1]\), i.e. \(\gamma(0)=0,\ \gamma(1)=1,\ \dot\gamma>0\)), the SRSF transforms by the isometric group action

\[ (q\ast\gamma)(t) \;=\; q\big(\gamma(t)\big)\,\sqrt{\dot\gamma(t)} . \]

Because the action is by isometries, \(\lVert q_1\ast\gamma - q_2\ast\gamma\rVert = \lVert q_1 - q_2\rVert\), and every distance below is invariant to simultaneous rewarping.

Amplitude distance — the residual shape difference after optimal time-warping. It is the Fisher-Rao distance minimized over the warping group \(\Gamma\):

\[ d_a(f_1,f_2) \;=\; \min_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\; \big\lVert\, q_1 \;-\; (q_2\ast\gamma) \,\big\rVert_{\mathbb{L}^2}. \]

This is exactly the objective elastic alignment solves by dynamic programming, so elastic_distance and amplitude_distance coincide (verify below: both return the same value).

Phase distance — the amount of timing difference removed to achieve that match. Warps live on a sphere in SRSF coordinates via \(\psi=\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\) with \(\lVert\psi\rVert=1\), so phase difference is the geodesic (arc) distance on that sphere between the optimal warp \(\gamma^\ast\) and the identity, measured through the Fisher-Rao angle:

\[ d_p(f_1,f_2) \;=\; \cos^{-1}\!\Big(\textstyle\int_0^1 \sqrt{\dot\gamma^\ast(t)}\;dt\Big). \]

Together the pair splits total variation into what the curve looks like (\(d_a\)) and when it happens (\(d_p\)) — the amplitude-phase separation that alignment exists to produce.

Warp complexity — how far a single warp \(\gamma\) departs from doing nothing, again as a Fisher-Rao geodesic distance but now between \(\gamma\) and the identity \(\gamma_{\mathrm{id}}(t)=t\):

\[ c(\gamma) \;=\; d_{FR}(\gamma,\gamma_{\mathrm{id}}) \;=\; \cos^{-1}\!\Big(\textstyle\int_0^1 \sqrt{\dot\gamma(t)}\;dt\Big)\in[0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}). \]

Larger \(c\) means more time-warping was applied; \(c=0\) means the curve was already aligned.

Warp smoothness — the roughness (bending energy) of a warp, penalizing kinks:

\[ s(\gamma) \;=\; \int_0^1 \big(\ddot\gamma(t)\big)^2\,dt . \]

A smooth diffeomorphism has small \(s\); a piecewise-linear landmark warp has \(\ddot\gamma\) concentrated at its kinks, so its bending energy is large — the mechanistic reason landmark and elastic warps look different in the next section.

The figure below computes all four quantities on the phase-varying dataset, each curve measured against the elastic Karcher mean.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import (karcher_mean, amplitude_distance, phase_distance,
                             elastic_distance, warp_complexity, warp_smoothness)

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n, m = 14, 150
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
base = np.exp(-((t - 0.35) ** 2) / 0.006) + 0.8 * np.exp(-((t - 0.70) ** 2) / 0.006)
data = np.zeros((n, m))
for i in range(n):
    w = t ** rng.uniform(0.7, 1.6)
    data[i] = np.interp(t, (w - w.min()) / np.ptp(w), base)

km = karcher_mean(data, t, max_iter=20)
mu = np.asarray(km["mean"])
gam = np.asarray(km["gammas"])

amp = np.array([amplitude_distance(data[i], mu, t) for i in range(n)])
pha = np.array([phase_distance(data[i], mu, t) for i in range(n)])
cx = np.array([warp_complexity(gam[i], t) for i in range(n)])
sm = np.array([warp_smoothness(gam[i], t) for i in range(n)])

f, axes = fig(ncols=2, figsize=(11, 3.8))
axes[0].scatter(amp, pha, c=cx, cmap="viridis", s=45, edgecolor="k", lw=0.4)
axes[0].set(title="Per-curve split to the elastic mean",
            xlabel=r"amplitude distance $d_a$", ylabel=r"phase distance $d_p$")
cb = f.colorbar(axes[0].collections[0], ax=axes[0])
cb.set_label("warp complexity $c(\\gamma)$", fontsize=8)

axes[1].scatter(cx, sm, color="#6f42c1", s=45, edgecolor="k", lw=0.4)
axes[1].set(title="Warp complexity vs. bending energy",
            xlabel=r"complexity $c(\gamma)$", ylabel=r"smoothness $s(\gamma)$")
print(render(f))

# amplitude distance IS the minimized elastic distance
d_el = np.array([elastic_distance(data[i], mu, t) for i in range(n)])
print(f"max |amplitude_distance - elastic_distance| = {np.abs(amp - d_el).max():.2e}")
print(f"mean phase distance d_p = {pha.mean():.4f} rad "
      f"({np.degrees(pha.mean()):.1f} deg on the warp sphere)")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ max |amplitude_distance - elastic_distance| = 0.00e+00 mean phase distance d_p = 0.1392 rad (8.0 deg on the warp sphere)

The left panel shows the amplitude-phase split per curve, coloured by how much warping each needed; curves needing large warps (bright) sit high on the phase axis. The right panel confirms these elastic warps are simultaneously non-trivial (positive complexity) yet smooth (modest bending energy) — the property landmark warps lack. The printout verifies \(d_a\) equals the minimized elastic distance to machine precision.

docs.title: Warping functions: the mechanism differs
docs.text:
The warps expose the fundamental difference. Elastic produces smooth diffeomorphisms; landmark produces piecewise-linear paths kinked at the landmarks; constrained is smooth but passes through the landmark anchors.

import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import find_peaks
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import karcher_mean, elastic_align_pair_constrained

rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
n, m = 16, 150
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
base = np.exp(-((t - 0.35) ** 2) / 0.006) + 0.8 * np.exp(-((t - 0.70) ** 2) / 0.006)
data = np.zeros((n, m))
for i in range(n):
    w = t ** rng.uniform(0.7, 1.5)
    data[i] = np.interp(t, (w - w.min()) / np.ptp(w), base)

# elastic warps
gam_el = np.asarray(karcher_mean(data, t, max_iter=20)["gammas"])

# landmark warps
def top_peaks(y, k, mp=0.2):
    idx, props = find_peaks(y, prominence=mp)
    return np.sort(t[idx[np.argsort(props["prominences"])[::-1][:k]]])
L = np.array([top_peaks(r, 2) for r in data]); target = L.mean(0)
gam_lm = np.array([np.interp(t, np.concatenate(([0.], target, [1.])),
                             np.concatenate(([0.], L[i], [1.]))) for i in range(n)])

# constrained warps
ref = data[0]
gam_c = np.array([np.asarray(elastic_align_pair_constrained(
    ref, data[i], t, target, L[i], lambda_=0.0)["gamma"]) for i in range(n)])

f, axes = fig(ncols=3, figsize=(12, 3.6))
for ax, (g, title, c) in zip(axes, [
        (gam_el, "Elastic (smooth)", "#198754"),
        (gam_lm, "Landmark (kinked)", "#6f42c1"),
        (gam_c, "Constrained (smooth + anchored)", "#0dcaf0")]):
    ax.plot(t, g.T, color=c, lw=1.0, alpha=0.6)
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="#6c757d", ls="--", lw=1.2)
    for x in target:
        ax.axvline(x, color="#adb5bd", ls=":", lw=0.8)
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="t", aspect="equal")
axes[0].set(ylabel="$\\gamma(t)$")
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The landmark warps have visible corners at the landmark times (dotted verticals); the elastic and constrained warps are smooth, but only the constrained one is pinned to pass through those same times.

docs.title: Quantifying alignment quality
docs.text:
The distances above act per pair; to score a whole method we aggregate. Sharper means come from lower cross-sectional variance, so the headline metric is variance reduction

\[ \mathrm{VR} \;=\; 1-\frac{\overline{\operatorname{Var}}_{\text{aligned}}}{\overline{\operatorname{Var}}_{\text{original}}}, \qquad \overline{\operatorname{Var}} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\operatorname{Var}_i\!\big(f_i(t_j)\big), \]

the fraction of mean pointwise variance each method removes (\(\mathrm{VR}=1\) is perfect collapse; \(\mathrm{VR}=0\) is no help). We compare all three on two datasets: smooth global phase shifts, and distinct independently-shifting features.

import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import find_peaks
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import karcher_mean, elastic_align_pair_constrained

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 160)

def make_smooth(seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    out = np.zeros((15, len(t)))
    for i in range(15):
        s = rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1); a = rng.normal(1, 0.15)
        out[i] = a * np.sin(2 * np.pi * (t - s)) + 0.4 * a * np.sin(4 * np.pi * (t - 0.7 * s))
    return out

def make_features(seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    out = np.zeros((15, len(t)))
    for i in range(15):
        p1 = rng.uniform(0.15, 0.35); p2 = rng.uniform(0.55, 0.75)
        out[i] = rng.normal(1, 0.2) * np.exp(-200 * (t - p1) ** 2) + \
                 rng.normal(0.8, 0.15) * np.exp(-200 * (t - p2) ** 2)
    return out

def vr(orig, aligned):
    return 1 - np.var(aligned, axis=0).mean() / np.var(orig, axis=0).mean()

def top_peaks(y, k, mp):
    idx, props = find_peaks(y, prominence=mp)
    if len(idx) == 0:
        return np.array([t[np.argmax(y)]] * k)
    o = np.argsort(props["prominences"])[::-1][:k]
    pk = np.sort(t[idx[o]])
    return np.pad(pk, (0, k - len(pk)), constant_values=pk[-1]) if len(pk) < k else pk

def landmark_align(data, k, mp):
    L = np.array([top_peaks(r, k, mp) for r in data]); target = L.mean(0)
    def reg(y, s):
        kt = np.concatenate(([0.], target, [1.])); ks = np.concatenate(([0.], s, [1.]))
        return np.interp(np.interp(t, kt, ks), t, y)
    return np.array([reg(data[i], L[i]) for i in range(len(data))]), L, target

def constrained_align(data, L, target):
    ref = data[0]
    return np.array([np.asarray(elastic_align_pair_constrained(
        ref, data[i], t, target, L[i], lambda_=0.0)["f_aligned"]) for i in range(len(data))])

results = {}
for name, mk, k, mp in [("smooth", make_smooth, 1, 0.3), ("features", make_features, 2, 0.2)]:
    data = mk(42)
    el = np.asarray(karcher_mean(data, t, max_iter=20)["aligned_data"])
    lm, L, target = landmark_align(data, k, mp)
    cn = constrained_align(data, L, target)
    results[name] = {"Elastic": vr(data, el), "Landmark": vr(data, lm), "Constrained": vr(data, cn)}

methods = ["Elastic", "Landmark", "Constrained"]
x = np.arange(len(methods)); w = 0.38
f, ax = fig()
ax.bar(x - w / 2, [results["smooth"][m] for m in methods], w,
       color="#3f51b5", label="smooth shifts")
ax.bar(x + w / 2, [results["features"][m] for m in methods], w,
       color="#e8710a", label="distinct features")
ax.set(title="Variance reduction by method and dataset",
       ylabel="VR (higher = better)", xticks=x, ylim=(0, 1.05))
ax.set_xticklabels(methods)
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
print(render(f))

for ds in ("smooth", "features"):
    print(ds, {m: round(results[ds][m], 3) for m in methods})
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ smooth {'Elastic': np.float64(0.582), 'Landmark': np.float64(0.372), 'Constrained': np.float64(0.594)} features {'Elastic': np.float64(0.932), 'Landmark': np.float64(0.829), 'Constrained': np.float64(0.918)}

The pattern mirrors the R reference: on smooth global shifts, elastic and constrained lead and landmark trails (broad oscillations give it few clean anchors); on distinct features, all three do well, with elastic and constrained excellent because the peaks are unambiguous.

docs.title: Elastic diagnostics
docs.text:
For the elastic method, alignment_quality decomposes the variance and warp_statistics summarizes the warps -- reporting how much work alignment did and how the total splits into amplitude and phase.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import karcher_mean, alignment_quality, warp_statistics

rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
n, m = 16, 140
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
base = np.exp(-((t - 0.35) ** 2) / 0.006) + 0.8 * np.exp(-((t - 0.70) ** 2) / 0.006)
data = np.zeros((n, m))
for i in range(n):
    w = t ** rng.uniform(0.7, 1.5)
    data[i] = np.interp(t, (w - w.min()) / np.ptp(w), base)

q = alignment_quality(data, t, lambda_=0.0, max_iter=15)
km = karcher_mean(data, t, max_iter=20)
ws = warp_statistics(np.asarray(km["gammas"]), t, confidence_level=0.95)

f, ax = fig()
labels = ["amplitude\nvariance", "phase\nvariance"]
vals = [float(q["amplitude_variance"]), float(q["phase_variance"])]
ax.bar(labels, vals, color=["#198754", "#6f42c1"])
for i, v in enumerate(vals):
    ax.text(i, v, f"{v:.4f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9)
ax.set(title=f"Variance decomposition "
             f"(phase share {float(q['phase_amplitude_ratio']):.0%})",
       ylabel="variance")
print(render(f))

print(f"mean variance reduction : {float(q['mean_variance_reduction']):.4f}")
print(f"phase / amplitude ratio : {float(q['phase_amplitude_ratio']):.4f}")
print(f"mean warp complexity    : {float(q['mean_warp_complexity']):.4f}")
print(f"mean geodesic dist warps: {np.asarray(ws['geodesic_distances']).mean():.4f}")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ mean variance reduction : 0.0274 phase / amplitude ratio : 0.9992 mean warp complexity : 0.1121 mean geodesic dist warps: 0.1121

The bar chart splits the total variation into an amplitude part (genuine shape differences) and a phase part (timing), and here the phase bar dominates -- the printed phase/amplitude ratio confirms most of the spread was timing that alignment could remove. The variance-reduction and warp-complexity numbers quantify how much was removed and how hard the warps had to work to do it.

alignment_quality key Meaning mean_variance_reduction Fraction of pointwise variance removed (the VR metric) total_variance Total variance before decomposition amplitude_variance / phase_variance Variance attributed to amplitude / to phase phase_amplitude_ratio Phase share of total -- high means phase-dominated mean_warp_complexity / mean_warp_smoothness Average warp magnitude / roughness pointwise_variance_ratio Per-point post/pre variance ratio, shape (m,)

A high phase_amplitude_ratio (near 1) confirms the variation is mostly timing -- precisely where alignment helps most.

docs.title: When each method succeeds -- and fails
docs.text:
Real data is messier than tidy examples. These scenarios show where each method shines and where it breaks.

import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import find_peaks
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import karcher_mean

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)

# Scenario A: smooth global warp -- no clean features (elastic wins, landmark struggles)
rng = np.random.default_rng(101)
smooth = np.zeros((12, 200))
for i in range(12):
    ws_ = rng.uniform(-0.15, 0.15)
    tw = t + ws_ * np.sin(np.pi * t)
    tw = (tw - tw.min()) / np.ptp(tw)
    smooth[i] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * tw) + 0.3 * np.cos(6 * np.pi * tw)

# Scenario B: mixed 1-peak & 2-peak curves (elastic handles, landmark forced-template fails)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
mixed = np.zeros((12, 200))
for i in range(12):
    if i < 6:
        mixed[i] = 1.5 * np.exp(-300 * (t - rng.uniform(0.3, 0.5)) ** 2)
    else:
        mixed[i] = np.exp(-300 * (t - rng.uniform(0.2, 0.35)) ** 2) + \
                   np.exp(-300 * (t - rng.uniform(0.6, 0.75)) ** 2)

# Scenario C: noisy -- raw vs pre-smoothed elastic
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
noisy = np.array([np.sin(2 * np.pi * (t - rng.uniform(-0.08, 0.08))) + rng.normal(0, 0.35, 200)
                  for _ in range(12)])
# simple moving-average pre-smoothing
kern = np.ones(11) / 11
smoothed = np.array([np.convolve(y, kern, mode="same") for y in noisy])

el_smooth = np.asarray(karcher_mean(smooth, t, max_iter=20)["aligned_data"])
el_mixed = np.asarray(karcher_mean(mixed, t, max_iter=20)["aligned_data"])
el_noisy_raw = np.asarray(karcher_mean(noisy, t, max_iter=20)["aligned_data"])
el_noisy_sm = np.asarray(karcher_mean(smoothed, t, max_iter=20)["aligned_data"])

f, axes = fig(ncols=3, figsize=(12.5, 3.6))
axes[0].plot(t, el_smooth.T, color="#198754", lw=0.9, alpha=0.5)
axes[0].plot(t, el_smooth.mean(0), color="#e8710a", lw=2.2)
axes[0].set(title="A: smooth warp -> elastic aligns cleanly", xlabel="t", ylabel="f(t)")

axes[1].plot(t, el_mixed.T, color="#3f51b5", lw=0.9, alpha=0.5)
axes[1].plot(t, el_mixed.mean(0), color="#e8710a", lw=2.2)
axes[1].set(title="B: mixed 1-/2-peak -> elastic copes", xlabel="t")

axes[2].plot(t, el_noisy_raw.mean(0), color="#dc3545", lw=2.0, label="raw (over-warps)")
axes[2].plot(t, el_noisy_sm.mean(0), color="#198754", lw=2.0, label="smooth then align")
axes[2].set(title="C: noisy -> smooth first", xlabel="t")
axes[2].legend(fontsize=8)
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Each panel isolates a regime where the method choice matters, and the sharpened orange means show the fix working in every case:

  • A -- elastic excels on smooth warping. Broad overlapping oscillations have no clear anchors, so landmark detection has nothing to grab; the Fisher-Rao metric captures the continuous phase change naturally.
  • B -- elastic copes with a variable feature count. Half the curves have one peak, half have two. Elastic makes no template assumption; a landmark method with a fixed expected_count=2 would force a spurious second peak onto the single-peak curves.
  • C -- smooth before aligning noisy data. The SRSF differentiates the curve, so noise drives over-warping. Pre-smoothing (here a moving average; splines or a kernel smoother work too) or a larger lambda_ tames it.

docs.title: Scenario summary
docs.text: Scenario Best method Why Smooth global warping Elastic No features to anchor; optimal continuous warp Independent feature shifts Landmark Guarantees feature-to-feature correspondence Noisy data Elastic (with lambda_) or pre-smoothing Penalty / smoothing controls over-warping Variable number of features Elastic No feature template required Features + smooth variation between them Constrained elastic Anchors features and smooths between them

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text:
The tables below compare the three methods examined in detail on this page. For every method, including shift, affine, continuous, sparse, likelihood-based, Bayesian and DTW alignment, use the decision tree on Choosing an Alignment Method.

Warping Automation Cost Smoothness Feature control Elastic Smooth diffeomorphism Fully automatic \(O(nm^2)\) High None Landmark Piecewise-linear Needs feature type \(O(nm+nk)\) Low (corners) Full Constrained Smooth with anchors Needs feature type \(O(nm^2/k)\) High between anchors Partial TSRVF (uses elastic) Fully automatic \(O(nm^2)\) + PCA High None Situation Recommended No prior on which features correspond; smooth timing differences Elastic (karcher_mean) Want a principled metric / amplitude-phase decomposition Elastic + Shape Analysis Well-defined, domain-meaningful features; need guaranteed correspondence Landmark (Landmark Registration) Features must align exactly and the warp between them should be smooth Constrained (elastic_align_pair_constrained) PCA / regression / clustering on aligned curves Elastic + TSRVF

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: Method Common pitfall Mitigation Elastic Over-warping ("pinching") on noisy data Increase lambda_, or pre-smooth Landmark Mismatched landmark correspondence Use a fixed count, raise the prominence threshold Constrained Too few landmarks = barely constrained Detect more / multiple landmark types TSRVF Linearization error for curves far from the mean Check reconstruction quality

docs.title: A worked workflow
docs.text:
A typical analysis chains the methods: explore, detect features to understand structure, align with the method the structure suggests, then linearize with TSRVF for downstream statistics.

import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import find_peaks
from fdars.alignment import karcher_mean, tsrvf_transform

# 1) explore, 2) understand structure via landmark counts
counts = [len(find_peaks(row, prominence=0.2)[0]) for row in data]
print("peaks per curve:", counts)   # variable count -> prefer elastic

# 3) align (elastic here, since the feature count varies)
km = karcher_mean(data, t, max_iter=15)

# 4) linearize for PCA on the tangent vectors
V = np.asarray(tsrvf_transform(data, t, max_iter=15)["tangent_vectors"])
Vc = V - V.mean(0)
s = np.linalg.svd(Vc, compute_uv=False)
cum = np.cumsum(s ** 2) / np.sum(s ** 2)
print("variance explained (first 3 PCs):", (cum[:3] * 100).round(1))

See Elastic Alignment, Advanced Elastic Alignment, Landmark Registration, and TSRVF for the individual methods, and Shape Analysis for the amplitude/phase decomposition that alignment enables.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
The elastic framework, SRSF transform, Fisher-Rao metric, and the amplitude/phase distances used above:

  • Srivastava, A. and Klassen, E. P. (2016). Functional and Shape Data Analysis. Springer Series in Statistics. Springer, New York. (Canonical reference for the SRSF, the Fisher-Rao metric, and the amplitude-phase geometry; see Ch. 4-8.)
  • Srivastava, A., Wu, W., Kurtek, S., Klassen, E., and Marron, J. S. (2011). Registration of Functional Data Using Fisher-Rao Metric. arXiv:1103.3817. (Introduces the elastic alignment objective \(\min_\gamma \lVert q_1 - (q_2\ast\gamma)\rVert\) and the amplitude/phase separation.)
  • Tucker, J. D., Wu, W., and Srivastava, A. (2013). Generative models for functional data using phase and amplitude separation. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 61, 50-66. doi:10.1016/j.csda.2012.12.001. (Karcher mean under the elastic metric, variance decomposition, and the alignment-quality diagnostics.)
  • Marron, J. S., Ramsay, J. O., Sangalli, L. M., and Srivastava, A. (2015). Functional Data Analysis of Amplitude and Phase Variation. Statistical Science, 30(4), 468-484. doi:10.1214/15-STS524. (Survey contrasting landmark registration with metric-based elastic alignment.)
  • Kneip, A. and Gasser, T. (1992). Statistical Tools to Analyze Data Representing a Sample of Curves. The Annals of Statistics, 20(3), 1266-1305. (Foundational treatment of landmark registration and structural averaging.)

docs.title: Inference after Alignment
docs.text:
Once curves are registered, the usual questions come back with a twist: do two groups differ, and is the difference in amplitude or in timing? Which curves are unusual, and in which way? How uncertain is the mean shape? What will the rest of this half-observed curve look like? This page collects the tools in fdars that answer them on top of an elastic alignment, and the one rule that makes their answers valid.

Align the pooled sample once, then permute labels on fixed amplitude and phase distances.

docs.title: The golden rule: align without the labels
docs.text:
Alignment is itself an estimate, and it is estimated from the data. If you align each group to its own template and then compare the groups, the registration has already used the group labels: each group's curves are pulled towards its own mean, which exaggerates between-group differences in amplitude and erases them in phase. A permutation test on such data is not valid, because relabelling the curves does not reproduce the alignment step.

Align the pooled sample once, ignoring the labels; then compare the groups on the aligned data. Every statistic below that depends on alignment does this internally.

docs.title: Testing for amplitude and phase differences
docs.text:
elastic_phase_amplitude_test(data, argvals, labels, n_perm=999, amplitude_metric="pairwise", joint=True):

  1. aligns all curves jointly to the elastic Karcher mean, without the labels;
  2. computes two \(n \times n\) distance matrices: the amplitude distance \(d_A(i,j) = \inf_\gamma \lVert q_i - (q_j\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\gamma'}\rVert\) (pairwise elastic distance; amplitude_metric="template_aligned" uses the cheaper \(L^2\) distance between the template-aligned SRSFs instead) and the phase distance \(d_P(i,j) = \arccos\langle\psi_i, \psi_j\rangle\) between the warps (\(\psi = \sqrt{\gamma'}\)); with joint=True also \(d_J^2 = d_A^2/\overline{d_A^2} + d_P^2/\overline{d_P^2}\);
  3. runs a one-way PERMANOVA (Anderson 2001) on each matrix: pseudo-\(F = \dfrac{SS_A/(k-1)}{SS_W/(N-k)}\) and the permutation p-value \((\#\{F^* \ge F\} + 1)/(n_{\text{perm}} + 1)\).

The distance matrices depend only on the unlabelled sample, so permuting the labels with the matrices held fixed gives the exact conditional null distribution. Each result (amplitude, phase, joint) reports statistic, p_value, r_squared, the sums of squares and degrees of freedom; the distance matrices and the full alignment are returned too. The generic fdars.inference.permanova(dist, labels) runs PERMANOVA on any distance matrix (Functional Inference).

Reading the p-values

PERMANOVA detects any difference in distribution of the distances: a shift of the group centres, and, with unequal group sizes, also a difference in spread. The amplitude and phase p-values use the same permutations, so they are not independent, and no multiplicity correction is applied. With two equal groups the smallest attainable p-value is \(2/(n_{\text{perm}}+1)\).

docs.title: Example: phase-only differences, and why noise matters
docs.text:
Two groups of 15 curves; group 2 has systematically later features (a phase difference only), and every curve carries random amplitude scaling and white noise. Over several simulated data sets, how often does each test reject at the 5 % level?

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fast
from fdars import alignment as A

m = 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.008) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.68) ** 2 / 0.01)

def simulate(seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X, labels = [], []
    for g in (0, 1):
        for _ in range(15):
            c = rng.normal(0.3 * g, 0.15)                       # group 1: later features
            X.append(rng.uniform(0.85, 1.15) * mu(t + c * t * (1 - t)) + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(m))
            labels.append(g)
    return np.array(X), np.array(labels)

n_sets = fast(10, 4)
rej = {"raw": np.zeros(2), "pre-smoothed": np.zeros(2)}
for seed in range(n_sets):
    X, labels = simulate(seed)
    for name, D in (("raw", X), ("pre-smoothed", np.asarray(A.srsf_presmooth(X, t, smoothing="box", passes=5)))):
        r = A.elastic_phase_amplitude_test(D, t, labels, n_perm=199, joint=False)
        rej[name] += [r["amplitude"]["p_value"] < 0.05, r["phase"]["p_value"] < 0.05]
for name, v in rej.items():
    print(f"{name:13s} rejection rate: amplitude {v[0] / n_sets:.2f}  phase {v[1] / n_sets:.2f}   ({n_sets} data sets)")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

raw           rejection rate: amplitude 0.50  phase 1.00   (10 data sets)
pre-smoothed  rejection rate: amplitude 0.10  phase 0.90   (10 data sets)
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The phase test detects the timing difference. On the raw curves the amplitude test also rejects far more often than 5 %, although the groups do not differ in amplitude at all: noise in the SRSF interacts with the warps (a stretched stretch of curve has its derivative noise rescaled), so curves warped more strongly look slightly different in amplitude. Light pre-smoothing (srsf_presmooth, a few box-filter passes) removes this leak and keeps the phase test's power. Heavy smoothing does the opposite: it flattens the features until the timing difference is hard to see (25 passes on these 101-point curves cut the phase rejection rate by half). Smooth just enough to tame the derivative noise; a finer grid helps too.

docs.title: Localised differences: where do the groups differ?
docs.text:
elastic_phase_amplitude_test answers whether the groups differ in amplitude or phase, with one p-value each. elastic_local_difference_test(data, argvals, labels, test="itp") answers where, and in which direction:

  1. it aligns all curves to one elastic Karcher mean, without the labels (the golden rule above), with the same warp options as elastic_align_pair_with_config;
  2. amplitude: it runs a local two-sample test on the aligned curves;
  3. phase: it runs the same local test on the warps, as the time displacement \(\gamma_i(t) - t\) (default, in argvals units) or as \(\psi_i = \sqrt{\gamma_i'}\) (phase_representation="psi").

The local test is either the interval-wise testing procedure (test="itp", Pini & Vantini 2016, as itp_two_pop_regions), which controls the interval-wise error rate at alpha, or a simultaneous confidence band for the mean difference (test="scb", Degras 2011, as scb_two_sample_band), which is family-wise over the grid. Amplitude and phase are tested separately, with no correction across the two.

Each of result["amplitude"] and result["phase"] holds regions, a list of contiguous grid intervals with t_start, t_end, direction and (ITP) min_adjusted_pvalue, plus the pointwise effect (A − B) and, for ITP, the pointwise adjusted p-values. Group A is the smaller label, B the larger:

Part direction="positive" direction="negative" amplitude A's aligned curves lie above B's A below B phase, displacement A's features occur later (timing="a_later") A's features occur earlier (timing="a_earlier") phase, psi A's warps run faster around \(t\) A's warps run slower

Below, two groups of 20 curves share a two-peak shape with individual timing jitter. Group 1 (B) has a taller first peak (a localised amplitude difference near \(t = 0.3\)) and a later second peak (a localised timing difference near \(t = 0.7\)):

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars import alignment as A

m = 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
bump = lambda s, c: np.exp(-(s - c) ** 2 / 0.004)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X, labels = [], []
for g in (0, 1):
    for _ in range(20):
        s = t + rng.normal(0, 0.02) * np.sin(np.pi * t)            # individual timing jitter
        h1 = rng.normal(1.0 + 0.3 * g, 0.08)                      # group 1: taller first peak
        c2 = 0.68 + 0.04 * g + rng.normal(0, 0.01)                # group 1: later second peak
        X.append(h1 * bump(s, 0.3) + 0.8 * bump(s, c2) + 0.005 * rng.standard_normal(m))
        labels.append(g)
X = np.asarray(A.srsf_presmooth(np.array(X), t, smoothing="box", passes=5))
labels = np.array(labels)

res = {test: A.elastic_local_difference_test(X, t, labels, test=test, nbasis=30) for test in ("itp", "scb")}

r = res["itp"]
aligned, phase = np.asarray(r["alignment"]["aligned_data"]), np.asarray(r["phase_data"])
f, (a1, a2) = fig(ncols=2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
for ax, Y, part, title, ylab in ((a1, aligned, "amplitude", "Amplitude: aligned curves", "f"),
                                 (a2, phase, "phase", "Phase: displacement $\\gamma_i(t) - t$", "time shift")):
    for reg in r[part]["regions"]:
        ax.axvspan(reg["t_start"], reg["t_end"], color="#ffc107", alpha=0.3, lw=0)
    ax.plot(t, Y[labels == 0].mean(0), color="#3f51b5", lw=2, label="group 0 (A)")
    ax.plot(t, Y[labels == 1].mean(0), color="#e8710a", lw=2, label="group 1 (B)")
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="t", ylabel=ylab)
a1.legend(fontsize=8)
print(render(f))

rows = "".join(
    f"<tr><td>{test.upper()}</td><td>{part}</td><td>[{g['t_start']:.2f}, {g['t_end']:.2f}]</td>"
    f"<td>{g.get('timing') or g['direction']}</td>"
    f"<td>{'' if g['min_adjusted_pvalue'] is None else format(g['min_adjusted_pvalue'], '.3f')}</td></tr>"
    for test, rr in res.items() for part in ("amplitude", "phase") for g in rr[part]["regions"])
print("<table><tr><th>test</th><th>part</th><th>region</th><th>direction</th><th>min adj. p</th></tr>"
      f"{rows}</table>")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ testpartregiondirectionmin adj. pITPamplitude[0.23, 0.38]negative0.005ITPphase[0.63, 0.86]a_earlier0.010SCBamplitude[0.11, 0.44]negativeSCBamplitude[0.51, 0.52]positiveSCBphase[0.50, 0.94]a_earlier

Both tests find the amplitude difference around the first peak, with group 0 below group 1, and the timing difference around the second peak, with group 0 earlier (the shaded regions in the plot are the ITP ones). The phase regions are wider than the peak itself: once the second peak is later, the displacement \(\gamma(t) - t\) differs on the whole stretch of time that has to be stretched or compressed to move it, not only at the peak. The SCB also flags a sliver of amplitude around \(t = 0.51\); it comes from the timing difference (it stays if the planted amplitude difference is removed from the simulation, and goes if the timing difference is removed): a single label-free alignment does not absorb a group-level timing difference completely, and a little of it shows up as amplitude next to the moved feature. Removing either planted difference removes the corresponding phase or amplitude regions.

Choose nbasis for the width of the effect

The ITP tests B-spline coefficients, so its resolution is set by the spacing of the components, and with a strong effect and too few components, components far from the effect reject as well. Here the peaks are about 0.1 wide, so the example uses nbasis=30. With the default nbasis=15 the amplitude test flags most of the domain, split into short alternating "above" and "below" regions by the sign of the noisy mean difference; those directions are not supported by the data. See Power and resolution of the ITP, and cross-check with test="scb".

When to use which:

  • elastic_phase_amplitude_test for a single global decision (do the groups differ at all, in amplitude, in phase?); it uses the full elastic distances and has no basis to tune.
  • elastic_local_difference_test to locate and sign the differences. Use test="itp" for interval-wise error control and adjusted p-values (it is conservative), test="scb" for a band that is family-wise over the grid and needs no basis (its multiplier bootstrap is liberal for small groups: about 35 of 200 null data sets rejected at 10 curves per group in fdars-core's study, 6 of 200 at 30).

The same pre-smoothing advice as for the global test applies: SRSF noise leaks phase differences into the amplitude part.

docs.title: Elastic box plots
docs.text:
The elastic functional box plots of Xie, Kurtek, Bharath & Sun (2017) (ports of fdasrsf ampbox / phbox) summarise amplitude and phase separately, after aligning the sample to its Karcher median:

  • Amplitude box plot (amplitude_boxplot_from_aligned): distances \(\lVert q_{\text{median}} - q_i\rVert\) between aligned SRSFs; the 50 % and \((1-\alpha)\) central regions are the closest \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) and \(\operatorname{round}(n(1-\alpha))\) curves; the quartile curves Q1/Q3 are chosen inside them to be far from the median in opposite directions; whiskers extend them by k_a × the inter-quartile distance; curves beyond the whisker distance are outliers.
  • Phase box plot (elastic_phase_boxplot): the same construction on warps, in the Fisher–Rao geometry of \(\psi = \sqrt{\gamma'}\), around the Karcher median warp (Weiszfeld steps); distances are shooting-vector lengths.
  • elastic_boxplots(data, argvals) does the alignment and both plots; its model.classify(new_data, argvals) aligns new curves to the template and assigns each to a region (level 1 = inside the 50 % region, 2 = inside the \((1-\alpha)\) region, 3 = within the whiskers, 4 = outlier) and a side (Q1 or Q3), separately for amplitude and phase.
import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n, m = 30, 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.008) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.68) ** 2 / 0.01)
X = np.array([rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1) * mu(t + rng.uniform(-0.3, 0.3) * t * (1 - t))
              + 0.005 * rng.standard_normal(m) for _ in range(n)])
X[4] = mu(t ** 3)                                            # timing outlier: features much later
X[11] = mu(t) + 0.6 * np.exp(-(t - 0.52) ** 2 / 0.004)       # shape outlier: an extra bump

b = A.elastic_boxplots(X, t)
print("amplitude box plot outliers:", [int(i) for i in b["amplitude"]["outlier_indices"]])
print("phase box plot outliers:    ", [int(i) for i in b["phase"]["outlier_indices"]])

new = np.array([mu(t ** 3), mu(t), mu(t) + 0.6 * np.exp(-(t - 0.52) ** 2 / 0.004)])
c = b["model"].classify(new, t)
print("new curves (late / typical / extra bump):")
print("  amplitude regions", [int(v) for v in c["amplitude"]["regions"]], "  phase regions", [int(v) for v in c["phase"]["regions"]])
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

amplitude box plot outliers: [11]
phase box plot outliers:     [4]
new curves (late / typical / extra bump):
  amplitude regions [3, 2, 4]   phase regions [4, 3, 3]
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Each outlier is flagged by the box plot of its own kind: the extra bump in amplitude, the late curve in phase. New curves are classified the same way: the late curve lands in phase region 4 (outlier) and amplitude region 3 (within the whiskers), the extra-bump curve in amplitude region 4, and the typical curve inside the central regions. The phase whiskers are long: the late curve's phase distance is about twice the next largest, yet only just beyond the whisker; lower k_a for a stricter phase fence.

Band-depth phase box plot. phase_boxplot(gammas, argvals, factor=1.5) is a different, simpler construction: it ranks the warps by modified band depth (López-Pintado & Romo 2009) as ordinary functions on \([0,1]\), takes the deepest as the median and the 50 % deepest as the central region, and flags warps outside the fences central band ± factor × its width. It works in the Euclidean geometry of \(\gamma\), not the Fisher–Rao geometry of the elastic phase box plot; phase_boxplot_classify classifies new warps (levels 1, 3, 4).

docs.title: Elastic depth and outlier detection
docs.text:
elastic_depth(data, argvals) returns, for every curve, an amplitude depth and a phase depth computed from the pairwise amplitude and phase distance matrices,

\[ D_i = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j \ne i} d_{ij}}, \]

and their geometric mean combined_depth. (The crate documentation calls this a lens depth; it is an inverse-mean-distance depth. Amplitude and phase distances live on different scales, so the geometric mean weighs them unevenly: compare amplitude and phase depths separately.) Cost: two \(O(n^2)\) pairwise-alignment matrices.

elastic_outlier_detection(data, argvals, threshold_method="tukey", tukey_k=1.5) (fdasrvf outlier.detection) computes each curve's elastic distance to a robust reference, the Karcher median by default (use_median=True), and flags curves whose distance exceeds a threshold:

  • threshold_method="tukey" (default): \(Q_3 + k\cdot\mathrm{IQR}\) of the distances (tukey_k, default 1.5);
  • threshold_method="quantile": the empirical \((1-\alpha)\) quantile, which flags about \(\alpha n\) curves in any sample: a screening rule, not a test.

The elastic distance is invariant to warping, so the threshold catches shape outliers only. The result also reports amplitude_distances and phase_distances to the reference; fence the phase distances yourself to catch timing outliers:

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import elastic_outlier_detection

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n, m = 28, 120
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
base = np.exp(-((t - 0.5) ** 2) / (2 * 0.12 ** 2))
data = np.array([rng.normal(1, 0.05) * np.interp(
    t, np.clip(t + rng.normal(0, 0.03), 0, 1), base) for _ in range(n)])
data[3] *= 1.8                                         # amplitude (shape) outlier
data[7] = np.interp(t, np.clip(t - 0.18, 0, 1), base)  # phase (timing) outlier

out = elastic_outlier_detection(data, t, threshold_method="tukey", tukey_k=1.5)
amp = np.asarray(out["amplitude_distances"])
pha = np.asarray(out["phase_distances"])

def fence(x, k=2.0):                                   # Tukey upper fence on each component
    q1, q3 = np.percentile(x, [25, 75]); return q3 + k * (q3 - q1)
fa, fp = fence(amp), fence(pha)
amp_out = np.where(amp > fa)[0]
pha_out = np.where(pha > fp)[0]

f, ax = fig()
ax.scatter(amp, pha, s=26, color="#adb5bd", zorder=2)
ax.axvline(fa, color="#3f51b5", ls="--", lw=1, label="amplitude fence")
ax.axhline(fp, color="#e8710a", ls="--", lw=1, label="phase fence")
for i in amp_out:
    ax.scatter(amp[i], pha[i], s=70, color="#3f51b5", zorder=3)
    ax.annotate(f"{i} · shape", (amp[i], pha[i]), (6, 4), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8, color="#3f51b5")
for i in pha_out:
    ax.scatter(amp[i], pha[i], s=70, color="#e8710a", zorder=3)
    ax.annotate(f"{i} · timing", (amp[i], pha[i]), (6, -11), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8, color="#e8710a")
ax.set(title="Outlier type: amplitude (shape) vs phase (timing)", xlabel="amplitude distance", ylabel="phase distance")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
print(render(f))
print(f"<p>built-in (total elastic distance) flags: {[int(i) for i in out['outlier_indices']]}; "
      f"amplitude fence: {[int(i) for i in amp_out]}; phase fence: {[int(i) for i in pha_out]}</p>")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

built-in (total elastic distance) flags: [3, 13]; amplitude fence: [3]; phase fence: [7]

The built-in threshold flags the shape outlier (curve 3) and one borderline curve, but not the timing outlier: curve 7 has a large phase distance but an ordinary amplitude distance, and is found only by fencing the phase distances. The reference median is estimated with the outliers included, which can mask a cluster of similar outliers.

docs.title: Uncertainty of the mean shape
docs.text: shape_confidence_interval(data, argvals, n_bootstrap=200, confidence_level=0.95) bootstraps the elastic Karcher mean: it resamples the curves, computes each resample's Karcher mean, aligns it to the full-sample mean (otherwise leftover phase would inflate the band) and reports pointwise percentile bands lower_band / upper_band and the bootstrap_means. The bands are pointwise, not simultaneous, and come with no formal coverage guarantee; the cost is n_bootstrap Karcher means. For curves in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), curve_shape_confidence_interval offers a geodesic bootstrap radius and fdasrvf's model-based region (Shapes of Curves in R^d). For posterior bands on warps and template, see Bayesian Alignment.

docs.title: Clustering without choosing \(k\): elastic DP-means
docs.text:
elastic_dpmeans(data, argvals, penalty=None) (port of fdasrsf kmeans.dpmeans_align) is the small-variance limit of a Dirichlet-process mixture in the elastic metric (Kulis & Jordan 2012). Each pass aligns every curve to every template, and a curve whose elastic distance to all templates exceeds the penalty \(\lambda\) opens a new cluster; empty clusters are dropped, warps are centred, and templates are the mean aligned SRSFs. The objective is \(\sum_i d_i^2 + \lambda^2 K\). The number of clusters is therefore set by \(\lambda\), a distance scale: a curve farther than \(\lambda\) from every template starts its own cluster.

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
m = 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
shapes = [lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.5) ** 2 / 0.01),
          lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.006) + np.exp(-(s - 0.68) ** 2 / 0.006),
          lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.3) ** 2 / 0.006) - 0.6 * np.exp(-(s - 0.7) ** 2 / 0.006)]
X, label = [], []
for k, f in enumerate(shapes):                      # 3 shapes x 10 curves, random warps and scales
    for _ in range(10):
        X.append(rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2) * f(t + rng.uniform(-0.4, 0.4) * t * (1 - t)) + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(m))
        label.append(k)
X, label = np.array(X), np.array(label)

D = np.asarray(A.elastic_self_distance_matrix(X, t))
same = label[:, None] == label[None, :]
print(f"within-shape distances: 95th percentile {np.percentile(D[same & (D > 0)], 95):.2f};"
      f"  between-shape: 5th percentile {np.percentile(D[~same], 5):.2f}")
for penalty in (None, 0.5, 0.8, 2.0):
    r = A.elastic_dpmeans(X, t, penalty=penalty)
    purity = sum(np.bincount(label[r["labels"] == c]).max() for c in np.unique(r["labels"])) / len(label)
    print(f"penalty={str(penalty):5s} (used {r['penalty']:.2f}): k = {r['k']}, purity {purity:.2f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

within-shape distances: 95th percentile 0.58;  between-shape: 5th percentile 0.95
penalty=None  (used 0.64): k = 3, purity 1.00
penalty=0.5   (used 0.50): k = 9, purity 1.00
penalty=0.8   (used 0.80): k = 3, purity 1.00
penalty=2.0   (used 2.00): k = 1, purity 0.33
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Any penalty between the typical within-cluster distance and the typical between-cluster distance recovers the three shapes. Too small a penalty splits clusters (with \(\lambda = 0.5\) some curves sit farther than that from their own template), too large a penalty merges everything into one. With penalty=None a seeded k-means++ heuristic picks it; it worked here, but on small samples it can be far too small, so read the scale off the distance matrix as above. The result depends on the order of the sweep. For a fixed number of clusters see align_cluster_fd and the other methods on Elastic Clustering.

docs.title: Predicting the rest of a partially observed curve
docs.text:
When a new curve has been observed only up to time \(s\) (or on fragments, or at scattered points), partial-curve conformal prediction (Wang, Kurtek & Zhang 2026) predicts the registered version of the complete curve with finite-sample guarantees:

  • an amplitude band \(I_t\) with \(P\bigl(Y_{n+1}(t) \in I_t\bigr) \ge 1 - \alpha\) for every \(t\) (band="pointwise"), or for all \(t\) simultaneously (band="simultaneous"), where \(Y_{n+1}\) is the new curve aligned to the template;
  • a phase set \(I_\gamma\) with \(P(\gamma^*_{n+1} \in I_\gamma) \ge 1 - \alpha\) for the warp that registers the complete curve (prediction.phase_set_contains(gamma) tests membership exactly).

The reference curves are split into a training part, which only estimates an elastic template, and a calibration part, which is registered to it; responses are predicted by Nadaraya–Watson weighting of calibration curves whose observed part resembles the new curve's. The guarantees need exchangeable curves, an observation pattern independent of the curves, and a template independent of the calibration curves.

The functions are partial_conformal_fit, partial_conformal_predict, partial_conformal_predict_observed (prefix, fragments or sparse times) and partial_conformal_select_bandwidth in fdars.conformal; the full walk-through with a coverage check is on Partial-Curve Conformal Prediction.

docs.title: Other inference built on alignment
docs.text:
• Conformal elastic regression. conformal_elastic_regression and conformal_elastic_pcr (fdars.conformal) wrap elastic scalar-on-function regression in split conformal intervals. Test and calibration curves are aligned with \(\lambda = 0\) regardless of the fitted model's \(\lambda\), and a uniform grid is assumed. See Conformal Prediction.
  • Elastic conformal anomaly detection. elastic_conformal_anomaly (fdars.tolerance) computes conformal p-values for new curves from amplitude, phase or combined elastic non-conformity scores against a calibration set. See Outlier Detection.
  • Elastic changepoints. elastic_changepoint(data, argvals, kind="amplitude" | "phase" | "fpca") looks for a single change in a time-ordered sample of curves (Tucker & Yarger 2024): a functional CUSUM on the aligned curves (amplitude), on the warps' shooting vectors (phase), or a Hotelling CUSUM on elastic FPCA scores; the p-value comes from permuting the curves with the alignment held fixed, which assumes no serial dependence under the null.

docs.title: Banded Elastic Alignment
docs.text:
The elastic dynamic program searches warps over the full \(m \times m\) grid of index pairs, which costs \(O(m^2)\) per pair of curves. A Sakoe–Chiba band restricts the search to a corridor around the diagonal, \(|i - j| \le R\) with \(R = \lceil \texttt{band\_frac}\cdot m\rceil\), so that the per-pair cost drops to \(O(m R)\). For long curves whose phase variation is small compared with the domain, the optimal warp lies inside the band and the result is unchanged.

The diagram shows the DP table: cells inside the diagonal stripe are evaluated, cells outside are skipped, and the warp path has to stay inside the stripe.

The band is one option of the elastic optimiser and is documented with the others on Elastic Optimisers & Penalties, including how it interacts with RBFGS and a timing/accuracy experiment. This page summarises the practical side.

docs.title: Two ways to set a band
docs.text:
from fdars import alignment as A

# classic functions
A.karcher_mean_with_band(data, argvals, lambda_=0.0, max_iter=20, tol=1e-4, band_frac=0.2)
A.elastic_self_distance_matrix_with_band(data, argvals, band_frac=0.2)
A.elastic_cross_distance_matrix_with_band(data1, data2, argvals, band_frac=0.2)

# any *_with_config function (DP or RBFGS)
A.karcher_mean_with_config(data, argvals, band_frac=0.2)
A.elastic_align_pair_with_config(f1, f2, argvals, band_frac=0.2, method="rbfgs")

band_frac=None (in the *_with_band functions) or 0.0 (in *_with_config) means no band. With the DP optimiser both routes give identical results, and the result dicts have the same keys as karcher_mean and the plain distance matrices. The landmark-constrained and curve-shape functions do not accept a band.

docs.title: What the band does to the model
docs.text:
The band is a constraint: the warp can move a time point by at most \(R h\) (about band_frac of the domain on a uniform grid). Within that constraint the DP is still exact. Therefore:

  • If the true displacement is smaller than the band, banded and unbanded results are identical, and the band is a free speed-up.
  • If it is larger, the warps are clipped at the band edge, residual phase stays in the aligned curves, the Karcher mean blurs, and distances are over-estimated.

Signs of clipping: warps that run along \(t \pm\) band_frac for a stretch, a variance reduction that drops when the band is narrowed, a mean that changes with band_frac.

docs.title: Choosing band_frac
docs.text:
There is no automatic choice: band_frac encodes how far you believe any feature can move. Practical rules:

  1. Estimate the largest plausible displacement, for example from an unbanded run on a subsample: np.abs(gammas - t).max() (in units of the domain length if \(t\) spans \([0, 1]\)).
  2. Set band_frac comfortably above it; check that the mean and the variance reduction do not change when you widen it.
  3. If the phase includes a large rigid offset, remove it first with shift registration and band only the remainder.

The speed-up grows as the band narrows: in the experiment on the optimiser page (20 curves, \(m = 201\), displacements up to 0.1), band_frac=0.1 reproduced the unbanded Karcher mean exactly in a quarter of the time, while band_frac=0.05 clipped the warps and left 8 % of the variance.

docs.title: Worked example: Canadian temperature
docs.text:
Eight stations, 365 days. The warps of an unbanded Karcher mean move points by up to about 19 days, about 5 % of the year; a band of 20 % contains that, a band of 5 % does not.

import time
import numpy as np
from docs_data import load_canadian_weather
from fdars import alignment as A

day, X, meta = load_canadian_weather("temperature")
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
Xs = X[rng.choice(X.shape[0], 8, replace=False)]

ref = None
for bf in (None, 0.2, 0.05):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    r = A.karcher_mean_with_band(Xs, day, band_frac=bf)
    dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
    ref = r if ref is None else ref
    shift = np.abs(np.asarray(r["gammas"]) - day).max()
    diff = np.abs(np.asarray(r["mean"]) - np.asarray(ref["mean"])).max()
    print(f"band_frac={str(bf):5s} {dt:5.2f} s   max |gamma - t| = {shift:4.1f} days   "
          f"max |mean - unbanded mean| = {diff:.3f} C")

D = np.asarray(A.elastic_self_distance_matrix_with_band(Xs, day, band_frac=0.2))
print(f"banded distance matrix {D.shape}, max asymmetry {np.abs(D - D.T).max():.1e} (upper triangle mirrored)")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

band_frac=None   2.84 s   max |gamma - t| = 18.9 days   max |mean - unbanded mean| = 0.000 C
band_frac=0.2    1.28 s   max |gamma - t| = 18.9 days   max |mean - unbanded mean| = 0.000 C
band_frac=0.05   0.39 s   max |gamma - t| = 17.1 days   max |mean - unbanded mean| = 2.598 C
banded distance matrix (8, 8), max asymmetry 0.0e+00 (upper triangle mirrored)
FDARS_FENCE_OK

With band_frac=0.2 the mean is unchanged and the run is about twice as fast. At 0.05 the band (\(\lceil 0.05\cdot 365\rceil = 19\) days) is right at the size of the largest warp: the largest displacement is cut and the mean moves. Note that converged is False for these runs at the default max_iter=20; raise max_iter (the Karcher iteration reports, but does not raise, non-convergence).
