docs.title: Bayesian Alignment
docs.text:
Every other aligner in fdars returns one warp per curve. That point estimate hides two things you sometimes need to know: how certain the timing is (a warp estimated from a flat stretch of curve is not), and whether the data support several different alignments (a curve with two similar peaks can be matched either way). Bayesian alignment answers both by sampling the posterior distribution of the warps, and of the template, by Markov chain Monte Carlo.

fdars has two samplers: bayesian_align_pair for one pair of curves, and bayesian_align_group, a port of fdasrsf's time_warping_bayes / time_warping_bayes_infHMC for a whole sample with a jointly estimated template, several chains, convergence diagnostics and parallel tempering.

Fourier tangent warps, a B-spline template and Gibbs \(\sigma^2\); check \(\hat R\) across chains, temper if stuck.

docs.title: Group alignment: the model
docs.text:
bayesian_align_group(data, argvals, ...) models the SRSF of each curve, after warping, as a common template plus noise:

\[ q^*(t_j) = q_i\bigl(\gamma_i(t_j)\bigr)\sqrt{\gamma_i'(t_j)} + \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad \varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \text{ iid}, \]

where \(q_i\) is the SRSF of curve \(i\) and \(q^*\) the template SRSF. Three blocks of unknowns are sampled jointly:

  • Warps. Each warp is parametrised on the Hilbert sphere of \(\psi = \sqrt{\gamma'}\): \(\psi_i = \exp_1(v_i)\), \(\gamma_i(t) = \int_0^t \psi_i^2\), with the shooting vector \(v_i = \sum_k c_{ik}\phi_k\) in the Fourier tangent basis \(\sqrt2\sin(2\pi jt), \sqrt2\cos(2\pi jt)\), \(j = 1, \dots, M\) (n_warp_harmonics, default 10). The prior is \(c_{ik} \sim N\bigl(0, (\sigma_g / j)^2\bigr)\) with \(\sigma_g\) = warp_prior_sd (default 4), so higher harmonics are shrunk harder.
  • Template. A quadratic B-spline \(q^* = \sum_k a_k B_k\) with n_template_basis functions (default 30) and prior \(a_k \sim N\bigl(0, (\sigma_q/\lceil k/2\rceil)^2\bigr)\), \(\sigma_q\) set from the spread of the observed SRSFs.
  • Noise. \(\sigma^2 \sim \text{InvGamma}(\alpha_0, \beta_0)\) (alpha0, beta0, default 0.1 each), drawn exactly by a Gibbs step.

Warps and template are only identified up to a common warp; every center_every iterations (default 100) the warps are re-centred so that their Karcher mean is the identity, and by default (center_draws=True) every retained draw is re-centred exactly before it is summarised. The chains start from the DP alignment (init_dp=True; fdasrsf starts at the identity).

docs.title: Two samplers
docs.text:
• sampler="pcn" (default): a Z-mixture preconditioned Crank–Nicolson proposal \(c' = \sqrt{1-\beta^2}\,c + \beta\,\xi\), \(\xi\) drawn from the prior, with \(\beta\) drawn from a mixture (pcn_betas = 0.5, 0.5, 0.005, 0.0001 with probabilities pcn_probs = 0.1, 0.1, 0.7, 0.1): small steps explore locally, large ones jump. One Metropolis–Hastings step per curve per iteration. Cheap per iteration, but it mixes slowly when the posterior is concentrated.
  • sampler="infhmc": infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Beskos et al. 2011) for each curve's warp coefficients, with the exact gradient of the SRSF likelihood: the Gaussian prior part of the dynamics is integrated exactly by a rotation, the likelihood enters through half kicks, the number of leapfrog steps is drawn from \(1, \dots,\) hmc_max_leapfrog, and per-curve step sizes are adapted by dual averaging during burn-in (Hoffman & Gelman 2014). The template is drawn exactly from its Gaussian full conditional. infHMC always restricts warps to \(\lVert v\rVert < \pi\) (injective_warps). It targets the same posterior as pCN with a much higher effective sample size per iteration.

docs.title: Several chains and the diagnostics
docs.text:
With n_chains = K, chain \(k\) runs with seed seed + k (in parallel; results do not depend on the thread count). The result reports:

Diagnostic Meaning Look for rhat_sigma2, rhat_log_likelihood, rhat_warps (per curve) split-\(\hat R\) (BDA3 form); a single chain is split into halves \(\le 1.01\)–\(1.05\) ess_sigma2, ess_log_likelihood, ess_warps Geyer effective sample size, summed over chains hundreds or more mode_spread (per curve) largest \(L^2\) distance between the chains' mean warps below about 0.01 warp_bimodality, multimodal_curves Sarle's bimodality coefficient of each curve's pooled draws (≈ 1/3 for a Gaussian), flagged above 5/9 flags = chains in different modes, or a genuinely bimodal warp chains[k] per-chain log_likelihood_trace, sigma2_trace, posterior_mean_gammas, mode, acceptance, warp_step_sizes, swap_acceptance a chain whose log-likelihood sits tens of units below the others is in a poor mode

The summaries are pooled over chains: gammas (posterior mean in \(\psi\) space), gammas_median, pointwise gammas_lower / gammas_upper at credible_level, aligned_data, the template (template, template_srsf, with bands) and \(\sigma^2\) (sigma2_mean, _lower, _upper). With return_draws=True (default) the draws themselves are returned (gamma_draws of shape \((n, \text{draws}, m)\), template_srsf_draws, sigma2_draws).

docs.title: Example: reading the diagnostics
docs.text:
Eight noisy two-bump curves with smooth random warps. The posterior is run with infHMC, four chains and four warp harmonics, on the raw curves and on pre-smoothed curves:

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fast
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, m = 8, 51
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.01) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.68) ** 2 / 0.012)
X = np.array([mu(t + rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) * t * (1 - t)) + 0.02 * rng.standard_normal(m) for _ in range(n)])
Xs = np.asarray(A.srsf_presmooth(X, t, smoothing="box", passes=25))

def report(label, r):
    ll = [np.mean(c["log_likelihood_trace"]) for c in r["chains"]]           # retained draws
    print(f"{label:30s} Rhat sigma2 {r['rhat_sigma2']:.3f}  loglik {r['rhat_log_likelihood']:.3f}"
          f"  warps(max) {np.max(r['rhat_warps']):.3f}  mode_spread(max) {np.max(r['mode_spread']):.4f}")
    print(f"{'':30s} chain mean log-likelihoods {np.round(ll, 1)}")

common = dict(n_iter=fast(3000, 1500), burn_in=fast(1500, 750), n_chains=4, sampler="infhmc",
              n_warp_harmonics=4, return_draws=False)
report("raw curves", A.bayesian_align_group(X, t, **common))
report("pre-smoothed (box, 25 passes)", A.bayesian_align_group(Xs, t, **common))
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

raw curves                     Rhat sigma2 1.054  loglik 1.133  warps(max) 1.799  mode_spread(max) 0.0221
                               chain mean log-likelihoods [-216.9 -203.6 -212.9 -208.6]
pre-smoothed (box, 25 passes)  Rhat sigma2 1.008  loglik 1.006  warps(max) 1.041  mode_spread(max) 0.0020
                               chain mean log-likelihoods [182.6 184.3 186.4 180.4]
FDARS_FENCE_OK

On the raw curves the chains disagree: \(\hat R\) is clearly above 1, mode_spread above 0.01, and the chains' average log-likelihoods differ by more than ten units, so they explore different joint modes (some curves aligned to slightly different features, with the template adapted to them). On pre-smoothed curves all diagnostics are fine. The reason is the likelihood: it is defined on the SRSF, which differentiates the data, so white noise in the curves becomes rough, heavy-tailed noise in \(q\) that creates many small local modes. The crate's documentation recommends modest grids and pre-smoothed curves for exactly this reason.

docs.title: pCN or infHMC?
docs.text:
On the pre-smoothed sample, both samplers at the same number of iterations:

import time
import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fast
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, m = 8, 51
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.01) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.68) ** 2 / 0.012)
X, H = [], []
for _ in range(n):
    w = t + rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) * t * (1 - t)
    X.append(mu(w) + 0.02 * rng.standard_normal(m))
    H.append(np.interp(t, w, t))                                  # true registering warp
X, H = np.array(X), np.array(H)
Xs = np.asarray(A.srsf_presmooth(X, t, smoothing="box", passes=25))
inner = (t > 0.1) & (t < 0.9)

n_iter, burn = fast(3000, 1500), fast(1500, 750)
draws = 4 * (n_iter - burn)
for sampler in ("pcn", "infhmc"):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    r = A.bayesian_align_group(Xs, t, n_iter=n_iter, burn_in=burn, n_chains=4, sampler=sampler,
                               n_warp_harmonics=4, return_draws=False)
    G = np.asarray(r["gammas"])
    err = 1000 * np.abs(((G - G.mean(0)) - (H - H.mean(0)))[:, inner]).mean()
    band = (np.asarray(r["gammas_upper"]) - np.asarray(r["gammas_lower"]))[:, inner].mean()
    print(f"{sampler:6s} Rhat loglik {r['rhat_log_likelihood']:.3f}  max Rhat warps {np.max(r['rhat_warps']):.3f}"
          f"  min ESS/draw (warps) {np.min(r['ess_warps']) / draws:.3f}"
          f"  95% band width {band:.4f}  warp error {err:.1f}e-3  ({time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s)")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

pcn    Rhat loglik 1.639  max Rhat warps 1.303  min ESS/draw (warps) 0.004  95% band width 0.0132  warp error 3.4e-3  (0.4 s)
infhmc Rhat loglik 1.006  max Rhat warps 1.041  min ESS/draw (warps) 0.037  95% band width 0.0136  warp error 4.1e-3  (1.1 s)
FDARS_FENCE_OK

pCN is two to three times faster per iteration, but its slowest-mixing warp has roughly a tenth of infHMC's effective sample size per draw, and its \(\hat R\) for the log-likelihood shows it has not converged. infHMC is the better default whenever you report the posterior; use pCN only with long chains and checked diagnostics. Both posterior-mean warps are close to the truth here (the DP point estimate of the same curves has a warp error of about \(5\times10^{-3}\)).

docs.title: Multimodality and parallel tempering
docs.text:
infHMC (and, more slowly, pCN) moves locally: a chain can settle in a poor, well-separated joint mode and never leave it. The diagnostics above detect this; the principled remedy is parallel tempering (Geyer 1991). With n_temperatures = K > 1, each chain runs \(K\) replicas at inverse temperatures \(1 = \beta_0 > \dots > \beta_{K-1} =\) pt_min_inv_temp, spaced geometrically (\(\beta_k = \beta_{\min}^{k/(K-1)}\)). Replica \(k\) targets the likelihood raised to \(\beta_k\) times the prior, so the hot replicas see a flatter posterior and cross barriers; after every sweep, adjacent replicas swap states with an exact Metropolis–Hastings acceptance. Only the \(\beta = 1\) replica is reported, so the posterior is unchanged. The cost is linear in \(K\).

chains[k]["swap_acceptance"] sizes the ladder: a rate near 0 for a pair of temperatures means the replicas cannot exchange there. The number of temperatures needed grows roughly with \(\sqrt{n\,T}\) (the log-likelihood fluctuations grow with the number of observations), so larger problems need longer or narrower ladders.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fast
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, m = 8, 51
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.01) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.68) ** 2 / 0.012)
X = np.array([mu(t + rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) * t * (1 - t)) + 0.02 * rng.standard_normal(m) for _ in range(n)])

common = dict(n_iter=fast(3000, 1000), burn_in=fast(1500, 500), n_chains=4, sampler="infhmc", return_draws=False)
for label, kw in [("no tempering", {}),
                  ("6 temperatures, beta_min 0.1", dict(n_temperatures=6)),
                  ("12 temperatures, beta_min 0.3", dict(n_temperatures=12, pt_min_inv_temp=0.3))]:
    r = A.bayesian_align_group(X, t, **common, **kw)
    ll = [np.mean(c["log_likelihood_trace"]) for c in r["chains"]]           # retained draws
    swaps = r["chains"][0]["swap_acceptance"]
    print(f"{label:30s} Rhat loglik {r['rhat_log_likelihood']:.3f}  chain log-lik spread {np.ptp(ll):5.1f}"
          + (f"  swap rates chain 0: {np.round(swaps, 2)}" if len(swaps) else ""))
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

no tempering                   Rhat loglik 1.179  chain log-lik spread  14.3
6 temperatures, beta_min 0.1   Rhat loglik 1.575  chain log-lik spread  35.6  swap rates chain 0: [0.   0.   0.   0.01 0.23]
12 temperatures, beta_min 0.3  Rhat loglik 1.094  chain log-lik spread   4.0  swap rates chain 0: [0.29 0.35 0.3  0.33 0.27 0.35 0.37 0.42 0.27 0.37 0.3 ]
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The default ladder (6 temperatures down to \(\beta = 0.1\)) is too coarse for this problem: the swap rates between the coldest replicas are essentially 0, so the \(\beta = 1\) chain never receives a state from the hot replicas and tempering cannot help. A narrower, longer ladder (12 temperatures down to 0.3) swaps at rates of about 0.3 throughout and brings the chains much closer together (\(\hat R\) 1.09, log-likelihood spread 4 instead of 14), at twelve times the cost. (Here, pre-smoothing fixes the problem more cheaply; tempering is for posteriors that are genuinely multimodal.)

When may a chain be discarded?

Only when its log-likelihood is lower by tens of units than that of the other chains and the other chains agree with each other: its mode then carries negligible posterior mass (weight about \(e^{-\text{gap}}\)). If chains split between modes of similar log-likelihood, the posterior itself is multimodal and every mode must be kept.

docs.title: Calibration: what the bands mean
docs.text:
The crate's own simulation study (data simulated from the model, 5 curves × 31 points) found nominal-95 % pointwise bands to cover the centred warps 0.93–0.96 of the time and the template 0.91–0.95, for infHMC and for long pCN runs. Three caveats remain:

  • \(\sigma^2\) is underestimated when the noise is large (posterior/true ratio 0.90 at SRSF noise 0.1, 0.74 at 0.3), because the likelihood evaluates a linear interpolant of the noisy SRSF at the warped points; warps can lower the residual by "smoothing" the noise. Bands come out slightly narrow.
  • Noise in the curves, not in the SRSF (the usual case): the SRSF noise is then heteroscedastic, correlated and heavy-tailed where \(f' \approx 0\), and warp bands covered only 0.83–0.87. Treat them as approximate; prefer modest grids and pre-smoothed curves.
  • The \(\sigma^2\) prior matters when the noise is small: fdasrsf's \(\beta_0 = 0.1\) adds about \(2\beta_0/(nT)\) to the posterior \(\sigma^2\), which widens the bands (over-coverage). Lower alpha0 and beta0 (for example \(10^{-6}\)) when the SRSF noise is known to be small.

Raw-state bands (center_draws=False, fdasrsf's convention) include the non-identified common warp and over-cover (about 0.98).

docs.title: Recommended settings
docs.text:
• sampler="infhmc", n_chains >= 4; read \(\hat R\), ESS, mode_spread and multimodal_curves together before using the bands.
  • Pre-smooth noisy curves (srsf_presmooth), and keep \(m\) moderate (50–100 points; n_points resamples internally).
  • Fewer warp harmonics (n_warp_harmonics 3–5) when the phase is smooth: fewer parameters, faster mixing.
  • Add tempering (n_temperatures > 1) when chains disagree on smoothed data; check swap_acceptance (aim for roughly 0.2–0.4 between neighbours) and add temperatures or raise pt_min_inv_temp if a pair is near 0.
  • Increase n_iter / burn_in until the diagnostics settle; thin only saves memory.

docs.title: Pairwise posterior: bayesian_align_pair
docs.text:
For a single pair, bayesian_align_pair(f1, f2, argvals, n_samples=1000, burn_in=200, step_size=0.1, proposal_variance=1.0, seed=42) samples the posterior of the warp \(\gamma\) that aligns f2 to f1, with likelihood \(-\tfrac12\sum_j w_j\bigl(q_{1}(t_j) - (q_2\circ\gamma)(t_j)\sqrt{\gamma'(t_j)}\bigr)^2\) (Simpson weights) and a pCN proposal \(v' = \sqrt{1-\beta^2}\,v + \beta\,\xi\) on the tangent space of the \(\psi\) sphere (\(\beta\) = step_size), started from the DP alignment.

Limits of the pairwise sampler

The noise variance is fixed at 1, so the band width depends on the scale of the data (rescale the curves and the band changes). It runs a single chain with no convergence diagnostics, and the credible band is the fixed 2.5 %–97.5 % range of the draws. For calibrated uncertainty use bayesian_align_group, which samples the noise variance, runs several chains and reports \(\hat R\) and ESS.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import bayesian_align_pair

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 120)
base = np.exp(-((t - 0.5) ** 2) / (2 * 0.10 ** 2))
f1 = base
f2 = np.interp(t, np.clip(t + 0.08, 0, 1), base)   # phase-shifted target

ba = bayesian_align_pair(f1, f2, t, n_samples=500, burn_in=100, seed=0, step_size=0.85)
f2_aligned = np.asarray(ba["f_aligned_mean"])
gam_lo = np.asarray(ba["credible_lower"])
gam_hi = np.asarray(ba["credible_upper"])
gam_mean = np.asarray(ba["posterior_mean_gamma"])

f, (a1, a2) = fig(ncols=2, figsize=(9.5, 4.0))
a1.plot(t, f1, color="#6c757d", lw=2, label="f1 (reference)")
a1.plot(t, f2, color="#dc3545", lw=1.6, ls="--", label="f2 (original)")
a1.plot(t, f2_aligned, color="#3f51b5", lw=2, label="f2 (aligned)")
a1.set(title=f"Bayesian alignment (accept. {float(ba['acceptance_rate']):.2f})",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="f(t)")
a1.legend(fontsize=8)

a2.fill_between(t, gam_lo, gam_hi, color="#6f42c1", alpha=0.2, label="95% credible")
a2.plot(t, gam_mean, color="#6f42c1", lw=2, label="posterior mean $\\gamma$")
a2.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="#6c757d", ls="--", lw=1.2)
a2.set(title="Posterior over the warp", xlabel="t",
       ylabel="$\\gamma(t)$", aspect="equal")
a2.legend(fontsize=8)
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The left panel shows the aligned f2 tracking the reference; the right panel replaces the point-estimate warp with a posterior: the band is the 95 % credible region around the posterior-mean \(\gamma\). Where the band hugs the mean, the timing is well determined; where it widens (in the flat tails, where the curves carry no timing information) the data are ambiguous about how much to warp.

Key Description posterior_gammas MCMC draws of the warp, shape (n_samples, m) posterior_mean_gamma posterior mean warp credible_lower / credible_upper pointwise 2.5 % / 97.5 % band on the warp acceptance_rate MCMC acceptance rate; lower step_size if it is too low, raise it if too high f_aligned_mean f2 aligned under the posterior-mean warp

docs.title: Parameters of bayesian_align_group
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect n_iter, burn_in, thin 2000, 1000, 1 chain length, discarded burn-in, thinning n_chains, seed 1, 42 chains (seed + k) sampler "pcn" or "infhmc" alpha0, beta0 0.1, 0.1 inverse-gamma prior on \(\sigma^2\) warp_prior_sd, n_warp_harmonics 4.0, 10 warp prior scale and Fourier size n_template_basis 30 template B-splines n_points 0 internal grid (0 = the input grid; fdasrsf uses 200) center_every, center_draws 100, True re-centring of states and of retained draws credible_level 0.95 pointwise band level init_dp True start from the DP alignment pcn_betas, pcn_probs (0.5, 0.5, 0.005, 0.0001), (0.1, 0.1, 0.7, 0.1) Z-mixture pCN hmc_step_size, hmc_max_leapfrog, hmc_adapt, hmc_target_accept 0.1, 10, True, 0.65 infHMC controls injective_warps False restrict to \(\lVert v\rVert < \pi\) (always on for infHMC) n_temperatures, pt_min_inv_temp 1, 0.1 parallel tempering return_draws True False drops the large draw arrays

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Use it when you must report uncertainty in the warps or the template, or when you suspect several plausible alignments (similar repeated features).
  • Use a point estimate (elastic Karcher mean) when you only need registered curves: it is faster and, for well-determined warps, nearly identical to the posterior mean.
  • Cost. Each iteration updates every warp (pCN: one likelihood evaluation each; infHMC: up to hmc_max_leapfrog gradient evaluations), times the number of replicas and chains. The examples above take about a second per run; samples of hundreds of curves on fine grids take much longer.

docs.title: Choosing an Alignment Method
docs.text: fdars.alignment offers more than a dozen ways to register curves, from one shift per curve to a full posterior over warping functions. They are not interchangeable: each assumes a particular kind of phase variability, and each pays for flexibility with variance, cost or interpretability. This page is the map. It asks a few questions about your data, points to the method whose assumptions match, explains why, and lists the traps.

docs.title: Two questions first
docs.text:
Every registration method splits the variability of a sample into two parts:

  • Amplitude: how tall or deep the features are.
  • Phase: when the features happen, encoded by a warping function \(h_i\) per curve.

Write the registered curve as \(\tilde x_i(t) = x_i(h_i(t))\). Methods differ in which set the warps \(h_i\) may come from and what criterion picks them. So before choosing, answer:

  1. What does one observation look like? A real-valued function on a shared interval, a curve in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) whose rotation and size are irrelevant, or a discrete time series that you only want to compare, not model?
  2. What does the phase variability look like? A constant delay, a delay plus a change of tempo, a few identifiable events, or a smooth but otherwise arbitrary time distortion?

The answer to the second question is a warp class. The smaller the class that still contains the true warps, the better: a flexible method fitted to data whose phase is really a shift will "explain" some amplitude noise as phase (over-registration).

The classes are nested only loosely: shift ⊂ affine ⊂ \(\Gamma\) (all increasing diffeomorphisms of the interval), and landmark (monotone cubic) and continuous (Ramsay–Li \(\int \exp W\)) warps are smooth subsets of \(\Gamma\). The elastic dynamic program searches a discretised \(\Gamma\) whose local slopes are limited to \([1/7, 7]\) by default.

docs.title: The decision tree in words
docs.text:
Q0. What is one observation?

  • A curve in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (an outline, a trajectory, handwriting), where rotation, scale or starting point are nuisance: use the shape-space functions curve_shape_* (with closed=True for contours, and warp_optim={"method": "rbfgs"} with align_iter >= 4 for an accurate reparametrisation). When bending and stretching should cost differently, pass metric="elastic" with weights a, b (planar curves). For small polygons where an exact distance matters, ab_elastic_distance_pl. For a few irregularly placed points per curve, sparse_elastic_align_pair / sparse_elastic_mean. See Shapes of Curves in R^d and Sparse & Irregular Curves.
  • A discrete time series (possibly of different lengths) where the goal is nearest-neighbour search, classification or clustering, not a warp model: the DTW family (dtw_*, soft_dtw_*, the elastic time-series distances in fdars.metric). DTW returns a cost, not a metric, and it warps amplitude differences away; see Dynamic Time Warping.
  • A real-valued function on a common interval: go to Q1.

Q1. What kind of values?

  • Binary, counts or positive-skewed (on/off activity, spike counts): register_fpca(family="binomial" | "poisson" | "gamma") registers on the likelihood scale and estimates a generalised FPCA jointly (Non-Gaussian Registration).
  • Irregular grids or curves cut off at the start or end: register_fpca(incompleteness=...); to predict the unobserved rest with finite-sample guarantees, the partial-curve conformal tools in fdars.conformal.
  • Dense, roughly Gaussian, shared grid: go to Q2.

Q2. What does the phase look like?

Phase variability Method Page Pure time offset, one reliable marker landmark_shift_registration Shift Pure time offset, no single marker iterative_shift_registration (extrapolation="periodic" for cyclic data); least_squares_shift_registration only as a baseline or seed Shift Offset plus a uniform change of speed (tempo) affine_registration(warp_class="dilation" \| "affine") Affine Named features with known correspondence, and the features are the phase landmark_register Landmark Features must be pinned, but the timing between them is free elastic_align_pair_constrained_with_config(method="rbfgs") Landmark Smooth non-linear phase, classical FDA workflow, amplitude scale varies between curves continuous_registration (periodic=True for cyclic data, r_defaults=True for R parity) Continuous General non-linear phase; you need a metric, an amplitude/phase split, elastic FPCA or regression karcher_mean_with_config (DP by default; method="rbfgs" with a penalty for smooth warps) Elastic, Optimisers Noisy curves or no trustworthy template; simple, low-dimensional phase pairwise_synchronization (Tang–Müller) Pairwise Synchronisation You must report uncertainty in the warps or the template bayesian_align_group (sampler="infhmc", several chains) Bayesian Alignment

Q3. Modifiers, whatever Q2 chose:

  • Noisy curves. Pre-smooth before any SRSF or derivative-based method (srsf_presmooth), and use \(\lambda > 0\).
  • Large \(n \cdot m\). A band (band_frac), the coarse-to-fine Karcher mean (automatic for \(m > 50\)), a coarse DP for long pairs (elastic_align_pair_multires with n_refine_steps=0), or a cheaper warp class.
  • Outliers. karcher_median, robust_karcher_mean; flag them with elastic_outlier_detection.
  • Periodic or closed data. karcher_mean_closed / elastic_align_pair_closed (elastic), periodic=True (continuous), extrapolation="periodic" (shift).
  • Groups to compare. Align all curves together without labels, then test whether the groups differ in amplitude or phase with elastic_phase_amplitude_test, or where and in which direction with elastic_local_difference_test (Inference after Alignment).

docs.title: Recommendations, with reasons
docs.text:
1. Default for dense 1-D functional data: the elastic Karcher mean with DP and \(\lambda = 0\), then check the diagnostics. It is the only family with a proper amplitude metric (Fisher–Rao, invariant to simultaneous reparametrisation), it separates amplitude from phase, and its output feeds vert_fpca, horiz_fpca, joint_fpca, elastic regression and the PERMANOVA test.
  2. Switch to method="rbfgs" with penalty="l2gam" and \(\lambda > 0\) (or penalty="roughness") when the warps look jagged or pinch, or when landmarks must be hit exactly. DP slopes are quantised and leave a residual floor (about 0.02 in SRSF distance for exactly warped copies); RBFGS is local, but it is seeded by DP and, when penalised, also restarted from the identity. See Elastic Optimisers.
  3. If the phase is a shift, use a shift model. An elastic warp has hundreds of degrees of freedom and will absorb amplitude noise as phase; the bake-off below shows the elastic warp error is about three times the shift model's on pure-shift data. Iterative shift is interpretable and costs \(O(n\,m)\) per iteration. Centre the shifts yourself afterwards: the iterative method does not.
  4. Continuous registration is the right tool when amplitude scale legitimately varies. Its default min-eigenvalue criterion is zero whenever the registered curve is proportional to the target, so it does not warp to fix amplitude, where least-squares and elastic criteria would. Use r_defaults=True for results comparable to R register.fd; use the default six-basis \(W\) only with \(\lambda > 0\) (unpenalised, it overfits).
  5. Landmarks first when they exist and are unambiguous. The warp is interpretable ("age at peak growth velocity"). Detection matches by order, so one spurious peak shifts every pairing after it: always check the detection counts per curve.
  6. Never compute SRSFs of noisy raw data. The SRSF differentiates the curve. Pre-smooth with srsf_presmooth(..., smoothing="box", passes=25) or smoothing="spline"; the aligners do not smooth for you.
  7. For \(\mathbb{R}^d\) outlines use curve_shape_*, not the *_nd_with_config functions. The _nd aligners share one warp across coordinates but have no rotation or scale quotient, and they normalise each coordinate on its own.
  8. For binary or count curves, register_fpca beats aligning logit(p̂) or \(\sqrt{\text{counts}}\): it registers on the likelihood scale. Prefer fpca_type="two_step" for Gamma and Poisson data, because the variational EM treats them as Gaussian.
  9. For warp uncertainty, use bayesian_align_group(sampler="infhmc", n_chains>=4) and read \(\hat R\) and the ESS; add tempering (n_temperatures>1) if the multimodality flags fire. Do not trust single pCN chains without diagnostics.
  10. When comparing groups, align all curves together without the labels, then run elastic_phase_amplitude_test(amplitude_metric="pairwise") for a global answer, or elastic_local_difference_test to find the time intervals where amplitude or timing differ. Per-group templates break the validity of the permutation test, and noisy curves should be pre-smoothed lightly, or SRSF noise leaks phase differences into the amplitude test (Inference after Alignment).

docs.title: Same data, five methods
docs.text:
The claims above can be checked. The block below simulates three samples of 20 noisy two-bump curves whose true phase is, respectively, a pure shift, an affine warp, and a smooth non-linear warp \(w(t) = t + c\,t(1-t)\). Each curve also carries ±10 % amplitude scaling and white noise. Five methods register each sample, and the table reports the mean absolute error between the estimated and the true registering warp (on the interior \([0.15, 0.85]\), after removing the common template warp that no method can identify). A * marks the best method per column.

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, m = 20, 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.008) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.68) ** 2 / 0.01)

def simulate(kind):
    """x_i(t) = a_i * mu(w_i(t)) + noise; returns the data and the registering warps w_i^-1."""
    X, H = [], []
    for _ in range(n):
        if kind == "shift":
            w = t - rng.uniform(-0.06, 0.06)
        elif kind == "affine":
            w = rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1) * t + rng.uniform(-0.05, 0.05)
        else:  # smooth non-linear
            w = t + rng.uniform(-0.6, 0.6) * t * (1 - t)
        X.append(rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1) * mu(w) + 0.02 * rng.standard_normal(m))
        H.append(np.interp(t, w, t))
    return np.array(X), np.array(H)

def warp_error(Hhat, H):
    """Mean |h_hat - h| on [0.15, 0.85] after removing the common (template) warp."""
    inner = (t > 0.15) & (t < 0.85)
    d = (Hhat - Hhat.mean(0)) - (H - H.mean(0))
    return np.abs(d[:, inner]).mean()

def methods(X):
    # registered curve x(h(t)); each method's warp converted to h
    seed = A.least_squares_shift_registration(X, t, 0.15)["shifts"]
    r = A.iterative_shift_registration(X, t, initial=seed, max_iter=20, tol=1e-6)
    yield "iterative shift", t - r["shifts"][:, None]
    r = A.affine_registration(X, t)
    yield "affine", (t - r["shifts"][:, None]) / r["dilations"][:, None]
    r = A.landmark_detect_and_register(X, t, kind="peak", min_prominence=0.2, expected_count=2)
    yield "landmark", r["gammas"]
    r = A.continuous_registration(X, t, lambda_=1e-3, max_template_iter=5)
    yield "continuous", r["warps"]
    yield "elastic (DP)", A.karcher_mean(X, t)["gammas"]

rows = {}
for kind in ["shift", "affine", "smooth"]:
    X, H = simulate(kind)
    for name, Hhat in methods(X):
        rows.setdefault(name, {})[kind] = warp_error(np.asarray(Hhat), H)

print("mean |warp error| x 1000   true warp:   shift   affine   smooth")
for name, r in rows.items():
    best = lambda k: "*" if r[k] == min(v[k] for v in rows.values()) else " "
    print(f"  {name:16s}          " + "".join(f"{1000 * r[k]:8.2f}{best(k)}" for k in ["shift", "affine", "smooth"]))
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

mean |warp error| x 1000   true warp:   shift   affine   smooth
  iterative shift               1.43     9.21    40.62 
  affine                        1.28*    1.30*    7.03 
  landmark                      6.69     8.76     7.80 
  continuous                    3.12     6.26     4.79*
  elastic (DP)                  4.26     4.26     4.95 
FDARS_FENCE_OK

How to read it:

  • Shift data. The rigid models (iterative shift, affine) recover the warps to about \(1.3\)–\(1.4 \times 10^{-3}\). The elastic DP is roughly three times worse: with hundreds of free warp values it fits part of the noise and the amplitude scaling as phase. Affine edges out pure shift here only because it re-centres its warps every iteration.
  • Affine data. The shift model can no longer follow the tempo change (error ×7); affine, the matching model, stays at \(1.3 \times 10^{-3}\).
  • Smooth non-linear data. Shift and affine are now misspecified. The penalised continuous registration and the elastic Karcher mean, whose warp classes contain \(t + c\,t(1-t)\), do best. Landmark registration is competitive throughout because the two peaks are the phase here, but it uses only two points per curve, so it cannot beat a model that uses the whole curve.

The lesson is the rule of thumb behind the decision tree: pick the smallest warp class that contains the phase you believe in. The extra flexibility of elastic alignment is a cost when it is not needed, and a necessity when it is.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Common ways to get alignment wrong

Template and warp behaviour

  • Pinching and over-registration. At \(\lambda = 0\) the elastic DP can compress a whole region down to slope \(1/7\), and SRSF alignment can explain amplitude differences as phase. Remedies: \(\lambda > 0\), a band, method="rbfgs" with penalty="roughness", or a smaller warp class.
  • \(\lambda\) is not portable. The same number means a different strength on different grids and under DP vs RBFGS. Use lambda_scale to convert between optimisers; lambda_cv tends to pick the smallest candidate.
  • Templates drift. Iterative shift and continuous registration do not centre their warps, so the registered sample can sit early or late as a whole. Affine registration and the elastic Karcher mean centre them.
  • Boundaries. Shift and affine registration fill the uncovered edge by clamping (extrapolation="boundary"), so flat edges enter the criterion. Use restrict_domain=True, domain="overlap" or extrapolation="periodic" where appropriate.
  • converged is about the optimiser, not the warps. In continuous_registration it means the tolerance was met (termination says why a curve stopped otherwise: "stalled", "coef_limit" or "max_iter"); in the Karcher mean, converged=False is reported, not raised. Inspect the criterion and the warps as well.

Distances and metrics

  • Elastic distance is only approximately symmetric. elastic_distance(f1, f2) warps f2 onto f1, and the DP is a one-sided discretisation. On coarse grids the asymmetry can be large (a one-bump vs a two-bump curve: 0.56 vs 0.94 at \(m = 30\), 0.92 vs 0.94 at \(m = 301\)). Use fine grids, or symmetrise with \(\tfrac12(d_{12} + d_{21})\). The distance-matrix functions compute the upper triangle and mirror it.
  • DTW costs are not metrics, and fdars DTW costs are not rooted: tslearn's value is the square root of fdars' for \(p = 2\).
  • SRSFs ignore vertical offsets. Curves that differ only by \(+c\) have elastic distance 0.

Method-specific traps

  • Landmark detection matches by order and landmark_detect_and_register raises if any curve has fewer than expected_count features; landmark_register does not raise on inconsistent input (for example, fewer landmark lists than curves) but returns identity warps and the curves unchanged.
  • The closed-curve start-point search is heuristic (coarse, then fine).
  • elastic_partial_match distances are not comparable across window lengths.
  • elastic_depth is not a lens depth: it is \(1/(1 + \text{mean distance})\), separately for amplitude and phase, which live on different scales.

docs.title: Warp conventions at a glance
docs.text:
All pages show warps as registering warps, \(\tilde x_i(t) = x_i(h_i(t))\). The functions return them in their own conventions:

Family What is returned Registered curve least_squares_shift_registration, iterative_shift_registration, landmark_shift_registration shifts \(\delta_i\) \(x_i(t - \delta_i)\); \(\delta > 0\) moves the curve right (opposite sign to scikit-fda's deltas_) affine_registration dilations \(a_i\), shifts \(b_i\) \(x_i((t - b_i)/a_i)\); dilation is about \(t = 0\) landmark_register gammas, mapping target time to source time \(x_i(\gamma_i(t))\) continuous_registration warps \(h_i\) \(x_i(h_i(t))\) elastic (karcher_mean*, elastic_align_pair*) gammas \(x_i(\gamma_i(t))\); elastic_align_pair(f1, f2) warps f2 onto f1 register_fpca t_hat, the inverse warp \(h_i^{-1}\) at each observation plot \(Y_{ij}\) against \(\hat t_{ij}\); see Non-Gaussian Registration pairwise_synchronization warps and inverse_warps built from the inverse of the averaged pairwise warps

docs.title: Continuous Registration
docs.text:
Continuous registration (Ramsay & Li, 1998; R fda::register.fd) is the classical FDA answer to smooth, non-linear phase variability. Each curve gets a smooth, strictly increasing warp built from an exponentiated B-spline expansion, fitted to a target curve by a penalised Gauss–Newton method. Its default criterion has a property no other aligner in fdars has: it is blind to the amplitude scale of the curve, so it does not distort the time axis to compensate for a curve that is simply taller or shorter than the target.

Use it when the phase is smooth but not rigid, when you want warps that are guaranteed smooth and invertible, when amplitude legitimately varies between curves, or when you need results comparable to R's register.fd.

Top row: a B-spline expansion \(W\) (with its first coefficient fixed at 0) is exponentiated, giving a positive function, whose normalised integral is a smooth monotone warp \(h\). Bottom row: for a curve \(\hat y = 2 y_0\) with the same timing as the target, the points \((y_0(t), \hat y(t))\) lie on a line, so the minimum-eigenvalue criterion is 0 ("already aligned") while the least-squares criterion is positive and would push the optimiser to warp.

docs.title: The warp model
docs.text:
For a curve \(y_i\) on \([a, b]\), the warp is

\[ h_i(t) = a + (b - a)\,\frac{F_i(t)}{F_i(b)}, \qquad F_i(t) = \int_a^t \exp W_i(s)\,ds, \qquad W_i(s) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} c_{ik}\,\phi_k(s), \]

with \(\phi_k\) a clamped B-spline basis (nbasis \(= K\) functions of order norder). Because \(\exp W_i > 0\), \(F_i\) is strictly increasing, so every coefficient vector gives a valid warp: smooth, strictly monotone, with \(h_i(a) = a\) and \(h_i(b) = b\). No constraint has to be enforced during the optimisation. The first coefficient is fixed at \(c_{i1} = 0\), because adding a constant to \(W\) multiplies \(F\) by a constant that the normalisation cancels.

The registered curve is \(\tilde y_i(t) = y_i(h_i(t))\), returned as registered_data, with the warps in warps, the coefficients in w_coefficients and the knot vector in w_knots.

docs.title: The criteria
docs.text:
criterion chooses how a registered curve is compared with the target \(y_0\) (by default the cross-sectional mean; or pass target):

"least_squares" (R crit=1):

\[ \int \bigl(y_0(t) - \tilde y_i(t)\bigr)^2 dt . \]

"min_eigenvalue" (R crit=2, the default): form the \(2\times 2\) cross-product matrix

\[ T_i = \begin{pmatrix} \int y_0^2 & \int y_0\,\tilde y_i \\ \int \tilde y_i\, y_0 & \int \tilde y_i^2 \end{pmatrix} \]

and minimise twice its smallest eigenvalue. \(T_i\) is the second-moment matrix of the points \((y_0(t), \tilde y_i(t))\); its smallest eigenvalue is zero exactly when those points lie on a line through the origin, that is when \(\tilde y_i = c\,y_0\) for some constant \(c\). The criterion therefore measures how far the registered curve is from being proportional to the target, and ignores the factor \(c\).

Both criteria add a roughness penalty \(\lambda \int (D^{L} W_i)^2\), with lambda_ the weight and lfd_order \(= L\) the derivative order (\(L <\) norder).

What the scale invariance buys

If curve \(i\) is a time-warped copy of the target and twice as tall, least squares sees a large residual even after perfect alignment, and its optimiser warps the time axis to shrink the residual (for example, compressing the peaks). The min-eigenvalue criterion is already 0 at the correct warp and has no incentive to distort it. It is not invariant to vertical offsets: \(\tilde y_i = y_0 + c\) does not give a zero eigenvalue.

docs.title: The optimiser
docs.text:
Each curve is registered independently by penalised Gauss–Newton with Levenberg–Marquardt damping, on a fine grid of n_fine points (default \(\max(201, m)\)):

  • each accepted step strictly decreases the penalised criterion;
  • coefficients with \(|c_k| > 50\) are rejected (R's climit), which keeps \(\exp W\) finite;
  • the iteration stops when the relative decrease falls below tol (default \(10^{-8}\)), when no damping gives a decrease (a stall), or after max_iter iterations (default 50).

The result records why each curve stopped in termination[i]:

termination Meaning "converged" the relative decrease fell below tol "stalled" no damped step decreased the criterion before tol was met "coef_limit" a stall in which a candidate step was rejected by the coefficient limit "max_iter" the iteration budget ran out

converged[i] is True exactly when termination[i] == "converged". A stall is often a local optimum, but the tolerance was not met. Convergence is a statement about the optimiser, not about the warps: also inspect criterion and the warps themselves.

Template passes. By default the target is the cross-sectional mean of the unregistered curves, which is blurred. max_template_iter > 1 re-estimates the target as the mean of the registered curves and registers again (a Procrustes-style loop that R does not offer), stopping when the target changes by less than template_tol. The warps are not centred, so the registered sample can drift as a whole.

Periodic data. With periodic=True each curve is treated as one period on \([a, b]\), and the warp gains a free time shift (the first coefficient becomes a shift on the periodic extension, returned in shift). The curves should satisfy \(y(a) \approx y(b)\). The full timing displacement of curve \(i\) at time \(t\) is \(h_i(t) - t\); shift is only its constant part when the warp also has a slope.

docs.title: fdars defaults vs R defaults
docs.text:
fdars default r_defaults=True (R register.fd) nbasis, norder 6, 4 (cubic B-spline \(W\)) 2, 2 (linear \(W\)) lfd_order 2 0 max_iter 50 20

The fdars default is much more flexible than R's: six cubic B-splines let \(W\) bend, while R's linear \(W\) only allows a monotone change of speed. Explicitly passed values override r_defaults. Use the flexible default only with \(\lambda > 0\), as the next example shows.

docs.title: Scale invariance in action
docs.text:
Twenty curves are smooth warps of a two-bump template, \(y_i(t) = s_i\,\mu(w_i(t))\), whose amplitude \(s_i\) varies more than six-fold. Registered to the true template with each criterion, the min-eigenvalue warps match the truth almost exactly, while least squares distorts them:

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n, m = 20, 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.008) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.68) ** 2 / 0.01)
X, H = [], []
for _ in range(n):
    w = t + rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) * t * (1 - t)                 # smooth data warp
    X.append(rng.uniform(0.3, 2.0) * mu(w) + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(m))
    H.append(np.interp(t, w, t))                                 # true registering warp
X, H = np.array(X), np.array(H)
inner = (t > 0.15) & (t < 0.85)
err = lambda W: 1000 * np.abs((np.asarray(W) - H)[:, inner]).mean()

for crit in ("min_eigenvalue", "least_squares"):
    r = A.continuous_registration(X, t, target=mu(t), criterion=crit)
    print(f"criterion={crit!r:17s} mean |h_hat - h| = {err(r['warps']):6.2f} x 1e-3")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

criterion='min_eigenvalue'  mean |h_hat - h| =   0.66 x 1e-3
criterion='least_squares'   mean |h_hat - h| =  27.17 x 1e-3
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The least-squares warps are about forty times further from the truth: to make a tall curve look like the target, they shrink its peaks by squeezing time. This is the reason the min-eigenvalue criterion is the default.

docs.title: Regularisation and template passes
docs.text:
The same sample, now registered without knowing the template. Without a penalty the six-function \(W\) overfits: noise and the blurred initial target pull the warps around. A small \(\lambda\) and a few template passes fix both:

import numpy as np
from collections import Counter
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n, m = 20, 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.008) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.68) ** 2 / 0.01)
X, H = [], []
for _ in range(n):
    w = t + rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) * t * (1 - t)
    X.append(rng.uniform(0.3, 2.0) * mu(w) + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(m))
    H.append(np.interp(t, w, t))
X, H = np.array(X), np.array(H)
inner = (t > 0.15) & (t < 0.85)
# the template is estimated, so compare warps after removing their common part
err = lambda W: 1000 * np.abs(((np.asarray(W) - np.mean(W, 0)) - (H - H.mean(0)))[:, inner]).mean()

for kw in (dict(), dict(lambda_=1e-3), dict(lambda_=1e-3, max_template_iter=5), dict(r_defaults=True, max_template_iter=5)):
    r = A.continuous_registration(X, t, **kw)
    stops = ", ".join(f"{k} {v}" for k, v in sorted(Counter(r["termination"]).items()))
    print(f"{str(kw):45s} warp error {err(r['warps']):6.2f} x 1e-3   {stops}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

{}                                            warp error  16.58 x 1e-3   converged 16, max_iter 4
{'lambda_': 0.001}                            warp error   4.23 x 1e-3   converged 20
{'lambda_': 0.001, 'max_template_iter': 5}    warp error   3.76 x 1e-3   converged 20
{'r_defaults': True, 'max_template_iter': 5}  warp error   4.71 x 1e-3   converged 19, stalled 1
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The penalty matters most: it cuts the error four-fold. R's linear \(W\) (r_defaults=True) is stiff enough not to need a penalty, but it cannot express warps that speed up and then slow down, so it stays at a similar error level. The stop reasons show the unpenalised fit running out of iterations on 4 of the 20 curves while every curve meets the tolerance in the other three runs.

docs.title: Periodic data: the Canadian temperature cycle
docs.text:
Each station's annual temperature cycle is one period. periodic=True lets the warp wrap around the year, so a station can be registered by both a delay and a smooth change of pace. With R's linear \(W\) and a mild penalty:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from docs_data import load_canadian_weather
from fdars import alignment as A

day, T, meta = load_canadian_weather("temperature")
r = A.continuous_registration(T, day, periodic=True, r_defaults=True, lambda_=1.0)
lag = (np.asarray(r["warps"]) - day).mean(axis=1)          # mean displacement h_i(t) - t, days
lag -= lag.mean()                                          # relative to the average station

shift = A.iterative_shift_registration(T, day, extrapolation="periodic", max_iter=50, tol=0.5)["shifts"]
shift_lag = -(shift - shift.mean())                        # same sign convention (positive = late)

region = meta["region"].to_numpy()
print("mean lag by region (days; positive = cycle runs late):")
print(pd.DataFrame({"continuous": pd.Series(lag).groupby(region).mean(),
                    "iterative shift": pd.Series(shift_lag).groupby(region).mean()}).round(1).to_string())
print(f"correlation of per-station lags: {np.corrcoef(lag, shift_lag)[0, 1]:.2f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

mean lag by region (days; positive = cycle runs late):
             continuous  iterative shift
Arctic              4.6              2.6
Atlantic            2.1              3.0
Continental        -2.6             -2.7
Pacific            -2.6             -4.2
correlation of per-station lags: 0.82
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Both methods agree on the picture (Atlantic and Arctic stations a few days late, Pacific and continental stations early) and on the per-station ordering. The continuous warps additionally allow the pace to change through the year. Measure lags from \(h_i(t) - t\), not from shift alone.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
from fdars import alignment as A

r = A.continuous_registration(
    data, argvals,
    target=None,                    # default: cross-sectional mean
    criterion="min_eigenvalue",     # or "least_squares"
    nbasis=None, norder=None,       # default 6, 4  (2, 2 with r_defaults)
    lambda_=0.0, lfd_order=None,    # default L = 2 (0 with r_defaults)
    max_iter=None, tol=1e-8,        # default 50 iterations (20 with r_defaults)
    n_fine=None,                    # default max(201, m)
    max_template_iter=1, template_tol=1e-4,
    initial_coefficients=None,      # (n, nbasis); column 0 = initial shift when periodic
    periodic=False, r_defaults=False,
)
Key Description registered_data \((n, m)\) registered curves \(y_i(h_i(t))\) warps \((n, m)\) warps \(h_i\) w_coefficients, w_knots coefficients \((n, K)\) and knots of \(W_i\) criterion \((n,)\) final criterion values target \((m,)\) final target n_iter, converged \((n,)\) per-curve iterations and convergence flags (tolerance met) termination list of \(n\) stop reasons: "converged", "stalled", "coef_limit" or "max_iter" n_template_iter template passes used shift \((n,)\) periodic shift (0 unless periodic=True)

max_iter=0 returns identity warps.

docs.title: Continuous or elastic?
docs.text:
Both handle smooth non-linear phase. Choose continuous registration when:

  • amplitude scale varies between curves and should not be explained as phase (min-eigenvalue);
  • you need warps that are smooth and strictly increasing by construction, with a known low-dimensional parametrisation;
  • you need parity with R's register.fd (r_defaults=True).

Choose elastic alignment when:

  • you need a proper metric between curves, an amplitude/phase decomposition, elastic FPCA, regression or inference;
  • the phase is complex (many features moving independently), beyond what a smooth \(W\) with few basis functions expresses;
  • there is no good target: the Karcher mean estimates the template within the metric.

The method chooser shows penalised continuous registration and the elastic Karcher mean performing alike on smooth non-linear warps, and both beating the rigid models there.

docs.title: Shapes of Curves in \(\mathbb{R}^d\)
docs.text:
An outline, a handwritten letter, a vertebra contour or a movement trajectory is a curve \(\beta:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^d\). When you compare two of them you rarely care where they sit, how large they are, which way they are turned, how fast they were traced or, for a closed contour, where tracing started. These are nuisance transformations. Elastic shape analysis removes all of them at once and measures what is left: the shape.

The curve_shape_* functions in fdars.alignment implement this for open and closed curves in any dimension (ports of fdasrsf curve_functions / curve_stats and fdasrvf multivariate_karcher_mean, curve_depth, curve_boxplot and shape_CI), plus the planar \((a,b)\) elastic metrics of Needham & Kurtek and an exact distance for polygons.

Translation, scale, rotation, re-parametrisation and the starting point all map a contour to the same shape; the distance is a great-circle arc on the pre-shape sphere.

Which page?

For real-valued curves \(f(t)\) use the 1-D elastic tools (Elastic Alignment, Shape Analysis (1-D)). The *_nd_with_config functions share one warp across the coordinates of an \(\mathbb{R}^d\) curve but have no rotation or scale quotient and normalise each coordinate on its own, so they are not shape analysis. For curves observed at a few irregular points, see Sparse & Irregular Curves.

docs.title: Curves as arrays
docs.text:
A curve is a (d, m) array: row \(k\) holds coordinate \(k\) at the \(m\) points of an implicit uniform grid \(t_j = j/(m-1)\). A set of \(n\) curves is an (n, d, m) array or a list of (d, m) arrays. A closed contour repeats its first point at the end, and you pass closed=True.

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

m = 61
s = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
th = 2 * np.pi * s
star = np.stack([(1 + 0.25 * np.cos(3 * th)) * np.cos(th),
                 (1 + 0.25 * np.cos(3 * th)) * np.sin(th)])     # (2, 61), last point == first

R = np.array([[0, -1], [1, 0]])                                 # rotate by 90 degrees
copy = 3.0 * R @ star + np.array([[5.0], [-2.0]])              # rotate, scale x3, translate
print("same shape, different pose:      d =", round(A.curve_shape_distance(star, copy, closed=True), 4))
print("same pose, rotation not removed: d =", round(A.curve_shape_distance(star, copy, closed=True, rotation=False), 4))
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

same shape, different pose:      d = 0.0
same pose, rotation not removed: d = 0.3615
FDARS_FENCE_OK

With all quotients on (the default) the rotated, scaled and shifted copy is at distance zero (up to the optimiser's residual). Switching rotation off makes the same pair look very different.

docs.title: The quotient, one group at a time
docs.text:
Write \(q = \beta'/\sqrt{\lVert\beta'\rVert}\) for the square-root velocity function (SRVF) of \(\beta\). Each nuisance group is removed by one ingredient:

Nuisance How it is removed Option translation the SRVF depends only on \(\beta'\); returned curves are centred on their arc-length centroid always scale each curve is rescaled to unit length, so \(\lVert q\rVert = 1\): SRVFs live on the unit sphere (the pre-shape sphere), and the distance is the great-circle angle \(\arccos\langle q_1, q_2^*\rangle\). With scale=False the distance is the flat \(\lVert q_1 - q_2^*\rVert\) scale=True; include_length=True adds the log length ratio, \(d = \sqrt{\theta^2 + \ln^2(\lVert q_1\rVert/\lVert q_2\rVert)}\) rotation the best \(R \in SO(d)\) by SVD Procrustes (Kabsch); with allow_reflection=True, over \(O(d)\) rotation=True re-parametrisation the elastic DP over warps \(\gamma\), acting as \((q\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\gamma'}\), summed over coordinates; or RBFGS / a finer DP via warp_optim reparam=True, lambda_ penalty starting point (closed curves) a seed search over circular shifts of the sample (stride seed_step, then refined around the best seed), plus projection of the SRVF onto the closed-curve manifold \(\{q : \int q\lVert q\rVert = 0\}\) closed=True, seed_search, seed_step=4

Rotation and warp are estimated alternately: Procrustes, then DP, then Procrustes again, for align_iter rounds (default 2), keeping the best candidate per seed. With reparam=False you get rigid (Procrustes) shape analysis.

The distance is therefore

\[ d([\beta_1],[\beta_2]) = \min_{R,\;\gamma,\;\text{seed}} \arccos\bigl\langle q_1,\; R\,(q_2\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\gamma'}\bigr\rangle , \]

computed by curve_shape_distance; curve_shape_align_pair returns the minimisers too (rotation, gamma, seed, beta2_aligned, q2_aligned), and curve_shape_self_distance_matrix the \(n\times n\) matrix (curve \(j\) aligned to curve \(i\) for \(i<j\), then mirrored).

docs.title: Example: contours that differ only in pose
docs.text:
Twelve closed contours, six three-lobed and six five-lobed stars, each randomly rotated, scaled, translated, re-parametrised and with a random starting point. With every quotient on, the within-class distances collapse; with rotation left in, they do not:

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
m = 81
s = np.linspace(0, 1, m)

def contour(lobes):
    w = s + rng.uniform(-0.08, 0.08) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * s)          # re-parametrise
    th = 2 * np.pi * w
    r = 1 + 0.25 * np.cos(lobes * th)
    pts = np.stack([r * np.cos(th), r * np.sin(th)])[:, :-1]
    pts = np.roll(pts, -rng.integers(0, m - 1), axis=1)                 # new start point
    pts = np.concatenate([pts, pts[:, :1]], axis=1)                     # close the contour
    a = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
    R = np.array([[np.cos(a), -np.sin(a)], [np.sin(a), np.cos(a)]])
    return rng.uniform(0.5, 2.0) * R @ pts + rng.normal(0, 1, (2, 1))   # rotate, scale, shift

curves = np.array([contour(3) for _ in range(6)] + [contour(5) for _ in range(6)])
label = np.repeat([0, 1], 6)
same = label[:, None] == label[None, :]
off = ~np.eye(12, dtype=bool)
for rot in (True, False):
    D = np.asarray(A.curve_shape_self_distance_matrix(curves, closed=True, rotation=rot))
    print(f"rotation={rot!s:5}  within-class mean {D[same & off].mean():.3f} (max {D[same & off].max():.3f})"
          f"   between-class min {D[~same].min():.3f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

rotation=True   within-class mean 0.062 (max 0.095)   between-class min 0.452
rotation=False  within-class mean 0.327 (max 0.605)   between-class min 0.466
FDARS_FENCE_OK

With rotation removed, the largest within-class distance is far below the smallest between-class distance, so any distance-based method (k-medoids, hierarchical clustering, 1-NN) separates the two shapes perfectly. Without the rotation quotient, the within-class distances grow five-fold, because they now include the arbitrary orientation, and they overlap the between-class distances: the classes are no longer separable by distance. (The remaining within-class distances of about 0.06 with rotation removed are mostly the DP residual discussed next.)

docs.title: Getting the warp right: DP floor, RBFGS and DP2
docs.text:
The elastic dynamic program only allows warp slopes from a small set of ratios, so even an exactly re-parametrised copy is not matched exactly: the distance stalls at a grid-independent floor of about 0.02 for smooth curves, and more for sharp features. The fix is the same as for 1-D curves (see Elastic Optimisers): refine with RBFGS (warp_optim={"method": "rbfgs"}) and give rotation and warp more alternation rounds (align_iter >= 4), or use the finer DP2 lattice.

import time
import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

m = 81
s = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
def star(w):
    th = 2 * np.pi * w
    r = 1 + 0.25 * np.cos(5 * th)
    return np.stack([r * np.cos(th), r * np.sin(th)])

b1 = star(s)
b2 = star(s + 0.06 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * s))          # the same outline, traced at a different speed
for name, kw in [("DP (default)", {}),
                 ("DP2: nbhd_dim=10, piecewise_linear", {"warp_optim": {"nbhd_dim": 10, "dp_cost": "piecewise_linear"}}),
                 ("RBFGS, align_iter=4", {"warp_optim": {"method": "rbfgs"}, "align_iter": 4})]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    d = A.curve_shape_distance(b1, b2, closed=True, **kw)
    print(f"{name:36s} residual distance {d:.4f}   ({time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s)")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

DP (default)                         residual distance 0.0563   (0.33 s)
DP2: nbhd_dim=10, piecewise_linear   residual distance 0.0325   (1.90 s)
RBFGS, align_iter=4                  residual distance 0.0180   (0.37 s)
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The true distance is 0. RBFGS cuts the DP residual about three-fold at no extra cost; DP2 halves it at several times the cost. In warp_optim, leave lambda_ at 0 (the penalty weight is the top-level lambda_) and do not set band_frac (curves reject a band).

docs.title: Means, covariance and principal components
docs.text:
curve_shape_karcher_mean computes the Fréchet (Karcher) mean on the shape space by gradient descent: every sweep aligns each curve to the current mean (rotation, warp and seed), maps it to the tangent space at the mean with the inverse exponential map (sphere geometry when scale=True, flat otherwise, projected to the closed-curve tangent space when closed=True), and moves the mean along the average shooting vector. It starts at the first curve, and stops when the average shooting vector is shorter than tol, when the energy \(\sum_i d_i^2\) would increase, or after max_iter sweeps.

curve_shape_karcher_median minimises \(\sum_i d_i\) instead (Weiszfeld steps, started at the medoid) and is robust to outlying shapes; its result is returned in the mean field.

The shooting vectors are linear coordinates on which ordinary multivariate statistics work:

  • curve_shape_karcher_covariance(model) is their \((d\,m)\times(d\,m)\) sample covariance (capped at \(d\,m \le 10\,000\));
  • curve_shape_pca(model, ncomp) is principal geodesic analysis (an \(L^2\)-weighted PCA of the shooting vectors through the \(n\times n\) Gram matrix, no size cap), and pca["model"].mode_shape(mean_model, k, c) maps \(\bar v + c\sqrt{\lambda_k}\,\phi_k\) back to a curve;
  • curve_shape_tsrvf(model, curves) gives the tangent vectors of new curves on the same grid (reproducing the training shooting vectors exactly), and curve_shape_tangent_to_curve inverts the map.

docs.title: Example: a one-parameter family of shapes
docs.text:
Twelve three-lobed contours whose lobe depth varies, each in a random pose. The first principal direction of shape variation should be the lobe depth:

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
m = 61
s = np.linspace(0, 1, m)

def contour(depth):
    w = s + rng.uniform(-0.05, 0.05) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * s)
    th = 2 * np.pi * w
    r = 1 + depth * np.cos(3 * th)
    pts = np.stack([r * np.cos(th), r * np.sin(th)])[:, :-1]
    pts = np.roll(pts, -rng.integers(0, m - 1), axis=1)
    pts = np.concatenate([pts, pts[:, :1]], axis=1)
    a = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
    return rng.uniform(0.5, 2.0) * np.array([[np.cos(a), -np.sin(a)], [np.sin(a), np.cos(a)]]) @ pts

depth = rng.uniform(0.1, 0.3, 12)
curves = np.array([contour(d) for d in depth])

km = A.curve_shape_karcher_mean(curves, closed=True)
pca = A.curve_shape_pca(km["model"], ncomp=3)
share = np.asarray(pca["eigenvalues"]) / np.sum(pca["eigenvalues"])
print("Karcher mean: n_iter", km["n_iter"], " energy per sweep", np.round(km["energy"], 4))
print("variance share of PC1..PC3:", np.round(share, 3))
print("|corr(PC1 score, lobe depth)| =", round(abs(np.corrcoef(np.asarray(pca["scores"])[:, 0], depth)[0, 1]), 4))
mode = pca["model"].mode_shape(km["model"], 0, 2.0)          # mean + 2 sd along PC1, shape (2, m)
print("mode shape array:", np.shape(mode))
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

Karcher mean: n_iter 5  energy per sweep [0.0983 0.087  0.0838 0.0828 0.0824]
variance share of PC1..PC3: [0.864 0.085 0.052]
|corr(PC1 score, lobe depth)| = 0.9994
mode shape array: (2, 61)
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The first component carries most of the shape variance and its scores track the simulated lobe depth almost perfectly, although every contour was in a different pose and traced from a different start. mode_shape(..., 0, ±2.0) gives the contours at two standard deviations along that direction, which is how shape PCA results are usually displayed.

Initialisation and convergence

The Karcher mean starts at the first curve, so with a multimodal energy the result can depend on the order of the curves. converged=False usually means the energy would have increased, which is normal near the optimum; check energy and n_iter rather than the flag.

docs.title: Depth, outliers and box plots
docs.text:
• curve_shape_depth(curves, ...) (fdasrvf curve_depth) aligns all pairs and returns an amplitude depth \(1/(1 + \operatorname{median}_j d_{ij})\) and a phase depth built from the warps' geodesic distance to the identity, both in \([0, 1]\), plus both distance matrices. Cost: \(n(n-1)/2\) alignments.
  • curve_shape_outlier_detection(curves, centre="median", threshold_method="tukey", tukey_k=1.5) computes each curve's distance to a centre (the Karcher median by default, so outliers do not pull it towards themselves) and flags distances above \(Q_3 + k\cdot\mathrm{IQR}\) (threshold_method="quantile" uses the empirical \(1-\alpha\) quantile instead, which flags about \(\alpha n\) curves in any sample: a screening rule, not a test).
  • curve_shape_boxplot(median_model, alpha=0.05, k_a=1.0) (fdasrvf curve_boxplot) builds the elastic shape box plot around a Karcher median: the 50 % and \((1-\alpha)\) central regions are the closest curves, the quartile curves are chosen far from the median in opposite directions, the whiskers extend them by k_a times the inter-quartile distance, and curves beyond the whisker distance are outliers. curve_shape_boxplot_from_aligned does the same from your own aligned SRVFs.
import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
m = 61
s = np.linspace(0, 1, m)

def contour(lobes, depth):
    w = s + rng.uniform(-0.05, 0.05) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * s)
    th = 2 * np.pi * w
    r = 1 + depth * np.cos(lobes * th)
    pts = np.stack([r * np.cos(th), r * np.sin(th)])[:, :-1]
    pts = np.roll(pts, -rng.integers(0, m - 1), axis=1)
    pts = np.concatenate([pts, pts[:, :1]], axis=1)
    a = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
    return rng.uniform(0.5, 2.0) * np.array([[np.cos(a), -np.sin(a)], [np.sin(a), np.cos(a)]]) @ pts

curves = np.array([contour(3, d) for d in rng.uniform(0.1, 0.3, 12)] + [contour(5, 0.2)])  # curve 12: five lobes
out = A.curve_shape_outlier_detection(curves, closed=True)
print("flagged:", [int(i) for i in out["outlier_indices"]], " Tukey threshold", round(float(out["threshold"]), 3))
print("distance of curve 12 to the median shape:", round(float(out["distances"][12]), 3),
      " largest of the others:", round(float(np.max(out["distances"][:12])), 3))
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

flagged: [12]  Tukey threshold 0.173
distance of curve 12 to the median shape: 0.423  largest of the others: 0.167
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The five-lobed contour is flagged; its distance to the median shape is about two and a half times the largest among the three-lobed ones.

docs.title: Confidence regions for the mean shape
docs.text:
curve_shape_confidence_interval(curves, method=...) offers two constructions:

  • method="bootstrap" (default): resample the curves n_bootstrap times, compute each resample's Karcher mean and align it to the full-sample mean. radius is the confidence_level quantile of the bootstrap distances (a geodesic ball around the mean shape), and lower_band / upper_band are pointwise coordinate bands. Cost: n_bootstrap Karcher means.
  • method="model_based" (fdasrvf shape_CI, requires scale=True): fit a Gaussian to the leading n_components principal directions at the Karcher median, sample n_samples shapes by geodesic shooting, pose them with random warps (from the horizontal FPCA of the median's warps) and random rotations (planar curves), and take the elastic box plot of the samples. The result's model holds the box plot, the PCA, the samples and fdasrvf's Q1a / Q3a as q1a / q3a. The random streams differ from R, so individual samples are not reproducible across the two libraries; the median and the model covariance are.
import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fast
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
m = 61
s = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
amp = rng.uniform(0.2, 0.4, 12)
curves = np.array([np.stack([s, a * np.sin(np.pi * s) + 0.1 * np.sin(3 * np.pi * s)]) for a in amp])  # open curves

boot = A.curve_shape_confidence_interval(curves, n_bootstrap=fast(100, 20), seed=1)
model = A.curve_shape_confidence_interval(curves, method="model_based", n_samples=fast(100, 50), seed=1)
print("bootstrap: 95% geodesic radius around the mean shape =", round(float(boot["radius"]), 4))
print("model-based: samples drawn =", np.shape(model["model"]["shape_samples"])[0],
      "  half of them within distance", round(float(model["model"]["boxplot"]["r50"]), 4), "of the median shape")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

bootstrap: 95% geodesic radius around the mean shape = 0.0423
model-based: samples drawn = 100   half of them within distance 0.061 of the median shape
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The bootstrap radius quantifies how far the mean shape could move under resampling (it shrinks like \(1/\sqrt n\)); the model-based region describes the spread of individual shapes under a fitted Gaussian model, which is what fdasrvf's shape_CI plots, so it is wider.

docs.title: Elastic metrics with bending and stretching weights
docs.text:
The SRVF distance treats bending and stretching of a curve in a fixed proportion. The \((a,b)\) elastic metrics (Needham & Kurtek 2020) let you weight them separately: for a deformation \(h\) of a planar curve,

\[ g_c(h, k) = \int a^2 \langle D_s h, N\rangle\langle D_s k, N\rangle + b^2 \langle D_s h, T\rangle\langle D_s k, T\rangle \, ds , \]

where \(T\) and \(N\) are the unit tangent and normal and \(D_s\) is the arc-length derivative. The normal part is bending (weight \(a^2\)), the tangential part is stretching (weight \(b^2\)). Only the ratio \(\lambda = a/(2b)\) changes the geometry; the SRVF is \(a = 1, b = 1/2\), i.e. \(\lambda = 1\).

\(a^2\) weights bending, \(b^2\) stretching; \(a/(2b) = 1\) is the SRVF.

They are computed through the F-transform \(F(c) = 2b\,\lvert c'\rvert^{1/2}\,(c'/\lvert c'\rvert)^{a/(2b)}\) (in complex notation), which maps the metric to a flat \(L^2\) metric, so every curve_shape_* function accepts metric="elastic", a=..., b=... and reuses the same Procrustes / DP machinery. Restrictions and details:

  • planar curves only (\(d = 2\)); other dimensions raise ValueError;
  • for \(\lambda \ne 1\) the transform is multivalued; the code uses one branch, and with rotation=True the Procrustes step quotients rotations and branches. With rotation=False, branch_search=True also tries the neighbouring branches;
  • closed contours use the matching closure condition (ab_closure_residual, ab_project_closed);
  • ab_transform / ab_transform_inverse expose the transform itself.
import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

m = 81
s = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
def arc(kappa):                                 # unit-length curve of constant curvature kappa
    th = kappa * (s - 0.5)
    return np.stack([np.cumsum(np.cos(th)), np.cumsum(np.sin(th))]) / (m - 1)
line, bent = arc(1e-6), arc(3.0)
wiggle = np.stack([s, 0.08 * np.sin(4 * np.pi * s)])

print("a/(2b)   d(line, bent arc)   d(line, wiggle)   nearer to the line")
for a in (0.25, 1.0, 4.0):
    d1, d2 = (A.curve_shape_distance(line, c, metric="elastic", a=a, b=0.5, rotation=False, scale=False)
              for c in (bent, wiggle))
    print(f"{a:6.2f}   {d1:17.3f}   {d2:15.3f}   {'bent arc' if d1 < d2 else 'wiggle'}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

a/(2b)   d(line, bent arc)   d(line, wiggle)   nearer to the line
  0.25               0.216             0.191   wiggle
  1.00               0.746             0.624   wiggle
  4.00               1.193             1.500   bent arc
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The weights change not only the scale of the distances but which shapes count as similar: with the SRVF and with cheap bending (\(\lambda \le 1\)) the gently wiggling curve is nearer to the straight line, with expensive bending (\(\lambda = 4\)) the smoothly bent arc is. There is no universally right \(\lambda\); choose it from the application (is a bend or a stretch the larger change?) or by the downstream performance of, for example, a nearest-neighbour classifier.

docs.title: Exact distance for polygons
docs.text:
For piecewise-linear curves the \((a,b)\) distance (quotient by translation and re-parametrisation only, no rotation or scale) can be computed exactly: ab_elastic_distance_pl(c1, c2, a, b) and ab_elastic_match_pl (which also returns the optimal matching path in normalised arc length and the similarity) implement the algorithm of Lahiri, Robinson & Klassen and Bauer et al. (2024). The vertex arrays may have different lengths, in any dimension. The cost is \(O(N_1^2 N_2^2 (N_1+N_2))\) for \(N_1\), \(N_2\) vertices, so it is meant for polygons with tens of vertices; for densely sampled curves use curve_shape_distance.

It is a useful ground truth for the discretised DP:

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
th = np.linspace(0, np.pi, 8)
P1 = np.stack([np.cos(th), np.sin(th)])                 # 8-vertex polygon (half circle)
P2 = P1 + 0.08 * rng.normal(size=(2, 8))                # a perturbed copy

def subdivide(P, k):                                    # the same polygon, k points per edge
    pts = [P[:, :1]]
    for i in range(P.shape[1] - 1):
        u = np.linspace(0, 1, k + 1)[1:]
        pts.append(P[:, i:i + 1] * (1 - u) + P[:, i + 1:i + 2] * u)
    return np.concatenate(pts, axis=1)

print("exact PL distance:", round(A.ab_elastic_distance_pl(P1, P2, 1.0, 0.5), 4))
for k in (5, 20, 60):
    c1, c2 = subdivide(P1, k), subdivide(P2, k)
    d = A.curve_shape_distance(c1, c2, rotation=False, scale=False)
    print(f"DP on {c1.shape[1]:3d}-point copies:  {d:.4f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

exact PL distance: 0.3894
DP on  36-point copies:  0.3854
DP on 141-point copies:  0.3878
DP on 421-point copies:  0.3901
FDARS_FENCE_OK

As the polygons are sampled more finely, the DP distance approaches the exact value, but only to within the DP's own error, in both directions: on coarse samples it comes out below the exact value, because the DP differentiates the sampled curve with central differences, which rounds the polygon's corners and makes two polygons look more alike; on fine samples its restricted warp slopes push it slightly above (the residual floor of the previous section). Use the exact distance when small differences between polygons matter, or to check a DP configuration.

docs.title: When it works, when it fails
docs.text:
• Works well for densely and roughly uniformly sampled outlines and trajectories whose differences are genuinely in shape: morphometrics, handwriting, gait and motion paths, contours from segmentation.
  • Sampling. All curves in a set share the number of points \(m\). Resample each curve to \(m\) points (by arc length is a good default) before calling. For a few irregular points per curve use the sparse elastic tools, which, however, do not quotient rotation or scale.
  • Cost. Each pair costs align_iter × (number of seeds) DP solves; closed curves search about \(m/\)seed_step seeds. Distance matrices are \(O(n^2)\) pairs (parallelised). Use moderate \(m\) (50–150) and seed_step 4–8 for large samples.
  • Residual floor. For near-identical shapes, distances around 0.02–0.06 can be pure optimiser error. Use warp_optim={"method": "rbfgs"}, align_iter=4 when small distances matter.
  • Symmetric shapes. A circle, or a star whose lobes are identical, has many equally good rotations and seeds; the optimal rotation and seed are then not unique even though the distance is.
  • Reflections. Mirror-image shapes are different unless allow_reflection=True.
