docs.title: Dynamic Time Warping
docs.text:
Dynamic time warping (DTW) is the oldest alignment method in signal processing (Sakoe & Chiba 1978) and still the default for comparing time series in classification and search. It finds the cheapest monotone matching of sample indices between two sequences and reports its accumulated cost. fdars has the full DTW family in fdars.metric: hard DTW with global windows and paths, lower bounds and exact nearest-neighbour search, soft-DTW and its expected alignment, DBA and soft-DTW barycentres, the global alignment kernel, the shape-based distance, multichannel DTW and ten further elastic time-series distances from aeon.

This page is about DTW as an alignment method: what its warping path is, how it differs from the warps of the functional-data aligners on the other pages, and when to choose it. The search and distance tools themselves are documented on DTW Search & Averaging and Elastic Time-Series Distances; clustering with DTW, SBD and k-Shape on Time-Series Clustering.

DTW: many-to-one matches, a monotone path through the cost matrix, and the soft-DTW expected alignment.

docs.title: The DTW path is a discrete warp
docs.text:
For sequences \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) and \(y_1, \dots, y_m\), DTW solves

\[ R(i,j) = c(x_i, y_j) + \min\{R(i-1,j),\; R(i,j-1),\; R(i-1,j-1)\}, \qquad c(a,b) = \lvert a-b\rvert^p, \]

with \(R(0,0) = 0\) and infinite borders. The optimal path \(\pi\) (from dtw_path) is a staircase of index pairs \((i, j)\) from \((1,1)\) to \((n,m)\), monotone in both coordinates. It is a warp in a discrete, weak sense:

  • Many-to-one matches. A horizontal or vertical run matches one sample to several: the path can "hold" a curve still while the other moves. Elastic warps can only slow down to a slope of \(1/7\) (DP) or any positive slope (RBFGS), never stop.
  • Index space, not time. The path relates sample indices; it ignores argvals, so both series must share a sampling rate, but they may have different lengths.
  • Cost, not distance. fdars reports \(\sum_{(i,j)\in\pi}\lvert x_i-y_j\rvert^p\) without a \(p\)-th root (tslearn and dtaidistance report the square root of the \(p=2\) cost). The value grows with the number of matched pairs, so it depends on the sampling density, and DTW does not satisfy the triangle inequality: treat it as a dissimilarity.

How does this compare with elastic alignment? Two experiments with a two-bump curve \(f_1\): a warped copy \(f_2 = f_1 \circ w\) (pure phase) and a scaled copy \(f_3 = 1.4\,f_1\) (pure amplitude). A good aligner recovers \(w^{-1}\) for the first pair and the identity for the second.

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A, metric as M

m = 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.008) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.68) ** 2 / 0.01)
w = t + 0.4 * t * (1 - t)
f1, f2, f3 = mu(t), mu(w), 1.4 * mu(t)          # reference, pure phase, pure amplitude
w_inv = np.interp(t, w, t)

def path_to_warp(path):                          # average matched index of y for each index of x
    P = np.asarray(path)
    return np.array([P[P[:, 0] == i, 1].mean() for i in range(m)]) / (m - 1)

print("                          phase pair: |warp - true|   amplitude pair: |warp - identity|")
print(f"DTW                       {np.abs(path_to_warp(M.dtw_path(f1, f2)['path']) - w_inv).mean():24.4f}"
      f"   {np.abs(path_to_warp(M.dtw_path(f1, f3)['path']) - t).mean():32.4f}")
for wp in (0.1, 1.0):
    a = path_to_warp(M.elastic_ts_alignment_path(f1, f2, "adtw", warp_penalty=wp)["path"])
    b = path_to_warp(M.elastic_ts_alignment_path(f1, f3, "adtw", warp_penalty=wp)["path"])
    print(f"ADTW, warp_penalty={wp:<4}    {np.abs(a - w_inv).mean():24.4f}   {np.abs(b - t).mean():32.4f}")
g2 = np.asarray(A.elastic_align_pair(f1, f2, t)["gamma"])
g3 = np.asarray(A.elastic_align_pair(f1, f3, t)["gamma"])
print(f"elastic (SRSF, DP)        {np.abs(g2 - w_inv).mean():24.4f}   {np.abs(g3 - t).mean():32.4f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

                          phase pair: |warp - true|   amplitude pair: |warp - identity|
DTW                                         0.0021                             0.0166
ADTW, warp_penalty=0.1                       0.0215                             0.0084
ADTW, warp_penalty=1.0                       0.0415                             0.0000
elastic (SRSF, DP)                          0.0011                             0.0000
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Both DTW and elastic alignment recover the pure phase difference. But DTW also warps the pure amplitude difference: to make a taller peak cheaper to match, it holds the shorter curve at its peak for several samples. Penalising warping (amplitude-penalised DTW, ADTW) removes the spurious warp only at a penalty that also suppresses the genuine one. DTW has no way to tell amplitude from phase, because its cost compares values pointwise. The elastic (Fisher–Rao) criterion is invariant to simultaneous warping and does not gain anything by warping a scaled copy, so it leaves it alone.

This is the core of the choice:

  • DTW answers "how similar are these two series if I may stretch time freely?", which is the right question for search and classification, where any warping that makes two signals match is welcome.
  • Registration methods answer "what is the timing of each curve, and what is left once timing is removed?", which needs warps that do not absorb amplitude.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
A global window restricts the path to a band around the diagonal. It speeds DTW up and limits how far one series may be pulled:

window= Parameters Admissible cells "none" (default) — all "sakoe_chiba" radius \(\lvert i-j\rvert \le r\) (widened by \(\lvert n-m\rvert\) for unequal lengths; tslearn) "itakura" max_slope \(\ge 1\) a parallelogram with slopes \(1/s\) and \(s\) (tslearn) "sakoe_chiba_fraction" window_fraction in \([0,1]\) half-width \(\lfloor f\cdot\min(n,m)\rfloor\) around the interpolated diagonal (aeon) "itakura_fraction" max_slope in \((0,1]\) aeon's Itakura parallelogram

dtw_window_mask(n, m, window=...) returns the boolean mask. A window is not a cure for amplitude-induced warping: in the example above a Sakoe–Chiba radius of 5 samples leaves the spurious warp of the scaled copy unchanged (it fits inside the band) and truncates the genuine warp of the phase pair, which needs about 10 samples. Choose the radius from the largest plausible time shift.

Legacy w argument

dtw_self_1d / dtw_cross_1d take an older band argument w with an asymmetric convention (\(j - i \in [1-w, w]\)); w=0 admits no cell and returns infinity without an error. It is not the same as window="sakoe_chiba", radius=w. Prefer the window= functions.

docs.title: Soft-DTW: a smooth expected alignment
docs.text: Soft-DTW (Cuturi & Blondel 2017) replaces the minimum in the recursion by the soft minimum \(-\gamma\log\sum e^{-a/\gamma}\), which makes the cost differentiable in the data. soft_dtw_alignment(x, y, gamma) returns the expected alignment matrix \(E\): entry \((i,j)\) is the probability that cell \((i,j)\) lies on the path under the Gibbs distribution over all paths (corners are 1; rows do not sum to 1). As \(\gamma \to 0\) it becomes the 0/1 hard path; larger \(\gamma\) spreads it out, which shows where the alignment is uncertain (in flat stretches of the curves many paths cost about the same). Raw soft-DTW can be negative and is not zero for identical series; use the soft-DTW divergence (soft_dtw_div_*) when you need a non-negative discrepancy.

docs.title: Averaging and registering a sample under DTW
docs.text:
To summarise a group of series under DTW, average along the alignment:

  • DBA (DTW barycentre averaging; Petitjean et al. 2011), dtw_barycenter_averaging(data, init=...): align the current barycentre to every series with dtw_path, replace each barycentre sample by the mean of the samples matched to it, repeat. The inertia never increases, but the result depends on the start: init="medoid" is more robust than the default pointwise mean.
  • Soft-DTW barycentre, soft_dtw_barycenter(data, gamma, n_restarts): minimise the sum of soft-DTW costs by L-BFGS; smaller \(\gamma\) is closer to DBA, larger \(\gamma\) closer to the pointwise mean.
import time
import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A, metric as M

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, m = 20, 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.008) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.68) ** 2 / 0.01)
X = np.array([mu(t + rng.uniform(-0.4, 0.4) * t * (1 - t)) + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(m) for _ in range(n)])

def peaks(f):
    return f"{f[:50].max():.3f}, {f[50:].max():.3f}"

print("true template peaks:           ", peaks(mu(t)))
print("pointwise mean:                ", peaks(X.mean(0)))
for init in ("mean", "medoid"):
    r = M.dtw_barycenter_averaging(X, init=init)
    print(f"DBA, init={init:7s}             ", peaks(np.asarray(r["barycenter"])), f"  inertia {r['cost']:.4f}")
for g in (0.01, 1.0):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    r = M.soft_dtw_barycenter(X, gamma=g, n_restarts=1)
    print(f"soft-DTW barycentre, gamma={g:<4}  ", peaks(np.asarray(r["barycenter"])), f"  ({time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s)")
print("elastic Karcher mean:          ", peaks(np.asarray(A.karcher_mean(X, t)["mean"])))
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

true template peaks:            1.000, 0.700
pointwise mean:                 0.774, 0.580
DBA, init=mean                 0.983, 0.691   inertia 0.0300
DBA, init=medoid               0.998, 0.704   inertia 0.0202
soft-DTW barycentre, gamma=0.01   0.982, 0.687   (1.3 s)
soft-DTW barycentre, gamma=1.0    0.927, 0.642   (0.3 s)
elastic Karcher mean:           1.015, 0.723
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Averaging along the alignment keeps the peak heights that the pointwise mean flattens; the medoid start brings DBA closest to the truth here, and the elastic Karcher mean recovers the template as well. DBA is the fastest of the three. The difference lies in what comes with it: the Karcher mean also returns smooth, invertible warps, the amplitude/phase split and the inputs for elastic FPCA, regression and tests; DBA returns a barycentre and index paths.

docs.title: Multichannel series
docs.text: dtw_distance_multivariate, dtw_path_multivariate, dtw_pairwise_distance_multivariate and dtw_barycenter_averaging_multivariate take (d, m) arrays (channels as rows) and use the dependent cost \(\lVert x_{\cdot,i} - y_{\cdot,j}\rVert_2^p\): one path for all channels, as in aeon and tslearn. With \(d = 1\) they reproduce the univariate results exactly. The functional-data counterpart is the shared-warp *_nd_with_config family (one elastic warp for all coordinates) or, when rotation and scale are nuisance, the curve shape space.

docs.title: Choosing within the DTW family
docs.text: Goal Use Page Nearest neighbour or classification over many references dtw_nearest_neighbor / dtw_k_nearest_neighbors with a Sakoe–Chiba window; the lower-bound cascade makes it exact and fast DTW Search A differentiable loss (neural networks, barycentres) soft-DTW; the divergence for a non-negative discrepancy Distance Metrics A representative series DBA (medoid start) or the soft-DTW barycentre with restarts DTW Search A kernel for an SVM the global alignment kernel gak_* (positive semi-definite once normalised; \(e^{-\text{DTW}}\) is not) DTW Search Shape matters, offset and scale do not SBD / k-Shape Elastic TS Distances Robustness to outliers or gaps EDR or LCSS (thresholded), ERP or TWE (gap costs), MSM Elastic TS Distances Penalise excessive warping ADTW (additive penalty) or WDTW (logistic weight) Elastic TS Distances Match slopes rather than values DDTW / WDDTW (derivative DTW) Elastic TS Distances Match local shape shape-DTW Elastic TS Distances Cluster series DTW k-means (DBA centroids), k-Shape, k-medoids on any matrix Time-Series Clustering

docs.title: When not to use DTW on functional data
docs.text:
Use elastic alignment (or another registration method from Choosing an Alignment Method) instead of DTW when you need:

  • an amplitude/phase decomposition: DTW warps away amplitude differences, as shown above;
  • a metric: Fréchet means, PERMANOVA, depth and many clustering criteria assume the triangle inequality, which DTW costs do not satisfy, and the cost scale depends on the number of samples;
  • smooth, invertible warps to transport curves, compute derivatives of registered data or report timing;
  • irregular sampling: DTW compares sample indices, so differently sampled curves must first be resampled to a common rate.

docs.title: The problem: amplitude vs. phase variability
docs.text:
Imagine recording the heartbeat signal of several patients. Every heartbeat has the same features -- a P wave, a QRS complex, a T wave -- but the timing of those features differs from patient to patient. Average the raw signals and the peaks blur out, because they do not line up. Two distinct sources of variation are at work whenever curves share a domain:

  • Amplitude variability -- differences in the height of features (peaks, valleys).
  • Phase variability -- differences in the timing of features (shifted or stretched along the domain axis).

Classical statistics -- the cross-sectional mean, ordinary FPCA -- treats all variation as amplitude. The result is a blurred mean and artificially inflated variance. Elastic alignment resolves this by finding time-warping functions \(\gamma\) that register each curve to a common template, isolating amplitude variation in the aligned curves and phase variation in the warps:

\[ f_{\text{aligned}}(t) = (f \circ \gamma)(t) = f(\gamma(t)). \]

The panels below show the same set of two-peak curves before alignment -- where the peaks land at different times, blurring the cross-sectional mean -- and after Karcher-mean alignment, where the peaks snap into register and the mean recovers a sharp two-peak profile.

image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

On the left the peaks arrive at different times, so the red cross-sectional mean is blunted and shifted -- it does not look like any single curve. On the right the Fisher-Rao alignment warps every curve onto the common Karcher mean, and the orange mean now reproduces the true peaked shape. This side-by-side is the canonical illustration of amplitude/phase separation.

Fisher-Rao framework

All alignment in fdars is performed under the elastic (Fisher-Rao) metric, the unique Riemannian metric on the function space that is invariant to simultaneous reparameterization. This guarantees the alignment is proper: the distance between two functions does not depend on how either is parameterized.

Numerical validation

Two ground-truth properties of the elastic machinery, asserted below:

  1. Alignment removes variance. After Karcher-mean alignment of a phase-varying sample, the mean pointwise variance must drop, so the variance reduction \(\text{VR}=1-\overline{\operatorname{Var}}(\tilde f)/\overline{\operatorname{Var}}(f)\) is strictly positive.
  2. Amplitude = elastic distance. For the residual after optimal alignment, amplitude_distance is by definition the elastic distance; the two must agree to machine precision.

variance reduction after alignment: 0.931 (> 0 required) amplitude vs elastic distance: 0.443239 vs 0.443239 (|diff| = 0.00e+00)

Both assertions pass: the variance reduction is strictly positive (alignment genuinely removed phase spread), and amplitude_distance reproduces elastic_distance to machine precision -- confirming they are the same quantity by construction, not merely close.

docs.title: How it works (intuition)
docs.text:
Elastic alignment stretches and compresses the time axis of each curve until corresponding features line up. The key trick is to work in the Square-Root Slope Function (SRSF) representation -- a transformed version of the curve that turns the awkward Fisher-Rao geometry into ordinary \(L^2\) geometry. In SRSF space, finding the best alignment reduces to a standard dynamic-programming problem that solves in \(O(m^2)\) time.

After alignment, variability splits cleanly into two parts:

  • Amplitude variability -- genuine differences in curve shape (how tall the peaks are, how deep the valleys).
  • Phase variability -- differences in timing (when the peaks occur), captured entirely by the warping functions.

The Karcher mean is the average shape, computed after alignment. Unlike the ordinary mean, it preserves sharp features because the peaks are registered before averaging.

docs.title: The space of warping functions
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be the space of absolutely continuous functions \(f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}\). The warping group is

\[ \Gamma = \{\gamma:[0,1]\to[0,1] \mid \gamma(0)=0,\;\gamma(1)=1,\;\dot\gamma > 0\}. \]

\(\Gamma\) acts on \(\mathcal{F}\) by composition: \((f\circ\gamma)(t)=f(\gamma(t))\). This reparameterizes a curve without changing its shape -- only the speed at which the curve is traversed changes.

docs.title: The Fisher-Rao metric
docs.text: The Fisher-Rao metric is the unique Riemannian metric (up to scaling) invariant under the action of \(\Gamma\). It is hard to compute directly because it involves \(f\)'s derivative in a denominator. The SRSF transform resolves this by isometrically mapping Fisher-Rao geometry onto a flat \(L^2\) space.

docs.title: SRSF transform
docs.text:
The Square-Root Slope Function of \(f\) is

\[ q(t) = \operatorname{sign}\!\big(\dot f(t)\big)\,\sqrt{\lvert \dot f(t)\rvert}. \]

It has three key properties:

  1. Isometry -- the Fisher-Rao distance between \(f_1,f_2\) equals the \(L^2\) distance between their SRSFs after optimal alignment.
  2. Equivariance -- under \(f\mapsto f\circ\gamma\) the SRSF transforms as \(q\mapsto(q\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\), the standard action of \(\Gamma\) on \(L^2\).
  3. Invertibility -- given \(q\) and an initial value \(f(0)\), the function is recovered by \(f(t)=f(0)+\int_0^t q(s)\lvert q(s)\rvert\,ds\).

The SRSF is available directly; the transform loses only the initial offset \(f(0)\), which you pass back to srsf_inverse to reconstruct the curve exactly.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import srsf_transform, srsf_inverse

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 100)
f = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) + 0.4 * np.sin(4 * np.pi * t)

q = srsf_transform(f, t)                    # forward
f_rec = srsf_inverse(q, t, initial_value=f[0])  # inverse (needs f(0))
print(f"Round-trip max error: {np.max(np.abs(f - f_rec)):.2e}")

f2, (a1, a2) = fig(ncols=2, figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
a1.plot(t, f, color="#3f51b5", lw=1.8)
a1.set(title="Original curve $f$", xlabel="t", ylabel="f(t)")
a2.plot(t, np.asarray(q), color="#6f42c1", lw=1.8)
a2.set(title="SRSF representation $q$", xlabel="t", ylabel="q(t)")
print(render(f2))
Round-trip max error: 1.58e-03 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The right panel is the curve's SRSF: it emphasizes the slopes of \(f\), crossing zero exactly where \(f\) has an extremum. The tiny printed round-trip error confirms the transform is losslessly invertible once \(f(0)\) is supplied, which is what lets us do all the geometry in SRSF space and map back.

Note

The SRSF drops \(f(0)\). Pass initial_value to srsf_inverse to recover the original function exactly (the round-trip error above is at the level of numerical integration).

docs.title: Alignment as optimization
docs.text:
Given \(f_1,f_2\) with SRSFs \(q_1,q_2\), optimal alignment finds

\[ \gamma^\* = \arg\min_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\;\big\lVert q_1 - (q_2\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\,\big\rVert_{L^2}, \]

The aligned function is \(f_2\circ\gamma^\*\), and the elastic distance is the residual \(L^2\) norm. On the continuous problem it is a metric on curves modulo warping and is invariant to simultaneous reparameterization: \(d_e(f_1,f_2)=d_e(f_1\circ\gamma, f_2\circ\gamma)\) for any \(\gamma\in\Gamma\).

How fdars computes it:

  • The search uses normalised SRSFs. The warp minimises \(\lVert \bar q_1 - (\bar q_2\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\rVert^2 + \lambda P(\gamma)\) with \(\bar q_j = q_j/\lVert q_j\rVert\), so the choice of warp does not depend on the overall size of the curves. The reported distance is then computed from the un-normalised SRSFs, by re-differentiating the warped curve \(f_2\circ\gamma^\*\), so it is in the units of the data.
  • The optimiser is a dynamic program over a discretised \(\Gamma\) by default (globally optimal among warps with slopes between 1/7 and 7), or a Riemannian quasi-Newton method; both, the penalties \(P\) and their weight \(\lambda\) are described on Elastic Optimisers & Penalties. Every function on this page has a *_with_config twin taking those options.
  • The discretised distance is only approximately symmetric. elastic_align_pair(f1, f2) warps f2 onto f1, and the DP is one-sided. On coarse grids \(d(f_1,f_2)\) and \(d(f_2,f_1)\) can differ a lot: for a one-bump and a two-bump curve, 0.56 vs 0.94 at \(m = 30\), 0.86 vs 0.94 at \(m = 101\), 0.92 vs 0.94 at \(m = 301\). The gap closes as the grid is refined. The distance-matrix functions compute the upper triangle and mirror it, so their output is symmetric by construction. On coarse grids, use \(\tfrac12(d_{12} + d_{21})\) or refine the grid.

docs.title: Amplitude-phase decomposition and variance reduction
docs.text:
For a sample \(f_1,\dots,f_n\) with aligned versions \(\tilde f_i=f_i\circ\gamma_i^\*\):

  • Amplitude variability is the residual variance in \(\tilde f_1,\dots,\tilde f_n\) -- genuine shape differences.
  • Phase variability is the variability in the warps \(\gamma_1^\*,\dots,\gamma_n^\*\) themselves -- timing differences.

The variance reduction (VR) quantifies how much of the total variance was phase,

\[ \text{VR} = 1 - \frac{\overline{\operatorname{Var}}(\tilde f_1,\dots,\tilde f_n)}{\overline{\operatorname{Var}}(f_1,\dots,f_n)}, \]

where \(\overline{\operatorname{Var}}\) is the mean pointwise variance. VR near 1 means the variation was almost all phase (and has been removed); VR near 0 means it was almost all amplitude.

docs.title: Karcher mean
docs.text:
The Karcher mean (Frechet mean under the elastic metric) minimizes the sum of squared elastic distances,

\[ \mu^\* = \arg\min_{\mu\in\mathcal{F}}\;\sum_{i=1}^n d_e(\mu, f_i)^2. \]

Because \(d_e\) accounts for reparameterization, \(\mu^\*\) is a shape-preserving average. karcher_mean computes it in SRSF space as follows:

  1. Template. Start from the observed curve whose SRSF is nearest the pointwise mean SRSF.
  2. Pre-centring. Align all curves to it, and move the template by the inverse of the mean warp (SqrtMeanInverse: the Karcher mean of the \(\psi_i=\sqrt{\dot\gamma_i}\) on the sphere, inverted), so that the starting template sits in the "average" time frame.
  3. Iterate. Align every curve to the current mean SRSF \(\mu_q\) and set \(\mu_q \leftarrow \frac1n\sum_i (q_i\circ\gamma_i)\sqrt{\dot\gamma_i}\), the \(L^2\) mean of the aligned SRSFs. Stop when the relative change of \(\mu_q\) is below tol. When \(m > 50\) and max_iter \(\ge 10\), the first half of the iterations runs on a grid four times coarser (coarse-to-fine), which is much cheaper.
  4. Post-centring. Compose the mean and all warps with the inverse of the mean warp, so that the warps average to the identity and the mean is not drifted early or late.
  5. Back to a curve. The mean curve is srsf_inverse of \(\mu_q\), anchored at the cross-sectional mean value at the first grid point.

converged=False is reported, not raised: check it and raise max_iter if needed. The result depends (weakly) on the starting template; there is no restart.

docs.title: Pairwise alignment
docs.text:
Align a single curve to a reference. The optimizer returns the aligned curve, the warp \(\gamma^\*\), and the elastic distance.

from fdars.alignment import elastic_align_pair

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
f1 = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
f2 = np.sin(2 * np.pi * (t - 0.1))  # phase-shifted

result = elastic_align_pair(f1, f2, t, lambda_=0.0)

f2_aligned = result["f_aligned"]   # f2 warped to match f1, shape (101,)
gamma      = result["gamma"]       # warping function, shape (101,)
distance   = result["distance"]    # elastic distance (scalar)

print(f"Elastic distance: {distance:.4f}")
print(f"Max alignment residual: {np.max(np.abs(f1 - f2_aligned)):.6f}")
Key Type Description f_aligned ndarray (m,) Second curve warped to match the first gamma ndarray (m,) Optimal warping function \(\gamma^\*\) distance float Elastic distance after alignment

Regularization

Increase lambda_ to penalize complex warping functions and obtain smoother alignments. 0.0 allows unconstrained warping; around 0.01 the warps become much smoother, and by 1.0 they are often close to the identity. The right value depends on the data: see Elastic Optimisers & Penalties for the four penalty forms, the RBFGS optimiser and the scale of \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Group alignment: Karcher mean
docs.text:
The Karcher mean simultaneously aligns all curves and computes their elastic average, iterating between aligning every curve to the current mean and recomputing the mean from the aligned curves.

from fdars import Fdata
from fdars.alignment import karcher_mean

# 30 curves with random phase shifts
np.random.seed(0)
n, m = 30, 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
shifts = np.random.uniform(-0.15, 0.15, n)
fd = Fdata(np.array([np.sin(2 * np.pi * (t - s)) for s in shifts]), argvals=t)

result = karcher_mean(fd.data, t, lambda_=0.0, max_iter=20, tol=1e-4)

mu        = result["mean"]          # Karcher mean, shape (m,)
mu_srsf   = result["mean_srsf"]     # mean in SRSF space, shape (m,)
aligned   = result["aligned_data"]  # aligned curves, shape (n, m)
gammas    = result["gammas"]        # warping functions, shape (n, m)
n_iter    = result["n_iter"]        # iterations used
converged = result["converged"]     # bool

print(f"Converged in {n_iter} iterations: {converged}")
Key Type Description mean ndarray (m,) Karcher mean function mean_srsf ndarray (m,) Mean in SRSF representation aligned_data ndarray (n, m) All curves aligned to the mean gammas ndarray (n, m) Warping functions for each curve n_iter int Number of iterations performed converged bool Whether the algorithm converged

The figure below contrasts the two averages directly: the cross-sectional mean is attenuated by the phase shifts, while the Karcher mean recovers the true amplitude.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import karcher_mean

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n, m = 20, 100
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
# shifted bumps
data = np.array([np.exp(-25 * (t - 0.5 - rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1)) ** 2)
                 for _ in range(n)])

km = karcher_mean(data, t, max_iter=30, tol=1e-4)
mu = np.asarray(km["mean"])

f, ax = fig()
ax.plot(t, data.T, color="#6c757d", lw=0.8, alpha=0.3)
ax.plot(t, data.mean(0), color="#3f51b5", lw=2.4, label="cross-sectional mean")
ax.plot(t, mu, color="#dc3545", lw=2.4, label="Karcher mean")
ax.set(title="Cross-sectional vs. Karcher mean (shifted bumps)",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="f(t)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The blue cross-sectional mean is shorter and wider than any real bump -- averaging shifted peaks pointwise smears them out. The red Karcher mean instead keeps the true peak height and width, because it averages shapes after warping rather than heights at fixed times. This height loss is the single clearest symptom of ignoring phase.

docs.title: Robust centres: Karcher median and trimmed mean
docs.text:
The Karcher mean minimises a sum of squared distances, so a few gross outliers can pull it away from the bulk of the sample. Two robust alternatives:

  • karcher_median approximately minimises \(\sum_i d_e(\mu, f_i)\) (unsquared) by a Weiszfeld iteration: start from a one-iteration Karcher mean, weight each curve by \(w_i \propto 1/d_i\), update the estimate as the weighted mean of the aligned curves (not of the SRSFs), re-align, and repeat until the SRSF of the estimate stops changing. Each iteration costs about \(2n\) alignments.
  • robust_karcher_mean computes a Karcher mean, drops the ceil(n * trim_fraction) farthest curves (keeping at least two), and recomputes the mean from the rest; all curves are then re-aligned to it. weights are 1 for kept and 0 for trimmed curves.
import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import karcher_mean, karcher_median, robust_karcher_mean

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n, m = 30, 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
bump = lambda c: np.exp(-((t - c) ** 2) / (2 * 0.12 ** 2))
data = np.array([rng.normal(3.0, 0.3) * bump(rng.normal(0.5, 0.08)) for _ in range(n)])
data[0] += 2.0 * np.exp(-((t - 0.2) ** 2) / 0.002)   # spurious early spike
data[1] *= -0.6                                        # flipped, depressed

mean = np.asarray(karcher_mean(data, t, max_iter=15)["mean"])
med = karcher_median(data, t, max_iter=15)
trim = robust_karcher_mean(data, t, trim_fraction=0.1, max_iter=15)

f, ax = fig()
ax.plot(t, data.T, color="#adb5bd", lw=0.7, alpha=0.4)
ax.plot(t, mean, color="#dc3545", lw=2.2, label="Karcher mean")
ax.plot(t, np.asarray(med["mean"]), color="#3f51b5", lw=2.2, label="Karcher median")
ax.plot(t, np.asarray(trim["mean"]), color="#198754", lw=2.2, ls="--", label="trimmed mean (10%)")
ax.set(title="Robust vs. standard elastic central shape", xlabel="t", ylabel="f(t)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
print(render(f))
w = np.asarray(med["weights"])
print(f"<p>median weights of the two outliers: {w[0]:.3f}, {w[1]:.3f} (median of all weights {np.median(w):.3f}); "
      f"curves trimmed: {list(np.flatnonzero(np.asarray(trim['weights']) == 0))}</p>")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

median weights of the two outliers: 0.003, 0.002 (median of all weights 0.031); curves trimmed: [np.int64(0), np.int64(1), np.int64(15)]

The spike and the flipped curve pull the plain Karcher mean; the median down-weights them and the trimmed mean drops them. Both return the keys of karcher_mean plus weights; karcher_median_with_config and robust_karcher_mean_with_config take the optimiser options. Setting trim_fraction too high removes legitimate variation: start at 0.05–0.10.

docs.title: Interpreting warping functions
docs.text:
A warping function \(\gamma:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) is a monotonically increasing diffeomorphism. Its position relative to the diagonal and its slope encode local timing:

Condition Interpretation \(\gamma(t) > t\) (above diagonal) Feature occurs later in the original curve; alignment looks forward \(\gamma(t) < t\) (below diagonal) Feature occurs earlier; alignment looks backward \(\dot\gamma(t) > 1\) Region is stretched -- features spread over more reference time \(\dot\gamma(t) < 1\) Region is compressed -- features happen faster \(\dot\gamma(t) = 1\) No timing distortion at \(t\)

Plotted together, the warps fan out around the identity diagonal: a \(\gamma\) bowing above the diagonal pulls features earlier, one bowing below pushes them later. Their spread is the phase variability that alignment separated out of the amplitude.

image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Differentiating \(\gamma\) gives its local warping speed \(\dot\gamma\), which makes the stretch/compress reading concrete.

# Inspect warping speed for the first curve
gamma_0 = gammas[0]
speed = np.gradient(gamma_0, t)

compressed = t[speed > 1.2]        # sped up
stretched  = t[speed < 0.8]        # slowed down
print(f"Compressed near t in {compressed[[0, -1]] if compressed.size else '(none)'}")

docs.title: Elastic distance and its decomposition
docs.text:
Compute the elastic (Fisher-Rao) distance between two curves without returning the warp explicitly, and the two quantities that describe what the alignment did:

  • the amplitude distance is the elastic distance itself, the residual after optimal warping: amplitude_distance(f1, f2) == elastic_distance(f1, f2);
  • the phase distance measures the optimal warp, \(d_{\text{phase}} = \arccos\bigl(\int_0^1 \sqrt{\dot\gamma^\*}\bigr)\), the Fisher–Rao distance of \(\gamma^\*\) from the identity.

They are two separate summaries (one of the residual, one of the warp), not an orthogonal split of a total distance.

from fdars.alignment import elastic_distance, amplitude_distance, phase_distance

d_amp   = amplitude_distance(f1, f2, t)
d_phase = phase_distance(f1, f2, t)
d_total = elastic_distance(f1, f2, t)

print(f"Amplitude distance: {d_amp:.4f}")
print(f"Phase distance:     {d_phase:.4f}")
print(f"Total (elastic):    {d_total:.4f}")

For two phase-shifted sines both are non-zero: the warp cannot move a periodic feature across the fixed end points \(\gamma(0)=0\), \(\gamma(1)=1\), so some of the shift remains as amplitude. Use the closed-curve aligner (below) for periodic signals.

The single-pair version, elastic_decomposition, returns the aligned curve and both distances in one call:

from fdars.alignment import elastic_decomposition

dec = elastic_decomposition(f1, f2, t, lambda_=0.0)
print(f"Amplitude: {dec['d_amplitude']:.4f}, Phase: {dec['d_phase']:.4f}")
f2_aligned = dec["f_aligned"]   # f2 aligned onto f1

docs.title: Distance matrices
docs.text:
Compute pairwise elastic distances for an entire dataset. These matrices feed nonparametric regression, clustering, or classification, and can be visualized with multidimensional scaling.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import elastic_self_distance_matrix

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n, m = 15, 100
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
data = np.array([np.sin(2 * np.pi * (t - rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1))) for _ in range(n)])

D = np.asarray(elastic_self_distance_matrix(data, t, lambda_=0.0))
print("Symmetric:    ", bool(np.max(np.abs(D - D.T)) < 1e-8), "(upper triangle mirrored)")
print("Zero diagonal:", bool(np.max(np.abs(np.diag(D))) < 1e-8))

# Classical MDS embedding of the elastic distances
n_ = D.shape[0]
J = np.eye(n_) - np.ones((n_, n_)) / n_
B = -0.5 * J @ (D ** 2) @ J
w, V = np.linalg.eigh(B)
emb = V[:, [-1, -2]] * np.sqrt(np.clip(w[[-1, -2]], 0, None))

f, ax = fig()
ax.scatter(emb[:, 0], emb[:, 1], color="#3f51b5", s=45)
ax.set(title="MDS of elastic distances", xlabel="MDS 1", ylabel="MDS 2")
print(render(f))
Symmetric: True (upper triangle mirrored) Zero diagonal: True image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Cross-distances between two datasets (e.g. train vs. test) come from elastic_cross_distance_matrix:

from fdars.alignment import elastic_cross_distance_matrix

fd_train, fd_test = fd[:20], fd[20:]
D_cross = elastic_cross_distance_matrix(fd_train.data, fd_test.data, fd.argvals, lambda_=0.0)
print("Cross-distance shape:", np.asarray(D_cross).shape)  # (20, 10)

docs.title: Alignment quality diagnostics
docs.text:
alignment_quality runs the elastic alignment internally and reports a suite of diagnostics -- how much variance is removed, and how the total splits into amplitude and phase.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import karcher_mean, alignment_quality

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n, m = 20, 100
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
data = np.array([np.sin(2 * np.pi * (t - rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1))) for _ in range(n)])

km = karcher_mean(data, t, max_iter=20, tol=1e-4)
aligned = np.asarray(km["aligned_data"])
q = alignment_quality(data, t, lambda_=0.0, max_iter=20)

# Pointwise variance before vs after -- where did alignment help?
var_before = np.var(data, axis=0)
var_after = np.var(aligned, axis=0)

f, ax = fig()
ax.fill_between(t, var_after, var_before, color="#3f51b5", alpha=0.18,
                label="variance removed")
ax.plot(t, var_before, color="#6c757d", ls="--", lw=1.6, label="before")
ax.plot(t, var_after, color="#3f51b5", lw=1.8, label="after")
ax.set(title="Pointwise variance: before vs. after alignment",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="variance")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
print(render(f))

print()
print(f"mean variance reduction : {float(q['mean_variance_reduction']):.4f}")
print(f"phase / amplitude ratio : {float(q['phase_amplitude_ratio']):.4f}")
print(f"mean warp complexity    : {float(q['mean_warp_complexity']):.4f}")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ mean variance reduction : 0.1478 phase / amplitude ratio : 0.7735 mean warp complexity : 0.0749

The shaded gap between the dashed (before) and solid (after) curves is the variance alignment removed, and it is largest exactly where the curves were most out of phase. The printed variance-reduction and phase/amplitude numbers put a single figure on that gap -- a compact summary of how much of the spread was timing.

alignment_quality key Meaning mean_variance_reduction Fraction of pointwise variance removed by alignment (the VR metric) total_variance Total variance before decomposition amplitude_variance / phase_variance Variance attributable to amplitude / to phase phase_amplitude_ratio Phase share of total variance -- high means phase-dominated mean_warp_complexity Average geodesic distance of warps from the identity mean_warp_smoothness Average bending energy of the warps pointwise_variance_ratio Per-point post/pre variance ratio, shape (m,)

A phase_amplitude_ratio near 1 confirms the variation is mostly timing -- precisely where alignment helps most.

docs.title: Per-curve health checks
docs.text:
diagnose_alignment flags individual curves whose warps are over-complex, under-improving, or too rough, and returns a global health score.

from fdars.alignment import diagnose_alignment

diag = diagnose_alignment(data, t, max_iter=15)
print(f"Health score : {float(diag['health_score']):.3f}")
print(f"Flagged      : {int(diag['n_flagged'])} of {len(data)} curves")
print(f"Flagged idx  : {list(np.asarray(diag['flagged_indices']))}")
Key Description health_score Overall alignment health in \([0,1]\) (1 = all curves healthy) flagged_indices / n_flagged Curves failing a diagnostic threshold flagged Per-curve flags warp_complexity / warp_smoothness Per-curve warp metrics residuals Per-curve post-alignment residual

The thresholds are over_alignment_threshold (warp complexity), max_bending_energy (warp smoothness), min_improvement_ratio and under_alignment_threshold. Note that the last one is applied as a minimum distance (curves whose post-alignment residual is below it count as suspiciously perfect), not as the ratio its name suggests.

pairwise_consistency complements this by checking whether alignment is internally coherent across triplets of curves; a low value can signal subgroups with genuinely different shapes.

from fdars.alignment import pairwise_consistency
pc = pairwise_consistency(data, t, max_triplets=100)
print(f"Pairwise consistency: {pc:.4f}")

docs.title: When elastic alignment works -- and when it does not
docs.text:
Elastic alignment is not a cure-all. It shines when variability is genuinely timing, and it can do harm (or nothing) otherwise. The table below is a compact version of the fdars scenario gallery; each row was measured with the code that follows.

Scenario Typical VR Verdict Shifted peaks / bumps 95--100% Best case -- localized features with timing shifts Multi-peak (ECG-like), spectral peaks 95--100% Excellent when peaks shift coherently Phase-shifted smooth curves (sine, sigmoid) 90--100% Works well Mixed amplitude + phase 40--65% Partial -- residual is real amplitude variation Pure amplitude differences ~0% Identity warps -- no harm, no help Genuinely different shapes low / negative Misuse -- forced warping; use depth/distance instead Very noisy raw data 0--30% Smooth first -- SRSF amplifies derivative noise 
import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import karcher_mean

def vr(data, t):
    aligned = np.asarray(karcher_mean(data, t, max_iter=20, tol=1e-4)["aligned_data"])
    return 1.0 - np.var(aligned, axis=0).mean() / np.var(data, axis=0).mean()

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 120)
scen = {}

# Shifted bumps -- best case
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
scen["bumps"] = np.array([np.exp(-200 * (t - 0.5 - rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1)) ** 2)
                          for _ in range(20)])
# Mixed amplitude + phase
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
scen["mixed"] = np.array([rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * (t - rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1)))
                          for _ in range(20)])
# Pure amplitude
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
scen["pure amp"] = np.array([rng.uniform(0.5, 2.0) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) for _ in range(20)])
# Different shapes
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
shapes = [np.sin(2 * np.pi * t), np.cos(6 * np.pi * t), t ** 3,
          np.exp(-((t - 0.5) ** 2) / 0.002)]
scen["diff shapes"] = np.array([shapes[i % 4] for i in range(20)])

vrs = {k: 100 * vr(v, t) for k, v in scen.items()}

f, ax = fig()
names = list(vrs.keys())
ax.bar(names, [vrs[k] for k in names],
       color=["#198754", "#e8710a", "#6c757d", "#dc3545"])
ax.axhline(0, color="#333", lw=0.8)
ax.set(title="Variance reduction by scenario", ylabel="VR (%)")
for i, k in enumerate(names):
    ax.text(i, vrs[k], f"{vrs[k]:.0f}%", ha="center",
            va="bottom" if vrs[k] >= 0 else "top", fontsize=9)
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The read is intuitive: shifted bumps align almost perfectly; the mixed case leaves real amplitude variance behind (not a failure); pure-amplitude data yields identity warps (VR \(\approx 0\)); and forcing unrelated shapes into register produces little or even negative VR -- a signal to use depth or distance methods instead.

Smooth noisy data first

The SRSF transform differentiates the curve, so measurement noise gets amplified and drives spurious warping. Pre-smooth noisy curves before aligning: with srsf_presmooth (next section), a B-spline basis or a kernel smoother. The aligners do not smooth for you. A minimum of 50--100 grid points is also recommended -- coarse grids limit the dynamic-programming resolution and make the distance asymmetric.

docs.title: Pre-smoothing for SRSFs
docs.text:
srsf_presmooth(data, argvals, smoothing=..., passes=...) returns smoothed curves, and srsf_transform_smoothed their SRSFs, with the two smoothers of fdasrvf:

  • smoothing="box", passes=k: \(k\) passes of a three-point moving average (fdasrvf smooth.data; 25 passes is its default);
  • smoothing="spline": a smoothing spline (fdasrvf f_to_srvf(smooth=TRUE));
  • smoothing="none" (default): unchanged.

Smooth, align the smoothed curves, then apply the warps to whatever version of the curves you need. Below, 20 curves with known smooth warps get white noise; the warps estimated from raw and from pre-smoothed data are applied to the clean curves, so the remaining variance measures how well the phase was recovered:

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
m = 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.01) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.7) ** 2 / 0.006)
clean = np.array([mu(t + rng.uniform(-0.4, 0.4) * t * (1 - t)) for _ in range(20)])
noisy = clean + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(clean.shape)

for label, X in [("raw", noisy),
                 ("box filter, 25 passes", A.srsf_presmooth(noisy, t, smoothing="box", passes=25)),
                 ("smoothing spline", A.srsf_presmooth(noisy, t, smoothing="spline"))]:
    gammas = np.asarray(A.karcher_mean(X, t)["gammas"])
    reg = np.array([A.reparameterize_curve(c, t, g) for c, g in zip(clean, gammas)])
    print(f"{label:22s} variance of the warped clean curves / before: {np.var(reg, 0).mean() / np.var(clean, 0).mean():.4f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

raw                    variance of the warped clean curves / before: 0.0383
box filter, 25 passes  variance of the warped clean curves / before: 0.0060
smoothing spline       variance of the warped clean curves / before: 0.0079
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Warps estimated from the raw noisy curves leave five to six times more phase variance in the signal than warps estimated after either smoother.

docs.title: Multi-bump scaling: a fundamental limit
docs.text:
A single monotone warp cannot independently retime many closely spaced features: stretching one inter-peak interval forces compression of another. Alignment therefore degrades gracefully as the number of independently shifting bumps grows.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import karcher_mean

def vr(data, t):
    aligned = np.asarray(karcher_mean(data, t, max_iter=20, tol=1e-4)["aligned_data"])
    return 100 * (1.0 - np.var(aligned, axis=0).mean() / np.var(data, axis=0).mean())

m = 200
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
n = 16
bump_counts = [2, 4, 6, 8]
scores = []
for nb in bump_counts:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    positions = np.linspace(0.12, 0.88, nb)
    data = np.zeros((n, m))
    for i in range(n):
        for p0 in positions:
            p = p0 + rng.uniform(-0.03, 0.03)
            data[i] += np.exp(-500 * (t - p) ** 2)
    scores.append(vr(data, t))

f, ax = fig()
ax.plot(bump_counts, scores, "o-", color="#3f51b5", lw=2, ms=8)
ax.set(title="Alignment degrades with more independently shifting bumps",
       xlabel="number of bumps", ylabel="VR (%)", ylim=(0, 105))
for x, y in zip(bump_counts, scores):
    ax.text(x, y - 6, f"{y:.0f}%", ha="center", fontsize=9)
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

With a handful of bumps alignment captures nearly all the phase spread; with many tightly packed bumps the monotonicity constraint bites. This is a property of the model, not a numerical artifact -- when features must move independently, a single warp cannot fully separate them.

docs.title: Elastic vs. DTW distance
docs.text:
Dynamic time warping (DTW) is a familiar alternative. Both are \(O(m^2)\) per pair, but DTW allows repeated indices (it can collapse a region to a point), so it is not a proper metric and can absorb amplitude differences into its warping. The elastic distance penalizes such "pinching" -- as \(\dot\gamma\to0\) the SRSF contribution \((q\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\) vanishes rather than concentrating -- so it stays a proper metric and keeps amplitude and phase cleanly separated.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import elastic_self_distance_matrix
from fdars.metric import dtw_self_1d

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n, m = 15, 120
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
data = np.zeros((n, m))
for i in range(n):
    p1 = 0.3 + rng.uniform(-0.06, 0.06)
    p2 = 0.7 + rng.uniform(-0.06, 0.06)
    data[i] = np.exp(-300 * (t - p1) ** 2) + np.exp(-300 * (t - p2) ** 2)

D_el = np.asarray(elastic_self_distance_matrix(data, t, lambda_=0.0))
D_dtw = np.asarray(dtw_self_1d(data))
iu = np.triu_indices(n, k=1)
corr = np.corrcoef(D_el[iu], D_dtw[iu])[0, 1]

f, ax = fig()
ax.scatter(D_el[iu], D_dtw[iu], color="#3f51b5", s=22, alpha=0.7)
ax.set(title=f"Elastic vs. DTW pairwise distances (corr = {corr:.2f})",
       xlabel="elastic distance", ylabel="DTW distance")
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The two distances correlate strongly on clean phase-shifted data. When amplitude variation is added, DTW partially absorbs it and the correlation weakens -- which is exactly why the elastic distance is preferable for downstream clustering or MDS when amplitude and phase carry distinct meaning.

Choosing a method

Use elastic alignment for localized features with independent timing shifts and when you need a principled mean (karcher_mean -- DTW has no equivalent). A plain DTW distance is fine for clustering when the metric property is not required, and is more robust on very noisy signals without pre-smoothing.

Periodic / circular data

karcher_mean and elastic_align_pair keep the end points fixed, \(\gamma(0)=0\), \(\gamma(1)=1\), so they cannot move a feature of a periodic signal across the boundary. For one period of a cyclic signal use elastic_align_pair_closed / karcher_mean_closed, which also search over the starting point; see Advanced Elastic Alignment.

docs.title: Warp statistics and phase boxplots
docs.text:
The warps are the phase. warp_statistics summarizes them -- a mean warp with a confidence band -- and phase_boxplot builds a functional boxplot of the warps that flags phase outliers.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import karcher_mean, warp_statistics, phase_boxplot

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n, m = 30, 100
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
data = np.array([np.sin(2 * np.pi * (t + rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1))) for _ in range(n)])

km = karcher_mean(data, t, max_iter=15)
gammas = np.asarray(km["gammas"])

ws = warp_statistics(gammas, t, confidence_level=0.95)
pb = phase_boxplot(gammas, t, factor=1.5)

f, (a1, a2) = fig(ncols=2, figsize=(9.5, 4.0))
a1.plot(t, gammas.T, color="#adb5bd", lw=0.8, alpha=0.5)
a1.fill_between(t, np.asarray(ws["lower_band"]), np.asarray(ws["upper_band"]),
                color="#3f51b5", alpha=0.18, label="95% band")
a1.plot(t, np.asarray(ws["mean"]), color="#3f51b5", lw=2.2, label="mean warp")
a1.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="#6c757d", ls="--", lw=1.2)
a1.set(title="warp_statistics", xlabel="t", ylabel="$\\gamma(t)$", aspect="equal")
a1.legend(fontsize=8)

a2.fill_between(t, np.asarray(pb["central_lower"]), np.asarray(pb["central_upper"]),
                color="#e8710a", alpha=0.25, label="central 50%")
a2.plot(t, np.asarray(pb["median"]), color="#e8710a", lw=2.2, label="median warp")
a2.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="#6c757d", ls="--", lw=1.2)
a2.set(title=f"phase_boxplot ({len(np.asarray(pb['outlier_indices']))} outliers)",
       xlabel="t", aspect="equal")
a2.legend(fontsize=8)
print(render(f))

print(f"mean geodesic distance of warps from identity: "
      f"{np.asarray(ws['geodesic_distances']).mean():.4f}")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ mean geodesic distance of warps from identity: 0.0794

Both panels summarize the warps themselves -- the phase variation -- against the diagonal identity. The left band shows the spread of individual \(\gamma_i\) around their mean, while the right phase boxplot flags warps whose timing deviates enough to count as outliers. Warps that hug the diagonal barely reparameterize their curve; those that bow away carry large phase shifts, and the printed mean geodesic distance measures that on average.

warp_statistics key Description mean Mean warp variance / std_dev Pointwise spread of the warps lower_band / upper_band Confidence band around the mean warp karcher_mean_warp Karcher-mean warp under the warp geometry geodesic_distances Each warp's distance from the identity, shape (n,) phase_boxplot key Description median / median_index Central (deepest) warp and its index central_lower / central_upper Central-50% envelope whisker_lower / whisker_upper Whisker envelope outlier_indices Warps flagged as phase outliers

Warps far from the identity indicate strong phase variation at those domain locations; curves outside the whiskers are phase outliers.

docs.title: Full example: aligning time-warped growth-like curves
docs.text:
Pulling the pieces together on one dataset -- align, inspect the warps, quantify the variance reduction, and decompose distances.

import numpy as np
from fdars import Fdata
from fdars.alignment import (
    karcher_mean,
    elastic_self_distance_matrix,
    amplitude_distance,
    phase_distance,
    warp_complexity,
    alignment_quality,
)

# --- Simulate: a double-peak template with amplitude + phase perturbations ---
np.random.seed(42)
n, m = 50, 201
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
base = 3 * np.exp(-((t - 0.3) ** 2) / 0.01) + 2 * np.exp(-((t - 0.7) ** 2) / 0.02)

data = np.zeros((n, m))
for i in range(n):
    amp = 1.0 + 0.2 * np.random.randn()
    shift = 0.05 * np.random.randn()
    t_warped = np.clip(t + shift * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t), 0, 1)
    data[i] = amp * np.interp(t, t_warped, base) + 0.1 * np.random.randn(m)

fd = Fdata(data, argvals=t)

# --- Align ---
result = karcher_mean(fd.data, fd.argvals, lambda_=0.1, max_iter=30, tol=1e-5)
print(f"Karcher mean converged: {result['converged']} ({result['n_iter']} iters)")
gammas = np.asarray(result["gammas"])

# --- Warp complexity ---
complexities = np.array([warp_complexity(gammas[i], fd.argvals) for i in range(n)])
print(f"Mean / max warp complexity: {complexities.mean():.4f} / {complexities.max():.4f}")

# --- Variance reduction ---
q = alignment_quality(fd.data, fd.argvals, lambda_=0.1, max_iter=20)
print(f"Variance reduction: {100 * float(q['mean_variance_reduction']):.1f}%")
print(f"Phase / amplitude ratio: {float(q['phase_amplitude_ratio']):.3f}")

# --- Distance decomposition for a pair ---
d_a = amplitude_distance(fd.data[0], fd.data[1], fd.argvals)
d_p = phase_distance(fd.data[0], fd.data[1], fd.argvals)
D = np.asarray(elastic_self_distance_matrix(fd.data, fd.argvals))
print(f"Curves 0 vs 1  amplitude {d_a:.4f}  phase {d_p:.4f}  elastic {D[0, 1]:.4f}")

See Elastic Optimisers & Penalties for DP, RBFGS, penalties and the band; Advanced Alignment for closed, partial, multiresolution and generative tools and the choice of \(\lambda\); Choosing an Alignment Method for when another warp class fits better; Landmark Registration for the classical feature-based approach; TSRVF for linearized statistics on aligned curves; and Shape Analysis for elastic FPCA and depth.

docs.title: Elastic Optimisers & Penalties
docs.text:
Every elastic aligner in fdars solves the same problem: find the warp \(\gamma\) that minimises the distance between one curve's SRSF and the warped SRSF of another, plus an optional penalty on \(\gamma\). How it is solved is configurable. The *_with_config functions (elastic_align_pair_with_config, elastic_distance_with_config, the distance-matrix and Karcher variants, the closed, \(\mathbb{R}^d\), robust and landmark-constrained versions, and align_to_target_with_config) all take the same optimiser keywords:

method="dp", lambda_=0.0, penalty="l2gam", optim_max_iter=30, scl=3,
nbhd_dim=7, dp_scl=1, dp_cost="piecewise_constant", dp_prune=True,
band_frac=0.0, lambda_scale="native"

With the defaults they reproduce the classic functions (elastic_align_pair, karcher_mean, …) bit for bit. This page explains each knob: the dynamic program and its accuracy limits, the Riemannian optimiser, the four warp penalties, the scale of \(\lambda\), and the Sakoe–Chiba band.

Left: the dynamic program searches monotone paths on the grid made of coprime moves (35 moves for nbhd_dim=7, slopes from 1/7 to 7), optionally inside a band. Middle: exact pruning skips a predecessor whose accumulated cost already reaches the target cell's best. Right: RBFGS optimises \(\psi = \sqrt{\dot\gamma}\) on the unit sphere, starting from a coarse DP warp.

docs.title: The objective
docs.text:
With SRSFs \(q_j = \operatorname{sign}(\dot f_j)\sqrt{|\dot f_j|}\), the optimisers minimise

\[ E(\gamma) = \bigl\lVert \bar q_1 - (\bar q_2\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\bigr\rVert^2 + \lambda\,P(\gamma), \]

where \(\bar q_j = q_j/\lVert q_j\rVert\) are the unit-normalised SRSFs. Normalising makes the alignment independent of the overall size of the curves. The reported distance, however, is computed after the search from the un-normalised SRSFs, by re-differentiating the warped curve \(f_2\circ\gamma\); it is the elastic distance in the units of the data.

docs.title: Dynamic programming (method="dp")
docs.text:
The DP discretises \(\gamma\) as a monotone path through the \(m\times m\) grid of index pairs and finds the globally optimal path among those it can represent.

Moves. From each cell the path may step by \((\Delta r, \Delta c)\) with \(1 \le \Delta r, \Delta c \le\) nbhd_dim and \(\gcd(\Delta r, \Delta c) = 1\). The default nbhd_dim=7 gives the classic 35 moves; the slope of the warp on each edge is \(\Delta r/\Delta c\), so slopes lie between 1/7 and 7. A larger neighbourhood contains the smaller one, so the optimum of its own objective can only decrease; the cost grows roughly with the number of moves, \(\approx 0.61\cdot\)nbhd_dim\(^2\).

Edge costs. The integral of \((\bar q_1 - \sqrt{\dot\gamma}\,\bar q_2\circ\gamma)^2\) along each edge is computed with

  • dp_cost="piecewise_constant" (default): SRSFs constant on each grid interval;
  • dp_cost="piecewise_linear": SRSFs linear between samples, integrated exactly. With nbhd_dim=10 this is fdasrsf's DP2;
  • dp_scl=k: resample the SRSFs \(k\) times finer for the edge integrals while the path stays on the input grid (no effect with the piecewise-linear cost).

Exact pruning (dp_prune=True, default). When filling cell \(T\), a predecessor \(s\) whose accumulated cost \(e[s]\) already reaches the best value found for \(T\) cannot win: every edge cost is non-negative, so \(e[s] + w \ge e[T]\). Skipping it without evaluating the edge changes nothing, so the warps are bit-identical to the unpruned fill, at about 1.4–1.6 times the speed. The engine only prunes when the edge costs are guaranteed non-negative (\(\lambda \ge 0\), strictly increasing argvals).

The residual floor. Because the slopes are quantised, the DP cannot represent a smooth warp exactly, and even an exactly warped copy of a curve keeps a non-zero distance. The floor shrinks with a finer neighbourhood, a better edge cost and a finer grid, and RBFGS removes most of it:

import time
import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.01) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.7) ** 2 / 0.006)
configs = {
    "DP  (nbhd_dim=7)":        dict(),
    "DP2 (nbhd_dim=10, pw-lin)": dict(nbhd_dim=10, dp_cost="piecewise_linear"),
    "RBFGS":                   dict(method="rbfgs"),
}
for m in (101, 201):
    t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
    f, g = mu(t), mu(t + 0.3 * t * (1 - t))           # g is an exactly warped copy of f
    for name, cfg in configs.items():
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        d = A.elastic_distance_with_config(f, g, t, **cfg)
        print(f"m={m}  {name:27s} distance {d:.4f}   {1e3 * (time.perf_counter() - t0):5.1f} ms")

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
a = A.elastic_align_pair_with_config(mu(t), mu(t + 0.3 * t * (1 - t)), t, dp_prune=True)
b = A.elastic_align_pair_with_config(mu(t), mu(t + 0.3 * t * (1 - t)), t, dp_prune=False)
print(f"pruning on vs off: identical warps = {np.array_equal(a['gamma'], b['gamma'])}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

m=101  DP  (nbhd_dim=7)            distance 0.1036     5.2 ms
m=101  DP2 (nbhd_dim=10, pw-lin)   distance 0.0626    27.3 ms
m=101  RBFGS                       distance 0.0375     3.2 ms
m=201  DP  (nbhd_dim=7)            distance 0.0580    20.7 ms
m=201  DP2 (nbhd_dim=10, pw-lin)   distance 0.0299   114.7 ms
m=201  RBFGS                       distance 0.0206     5.3 ms
pruning on vs off: identical warps = True
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The true distance is 0. On these sharp two-bump curves DP2 cuts the default DP's floor by 40–50 %, and RBFGS by about 65 %, while being the fastest of the three on a single pair. Doubling the grid roughly halves every floor. On smoother curves all floors are lower.

docs.title: RBFGS (method="rbfgs")
docs.text:
RBFGS is a Riemannian limited-memory BFGS (a port of fdasrsf's optimum_reparam(method="RBFGS"), after Huang, Gallivan, Srivastava & Absil). It represents the warp by \(\psi = \sqrt{\dot\gamma}\), which lies on the unit sphere of \(L^2[0,1]\) because \(\int\psi^2 = \gamma(1) - \gamma(0) = 1\), and optimises directly over smooth warps:

  1. Seed. A DP warp on a coarse grid (at most 51 points) gives the starting point; with a band, the banded DP on the full grid does.
  2. Refine. The SRSFs are resampled scl times finer (default 3) and L-BFGS steps along the sphere run for at most optim_max_iter iterations (default 30).
  3. Restart. When penalised (\(\lambda > 0\)), it is also started from the identity (\(\psi = 1\)) and the lower-cost result is kept.

It is a local optimiser: it usually reaches a lower cost than the DP and returns smooth warps, but it can settle in a different local minimum than the globally optimal DP path. Use it

  • when DP warps look jagged or have long flat (pinched) stretches,
  • to get below the DP residual floor,
  • for the "roughness" and "geodesic" penalties, which only RBFGS supports,
  • in landmark-constrained alignment, where it refines each segment between landmarks.

docs.title: Warp penalties
docs.text:
penalty chooses \(P(\gamma)\), weighted by lambda_:

penalty \(P(\gamma)\) DP RBFGS Penalises "l2gam" (default) \(\int(\dot\gamma - 1)^2\) yes yes departure of the speed from 1 (the classic fdars penalty) "l2psi" \(\int(\sqrt{\dot\gamma} - 1)^2\) yes yes the same on the \(\psi\) scale (fdasrsf's default) "roughness" \(\int\ddot\gamma^2\) — yes curvature of the warp: allows a constant change of speed, forbids wiggles "geodesic" \(\arccos\bigl(\int\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\bigr)^2\) — yes squared Fisher–Rao distance of \(\gamma\) from the identity

A DP can only add penalties that are sums of a function of the slope over its edges, which is why "roughness" (concentrated at the corners of the piecewise-linear path) and "geodesic" (a non-linear function of a global integral) need RBFGS; method="dp" with either of them and \(\lambda > 0\) raises ValueError.

elastic_align_pair_penalized is deprecated

Its penalty_type="second_order" and "combined" options smooth the DP warp after the search instead of penalising the objective. Use elastic_align_pair_with_config(method="rbfgs", penalty="roughness", lambda_=...).

The effect of \(\lambda\) on a noisy pair of curves, for the default penalty under both optimisers and for the roughness penalty. warp_smoothness is the bending energy \(\int\ddot\gamma^2\) of the warp and warp_complexity its geodesic distance from the identity:

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.01) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.7) ** 2 / 0.006)
m = 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
f = mu(t) + 0.03 * rng.standard_normal(m)
g = mu(t + 0.3 * t * (1 - t)) + 0.03 * rng.standard_normal(m)

def row(label, **cfg):
    r = A.elastic_align_pair_with_config(f, g, t, **cfg)
    print(f"{label:30s} bending {A.warp_smoothness(r['gamma'], t):8.1f}   "
          f"complexity {A.warp_complexity(r['gamma'], t):.3f}   distance {r['distance']:.3f}")

for lam in (0.0, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0):
    row(f"l2gam  dp    lambda={lam:g}", lambda_=lam)
    row(f"l2gam  rbfgs lambda={lam:g}", method="rbfgs", lambda_=lam)
for lam in (1e-4, 1e-2):
    row(f"roughness rbfgs lambda={lam:g}", method="rbfgs", penalty="roughness", lambda_=lam)
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

l2gam  dp    lambda=0          bending  10204.1   complexity 0.319   distance 1.017
l2gam  rbfgs lambda=0          bending   5107.1   complexity 0.340   distance 0.760
l2gam  dp    lambda=0.01       bending    738.2   complexity 0.150   distance 0.894
l2gam  rbfgs lambda=0.01       bending    304.2   complexity 0.133   distance 0.782
l2gam  dp    lambda=0.1        bending     36.0   complexity 0.070   distance 1.338
l2gam  rbfgs lambda=0.1        bending      5.2   complexity 0.066   distance 1.287
l2gam  dp    lambda=1          bending      0.0   complexity 0.000   distance 2.273
l2gam  rbfgs lambda=1          bending      0.1   complexity 0.021   distance 1.956
roughness rbfgs lambda=0.0001  bending      1.4   complexity 0.093   distance 1.008
roughness rbfgs lambda=0.01    bending      0.1   complexity 0.059   distance 1.472
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Reading it (the true warp has complexity 0.087 and bending energy 0.56):

  • At \(\lambda = 0\) both optimisers chase the noise: complexity 0.32–0.34, four times the truth, with huge bending energy (the DP's twice the RBFGS's).
  • l2gam with \(\lambda = 0.01\) cuts the bending by more than an order of magnitude but the warp is still too large (0.13–0.15); at \(\lambda = 0.1\) it is too small, and at \(\lambda = 1\) it collapses to the identity. The penalty shrinks the size and the roughness of the warp together.
  • The roughness penalty only targets the wiggles: at \(\lambda = 10^{-4}\) it returns a warp with the true complexity (0.093) and bending energy (1.4). It lives on a different scale, an absolute \(\int\ddot\gamma^2\): at \(10^{-2}\) it already flattens the warp, and on narrow features values like 0.1 give an essentially identity warp.
  • The reported distance is not monotone in \(\lambda\): it is the post-hoc un-normalised elastic distance, not the penalised objective.

docs.title: The scale of \(\lambda\)
docs.text:
The two optimisers read \(\lambda\) in slightly different conventions. The DP penalises in the fdars convention: edge costs on unit-norm SRSFs, integrated in argvals units. RBFGS follows fdasrsf: SRSFs resampled scl times finer, with fdasrsf's lamScale weighting. The objectives coincide when \(\lambda_{\text{rbfgs}} = \varphi\,\lambda_{\text{dp}}\), with a data-dependent factor \(\varphi\):

  • for 1-D curves \(\varphi = 1 + O(1/m)\): the conventions nearly coincide;
  • for \(\mathbb{R}^d\) curve shapes (raw, un-normalised SRVFs) \(\varphi \approx 1/(m\,\lVert q_1\rVert\,\lVert q_2\rVert)\): the same number means a very different strength.

lambda_scale removes the ambiguity: "native" (default) lets each optimiser read \(\lambda\) in its own convention; "dp" declares \(\lambda\) to be in the DP convention (RBFGS uses \(\varphi\lambda\)); "fdasrsf" declares it in the fdasrsf convention (DP uses \(\lambda/\varphi\)). Use "dp" or "fdasrsf" when you tune \(\lambda\) under one optimiser and switch to the other, or when you reproduce fdasrsf results. "roughness" and "geodesic" exist only under RBFGS and are never converted.

Even with a fixed convention, \(\lambda\) is not transferable between datasets: the data term is the distance between normalised SRSFs, whose size depends on how different the curves are. Choose it per dataset:

  • lambda_cv(data, argvals, lambdas) scores candidates by cross-validation. It is biased toward small \(\lambda\) and often returns the smallest candidate; treat its answer as a lower bound.
  • peak_persistence(data, argvals, lambdas) picks the \(\lambda\) at which the number of peaks of the Karcher mean is stable, useful when the number of features is what matters.
  • Look at the warps: bending energy, complexity, and whether long flat stretches (pinching) remain.

Both selectors are demonstrated on Advanced Elastic Alignment.

docs.title: The Sakoe–Chiba band (band_frac)
docs.text:
band_frac > 0 restricts the warp to a corridor around the identity: the index radius is \(R = \lceil \texttt{band\_frac}\cdot m\rceil\), so \(|\gamma(t) - t| \le R\,h\) on a uniform grid of spacing \(h\).

  • DP confines the path to \(|r - c| \le R\): it is exact within the band and costs about \(O(m R)\) instead of \(O(m^2)\).
  • RBFGS starts from the banded DP, runs unconstrained, then clamps the warp pointwise into the band (a clamp between two increasing bounds keeps it monotone) and returns the better of the clamped RBFGS warp and the DP seed. The result satisfies the band and is never worse than the banded DP; the band mainly speeds up the seed.
  • The landmark-constrained and curve-shape functions reject band_frac > 0.

The band is a constraint on the model, not only a speed-up: if the true displacement exceeds it, the warps are clipped and the alignment degrades.

import time
import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.35) ** 2 / 0.01) + 0.7 * np.exp(-(s - 0.7) ** 2 / 0.006)
m = 201
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = np.array([mu(t + rng.uniform(-0.4, 0.4) * t * (1 - t)) for _ in range(20)])   # |gamma - t| up to 0.1

ref = None
for bf in (0.0, 0.3, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    r = A.karcher_mean_with_config(X, t, band_frac=bf, max_iter=10)
    dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
    ref = r if ref is None else ref
    ratio = np.var(r["aligned_data"], 0).mean() / np.var(X, 0).mean()
    print(f"band_frac={bf:<4}  {dt:5.2f} s   variance after/before {ratio:.4f}   "
          f"max |mean - unbanded mean| {np.abs(r['mean'] - ref['mean']).max():.4f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

band_frac=0.0    1.12 s   variance after/before 0.0010   max |mean - unbanded mean| 0.0000
band_frac=0.3    0.63 s   variance after/before 0.0010   max |mean - unbanded mean| 0.0000
band_frac=0.1    0.23 s   variance after/before 0.0010   max |mean - unbanded mean| 0.0000
band_frac=0.05   0.13 s   variance after/before 0.0778   max |mean - unbanded mean| 0.0282
band_frac=0.02   0.06 s   variance after/before 0.4610   max |mean - unbanded mean| 0.1424
FDARS_FENCE_OK

While the band contains the true displacement (about 0.1 here), the banded Karcher mean is identical to the unbanded one and up to four times faster. At band_frac=0.05 the warps are clipped, 8 % of the variance stays, and the mean changes; at 0.02 the alignment mostly fails. Choose band_frac above the largest plausible displacement, or pre-align large shifts with a shift model. Banded Elastic Alignment has more on the band and the older *_with_band functions.

docs.title: Which optimiser?
docs.text:
Situation Setting Default; reference results; global optimum among quantised warps method="dp" fdasrsf parity, lower residual floor at DP's guarantees nbhd_dim=10, dp_cost="piecewise_linear" (DP2) Smooth warps, lowest cost, exact constrained segments method="rbfgs" Noisy curves \(\lambda > 0\) with "l2gam" (DP or RBFGS) or "roughness" (RBFGS), after pre-smoothing Long curves with small phase band_frac above the largest displacement Tuning \(\lambda\) under one optimiser, running under another lambda_scale="dp" or "fdasrsf"

RBFGS is not only more accurate: for group alignment it can also be faster than DP, because its coarse DP seed is cheap. In the band example above, karcher_mean_with_config(X, t, method="rbfgs") takes about a third of the unbanded DP's time.
