docs.title: Non-Gaussian Registration
docs.text:
Accelerometers record whether a person is active minute by minute (0/1). Neurons fire counts per time bin. Disease registries record yes/no states per visit. These are functional data with binary, count or positive-skewed values, and they have phase variability like any other: people get up at different times, trials start with different latencies. Aligning them with SRSF or least-squares methods does not work well: the raw values are discrete, derivatives are meaningless, and smoothing them first to "proportions" or \(\log\) counts throws information away and distorts the timing near 0 and 1.

register_fpca registers such curves on the likelihood scale. It is a port of the R package registr (Wrobel et al. 2019; Wrobel & Bauer 2021): each curve's time axis is warped so that its observations are most likely under an exponential-family model whose mean is a smooth template, and the template itself is a generalised functional principal component (GFPCA) model estimated jointly. It also handles irregular grids and curves cut off at the start or the end.

Binary curves registered on the logit scale by estimating inverse warps \(h_i^{-1}\).

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
For curve \(i\) observed at times \(t^*_{ij}\),

\[ g\bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y_i(t^*)]\bigr) = \theta_i\bigl(h_i^{-1}(t^*)\bigr), \qquad \theta_i(t) = \Theta(t)^\top(\alpha + \psi\, s_i), \]

with

  • \(g\) the canonical link of the chosen family: "gaussian" (identity), "binomial" (logit; values in \([0, 1]\)), "poisson" (log; values \(\ge 0\)), "gamma" (log; values \(> 0\), per-curve scale);
  • \(\Theta\) a cubic B-spline basis of size kt (default 8), \(\alpha\) the population mean coefficients, \(\psi\) the FPC coefficients and \(s_i \sim N(0, I)\) the subject scores (npc components, default 1);
  • \(h_i^{-1}\) the inverse warp: it maps the observed ("chronological") time \(t^*\) to the registered ("template") time. It is a monotone cubic B-spline with kh coefficients (default 4) on the curve's own observed range, with inner knots at quantiles of its time points.

This method estimates the inverse warp

Most aligners return a warp \(h_i\) with registered curve \(x_i(h_i(t))\). register_fpca returns \(\hat t_{ij} = h_i^{-1}(t^*_{ij})\) (registration["t_hat"], one array per curve): the registered time at which each observation sits. To plot registered data, plot \(Y_{ij}\) against \(\hat t_{ij}\) (or use registered_argvals / registered_values). evaluate_inverse_warp(hinv_beta[i], hinv_inner_knots[i], t_lo, t_hi, t) evaluates \(h_i^{-1}\) anywhere on the curve's range.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
register_fpca alternates registration and GFPCA:

  1. Template. A spline GLM \(g(\mathbb{E}[Y]) = \Theta^\top c\) is fitted to all observations pooled (iteratively reweighted least squares). The time range of template (default: the data) must equal the data's.
  2. Registration (register_expfam is this step alone). For every curve, the coefficients of \(h_i^{-1}\) maximise the curve's log-likelihood under the template. registr does this with a log-barrier constrOptim; fdars reparametrises the coefficients through a softmax of increments (so every candidate is strictly monotone) and uses L-BFGS with analytic gradients for all four families. Losses are therefore at most R's, and warps are strictly monotone.
  3. GFPCA of the registered data (see below).
  4. Re-registration. Every curve is re-registered to its own fitted curve \(\Theta^\top(\alpha + \psi\,\hat s_i)\), warm-started from the previous warp. This separates amplitude (the score \(s_i\)) from phase: a curve that is simply more active is not warped to look like the mean.
  5. Repeat 3–4 until the mean squared change of \(\hat t / t_{\max}\) is at most \(10^{-4}\), or for max_iterations (default 10), then run a final GFPCA.

docs.title: Two GFPCA engines
docs.text:
fpca_type Method Families Cost "variational_em" (default) registr bfpca / fpca_gauss: EM with the Jaakkola–Jordan variational bound for binary data (one variational parameter per observation), exact EM for Gaussian data likelihood-based for gaussian and binomial only; poisson and gamma data are treated as gaussian on the data scale, as in R fast "two_step" registr gfpca_twoStep (Gertheiss et al. 2017): (1) smooth covariance on the latent scale (Hall, Müller & Yao 2008: P-spline GLM mean, tensor-spline smooth of the off-diagonal cross-products, delta-method transform, near-PD projection); (2) eigen-decomposition; (3) scores and mean from a GLMM fitted natively (REML for gaussian, Laplace otherwise) family-specific for all four families much slower

Prefer "two_step" for Poisson and gamma data when the GFPCA itself matters; for registration alone the variational EM is usually enough (see the example below). npc_var_explained (and npc_min_component_share) choose the number of components by explained variance, registr's npc_criterion.

docs.title: Registering binary and count curves
docs.text:
Thirty curves are generated from a common latent template \(\theta\) evaluated at a known inverse warp, \(Y_i(t^*) \sim \text{Bernoulli}\bigl(\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\theta(h_i^{-1}(t^*))\bigr)\), and likewise with Poisson counts and a log link. The table compares the recovered inverse warps with the truth (mean absolute error after removing the common part, \(\times 10^{-3}\)), for register_fpca and for the usual workaround: smooth each curve, transform it to the logit or log scale, and align with the elastic Karcher mean.

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

def simulate(family, m, rng, n=30):
    t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
    theta = (lambda s: 3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * s) - 0.5) if family == "binomial" else \
            (lambda s: 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * s) + 0.5)
    Y, Hinv = [], []
    for _ in range(n):
        hinv = t + rng.uniform(-0.6, 0.6) * t * (1 - t)        # true inverse warp
        eta = theta(hinv)
        Y.append(rng.binomial(1, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-eta))) if family == "binomial" else rng.poisson(np.exp(eta)))
        Hinv.append(hinv)
    return t, np.array(Y, float), np.array(Hinv)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print("family     m    register_fpca   smooth + elastic   no registration")
for family in ("binomial", "poisson"):
    for m in (100, 200):
        t, Y, Hinv = simulate(family, m, rng)
        err = lambda T: 1000 * np.abs((T - T.mean(0)) - (Hinv - Hinv.mean(0))).mean()

        r = A.register_fpca_regular(Y, t, family=family)
        T = np.array([np.asarray(x) for x in r["registration"]["t_hat"]])

        K = np.exp(-0.5 * ((t[:, None] - t[None, :]) / 0.06) ** 2)   # Gaussian kernel smoother
        S = Y @ (K / K.sum(1, keepdims=True)).T
        S = np.log((S + 0.02) / (1.02 - S)) if family == "binomial" else np.log(S + 0.5)
        G = np.asarray(A.karcher_mean(S, t)["gammas"])
        Te = np.array([np.interp(t, g, t) for g in G])               # elastic warp -> inverse warp

        print(f"{family:9s} {m:4d}   {err(T):13.1f}   {err(Te):16.1f}   {err(np.tile(t, (len(Y), 1))):15.1f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

family     m    register_fpca   smooth + elastic   no registration
binomial   100            23.6               33.2              45.5
binomial   200            19.9               25.7              44.5
poisson    100            16.4               20.8              39.1
poisson    200            10.8               17.4              47.8
FDARS_FENCE_OK

register_fpca recovers the warps best in every setting, with 20–40 % lower error than the smoothing workaround. With more observations per curve both approaches improve. (The elastic warp \(\gamma_i\) registers \(x_i(\gamma_i(t))\), so its inverse is the comparable quantity.)

docs.title: Variational EM or two-step?
docs.text:
Count curves whose level also varies between subjects (a random intercept on the log scale, recovered as the first GFPCA score):

import time
import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fast
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n, m = 30, 100
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
Y, Hinv, level = [], [], []
for _ in range(n):
    hinv = t + rng.uniform(-0.6, 0.6) * t * (1 - t)
    s = rng.normal(0, 0.5)                                   # subject-level amplitude
    Y.append(rng.poisson(np.exp(1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * hinv) + 0.5 + s)))
    Hinv.append(hinv)
    level.append(s)
Y, Hinv, level = np.array(Y, float), np.array(Hinv), np.array(level)

for fpca_type in fast(("variational_em", "two_step"), ("variational_em",)):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    r = A.register_fpca_regular(Y, t, family="poisson", fpca_type=fpca_type, npc=1)
    T = np.array([np.asarray(x) for x in r["registration"]["t_hat"]])
    err = 1000 * np.abs((T - T.mean(0)) - (Hinv - Hinv.mean(0))).mean()
    score = np.asarray(r["fpca"]["scores"])[:, 0]
    print(f"{fpca_type:15s} GFPCA family {r['fpca']['em_family']:8s} warp error {err:5.1f}"
          f"  |corr(score, level)| {abs(np.corrcoef(score, level)[0, 1]):.3f}"
          f"  ({time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s)")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

variational_em  GFPCA family gaussian warp error  34.5  |corr(score, level)| 0.954  (0.1 s)
two_step        GFPCA family poisson  warp error  33.0  |corr(score, level)| 0.980  (15.3 s)
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Both engines recover the subject levels (correlation above 0.95) and similar warps. The variational EM reports em_family = "gaussian": it modelled the counts as Gaussian on the data scale. The two-step fit is Poisson-specific and slightly more accurate here, at more than a hundred times the run time. (In local DOCS_FAST builds only the variational EM runs.)

docs.title: Incomplete curves
docs.text:
A curve can stop before the process it records has finished (a recording that ends early), or start late. With incompleteness="trailing", "leading" or "full" the corresponding end(s) of \(h_i^{-1}\) are free: the curve's last observation does not have to map to the end of the template. Free ends are weakly identified, so the negative log-likelihood is penalised by \(n_i \cdot \lambda_{\text{inc}} \cdot \text{pen}\), where pen is the squared offset of the free end from the diagonal (or the squared difference in span for "full"), as in registr's loss_h. Incompleteness is not available with warping="piecewise_linear2".

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A
from fdars.pace_fpca import irreg_fdata_from_lists

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, m = 30, 150
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
times, values, true_hinv = [], [], []
for _ in range(n):
    hinv = t + rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) * t * (1 - t)
    y = rng.poisson(np.exp(1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * hinv) + 0.5)).astype(float)
    end = rng.integers(int(0.6 * m), m)                 # recording stops between 60% and 100%
    times.append(t[:end]); values.append(y[:end]); true_hinv.append(hinv[:end])
data = irreg_fdata_from_lists(times, values)

print("incompleteness  lambda_inc   warp error   end-point error   (x 1e-3)")
for inc, lam in [(None, 0.0), ("trailing", 0.0), ("trailing", 1.0), ("trailing", 10.0)]:
    r = A.register_fpca(data, family="poisson", incompleteness=inc, lambda_inc=lam)
    T = [np.asarray(x) for x in r["registration"]["t_hat"]]
    warp = 1000 * np.mean([np.abs(a - h).mean() for a, h in zip(T, true_hinv)])
    end = 1000 * np.mean([abs(a[-1] - h[-1]) for a, h in zip(T, true_hinv)])
    print(f"{str(inc):14s} {lam:10.1f}   {warp:10.1f}   {end:15.1f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

incompleteness  lambda_inc   warp error   end-point error   (x 1e-3)
None                  0.0         17.2              35.9
trailing              0.0         23.1              60.8
trailing              1.0         17.4              28.6
trailing             10.0         17.1              31.8
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Two lessons:

  • A free end needs a penalty. With \(\lambda_{\text{inc}} = 0\) the free end chases noise and the warps get worse than pretending the curves were complete.
  • With a moderate penalty (\(\lambda_{\text{inc}} \approx 1\)) the end points are estimated better than under the complete-curve assumption, while the overall warp error stays the same. The gain is modest here because the true inverse warps do not move the end far from the diagonal; it grows when curves stop at very different stages of the process.

Treat \(\lambda_{\text{inc}}\) as a tuning parameter: try a few values on a log scale and inspect where the free ends land.

docs.title: Piecewise-linear warps with priors
docs.text: warping="piecewise_linear2" replaces the B-spline by registr's two-knot polygon \((0,0) \to (x_1,y_1) \to (x_2,y_2) \to (1,1)\) on each curve's range scaled to \([0,1]\), with \(x_1 \ge 0.1\), \(x_2 - x_1 \ge 0.1\), \(x_2 \le 0.9\) (and the same for \(y\)). The binary likelihood is multimodal in these four numbers, so the optimiser adds a coarse grid start and a Nelder–Mead polish. For binomial data, prior_sd puts normal priors on the knots (means 0.25, 0.25, 0.75, 0.75). With this warping, t_hat is on the scaled domain. Use it when you want an interpretable, low-dimensional warp ("the morning came 40 minutes later").

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Effect family "gaussian" "binomial", "poisson", "gamma" kh 4 B-spline size of the inverse warp (≥ 4); more = more flexible warps warping "nonparametric" or "piecewise_linear2" prior_sd None knot prior (binomial + piecewise_linear2 only) incompleteness, lambda_inc None, 0 free ends and their penalty max_iterations 10 registration ⇄ GFPCA rounds warp_max_iter, warp_tol, gamma_scale_init 500, 1e-12, 1.5 per-curve optimiser fpca_type "variational_em" or "two_step" npc, kt 1, 8 GFPCA components and spline size (kt is also the template size) npc_var_explained, npc_min_component_share None choose npc by explained variance fpca_max_iter, error_thresh, seed 50, 1e-4, 1988 EM controls; psi_init, xi_init fix the random start periodic False periodic B-spline bases

Entry points:

  • register_fpca(data, template=None, ...) for an irregular data object from fdars.pace_fpca.irreg_fdata_from_lists(times, values); register_fpca_regular(data, argvals, ...) for a dense \((n, m)\) matrix.
  • register_expfam(data, ...): one registration pass to the population template, without GFPCA.
  • gfpca_variational(data, family, ...), gfpca_two_step(data, family, ...): GFPCA alone, without registration.

Results: registration (t_hat, hinv_beta, hinv_inner_knots, curve_loss, loss, template_knots, template_coefs, per-curve converged), fpca (mean, efunctions, evalues, scores, fitted, em_family, ...), registered_data (an irregular data object), registered_argvals, registered_values, iterations, converged, registration_loss.

Reproducing R

The random initialisation of the EM uses a different generator from R, so results agree with registr only up to the EM tolerance; pass psi_init / xi_init to fix the start. registr's subsampling of more than \(10^7\) rows is not ported.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Use it for binary, count or positive-skewed curves with phase variability; for irregular grids; for curves that stop early or start late; when you want the GFPCA of the registered data in the same step.
  • Prefer elastic or continuous registration for dense, roughly Gaussian curves: with family="gaussian" this model works, but the elastic and Ramsay–Li methods give metrics, amplitude/phase decompositions and smoother warp classes.
  • Check the warps. With few observations per curve or a nearly flat template, the likelihood carries little information about timing; inspect t_hat against the observed times.

docs.title: Landmark Registration
docs.text:
Landmark registration is the oldest and most transparent way to remove phase variation: identify a handful of landmarks on each curve (a peak, a valley, a zero crossing, an inflection) and warp every curve so that its landmarks land at common target times. You dictate the correspondence rather than search for it. That makes the result fast and interpretable ("this child's growth spurt happened 1.3 years after the average"), at the cost of needing features that can be detected reliably.

It is the natural choice for curves with meaningful, identifiable features: the peak of the pubertal growth spurt, the P/QRS/T waves of an ECG, the peak force of a gait cycle. Where elastic alignment optimises the whole curve, landmark registration anchors the warp at a few feature times and fills in between with a smooth monotone curve. A hybrid, landmark-constrained elastic alignment, pins the landmarks and optimises the elastic criterion between them.

From left to right: peaks found by detect_landmarks and matched by order; the steps of landmark_register; the resulting warps \(\gamma_i\), which pass exactly through the knots \((\tau_k^\*, t_{ik})\) and are smooth monotone cubics between them; and the registered curves \(x_i(\gamma_i(t))\) with every landmark on its target.

docs.title: The functions
docs.text: Function Does detect_landmarks(curve, argvals, kind="peak", min_prominence=0.0) Finds features in one curve: kind is "peak", "valley", "zero_crossing", "inflection" or "custom". Returns a list of dicts with position, kind, value, prominence, in time order. landmark_register(data, argvals, landmarks, target=None) Warps each curve so that its landmarks (one list per curve) map to target (default: per-landmark mean). Returns registered, gammas, landmarks, target_landmarks. landmark_detect_and_register(data, argvals, kind="peak", min_prominence=0.0, expected_count=1) Detection plus registration in one call, using the first expected_count features of each curve (raises ValueError if a curve has fewer). elastic_align_pair_constrained_with_config(f1, f2, argvals, landmark_targets, landmark_sources, ...) Elastic (SRSF) alignment of f2 to f1 whose warp passes through given landmark pairs.

docs.title: The warp
docs.text:
Given landmark times \(t_{i1} < \dots < t_{iK}\) on curve \(i\) and targets \(\tau_1^\* < \dots < \tau_K^\*\), the warp \(\gamma_i\) maps target time to source time and must satisfy

\[ \gamma_i(\tau_k^\*) = t_{ik}, \qquad \gamma_i(a) = a, \qquad \gamma_i(b) = b, \]

so that the registered curve \(\tilde x_i(t) = x_i(\gamma_i(t))\) shows landmark \(k\) at \(\tau_k^\*\). fdars builds \(\gamma_i\) as a monotone piecewise-cubic Hermite interpolant (Fritsch–Carlson) through the knots \((a, a), (\tau_1^\*, t_{i1}), \dots, (\tau_K^\*, t_{iK}), (b, b)\):

  1. Start from tangent slopes \(d_j\) at the knots.
  2. On each interval with secant slope \(\Delta_j\), set \(\alpha = d_j/\Delta_j\) and \(\beta = d_{j+1}/\Delta_j\). If \(\alpha^2 + \beta^2 > 9\), scale both tangents by \(3/\sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2}\). This is the Fritsch–Carlson condition that guarantees the cubic on that interval is monotone.
  3. Evaluate the Hermite cubic on every interval.

Unlike the piecewise-linear warp of the classical textbook recipe, the result has a continuous first derivative, so the registered curves have no kinks at the landmarks. Like it, the warp interpolates the landmarks exactly: there is no optimisation and no residual.

docs.title: The targets
docs.text: By default \(\tau_k^\* = \frac1n\sum_i t_{ik}\), the per-landmark mean, which keeps the registered sample near the "average" timing. Any fixed target works, for example the landmarks of a reference curve or round numbers.

docs.title: Prominence
docs.text: A peak at \(t_0\) has prominence \(x(t_0) - \max\bigl(\min_{[t_L, t_0]} x, \min_{[t_0, t_R]} x\bigr)\), where \(t_L, t_R\) are the nearest higher peaks (or the domain ends). A bump on the flank of a big peak has low prominence; an isolated peak has high prominence. min_prominence discards features below a threshold; valleys are peaks of \(-x\).

docs.title: Example: the pubertal growth spurt
docs.text:
The Berkeley growth data contain the heights of 93 children at 31 ages. The velocity (first derivative) has a peak, the pubertal growth spurt, whose timing varies by years between children. We take 15 boys and 15 girls, compute velocities on ages 8–18 from a cubic spline, pick each child's most prominent velocity peak, and register on it.

import numpy as np
from scipy.interpolate import CubicSpline
from docs_data import load_growth
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars import alignment as A

age, X, meta = load_growth()
idx = np.r_[0:15, 39:54]                       # 15 boys, 15 girls
t = np.linspace(8, 18, 101)
V = np.array([CubicSpline(age, x)(t, 1) for x in X[idx]])   # velocity, cm/year

# one landmark per child: the most prominent velocity peak (the spurt)
peaks = [A.detect_landmarks(v, t, kind="peak", min_prominence=1.0) for v in V]
L = [[max(p, key=lambda d: d["prominence"])["position"]] for p in peaks]

res = A.landmark_register(V, t, L)
R, G = np.asarray(res["registered"]), np.asarray(res["gammas"])
tau = res["target_landmarks"][0]

f, (a1, a2, a3) = fig(ncols=3, figsize=(11, 3.6))
a1.plot(t, V.T, color="#3f51b5", lw=0.8, alpha=0.5)
a1.plot(t, V.mean(0), color="#dc3545", lw=2.2, label="mean")
a1.set(title="Velocity (spurts drift)", xlabel="age", ylabel="cm / year")
a1.legend(fontsize=8)
a2.plot(t, R.T, color="#198754", lw=0.8, alpha=0.5)
a2.plot(t, R.mean(0), color="#e8710a", lw=2.2, label="mean")
a2.axvline(tau, color="#6c757d", ls=":", lw=1)
a2.set(title="Registered on the spurt", xlabel="registered age")
a2.legend(fontsize=8)
a3.plot(t, G.T, color="#6f42c1", lw=0.9, alpha=0.6)
a3.plot(t, t, color="#6c757d", ls="--", lw=1.2)
a3.set(title="Warps $\\gamma_i$", xlabel="registered age", ylabel="original age", aspect="equal")
print(render(f))

hit = max(abs(np.interp(tau, t, g) - l[0]) for g, l in zip(G, L))
print(f"<p>target spurt age {tau:.2f}; max |gamma_i(target) - landmark_i| = {hit:.1e}; "
      f"variance after/before = {np.var(R, 0).mean() / np.var(V, 0).mean():.2f}; "
      f"height of the mean peak {V.mean(0).max():.1f} -> {R.mean(0).max():.1f} cm/year "
      f"(average individual peak {np.mean(V.max(1)):.1f})</p>")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

target spurt age 12.83; max |gamma_i(target) - landmark_i| = 7.7e-04; variance after/before = 0.49; height of the mean peak 6.1 -> 8.7 cm/year (average individual peak 8.9)

The unregistered mean (left) is a low, broad hump: it averages spurts that happen between ages 11 and 15. After registration the mean spurt reaches almost the average individual peak height, and the warps (right) show who matured early (below the diagonal near the target) or late (above). The sampled warps pass through their knots to better than \(10^{-3}\) years (the warp is exact at the knot; the residual is linear interpolation between grid points). About half of the variance remains: the spurts differ in size and duration, which a single landmark cannot and should not remove.

docs.title: Automatic detection: check what was matched
docs.text:
landmark_detect_and_register is convenient, but it pairs features by order: it keeps the first expected_count detected features of each curve, in time order, and registers them. Two consequences:

  • A spurious early feature (a pre-pubertal bump) becomes "landmark 1" for that curve, and every later pairing shifts.
  • Every curve must have at least expected_count detected features (default 1). If one has fewer, the call raises ValueError rather than registering on mismatched landmarks; expected_count=0 is rejected too.
import numpy as np
from scipy.interpolate import CubicSpline
from docs_data import load_growth
from fdars import alignment as A

age, X, meta = load_growth()
t = np.linspace(8, 18, 101)
V = np.array([CubicSpline(age, x)(t, 1) for x in X[np.r_[0:15, 39:54]]])
ratio = lambda R: np.var(np.asarray(R), 0).mean() / np.var(V, 0).mean()

counts = [len(A.detect_landmarks(v, t, kind="peak", min_prominence=1.0)) for v in V]
print(f"peaks detected per curve: {counts}")
r = A.landmark_detect_and_register(V, t, kind="peak", min_prominence=1.0, expected_count=1)
print(f"expected_count=1: target {np.round(r['target_landmarks'], 2)}, variance after/before {ratio(r['registered']):.2f}")
try:
    A.landmark_detect_and_register(V, t, kind="peak", min_prominence=1.0, expected_count=2)
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"expected_count=2: ValueError: {e}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

peaks detected per curve: [2, 2, 2, 1, 2, 4, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 1, 1, 3, 1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1]
expected_count=1: target [11.48], variance after/before 0.95
expected_count=2: ValueError: curve 3 has only 1 detected landmark(s) but expected_count=2; lower expected_count or min_prominence
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Between one and four velocity peaks are detected per child. With expected_count=1 the first peak (often a small bump before the spurt) is registered, so the target lands at 11.5 years and the variance barely moves (0.95). Choosing the most prominent peak, as in the previous example, targets 12.8 years and halves it. Inspect the detections, choose the landmarks yourself when the features are ambiguous, and pass them to landmark_register.

Inconsistent input returns identity warps

landmark_register does not raise on inconsistent input (for example, fewer landmark lists than curves, or argvals of the wrong length): it returns identity warps on \([t_1, t_m]\) and the curves unchanged. A registration that changed nothing is therefore a hint to check that len(landmarks) == data.shape[0] and len(argvals) == data.shape[1].

Other properties to keep in mind:

  • Targets must be increasing within the domain; landmarks at or beyond the end points are dropped from the knots.
  • A zero secant (two equal consecutive source landmarks) gives a flat segment of the warp; the warp is then non-decreasing rather than strictly increasing.
  • Grid resolution. detect_landmarks reports grid points; refine the grid (as above, by evaluating a spline on 101 ages) or interpolate the feature when sub-grid accuracy matters.

docs.title: Landmarks + elastic between them
docs.text:
Sometimes the landmarks are trustworthy but the timing between them is not a smooth interpolation: the curve has further features that should be aligned too. elastic_align_pair_constrained_with_config solves the elastic problem

\[ \min_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\;\bigl\lVert q_1 - (q_2\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\bigr\rVert^2 + \lambda P(\gamma) \quad\text{subject to}\quad \gamma(\tau_k) = s_k , \]

where landmark_targets \(\tau_k\) are times on f1 and landmark_sources \(s_k\) the corresponding times on f2. The landmark pairs are first snapped to the grid (the pairs actually enforced are returned as enforced_landmarks); pairs that would cross are dropped. Then:

  • method="dp" runs the dynamic program separately on each segment between consecutive waypoints.
  • method="rbfgs" uses the segmented DP as a seed and refines each segment with the Riemannian optimiser, which reaches a lower cost and a smoother warp.

Both pass exactly through the enforced waypoints. The Sakoe–Chiba band is not supported (band_frac must be 0), and the "geodesic" penalty cannot be combined with \(\lambda > 0\) here.

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.3) ** 2 / 0.004) + 0.8 * np.exp(-(s - 0.7) ** 2 / 0.004)
w = t + 0.4 * t * (1 - t) * (t - 0.2)            # true warp
f1 = mu(t)
f2 = mu(np.interp(t, w, t))                       # f2(w(t)) = f1(t): peaks moved to w(0.3), w(0.7)
targets = np.array([0.3, 0.7])
sources = np.interp(targets, t, w)

free = A.elastic_align_pair(f1, f2, t)
print(f"unconstrained DP:  distance {free['distance']:.3f}, "
      f"|gamma(tau) - s| = {np.abs(np.interp(targets, t, free['gamma']) - sources).round(4)}")
for method in ("dp", "rbfgs"):
    r = A.elastic_align_pair_constrained_with_config(f1, f2, t, targets, sources, method=method)
    enf = np.asarray(r["enforced_landmarks"])
    hit = np.abs(np.interp(enf[:, 0], t, r["gamma"]) - enf[:, 1]).max()
    print(f"constrained {method:5s}: distance {r['distance']:.3f}, enforced pairs {enf.round(2).tolist()}, "
          f"max |gamma(tau) - s| at enforced pairs {hit:.1e}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

unconstrained DP:  distance 0.115, |gamma(tau) - s| = [0.0016 0.002 ]
constrained dp   : distance 0.115, enforced pairs [[0.3, 0.31], [0.7, 0.74]], max |gamma(tau) - s| at enforced pairs 0.0e+00
constrained rbfgs: distance 0.081, enforced pairs [[0.3, 0.31], [0.7, 0.74]], max |gamma(tau) - s| at enforced pairs 0.0e+00
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Here the unconstrained DP already lands within 0.002 of the true landmarks; the constraint guarantees it. Both constrained solvers hit the (grid-snapped) landmark pairs exactly; snapping moves a pair by up to half a grid step from the requested source (0.742 becomes 0.74). Within the constraint the DP warp is the same as the free one, while RBFGS, which is not limited to quantised slopes, lowers the elastic distance by about 30 %. The older elastic_align_pair_constrained(f1, f2, t, targets, sources, lambda_=0.0) is the DP version without the optimiser options. The landmark arrays must be NumPy arrays, not lists.

docs.title: Landmark, shift, or elastic?
docs.text:
Landmark (landmark_register) Landmark shift Constrained elastic Elastic (karcher_mean) Correspondence you specify it you specify one point you specify it, the rest is optimised found automatically Warp monotone cubic through the knots a translation elastic, through the knots elastic (\(\Gamma\)) Template none none pairwise (f1) Karcher mean Cost trivial trivial one DP (+ RBFGS) per pair iterative DP Best when features are the phase one marker, rigid phase features fixed, more to align between no reliable features

Landmark registration is ideal when the features to align are unambiguous (a clear systolic peak, a known stimulus onset). When features are noisy, hard to detect or absent, prefer elastic alignment, which uses the whole curve. See Choosing an Alignment Method for the full decision tree.

docs.title: Pairwise Synchronisation
docs.text:
Every other group aligner in fdars registers curves to a template: the cross-sectional mean, the Karcher mean, a landmark target. When the sample is heterogeneous or noisy, that template can be a poor reference, and errors in it propagate to every warp. Tang & Müller (2008) proposed a template-free alternative: estimate a warp between pairs of curves, which only requires the two curves to be comparable with each other, and obtain each curve's warp to the common time scale by averaging its pairwise warps.

pairwise_synchronization implements this method (R fdapace::WFDA).

Each curve's warp inverts the truncated mean of its pairwise warps; no template is needed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
For each curve \(i\):

  1. Partners. Draw \(K = \operatorname{round}(\text{subset\_prop}\cdot(n-1))\) partner curves at random (seeded with seed + i).

  2. Pairwise warps. For each partner \(k\), fit a monotone piecewise-linear warp \(h_{ik}\) with nknots equally spaced interior knots such that \(\tilde y_k \circ h_{ik} \approx \tilde y_i\):

    \[ \min_{h_{ik}} \sum_j \bigl(\tilde y_k(h_{ik}(w_j)) - \tilde y_i(w_j)\bigr)^2 + \lambda \sum_j \bigl(h_{ik}(w_j) - w_j\bigr)^2 , \]

    where \(\tilde y = y / \max\lvert y\rvert\) is the curve normalised by its maximum absolute value and \(w\) is the grid mapped to \([0, 1]\). The second term keeps pairwise warps near the identity; with lambda_=None, \(\lambda\) is fdapace's data-driven value \(10^{-4}\sqrt{\sum_i\int(\tilde y_i - \bar{\tilde y})^2/(n-1)}\). The knot heights are optimised by box-constrained Nelder–Mead with restarts (fdapace uses BOBYQA). 3. Average. The average of the pairwise warps estimates \(h_i^{-1}\): with choice="truncated" (default) partners whose fit cost exceeds the truncation_quantile (0.9) of the costs are dropped and the rest averaged; with choice="weighted" all partners are averaged with weights inversely proportional to their costs. 4. Invert. \(h_i\) is the inverse of that average, and the synchronised curve is \(y_i \circ h_i\).

Why does averaging work? If curve \(i\) runs on its own clock \(h_i\), the pairwise warp to partner \(k\) is roughly \(h_k \circ h_i^{-1}\). Averaging over many partners averages out the partners' clocks, and the common time scale is defined as the one in which the average warp is the identity. No template is ever estimated.

The result holds warps \(h_i\) (registered curve \(y_i(h_i(t))\), same convention as the other aligners), inverse_warps, the synchronised curves aligned, the per-curve costs, the lambda used, and the raw partners, pairwise_warps and pairwise_costs. All warps are on the argvals scale.

docs.title: Example: robustness to noise
docs.text:
Twenty curves are two-bump functions, each warped by a random piecewise-linear warp through two knots, plus white noise of increasing size. The table reports the error of the estimated registering warps (mean absolute, \(\times 10^{-3}\), after removing the common part, averaged over three samples) for pairwise synchronisation and for the elastic Karcher mean on raw curves, on pre-smoothed curves, and on pre-smoothed curves with a warp penalty:

import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

def simulate(seed, noise, n=20, m=101):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
    mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.33) ** 2 / 0.006) + 0.6 * np.exp(-(s - 0.67) ** 2 / 0.006)
    X, H = [], []
    for _ in range(n):
        knots = np.sort(rng.uniform(0.2, 0.8, 2))
        heights = np.sort(np.clip(knots + rng.uniform(-0.08, 0.08, 2), 0.05, 0.95))
        w = np.interp(t, [0, *knots, 1], [0, *heights, 1])        # piecewise-linear data warp
        X.append(mu(w) + noise * rng.standard_normal(m))
        H.append(np.interp(t, w, t))                              # true registering warp
    return t, np.array(X), np.array(H)

print("noise sd   pairwise   Karcher   Karcher (smoothed)   Karcher (smoothed, lambda=0.05)")
for noise in (0.02, 0.1, 0.2):
    errs = []
    for seed in range(3):
        t, X, H = simulate(seed, noise)
        inner = (t > 0.1) & (t < 0.9)
        err = lambda W: 1000 * np.abs(((W - W.mean(0)) - (H - H.mean(0)))[:, inner]).mean()
        Xs = np.asarray(A.srsf_presmooth(X, t, smoothing="box", passes=25))
        errs.append([err(np.asarray(A.pairwise_synchronization(X, t)["warps"])),
                     err(np.asarray(A.karcher_mean(X, t)["gammas"])),
                     err(np.asarray(A.karcher_mean(Xs, t)["gammas"])),
                     err(np.asarray(A.karcher_mean(Xs, t, lambda_=0.05)["gammas"]))])
    e = np.mean(errs, axis=0)
    print(f"{noise:8.2f}   {e[0]:8.1f}   {e[1]:7.1f}   {e[2]:18.1f}   {e[3]:31.1f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

noise sd   pairwise   Karcher   Karcher (smoothed)   Karcher (smoothed, lambda=0.05)
    0.02        9.6       8.0                  6.8                               7.4
    0.10       10.2      18.1                 12.4                               8.4
    0.20       11.4      35.6                 17.4                               9.2
FDARS_FENCE_OK

On clean data the elastic Karcher mean is slightly better: its warp class is richer and its template sharp. As noise grows, the elastic alignment of raw curves degrades fast, because the SRSF differentiates the noise. Pairwise synchronisation hardly changes: it compares function values, not derivatives, uses a four-parameter warp, and its penalty keeps pairwise warps near the identity. Elastic alignment catches up with it, and slightly overtakes it, only after pre-smoothing and a warp penalty, both of which need tuning.

docs.title: Choosing the settings
docs.text:
import time
import numpy as np
from fdars import alignment as A

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
mu = lambda s: np.exp(-(s - 0.33) ** 2 / 0.006) + 0.6 * np.exp(-(s - 0.67) ** 2 / 0.006)
m = 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
for n in (10, 20, 40):
    X, H = [], []
    for _ in range(n):
        knots = np.sort(rng.uniform(0.2, 0.8, 2))
        w = np.interp(t, [0, *knots, 1], [0, *np.sort(np.clip(knots + rng.uniform(-0.08, 0.08, 2), 0.05, 0.95)), 1])
        X.append(mu(w) + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(m))
        H.append(np.interp(t, w, t))
    X, H = np.array(X), np.array(H)
    inner = (t > 0.1) & (t < 0.9)
    err = lambda W: 1000 * np.abs(((W - W.mean(0)) - (H - H.mean(0)))[:, inner]).mean()
    for kw in ({}, {"choice": "weighted"}, {"subset_prop": 1.0}, {"nknots": 4}):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        r = A.pairwise_synchronization(X, t, **kw)
        print(f"n={n:2d}  {str(kw):24s} K={len(r['partners'][0]):2d}  warp error {err(np.asarray(r['warps'])):5.1f}"
              f"  ({time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s)")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

n=10  {}                       K= 4  warp error  16.4  (0.06 s)
n=10  {'choice': 'weighted'}   K= 4  warp error  13.8  (0.07 s)
n=10  {'subset_prop': 1.0}     K= 9  warp error   6.5  (0.15 s)
n=10  {'nknots': 4}            K= 4  warp error  16.7  (0.32 s)
n=20  {}                       K=10  warp error   8.9  (0.31 s)
n=20  {'choice': 'weighted'}   K=10  warp error   9.1  (0.31 s)
n=20  {'subset_prop': 1.0}     K=19  warp error   7.3  (0.59 s)
n=20  {'nknots': 4}            K=10  warp error   8.1  (1.61 s)
n=40  {}                       K=20  warp error   7.6  (1.28 s)
n=40  {'choice': 'weighted'}   K=20  warp error   7.5  (1.27 s)
n=40  {'subset_prop': 1.0}     K=39  warp error   6.3  (2.46 s)
n=40  {'nknots': 4}            K=20  warp error   7.2  (6.31 s)
FDARS_FENCE_OK
  • Cost grows as \(n^2\). Each curve fits \(K \approx (n-1)/2\) pairwise warps by default, so the number of pairwise fits quadruples when \(n\) doubles (the timings of these small runs are dominated by overheads and parallel scheduling). Lower subset_prop for large samples; a few dozen partners per curve are usually enough.
  • Few curves: use every partner. With \(n = 10\) the default gives only \(K = 4\) partners per curve, and the average of four warps is noisy; subset_prop=1.0 cuts the error substantially. With larger \(n\) the gain is small.
  • Truncated vs weighted averaging matter little on clean samples. Truncation protects against a few partners that cannot be matched at all (different shapes, outliers); weighting uses every partner.
  • More knots (nknots, up to 7) allow more complex warps but cost more and need more data per segment. The method targets smooth, low-complexity phase; for warps with many local features use elastic alignment.
  • is_pwl=False replaces knot optimisation by a random search over \(K^2\) sorted-uniform candidate warps (fdapace's alternative); it is rarely better.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Vertical offsets distort the fit. Curves are normalised by \(\max\lvert y\rvert\), not centred, so curves that differ by a baseline shift are compared at different relative levels. Subtract a baseline first if offsets are nuisance.
  • Identically zero curves are rejected (the normalisation fails). At least 2 curves and 3 points are required.
  • Boundaries are fixed. Warps map \([t_0, T]\) onto itself; a phase that runs off the end of the window is distorted.
  • fdapace parity. fdapace 0.6.0 computes the pairwise cost from a single matrix element (an R indexing bug). The default cost_measure="pairwise_fit" uses the intended data-fit cost; cost_measure="fdapace_legacy" reproduces fdapace. The random partner draws use a different generator from R; with subset_prop=1.0 the result does not depend on the generator.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect choice "truncated" "truncated" or "weighted" averaging subset_prop 0.5 fraction of the other curves used as partners, in \((0, 1]\) nknots 2 interior knots of the pairwise warps (1–7) is_pwl True knot optimisation (False: random search) lambda_ None warp penalty; None = fdapace's data-driven value truncation_quantile 0.9 cost quantile above which partners are dropped cost_measure "pairwise_fit" or "fdapace_legacy" max_evals, optim_tol 4000, 1e-12 optimiser budget per pairwise warp seed 666 partner draws (fdapace default)

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Use it when the sample is noisy, when no curve or mean is a credible template, when you want simple, low-dimensional warps without tuning an SRSF pre-smoother, or for parity with fdapace.
  • Prefer elastic alignment when you need a metric, an amplitude/phase decomposition, elastic FPCA or inference, or warps with many local features; prefer a shift or affine model when the phase is that simple.
  • The Comparing Methods bake-off shows it against every other aligner on one sample.

docs.title: Shape Analysis
docs.text:
Two curves can look different point-by-point yet share the same shape -- when the difference is only a matter of parameterization (timing), a vertical baseline shift, or an overall magnitude. This page covers real-valued (1-D) curves; for outlines and trajectories in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where rotation and scale are nuisance too, use the curve_shape_* functions (see Shapes of Curves in R^d). Shape analysis studies the geometry of functional data after factoring out such nuisance transformations. The formal device is a quotient space: curves that differ only by a nuisance transformation are identified as the same point. The elastic (Fisher-Rao) framework, via the SRSF representation, makes this quotient geometry computable.

fdars provides tools for shape representatives and distances (this quotient geometry), for the shape mean (a Karcher mean in quotient space), and -- going beyond the quotient basics -- for elastic depth and elastic FPCA that decompose variability into amplitude and phase components.

Function Role shape_distance Elastic distance between two curves modulo warping (equals elastic_distance) shape_mean Karcher mean (average shape) in a chosen quotient shape_self_distance_matrix All pairwise distances in a chosen quotient (for clustering/MDS) reparameterize_curve Apply a warp \(\gamma\) to a curve (move within an orbit)

A sample of curves that share a common shape but differ in amplitude and timing (left) collapses onto a single sharp template once the warping is factored out. The elastic mean shape -- the Karcher mean under the Fisher-Rao metric (right, orange) -- recovers that template, whereas the naive cross-sectional mean (right, dashed) is flattened by the phase spread.

image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The dashed red cross-sectional mean is a washed-out compromise -- it averages heights at fixed times across curves that peak at different times. The solid orange elastic mean shape instead recovers a crisp representative that actually resembles the individual curves, because it averages after removing phase. That contrast is the motivation for shape-space statistics.

docs.title: The quotient geometry
docs.text:
Shape analysis lives in a quotient space. Write a curve as a function \(f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}\). The nuisance transformations form a group \(\Gamma\) of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms (warps) \(\gamma:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) with \(\gamma(0)=0\), \(\gamma(1)=1\) and \(\dot\gamma>0\). The group acts on curves by composition,

\[ (f,\gamma)\;\longmapsto\; f\circ\gamma , \]

and the set of all curves reachable from \(f\) this way is its orbit \([f]=\{\,f\circ\gamma : \gamma\in\Gamma\,\}\). Two curves have the same shape iff they lie in the same orbit. The shape space is the quotient \(\mathcal{F}/\Gamma\), and a shape distance must be a proper distance on that quotient.

docs.title: Why the \(\mathbb{L}^2\) metric fails
docs.text:
The naive attempt — align by minimizing \(\|f_1 - f_2\circ\gamma\|_{\mathbb{L}^2}\) over \(\gamma\) — is not a distance on the quotient, because the \(\mathbb{L}^2\) inner product is not preserved by warping:

\[ \langle f\circ\gamma,\; g\circ\gamma\rangle_{\mathbb{L}^2} = \int_0^1 f(\gamma(t))\,g(\gamma(t))\,dt \;\neq\; \langle f,g\rangle_{\mathbb{L}^2}. \]

Reparameterizing both curves changes the value, so the "distance" depends on where in each orbit you happen to sit. This produces the pinching pathology: the optimizer buys artificially small residuals by warping mass into a thin spike. The elastic (Fisher-Rao) framework fixes this.

docs.title: The square-root slope function (SRSF)
docs.text:
Represent a curve by its square-root slope function (also called SRVF in the curve setting),

\[ q(t) \;=\; \operatorname{sgn}\bigl(\dot f(t)\bigr)\,\sqrt{\bigl|\dot f(t)\bigr|}, \qquad q \in \mathbb{L}^2([0,1],\mathbb{R}), \]

with inverse \(f(t)=f(0)+\int_0^t q(s)\,|q(s)|\,ds\). The map \(f\mapsto q\) trades the original curve for its (signed square-rooted) velocity. The decisive property is how the group action transforms in this representation. If \(\tilde f = f\circ\gamma\), its SRSF is

\[ \tilde q(t) \;=\; (q\circ\gamma)(t)\,\sqrt{\dot\gamma(t)} \;\;=:\;\; (q,\gamma). \]

The extra \(\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\) Jacobian factor is exactly what is needed to make the action an isometry of \(\mathbb{L}^2\):

\[ \bigl\langle (q,\gamma),\,(r,\gamma)\bigr\rangle_{\mathbb{L}^2} = \int_0^1 q(\gamma(t))\,r(\gamma(t))\,\dot\gamma(t)\,dt = \int_0^1 q(s)\,r(s)\,ds = \langle q,r\rangle_{\mathbb{L}^2}, \]

by the change of variables \(s=\gamma(t)\). So the complicated Fisher-Rao Riemannian metric on curve space becomes the flat \(\mathbb{L}^2\) metric on SRSF space — and warping is a norm-preserving rotation there. This is the whole point of the SRSF transform: it linearizes the elastic geometry.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import srsf_transform, reparameterize_curve

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
f = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) + 0.4 * np.sin(4 * np.pi * t)

# a warp and the warped curve
gamma = t ** 1.8
gamma = (gamma - gamma.min()) / np.ptp(gamma)
f_w = reparameterize_curve(f, t, gamma)

q   = np.asarray(srsf_transform(f, t))
q_w = np.asarray(srsf_transform(f_w, t))

# L2 norms: preserved in SRSF space, not in curve space
nrm = lambda a: np.sqrt(np.trapezoid(a ** 2, t))
f_norms = (nrm(f), nrm(f_w))
q_norms = (nrm(q), nrm(q_w))

f_, (a1, a2) = fig(ncols=2, figsize=(9.8, 4.0))
a1.plot(t, f,   color="#3f51b5", lw=2.0, label="$f$")
a1.plot(t, f_w, color="#e8710a", lw=2.0, label=r"$f\circ\gamma$")
a1.set(title=f"Curve space: $\\|f\\|$={f_norms[0]:.3f}, "
             f"$\\|f\\circ\\gamma\\|$={f_norms[1]:.3f}",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="f(t)")
a1.legend(fontsize=9)

a2.plot(t, q,   color="#3f51b5", lw=2.0, label="$q$")
a2.plot(t, q_w, color="#e8710a", lw=2.0, label=r"$(q,\gamma)$")
a2.set(title=f"SRSF space: $\\|q\\|$={q_norms[0]:.3f}, "
             f"$\\|(q,\\gamma)\\|$={q_norms[1]:.3f}",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="q(t)")
a2.legend(fontsize=9)
print(render(f_))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The two curves on the left have visibly different \(\mathbb{L}^2\) norms; their SRSFs on the right have (to discretization error) the same norm — the \(\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\) factor makes warping an isometry, which is precisely why the elastic metric behaves.

Numerical validation: the SRSF map is an \(\mathbb{L}^2\) isometry

The defining property is stronger than norm preservation: warping both curves by a common \(\gamma\) leaves the \(\mathbb{L}^2\) distance between their SRSFs unchanged, \(\|q_1 - q_2\|_{\mathbb{L}^2} = \|(q_1,\gamma) - (q_2,\gamma)\|_{\mathbb{L}^2}\). Below we take two curves, apply the same warp to both, and confirm the SRSF distance is invariant. The residual is pure discretization error (it shrinks as the grid refines), so we assert a relative tolerance.

SRSF distance before warp: 2.418271 SRSF distance after warp: 2.417427 relative deviation (isometry error): 3.49e-04

The two printed SRSF distances -- before and after applying the same warp to both curves -- agree to well under a percent, so warping is an isometry up to discretization. This is the property that makes shape distances well defined: reparameterizing both curves together leaves their separation unchanged.

docs.title: Geodesic distance in shape space
docs.text:
On the SRSF sphere the geodesic distance between two representatives is the arc length

\[ d(q_1,q_2)=\cos^{-1}\!\Bigl(\langle q_1,q_2\rangle_{\mathbb{L}^2}\Bigr), \]

and the shape distance of the classical theory minimises this arc length over the warping orbit of one curve:

\[ d_{\mathrm{shape}}\bigl([f_1],[f_2]\bigr) \;=\; \inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\; d\bigl(q_1,\;(q_2,\gamma)\bigr) \;=\; \inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\; \cos^{-1}\!\Bigl(\bigl\langle q_1,\,(q_2\circ\gamma)\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\bigr\rangle\Bigr). \]

Because the action is by isometries, this infimum is a genuine distance on the quotient \(\mathcal{F}/\Gamma\): it is symmetric, non-negative, zero exactly when the orbits coincide, and satisfies the triangle inequality.

Two practical remarks. First, the 1-D functions on this page (shape_distance, elastic_distance) report the \(L^2\) version, \(\inf_\gamma \lVert q_1 - (q_2,\gamma)\rVert\), on the un-normalised SRSFs; the arc-length (sphere) version is used when scale is quotiented out, as in the curve_shape_* functions with scale=True. Second, the infimum is computed by a discretised optimiser (dynamic programming by default), which makes the computed distance only approximately symmetric; see Elastic Alignment. curve_geodesic returns a whole path, not just its endpoints.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import curve_geodesic

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 120)
f1 = np.exp(-((t - 0.5) ** 2) / 0.01)           # one bump (unimodal)
f2 = (np.exp(-((t - 0.3) ** 2) / 0.008)
      + np.exp(-((t - 0.7) ** 2) / 0.008))       # two bumps (bimodal, a different shape)

geo = curve_geodesic(f1, f2, t, n_points=7)
path = np.asarray(geo["curves"])                # (7, m) curves along geodesic
s    = np.asarray(geo["parameter_values"])      # path parameter in [0, 1]
darc = np.asarray(geo["distances"])             # cumulative arc length

f_, (a1, a2) = fig(ncols=2, figsize=(9.8, 4.0))
cmap = __import__("matplotlib").cm.viridis
for k in range(path.shape[0]):
    a1.plot(t, path[k], color=cmap(s[k]), lw=1.8)
a1.plot(t, f1, color="#3f51b5", lw=2.8, label="$f_1$ (start)")
a1.plot(t, f2, color="#e8710a", lw=2.8, label="$f_2$ (end)")
a1.set(title="Geodesic path in shape space", xlabel="t", ylabel="f(t)")
a1.legend(fontsize=9)

a2.plot(s, darc, "o-", color="#3f51b5")
a2.set(title="Cumulative geodesic arc length",
       xlabel="path parameter s", ylabel="distance from start")
print(render(f_))

print(f"total shape geodesic distance: {darc[-1]:.4f}")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ total shape geodesic distance: 1.3371

The right panel is the cleanest diagnostic: the cumulative arc length grows linearly in the path parameter, the signature of a constant-speed geodesic. In curve space (left) the intermediates are drawn in \(f_1\)'s time frame: curve_geodesic first aligns \(f_2\) to \(f_1\) and interpolates the amplitude between \(f_1\) and the aligned \(f_2\circ\gamma\), so the final curve is that aligned version (its bumps sit where \(f_1\)'s features are), not \(f_2\) itself. The phase part of the path is carried by the returned warps.

docs.title: The Karcher mean as a shape average
docs.text:
There is no linear "average orbit," so the mean shape is defined intrinsically as the Karcher (Fréchet) mean — the orbit that minimizes the sum of squared shape distances:

\[ [\mu] \;=\; \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{[f]}\; \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_{\mathrm{shape}}\bigl([f],[f_i]\bigr)^2 . \]

It is computed by alternating between (i) aligning every curve's SRSF to the current mean by dynamic programming, and (ii) updating the mean to the \(\mathbb{L}^2\) average of the aligned SRSFs — a gradient descent on the shape manifold. shape_mean and karcher_mean implement this; the penalty \(\lambda\!\ge\!0\) regularizes the warps to prevent pinching on noisy data.

docs.title: Shape distance (quotient space)
docs.text:
The shape distance measures how different two curves are in the quotient space obtained by modding out the group of warping functions. shape_distance(f1, f2, argvals, lambda_=0.0) uses the reparameterisation quotient only, so it equals elastic_distance (it also returns the warp and the aligned curve). It removes phase and vertical offsets (the SRSF ignores those), not amplitude scale: shape_distance(f, 1.5 * f) is not zero. To quotient out scale, use shape_self_distance_matrix or shape_mean with quotient="reparameterization_translation_scale" (below).

import numpy as np
from fdars.alignment import shape_distance

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
f1 = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
f2 = 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * (t - 0.1))  # scaled and shifted

result = shape_distance(f1, f2, t)

d          = result["distance"]     # shape distance (scalar)
gamma      = result["gamma"]        # optimal warping function
f2_aligned = result["f2_aligned"]   # f2 after alignment
Key Type Description distance float Shape distance in quotient space gamma ndarray (m,) Optimal warping function f2_aligned ndarray (m,) Second curve aligned to first

Shape vs. elastic distance

For 1-D curves, shape_distance and elastic_distance are the same number. Amplitude differences are preserved by both; only the scale quotient of the matrix and mean functions removes (approximately) an overall size factor.

docs.title: Orbits and quotient choices
docs.text:
Each curve belongs to an orbit -- the set of all curves reachable from it by the nuisance transformations. reparameterize_curve moves a curve within its reparameterization orbit by applying a warp \(\gamma\); the shape tools compare curves across orbits. The quotient controls which transformations are factored out:

quotient Factors out Effect in fdars "reparameterization" (default) warping (timing) the elastic distance and Karcher mean "reparameterization_translation" + vertical offset each curve's integral mean is subtracted first; distances are unchanged (the SRSF already ignores offsets), only the returned mean is centred "reparameterization_translation_scale" + overall size each centred curve is also divided by the \(L^2\) norm of its SRSF; this is an approximate scale quotient (it rescales the SRSF by \(1/\sqrt{\lVert q\rVert}\), so representatives are not unit-norm and scaled copies end up close, not identical)

Spell the quotient exactly

Any other string, including the shorthand "translation" or "scale", raises ValueError. Use the full names above. (Older fdars versions silently fell back to "reparameterization" for unknown strings, so code that passed "translation" or "scale" computed the plain elastic quotient.)

import numpy as np
from fdars.alignment import shape_self_distance_matrix, shape_mean

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
f = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
X = np.array([f, 1.5 * f, 0.5 * f + 2, np.sin(2 * np.pi * t ** 1.3)])   # scaled, scaled+shifted, warped
for q in ("reparameterization", "reparameterization_translation", "reparameterization_translation_scale"):
    d = np.asarray(shape_self_distance_matrix(X, t, quotient=q))[0, 1:]
    mean = np.asarray(shape_mean(X, t, quotient=q)["mean"])
    print(f"{q:37s} d(f, .) = {np.round(d, 3)}   mean level {mean.mean():+.3f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

reparameterization                    d(f, .) = [0.449 0.585 0.071]   mean level +0.521
reparameterization_translation        d(f, .) = [0.449 0.585 0.071]   mean level -0.001
reparameterization_translation_scale  d(f, .) = [0.151 0.225 0.05 ]   mean level -0.000
FDARS_FENCE_OK

The warped copy (last column) is close to \(f\) under every quotient. The scaled copies stay at the same distance under the first two quotients; the scale quotient brings them closer, but not to zero.

from fdars.alignment import reparameterize_curve

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
f = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
gamma = t ** 1.4; gamma = (gamma - gamma.min()) / np.ptp(gamma)  # a monotone warp
f_warped = reparameterize_curve(f, t, gamma)   # same orbit, different parameterization

docs.title: A two-group worked example
docs.text:
The shape distance really earns its keep when groups differ in shape but each group also carries nuisance phase variation. Below, one group is unimodal (a single bump) and the other is bimodal (two bumps); within each group the peak positions jitter. Shape distance factors out that within-group jitter but preserves the unimodal-vs-bimodal difference, so within-group distances are small and cross-group distances are large -- and the distance matrix shows a clean block structure that ordinary hierarchical clustering separates perfectly. (Note: two curves that differ only in bump position -- e.g. a left bump vs. a right bump -- are the same shape under the reparameterization quotient, so they would not form separable groups; the groups must differ in genuine shape.)

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import shape_distance, shape_mean, shape_self_distance_matrix

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n, m = 30, 50
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
X = np.zeros((n, m))
for i in range(15):                       # unimodal group (one bump, jittered position)
    c = 0.5 + rng.normal(0, 0.05)
    X[i] = np.exp(-((t - c) ** 2) / 0.02) + rng.normal(0, 0.03, m)
for i in range(15, 30):                   # bimodal group (two bumps -> different shape)
    c = rng.normal(0, 0.05)
    X[i] = (np.exp(-((t - (0.3 + c)) ** 2) / 0.01)
            + np.exp(-((t - (0.7 + c)) ** 2) / 0.01)) + rng.normal(0, 0.03, m)

# within-group vs cross-group shape distance
d_same = shape_distance(X[0], X[5], t)["distance"]
d_diff = shape_distance(X[0], X[20], t)["distance"]

# shape means per group (Karcher mean in quotient space)
mu_left = np.asarray(shape_mean(X[:15], t, quotient="reparameterization", max_iter=20)["mean"])
mu_right = np.asarray(shape_mean(X[15:], t, quotient="reparameterization", max_iter=20)["mean"])

# full pairwise shape-distance matrix -> block structure
D = np.asarray(shape_self_distance_matrix(X, t, quotient="reparameterization"))

f, (a1, a2) = fig(ncols=2, figsize=(9.8, 4.0))
a1.plot(t, X[:15].T, color="#3f51b5", lw=0.7, alpha=0.3)
a1.plot(t, X[15:].T, color="#e8710a", lw=0.7, alpha=0.3)
a1.plot(t, mu_left, color="#3f51b5", lw=2.6, label="unimodal shape mean")
a1.plot(t, mu_right, color="#e8710a", lw=2.6, label="bimodal shape mean")
a1.set(title="Two shape groups + Karcher shape means", xlabel="t", ylabel="f(t)")
a1.legend(fontsize=8)

im = a2.imshow(D, cmap="plasma", origin="lower")
a2.set(title="Shape-distance matrix (block structure)",
       xlabel="curve", ylabel="curve")
f.colorbar(im, ax=a2, fraction=0.046, shrink=0.85)
print(render(f))

print(f"within-group shape distance (1 vs 5):  {d_same:.4f}")
print(f"cross-group  shape distance (1 vs 20): {d_diff:.4f}")

# hierarchical clustering on the shape distances recovers the two groups
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, fcluster
from scipy.spatial.distance import squareform
Z = linkage(squareform(D, checks=False), method="complete")
labels = fcluster(Z, t=2, criterion="maxclust")
group = np.array([0] * 15 + [1] * 15)
acc = max((labels == group + 1).mean(), (labels == 2 - group).mean())
print(f"2-cluster agreement with true groups: {acc:.0%}")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ within-group shape distance (1 vs 5): 0.7328 cross-group shape distance (1 vs 20): 1.3448 2-cluster agreement with true groups: 100%

The within-group distance is small because the only within-group difference -- peak position -- is exactly the phase variation the quotient factors out, while the cross-group distance stays large because unimodal and bimodal are genuinely different shapes. The distance matrix's two dark diagonal blocks confirm it, and complete-linkage clustering recovers the groups.

shape_mean returns the same keys as karcher_mean (mean, mean_srsf, aligned_data, gammas, n_iter, converged); pass quotient= to choose which nuisance to factor out.

Best practices

  • Pick the quotient to match the nuisance: "reparameterization" for timing; "reparameterization_translation_scale" when overall size is nuisance too (approximate). Spell the names in full.
  • Check shape_mean's converged; raise max_iter if it is False.
  • Use lambda_ > 0 to prevent extreme warps on noisy or sparse data.
  • Smooth curves on a common grid before analysis, and inspect the returned gammas to gauge how much reparameterization was needed.

docs.title: Uncertainty of the mean shape
docs.text:
A point estimate of the mean shape is not enough — we want a confidence band around it. shape_confidence_interval bootstraps the sample: it resamples curves with replacement, recomputes the Karcher mean of each resample, aligns each bootstrap mean to the full-sample mean, and reports pointwise percentile bands of those aligned means. It uses the reparameterisation quotient only. Because the mean is estimated after factoring out phase, the band reflects genuine shape (amplitude-in-quotient) uncertainty rather than being inflated by misalignment.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.alignment import shape_confidence_interval

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n, m = 24, 80
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
base = np.exp(-((t - 0.5) ** 2) / 0.03)         # common bump shape
data = np.zeros((n, m))
for i in range(n):
    warp = np.clip(t + 0.10 * rng.standard_normal() * np.sin(np.pi * t), 0, 1)
    data[i] = (1.0 + 0.15 * rng.standard_normal()) * np.interp(t, warp, base) \
              + 0.03 * rng.standard_normal(m)

ci = shape_confidence_interval(data, t, n_bootstrap=120, confidence_level=0.90,
                               max_iter=12, seed=1)
mu    = np.asarray(ci["mean"])
lower = np.asarray(ci["lower_band"])
upper = np.asarray(ci["upper_band"])

f, ax = fig()
ax.plot(t, data.T, color="#6c757d", lw=0.7, alpha=0.25)
ax.fill_between(t, lower, upper, color="#e8710a", alpha=0.25,
                label="90% bootstrap band")
ax.plot(t, mu, color="#e8710a", lw=2.6, label="mean shape")
ax.set(title="Mean shape with bootstrap confidence band",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="f(t)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
print(render(f))

width = float(np.trapezoid(upper - lower, t))
print(f"mean band width (integrated): {width:.4f}")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ mean band width (integrated): 0.1140

The orange band traces where the mean shape is precisely pinned (narrow) versus uncertain (wide), and because it is built from bootstrap resamples of aligned shapes it measures amplitude uncertainty rather than residual phase jitter. The integrated width printed below gives a single scalar for how tightly the sample determines the mean.

Key Type Description mean ndarray (m,) Estimated mean shape lower_band ndarray (m,) Pointwise lower confidence limit upper_band ndarray (m,) Pointwise upper confidence limit bootstrap_means ndarray (B, m) The n_bootstrap resampled mean shapes

Pointwise, not simultaneous

shape_confidence_interval returns pointwise percentile bands from the bootstrap distribution of the mean shape. They are not simultaneous (family-wise) bands and do not correct for multiplicity across t; for simultaneous coverage of an aligned mean, see the tolerance/simultaneous-band tools in fdars.tolerance.

docs.title: Elastic depth
docs.text:
Elastic depth ranks functional observations from center to periphery using the elastic metric. It decomposes into amplitude and phase components, enabling separate outlier detection in each source of variability. Each depth is \(1/(1 + \bar d_i)\), with \(\bar d_i\) the mean amplitude (or phase) distance of curve \(i\) to the others, and combined_depth is the geometric mean of the two. This is a distance-based centrality, not the lens depth of the literature, and amplitude and phase distances live on different scales, so the combination weights them unevenly.

import numpy as np
from fdars import Fdata
from fdars.alignment import elastic_depth

np.random.seed(0)
n, m = 40, 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
fd = Fdata(
    np.array([
        np.sin(2 * np.pi * (t - 0.1 * np.random.randn()))
        + 0.3 * np.random.randn()
        for _ in range(n)
    ]),
    argvals=t,
)

result = elastic_depth(fd.data, fd.argvals, lambda_=0.0)

amp_depth  = result["amplitude_depth"]    # (n,)
ph_depth   = result["phase_depth"]        # (n,)
comb_depth = result["combined_depth"]     # (n,)
amp_dists  = result["amplitude_distances"]  # (n, n)
ph_dists   = result["phase_distances"]      # (n, n)

# Most central curve (highest combined depth)
median_idx = np.argmax(comb_depth)
print(f"Elastic median: curve {median_idx}")
print(f"  Amplitude depth: {amp_depth[median_idx]:.4f}")
print(f"  Phase depth:     {ph_depth[median_idx]:.4f}")

# Potential outliers (lowest depth)
outlier_idx = np.argmin(comb_depth)
print(f"Most outlying:  curve {outlier_idx}")
Key Type Description amplitude_depth ndarray (n,) Depth based on amplitude distances phase_depth ndarray (n,) Depth based on phase distances combined_depth ndarray (n,) Joint amplitude+phase depth amplitude_distances ndarray (n, n) Pairwise amplitude distance matrix phase_distances ndarray (n, n) Pairwise phase distance matrix

Diagnostic plots

Plot amplitude depth vs. phase depth in a scatter plot. Curves far from the cluster center in either dimension are outlying in that specific source of variability.

Shading each curve by its combined elastic depth turns the sample into a visual centre-outward ordering: the deepest curve (the elastic median, orange) sits at the heart of the band, while shallow curves fade toward the edges.

image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Opacity encodes elastic depth: the darkest curve (highlighted orange) is the elastic median -- the most central shape -- while the faint outer curves are the shallowest, least typical members. Because depth is computed in the elastic space, a curve is "deep" when its shape is central, independent of whether its peaks arrived early or late.

docs.title: Elastic FPCA
docs.text: Standard FPCA conflates amplitude and phase variation into a single set of principal components. Elastic FPCA performs PCA in the aligned (elastic) space, yielding separate decompositions of amplitude and phase variability.

docs.title: Vertical (amplitude) FPCA
docs.text:
Extracts the principal modes of amplitude variation from the aligned curves.

from fdars.alignment import vert_fpca

result = vert_fpca(fd.data, fd.argvals, n_comp=3, lambda_=0.0, max_iter=20, tol=1e-4)

scores      = result["scores"]              # (n, 3) -- amplitude PC scores
eigfun_q    = result["eigenfunctions_q"]     # (3, m+1) -- eigenfunctions in SRSF space
eigfun_f    = result["eigenfunctions_f"]     # (3, m) -- eigenfunctions in original space
eigenvalues = result["eigenvalues"]          # (3,)
cum_var     = result["cumulative_variance"]  # (3,)
mean_q      = result["mean_q"]              # (m+1,) -- mean SRSF

print(f"Amplitude variance explained: {cum_var[-1]*100:.1f}%")
Key Type Description scores ndarray (n, k) Amplitude FPC scores eigenfunctions_q ndarray (k, m+1) Eigenfunctions in SRSF space eigenfunctions_f ndarray (k, m) Eigenfunctions in function space eigenvalues ndarray (k,) Eigenvalues cumulative_variance ndarray (k,) Cumulative proportion of variance mean_q ndarray (m+1,) Mean SRSF

The extra \((m+1)\)-th coordinate augments each SRSF with the curve's value at one point (as in fdasrvf, so that vertical level is part of the amplitude); fdars takes that value at the midpoint of the grid, not at \(t_0\) as its doc comment says.

docs.title: Horizontal (phase) FPCA
docs.text:
Extracts the principal modes of phase variation from the estimated warping functions.

from fdars.alignment import horiz_fpca

result = horiz_fpca(fd.data, fd.argvals, n_comp=3, lambda_=0.0, max_iter=20, tol=1e-4)

scores      = result["scores"]                # (n, 3) -- phase PC scores
eigfun_psi  = result["eigenfunctions_psi"]     # (3, m) -- in psi space
eigfun_gam  = result["eigenfunctions_gam"]     # (3, m) -- in gamma space
eigenvalues = result["eigenvalues"]            # (3,)
cum_var     = result["cumulative_variance"]    # (3,)
mean_psi    = result["mean_psi"]               # (m,) -- mean psi
shooting    = result["shooting_vectors"]       # (n, m) -- shooting vectors

print(f"Phase variance explained: {cum_var[-1]*100:.1f}%")
Key Type Description scores ndarray (n, k) Phase FPC scores eigenfunctions_psi ndarray (k, m) Eigenfunctions in \(\psi\) representation eigenfunctions_gam ndarray (k, m) Eigenfunctions as warping functions eigenvalues ndarray (k,) Eigenvalues cumulative_variance ndarray (k,) Cumulative proportion of variance mean_psi ndarray (m,) Mean \(\psi\) shooting_vectors ndarray (n, m) Shooting vectors (tangent space)

docs.title: Joint FPCA
docs.text:
Combines amplitude and phase variation into a single joint decomposition, weighting the two sources via a balance parameter \(c\).

from fdars.alignment import joint_fpca

result = joint_fpca(fd.data, fd.argvals, n_comp=3, lambda_=0.0, max_iter=20, tol=1e-4)

scores     = result["scores"]              # (n, 3)
eigenvalues = result["eigenvalues"]        # (3,)
cum_var    = result["cumulative_variance"]  # (3,)
balance_c  = result["balance_c"]           # automatic balance parameter
vert_comp  = result["vert_component"]      # (k, m) -- amplitude part
horiz_comp = result["horiz_component"]     # (k, m) -- phase part

print(f"Balance parameter c = {balance_c:.4f}")
print(f"Joint variance explained: {cum_var[-1]*100:.1f}%")
Key Type Description scores ndarray (n, k) Joint FPC scores eigenvalues ndarray (k,) Eigenvalues cumulative_variance ndarray (k,) Cumulative proportion of variance balance_c float Phase weight \(c\), chosen automatically to minimise the SRSF reconstruction error (as fdasrsf's jointFPCA) vert_component ndarray (k, m) Amplitude part of each eigenfunction horiz_component ndarray (k, m) Phase part of each eigenfunction

When to use which?

  • Vertical FPCA -- when you care only about amplitude variability (e.g., peak heights).
  • Horizontal FPCA -- when you care only about timing variability (e.g., event onset).
  • Joint FPCA -- when you want a unified low-dimensional representation for downstream tasks like regression or clustering.

docs.title: Full example: amplitude vs. phase decomposition
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from fdars import Fdata
from fdars.alignment import (
    karcher_mean,
    vert_fpca,
    horiz_fpca,
    elastic_depth,
)

# --- Simulate ---
np.random.seed(123)
n, m = 60, 151
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)

data = np.zeros((n, m))
for i in range(n):
    amp = 1.0 + 0.4 * np.random.randn()           # amplitude variation
    shift = 0.08 * np.random.randn()               # phase variation
    t_warp = np.clip(t + shift * np.sin(np.pi * t), 0, 1)
    data[i] = amp * np.sin(2 * np.pi * np.interp(t, t_warp, t))

fd = Fdata(data, argvals=t)

# --- Alignment ---
km = karcher_mean(fd.data, fd.argvals, lambda_=0.05)
print(f"Karcher mean converged: {km['converged']}")

# --- Amplitude FPCA ---
vfpca = vert_fpca(fd.data, fd.argvals, n_comp=3, lambda_=0.05)
print(f"Amplitude variance (3 PCs): {vfpca['cumulative_variance'][-1]*100:.1f}%")

# --- Phase FPCA ---
hfpca = horiz_fpca(fd.data, fd.argvals, n_comp=3, lambda_=0.05)
print(f"Phase variance (3 PCs):     {hfpca['cumulative_variance'][-1]*100:.1f}%")

# --- Elastic depth ---
depth = elastic_depth(fd.data, fd.argvals)
median_idx = np.argmax(depth["combined_depth"])
print(f"Elastic median: curve {median_idx}")
print(f"  Amp depth:  {depth['amplitude_depth'][median_idx]:.4f}")
print(f"  Phase depth: {depth['phase_depth'][median_idx]:.4f}")
