docs.title: Function-on-Scalar Regression
docs.text:
Function-on-scalar regression is the mirror image of scalar-on-function: it models a functional response \(y_i(t)\) as a function of scalar predictors \(x_{i1}, \dots, x_{ip}\):

\[ y_i(t) = \beta_0(t) + \sum_{j=1}^{p} x_{ij}\,\beta_j(t) + \varepsilon_i(t). \]

Each coefficient function \(\beta_j(t)\) describes how predictor \(j\) influences the response curve at every point \(t\). Typical questions it answers:

  • How does a treatment shift the entire response curve, and when is the effect strongest?
  • Do group mean functions differ across the domain?

fdars offers a penalised estimator (fosr), an FPC-based estimator (fosr_fpc), prediction (predict_fosr), and a permutation ANOVA test (fanova).

docs.title: Penalised estimation
docs.text:
Fitting the model by ordinary least squares independently at each \(t\) recovers \(\beta_j(t)\) but produces noisy, jagged curves. fosr instead adds a second-difference roughness penalty, minimising

\[ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big\|y_i - \beta_0 - \textstyle\sum_j x_{ij}\beta_j\big\|^2 \;+\; \lambda \sum_{j} \int \big[\beta_j''(t)\big]^2\,dt, \]

which yields the ridge-type estimator \(\hat\beta(\cdot) = (X^\top X + \lambda D^\top D)^{-1} X^\top Y(\cdot)\), where \(D\) is a second-difference operator. The penalty \(\lambda \ge 0\) trades data fidelity against smoothness.

A useful summary of fit quality is the pointwise \(R^2\),

\[ R^2(t) = 1 - \frac{\sum_i [y_i(t) - \hat y_i(t)]^2}{\sum_i [y_i(t) - \bar y(t)]^2}, \]

which reveals where along the domain the scalar predictors explain the response well, and where they do not.

docs.title: Function-on-Scalar Regression (FOSR)
docs.text:
fosr fits the model with an optional roughness penalty and returns coefficient functions, fitted curves, residuals, and a global \(R^2\).

import numpy as np
from fdars import Fdata
from fdars.regression import fosr

# --- Simulate data ---
np.random.seed(0)
n, m, p = 80, 101, 3
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)

# Scalar predictors
predictors = np.random.randn(n, p)

# True coefficient functions
beta_true = np.zeros((p, m))
beta_true[0] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)          # predictor 1 effect
beta_true[1] = 0.5 * np.cos(4 * np.pi * t)    # predictor 2 effect
beta_true[2] = t * (1 - t)                     # predictor 3 effect

# Functional response
fd = Fdata(predictors @ beta_true + 0.2 * np.random.randn(n, m), argvals=t)

# --- Fit FOSR ---
result = fosr(fd.data, predictors, lambda_=0.1)  # ridge penalty

fitted    = result["fitted"]      # (n, m) -- fitted functional responses
beta_hat  = result["beta"]        # (p, m) -- estimated coefficient functions
residuals = result["residuals"]   # (n, m)
r2        = result["r_squared"]   # scalar

print(f"R-squared: {r2:.4f}")
print(f"Beta shape: {np.asarray(beta_hat).shape}")
Key Type Description fitted ndarray (n, m) Fitted functional responses beta ndarray (p, m) Estimated coefficient functions residuals ndarray (n, m) Residual curves r_squared float Global \(R^2\)

Roughness penalty

Set lambda_=0.0 for ordinary least squares at each time point (fast but noisy). A positive lambda_ applies a fixed second-difference penalty; increase it until the coefficient functions are as smooth as the science warrants.

The estimated coefficient functions \(\hat\beta_j(t)\) (solid) track the true effects (dashed) closely, one curve per scalar predictor:

image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Each estimated curve hugs its dashed truth: the sinusoid, the higher-frequency cosine, and the parabolic bump are all recovered, confirming that the ridge penalty smooths without flattening the genuine signal.

docs.title: Interpreting coefficient functions
docs.text:
Each \(\hat{\beta}_j(t)\) describes the effect of predictor \(j\) on the response at time \(t\):

  • \(\hat{\beta}_j(t) > 0\): increasing predictor \(j\) raises the response at time \(t\).
  • \(\hat{\beta}_j(t) < 0\): increasing predictor \(j\) lowers the response at time \(t\).
  • \(\hat{\beta}_j(t) \approx 0\): predictor \(j\) has no effect at time \(t\).
# Check recovery of true coefficients
for j in range(p):
    corr = np.corrcoef(beta_true[j], np.asarray(beta_hat)[j])[0, 1]
    print(f"  Predictor {j}: correlation with truth = {corr:.4f}")

docs.title: FPC-based FOSR
docs.text:
Instead of penalising, fosr_fpc first compresses the response curves onto their leading functional principal components, regresses the FPC scores on the scalar predictors, and maps the result back to function space. It replaces the choice of \(\lambda\) with a choice of component count n_comp, and is efficient and stable when the response curves have strong low-rank structure. It also returns the pointwise \(R^2(t)\).

from fdars.regression import fosr_fpc

result = fosr_fpc(fd.data, predictors, n_comp=5)

print(f"FPC-based R-squared: {result['r_squared']:.4f}")
Key Type Description beta ndarray (p, m) Coefficient functions intercept ndarray (m,) Intercept function \(\hat\beta_0(t)\) fitted ndarray (n, m) Fitted response curves residuals ndarray (n, m) Residual curves r_squared float Global \(R^2\) r_squared_t ndarray (m,) Pointwise \(R^2(t)\) ncomp int Number of components used

The pointwise \(R^2(t)\) shows where the predictors explain the response — high in regions with real signal, low where the response is dominated by noise.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.regression import fosr_fpc

np.random.seed(3)
n, m, p = 60, 101, 2
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
X = np.random.randn(n, p)
beta_true = np.zeros((p, m))
beta_true[0] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
# Second effect concentrated in the first half of the domain
beta_true[1] = np.where(t < 0.5, np.cos(2 * np.pi * t), 0.0)
Y = X @ beta_true + 0.25 * np.random.randn(n, m)

res = fosr_fpc(Y, X, n_comp=5)
r2t = np.asarray(res["r_squared_t"])

f, ax = fig()
ax.plot(t, r2t, color="#3f51b5", lw=2)
ax.fill_between(t, 0, r2t, color="#3f51b5", alpha=0.15)
ax.set(title=r"Pointwise $R^2(t)$", xlabel="t", ylabel=r"$R^2(t)$", ylim=(0, 1))
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The curve is high on the left, where the second predictor's effect lives, and sags toward the right, where only the sinusoid contributes and noise dominates — a direct map of where the scalar predictors earn their keep.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
predict_fosr returns the fitted response curves for new predictor rows. Pass the training data and predictors plus the new predictor matrix; the returned array has one row per new observation.

new_pred = np.array([[1.0, 0.5, 0.0],   # e.g. treated, avg covariate
                     [0.0, -1.0, 1.0]]) # control
pred_curves = predict_fosr(fd.data, predictors, new_pred, lambda_=0.1)
print(np.asarray(pred_curves).shape)   # (2, m)

docs.title: Functional ANOVA
docs.text:
Functional ANOVA tests whether group mean functions differ across the domain — the functional analog of one-way ANOVA. The null is that all \(k\) group mean functions coincide:

\[ H_0: \mu_1(t) = \mu_2(t) = \cdots = \mu_k(t) \quad \text{for all } t \in \mathcal{T}. \]

A pointwise \(F\)-statistic is computed at each \(t\),

\[ F(t) = \frac{\sum_g n_g\,(\bar y_g(t) - \bar y(t))^2 / (k-1)} {\sum_g \sum_{i \in g} (y_i(t) - \bar y_g(t))^2 / (N-k)}, \]

and the global statistic \(\int F(t)\,dt\) is compared to its permutation distribution: group labels are shuffled \(B\) times, and the \(p\)-value is \((1 + \#\{F^*_b \ge F_{\text{obs}}\})/(B+1)\). This gives an exact, distribution-free test valid at any sample size.

import numpy as np
from fdars import Fdata
from fdars.regression import fanova

# --- Simulate three groups ---
np.random.seed(1)
n_per_group = 30
m = 101
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)

group_means = [
    np.sin(2 * np.pi * t),
    np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) + 0.5 * t,         # shifted group
    np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) - 0.3 * (1 - t),   # another shifted group
]

fd = Fdata(
    np.vstack([
        mean + 0.3 * np.random.randn(n_per_group, m)
        for mean in group_means
    ]),
    argvals=t,
)
groups = np.array([0]*n_per_group + [1]*n_per_group + [2]*n_per_group, dtype=np.int64)

# --- Run FANOVA ---
result = fanova(fd.data, groups, n_perm=999)

print(f"Global F-statistic: {result['global_statistic']:.4f}")
print(f"Permutation p-value: {result['p_value']:.4f}")
print(f"Group means shape: {np.asarray(result['group_means']).shape}")   # (3, 101)
print(f"Pointwise F(t) shape: {np.asarray(result['f_statistic_t']).shape}")  # (101,)
Key Type Description f_statistic_t ndarray (m,) Pointwise \(F\)-statistic p_value float Permutation-based \(p\)-value group_means ndarray (k, m) Estimated group mean functions global_statistic float Global (integrated) \(F\)-statistic

Permutation test

The n_perm parameter controls the number of random permutations. More permutations yield a more precise \(p\)-value but take longer. For publication-quality results, use n_perm=4999 or higher.

The two panels below show where the groups separate: the group mean functions on the left, and the pointwise \(F(t)\) on the right — its peaks mark the regions driving the rejection.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.regression import fanova

np.random.seed(1)
npg, m = 25, 81
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
means = [np.sin(2 * np.pi * t),
         np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) + 0.5 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * t),
         2 * t - 1]
Y = np.vstack([mu + 0.15 * np.random.randn(npg, m) for mu in means])
groups = np.repeat([0, 1, 2], npg).astype(np.int64)

res = fanova(Y, groups, n_perm=499)
gm = np.asarray(res["group_means"])
ft = np.asarray(res["f_statistic_t"])

f, (a0, a1) = fig(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
colors = ["#3f51b5", "#e8710a", "#198754"]
for g in range(3):
    a0.plot(t, gm[g], color=colors[g], lw=2, label=f"group {g+1}")
a0.set(title="Group mean functions", xlabel="t", ylabel="mean")
a0.legend()

a1.plot(t, ft, color="#b5179e", lw=2)
a1.set(title=f"Pointwise F(t)   (p = {res['p_value']:.3f})",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="F(t)")
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The three group means fan apart most strongly near the middle and right of the domain, and the \(F(t)\) trace peaks in exactly those regions — the permutation \(p\)-value confirms the separation is far beyond chance.

docs.title: Diagnostics: pointwise residual variance
docs.text:
A quick model check is the variance of the residual curves at each \(t\). Roughly constant variance supports the model; peaks flag regions where the scalar predictors fail to capture the response.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.regression import fosr

np.random.seed(5)
n, m, p = 70, 101, 2
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
X = np.random.randn(n, p)
beta_true = np.zeros((p, m))
beta_true[0] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
beta_true[1] = 0.5 * np.cos(4 * np.pi * t)
# Heteroscedastic noise: larger in the second half
noise = np.random.randn(n, m) * (0.1 + 0.4 * (t > 0.5))
Y = X @ beta_true + noise

res = fosr(Y, X, lambda_=0.1)
resid = np.asarray(res["residuals"])
rv = resid.var(axis=0)

f, ax = fig()
ax.plot(t, rv, color="#3f51b5", lw=2)
ax.set(title="Pointwise residual variance", xlabel="t", ylabel="Var(residual)")
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Residual variance is flat and small over the first half of the domain but climbs sharply past \(t=0.5\), exactly matching the heteroscedastic noise we injected — a clear signal that a constant-variance assumption would be violated there.

docs.title: Full example: treatment effect on functional responses
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from fdars import Fdata
from fdars.regression import fosr, fanova

np.random.seed(77)
n, m = 90, 121
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)

# Two-group design: treatment (1) vs control (0)
treatment = np.array([0]*45 + [1]*45, dtype=np.int64)
predictors = treatment.reshape(-1, 1).astype(np.float64)

# True treatment effect peaks in the middle of the domain
effect = 2.0 * np.exp(-((t - 0.5)**2) / 0.02)

# Simulate response
raw = np.zeros((n, m))
for i in range(n):
    baseline = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) + 0.5 * np.random.randn() * np.cos(np.pi * t)
    raw[i] = baseline + treatment[i] * effect + 0.4 * np.random.randn(m)
fd = Fdata(raw, argvals=t)

# --- FOSR: estimate the treatment effect curve ---
fosr_result = fosr(fd.data, predictors, lambda_=0.1)
beta_treatment = np.asarray(fosr_result["beta"])[0]  # estimated effect of treatment
print(f"FOSR R-squared: {fosr_result['r_squared']:.4f}")
print(f"Peak treatment effect at t={fd.argvals[np.argmax(beta_treatment)]:.2f}")

# --- FANOVA: test whether groups differ ---
fanova_result = fanova(fd.data, treatment, n_perm=999)
print(f"FANOVA p-value: {fanova_result['p_value']:.4f}")
if fanova_result["p_value"] < 0.05:
    print("Significant treatment effect detected.")
else:
    print("No significant treatment effect.")

The estimated treatment-effect curve \(\hat\beta_1(t)\) should localise the bump we built into the simulation. Plotting it against the truth confirms both its shape and its timing:

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.regression import fosr

np.random.seed(77)
n, m = 90, 121
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
treatment = np.array([0] * 45 + [1] * 45, dtype=np.int64)
predictors = treatment.reshape(-1, 1).astype(np.float64)
effect = 2.0 * np.exp(-((t - 0.5) ** 2) / 0.02)

raw = np.zeros((n, m))
for i in range(n):
    baseline = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) + 0.5 * np.random.randn() * np.cos(np.pi * t)
    raw[i] = baseline + treatment[i] * effect + 0.4 * np.random.randn(m)

beta_hat = np.asarray(fosr(raw, predictors, lambda_=0.1)["beta"])[0]

f, ax = fig()
ax.plot(t, effect, color="#6c757d", lw=1.5, ls="--", label="true effect")
ax.plot(t, beta_hat, color="#e8710a", lw=2, label=r"$\hat\beta_1(t)$")
ax.axvline(t[np.argmax(beta_hat)], color="#3f51b5", ls=":", lw=1.2,
           label=f"peak at t = {t[np.argmax(beta_hat)]:.2f}")
ax.set(title="Recovered treatment-effect curve", xlabel="t", ylabel="effect")
ax.legend()
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The recovered curve peaks near \(t=0.5\) and tapers to zero elsewhere, matching the localized Gaussian effect that was injected — the estimator correctly isolates both how large and when the treatment acts.

docs.title: When to use each method
docs.text:
Method Function Tuning Best for Penalised FOSR fosr \(\lambda\) smooth coefficient functions, large \(m\) FPC-based FOSR fosr_fpc \(K\) (# components) low-rank response structure, pointwise \(R^2\) Functional ANOVA fanova \(B\) (# permutations) testing group differences

2D function-on-scalar (R-only)

The R reference also documents fosr.2d for surface-valued responses \(y_i(s,t)\) (e.g. spatio-temporal fields, imaging). There is no fdars Python binding for this today, so it is omitted here rather than emulated.

  • Cuevas, Febrero & Fraiman (2004), An ANOVA test for functional data, Comput. Stat. Data Anal. 47(1), 111–122.

docs.title: Functional Generalized Linear Model
docs.text: Functional GLM extends scalar-on-function regression to exponential-family responses. Instead of a Gaussian error term, the response may be binary (binomial), a count (Poisson), a positive continuous value (gamma), or unrestricted Gaussian. fdars.regression.functional_glm first projects each observed curve onto a small number of functional principal components (FPCA), then fits a standard GLM on the resulting scores — one scalar score per FPC per subject. The coefficient function \(\hat\beta(t)\) is reconstructed back to the original domain by recombining the FPC loadings.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
Use functional_glm when your response variable is not Gaussian — binary outcomes, counts, or strictly positive continuous values — and your predictors are functional (curves). For a Gaussian response with a functional predictor, functional_glm with family="gaussian" produces the same fit as the linear scalar-on-function model, but the dedicated fregre_lm in fdars.regression is simpler.

Situation Recommended fdars function Binary response (0/1), pure classification task Specialized logistic fdars.regression.functional_logistic Binary response, need β(t) and GLM diagnostics Functional GLM functional_glm(..., family="binomial") Count response (non-negative integers) Functional GLM functional_glm(..., family="poisson") Positive continuous response Functional GLM functional_glm(..., family="gamma") Gaussian/unrestricted continuous response Linear SoF fdars.regression.fregre_lm

Quick rule: Start with functional_glm when the response distribution dictates a non-identity link. For binary classification where predicted classes matter more than the coefficient function, prefer functional_logistic — it returns predicted classes directly and supports bootstrap_ci_functional_logistic. For Gaussian responses, use the simpler scalar-on-function linear model.

When functional_logistic is preferred over binomial GLM

fdars.regression.functional_logistic is a dedicated binary classifier that predates functional_glm. It returns probabilities and predicted_classes directly, and it supports bootstrap_ci_functional_logistic for confidence intervals on the coefficient function. If your goal is to predict class labels rather than interpret β(t), use functional_logistic from fdars.regression.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
Let \(X_1(t), \dots, X_n(t)\) be \(n\) functional observations on grid \(t_1, \dots, t_m\), and let \(y_1, \dots, y_n\) be scalar responses from a specified exponential-family distribution. The model proceeds in two stages:

Stage 1 — FPCA projection. Decompose the functional data into n_comp leading functional principal components \(\phi_1(t), \dots, \phi_K(t)\) and form the score matrix \(S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times K}\) where \(s_{ik} = \int X_i(t)\,\phi_k(t)\,dt\). Each curve is now represented by \(K\) scalar scores.

Stage 2 — GLM in score space. Fit a GLM on the scores:

\[ g\!\bigl(\mathbb{E}[y_i \mid S_i]\bigr) \;=\; \alpha + S_i^\top \gamma, \]

where \(g(\cdot)\) is the link function for the chosen family and \(\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^K\) are scalar coefficients. The coefficient function on the original domain is

\[ \hat\beta(t) \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat\gamma_k\,\phi_k(t). \]

The GLM is fit by iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) with a maximum of max_iter iterations and convergence tolerance tol on the deviance change.

Link functions by family

Family Link \(g(\mu)\) Domain constraint Notes "gaussian" identity \(\mu\) \(y \in \mathbb{R}\) Reduces to ordinary functional linear model "binomial" logit \(\log(\mu / (1-\mu))\) \(y \in \{0, 1\}\) Binary response "poisson" log \(\log(\mu)\) \(y \geq 0\) Count response "gamma" inverse (canonical) \(1/\mu\) \(y > 0\) Positive continuous; NOT log-link

Gamma family uses the inverse canonical link, not log

fdars.regression.functional_glm with family="gamma" uses the inverse canonical link \(g(\mu) = 1/\mu\), not the log-link that R's glm(..., family=Gamma) defaults to. Results will differ from R if you assume a log-link. If you need a log-link for a Gamma response, transform the response before calling functional_glm with family="gaussian", or interpret the inverse-link coefficients appropriately.

AIC is not comparable to R glm() AIC

The AIC returned by functional_glm is computed from the score-space GLM log-likelihood, which treats the FPC scores as fixed predictors. This is not the same quantity as R's glm() AIC, which is based on the full-data likelihood. The AIC value here is useful for comparing models with different n_comp or family choices within fdars, but should not be compared numerically to AIC from R or other software.

Parameters

Parameter Type Default Description data ndarray (n, m) — Functional data matrix; rows are observations response ndarray (n,) — Scalar response vector family str "gaussian" Exponential family: "gaussian", "binomial", "poisson", "gamma" n_comp int 3 Number of FPC components for the FPCA projection scalar_covariates ndarray (n, q) or None None Additional scalar predictors to include in the GLM alongside the FPC scores max_iter int 25 Maximum IRLS iterations tol float 1e-6 Convergence tolerance on deviance change

Returns a dict with 15 keys:

Key Shape / Type Description "intercept" float GLM intercept on the link scale "beta_t" (m,) Functional coefficient \(\hat\beta(t)\) on the original domain "beta_se" (m,) Pointwise standard errors of \(\hat\beta(t)\) "gamma" (K,) Score-space GLM coefficients (\(K\) = actual n_comp used) "fitted_values" (n,) Fitted responses on the response scale (inverse-linked) "linear_predictors" (n,) Linear predictors \(\hat\eta_i = \alpha + S_i^\top \hat\gamma\) "ncomp" int Actual number of FPC components used "coefficients" (K+1,) Full coefficient vector (intercept + score coefficients) "std_errors" (K+1,) Standard errors of coefficients "log_likelihood" float Log-likelihood of the fitted score-space GLM "deviance" float Residual deviance "iterations" int Number of IRLS iterations taken "aic" float AIC from the score-space GLM (not comparable to R glm AIC — see note above) "bic" float BIC from the score-space GLM "family" str Family string echoed back

docs.title: 1. Binomial and Poisson examples
docs.text:
The code below fits the GLM for two families on synthetic data and plots the estimated coefficient functions. Each family uses a distinct link function and response domain.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
import fdars.regression as reg

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n, m = 30, 60
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
X = np.array([np.sin(2 * np.pi * t * (1 + 0.3 * rng.normal())) + rng.normal(0, 0.1, m)
              for _ in range(n)])

# --- Family 1: Binomial (binary response) ---
logit_true = X @ np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) / m
prob_true = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-3 * logit_true))
y_bin = rng.binomial(1, prob_true).astype(float)

res_bin = reg.functional_glm(X, y_bin, family="binomial", n_comp=3)
beta_bin = np.asarray(res_bin["beta_t"])

# --- Family 2: Poisson (count response, y >= 0) ---
# True log-rate is a linear functional of X; exp() ensures y >= 0.
log_rate_true = X @ np.cos(2 * np.pi * t) / m
y_poi = rng.poisson(np.exp(1.5 * log_rate_true)).astype(float)

res_poi = reg.functional_glm(X, y_poi, family="poisson", n_comp=3)
beta_poi = np.asarray(res_poi["beta_t"])

f, (a0, a1) = fig(1, 2, figsize=(12.0, 3.8))

a0.plot(t, beta_bin, color="#3f51b5", lw=2.2)
a0.set(title="Functional GLM (binomial) — β(t)",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="β(t)")

a1.plot(t, beta_poi, color="#e8710a", lw=2.2)
a1.set(title="Functional GLM (poisson) — β(t)",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="β(t)")

print(render(f))
print(f"binomial  deviance={res_bin['deviance']:.3f}  aic={res_bin['aic']:.3f}  "
      f"family={res_bin['family']}")
print(f"poisson   deviance={res_poi['deviance']:.3f}  aic={res_poi['aic']:.3f}  "
      f"family={res_poi['family']}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ binomial deviance=34.332 aic=42.332 family=binomial poisson deviance=25.588 aic=78.876 family=poisson FDARS_FENCE_OK

docs.title: 2. Gaussian family — reduces to the linear scalar-on-function model
docs.text:
With family="gaussian" and the identity link, the functional GLM is algebraically equivalent to the linear scalar-on-function model (fregre_lm). This fence verifies that claim by comparing fitted values from both estimators on the same data.

import numpy as np
from fdars.regression import functional_glm, fregre_lm

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n, m = 25, 40
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)

# Build functional data from 3 explicit FPC scores for good conditioning.
scores = rng.standard_normal((n, 3))
phi = np.array([np.sin((k + 1) * np.pi * t) for k in range(3)])
X = scores @ phi + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal((n, m))
y = X @ phi[0] / m + 0.2 * rng.standard_normal(n)

glm_g = functional_glm(X, y, family="gaussian", n_comp=3)
lm    = fregre_lm(X, y, n_comp=3)

corr = np.corrcoef(np.asarray(glm_g["fitted_values"]),
                   np.asarray(lm["fitted_values"]))[0, 1]
print(f"Correlation of fitted values (GLM gaussian vs fregre_lm): {corr:.6f}")
print(f"GLM  deviance={glm_g['deviance']:.4f}  aic={glm_g['aic']:.4f}")
print(f"fregre_lm r_squared={lm['r_squared']:.4f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

Correlation of fitted values (GLM gaussian vs fregre_lm): 1.000000 GLM deviance=0.8910 aic=9.7820 fregre_lm r_squared=0.8201 FDARS_FENCE_OK

The correlation between fitted values is essentially 1.0 — confirming that the Gaussian functional GLM and the linear scalar-on-function model are equivalent estimators for Gaussian responses.

docs.title: 3. Choosing n_comp — parameter selection
docs.text:
n_comp controls how many FPCA components are retained before fitting the GLM. Too few components miss signal; too many add noise. Use model_selection_ncomp from fdars.scalar_on_function to select n_comp by GCV (generalized cross-validation), AIC, or BIC before fitting the GLM.

import numpy as np
from fdars.scalar_on_function import model_selection_ncomp
from fdars.regression import functional_glm

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n, m = 25, 40
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)

scores = rng.standard_normal((n, 3))
phi = np.array([np.sin((k + 1) * np.pi * t) for k in range(3)])
X = scores @ phi + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal((n, m))
y = X @ phi[0] / m + 0.2 * rng.standard_normal(n)

# Select n_comp via GCV on the linear (Gaussian) sub-problem first.
sel = model_selection_ncomp(X, y, max_comp=6, criterion="gcv")
best = sel["best_ncomp"]

print(f"Best n_comp (GCV): {best}")
print("  n_comp | AIC      | BIC      | GCV")
for ncomp, aic, bic, gcv in sel["criteria"]:
    print(f"  {ncomp:6d} | {aic:8.2f} | {bic:8.2f} | {gcv:.5f}")

# Fit the GLM with the selected n_comp.
res = functional_glm(X, y, family="gaussian", n_comp=best)
print(f"\nGLM (gaussian, n_comp={best}): deviance={res['deviance']:.4f}  "
      f"aic={res['aic']:.4f}  iterations={res['iterations']}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

Best n_comp (GCV): 3 n_comp | AIC | BIC | GCV 1 | -51.36 | -48.92 | 0.12607 2 | -75.00 | -71.34 | 0.04997 3 | -75.36 | -70.48 | 0.04778 4 | -73.37 | -67.28 | 0.05560 5 | -71.65 | -64.33 | 0.05969 6 | -70.22 | -61.69 | 0.06502

GLM (gaussian, n_comp=3): deviance=0.8910 aic=9.7820 iterations=2 FDARS_FENCE_OK

Choosing n_comp in practice

  • Use model_selection_ncomp first on a Gaussian approximation of your problem (swap in family="gaussian" temporarily) to get a computationally cheap GCV/AIC profile over component counts. The selected n_comp is a good starting point for the non-Gaussian GLM.
  • Inspect deviance across n_comp using the GLM directly: fit the model for n_comp in [1, 2, …, max_comp] and plot result["deviance"] vs n_comp. The curve typically elbows where additional components no longer reduce deviance meaningfully.
  • Compare AIC and BIC from result["aic"] and result["bic"] (within-fdars comparisons only — not comparable to R; see note above).
  • Keep n_comp ≤ n / 5 as a rule of thumb to avoid over-fitting in the score-space GLM.

docs.title: 4. Gamma family example
docs.text:
The gamma family models strictly positive continuous responses using the inverse canonical link \(g(\mu) = 1/\mu\). Common use cases include response times, insurance claims, or any strictly positive measurement where variance scales with the mean.

Family domain constraints and lowercase family strings

  • "gamma" requires every response value y > 0 (strictly positive). Any non-positive value raises ValueError.
  • "binomial" requires y ∈ {0.0, 1.0} (binary, not a probability).
  • "poisson" requires y ≥ 0 (non-negative).
  • Family strings are always lowercase: "gaussian", "binomial", "poisson", "gamma". Passing "Gamma" or "Poisson" raises ValueError.
import numpy as np
from fdars.regression import functional_glm

rng = np.random.default_rng(17)
n, m = 25, 40
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)

scores = rng.standard_normal((n, 3))
phi = np.array([np.sin((k + 1) * np.pi * t) for k in range(3)])
X = scores @ phi + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal((n, m))

# Gamma response: construct y > 0 via exp of a linear functional of X.
log_rate = X @ phi[0] / m
y = np.exp(log_rate) + 0.1   # guaranteed y > 0

res = functional_glm(X, y, family="gamma", n_comp=3)
print(f"family:         {res['family']}")
print(f"deviance:       {res['deviance']:.4f}")
print(f"iterations:     {res['iterations']}")
print(f"fitted (first 5): {np.asarray(res['fitted_values'])[:5].round(4)}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

family: gamma deviance: 0.1943 iterations: 7 fitted (first 5): [1.842 0.6913 0.7887 0.9922 0.6114] FDARS_FENCE_OK

docs.title: Partial-Curve Conformal Prediction
docs.text:
Some curves are only partly observed when a decision has to be made: a growth curve up to the current age, a batch profile up to the current hour, a signal with dropouts. Partial-curve conformal prediction answers two questions about the unobserved remainder, both with a finite-sample coverage guarantee:

  • Amplitude: after registration to a common template, where will the complete curve lie? This is a prediction band for the aligned curve.
  • Phase: how will the complete curve be warped relative to the template? This is a prediction set of warping functions.

fdars.conformal implements the split-conformal SFCP (amplitude) and SFCPP (phase) procedures of Wang, Kurtek & Zhang (2026). It extends them with simultaneous bands, held-out bandwidth tuning and fragmented or sparse observation patterns. For conformal intervals of a scalar response, see Conformal Prediction; for bands that should contain whole new curves, see Tolerance Bands.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Fully observed curves \(f_1, \dots, f_n\) are available; a new curve \(f_{n+1}\) is observed only on part of the domain.

  1. Split. The curves are split at random (cal_fraction, seed) into a training part and a calibration part of size \(n_2\). The training part is used only to estimate the elastic template \(\bar f\), a Karcher mean.
  2. Register. Each calibration curve is registered to the template, \(\gamma_i^* = \arg\min_\gamma \lVert \bar q - (q_i \circ \gamma)\sqrt{\dot\gamma}\rVert\) (SRSF dynamic programming, penalty lambda_). This gives an amplitude response \(Y_i = f_i \circ \gamma_i^*\) (the aligned curve) and a phase response \(\gamma_i^*\).
  3. Predict from the observed part. The new curve's responses are predicted by Nadaraya–Watson smoothing over the calibration curves, with Gaussian kernel weights on the distance between the observed parts (distance="l2", "srsf" or "elastic"; bandwidth bandwidth, by default the median pairwise distance).
  4. Calibrate. The leave-one-out residuals of the calibration curves, together with a trial value for the new curve (full conformal within the calibration set), give the band. For the amplitude the conformal interval is computed exactly in closed form at every grid point. For the phase, residuals are Fisher–Rao distances \(d(\gamma_1, \gamma_2) = \arccos \int \sqrt{\dot\gamma_1 \dot\gamma_2}\) between warps.

Because the template comes from curves that are not used for calibration, the calibration curves and the new curve are exchangeable. That gives, for any sample size,

\[ P\big(Y_{n+1}(t) \in I_t\big) \ge 1 - \alpha \ \text{ for every } t, \qquad P\big(\gamma_{n+1}^* \in I_\gamma\big) \ge 1 - \alpha, \]

where \(Y_{n+1}\) and \(\gamma^*_{n+1}\) are the aligned curve and warp of the complete new curve, which are unknown at prediction time. The guarantee needs \(\alpha \ge 1/(n_2 + 1)\); a smaller alpha raises a ValueError naming the number of calibration curves required.

docs.title: Example: a curve observed up to \(t = 0.58\)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
import fdars.conformal as cf
from fdars.alignment import elastic_align_pair

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
m = 51
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
def curve():                     # a main peak and a shoulder, random height and timing
    a, s = rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2), rng.uniform(-0.08, 0.08)
    w = t + s * np.sin(np.pi * t)
    return a * np.exp(-0.5 * ((w - 0.5) / 0.12) ** 2) + 0.3 * a * np.exp(-0.5 * ((w - 0.8) / 0.06) ** 2)

X = np.array([curve() for _ in range(30)])          # fully observed reference curves
new = curve()
k = 30                                              # only the first 30 grid points are observed

model = cf.partial_conformal_fit(X, t, alpha=0.2, seed=1)
pred = cf.partial_conformal_predict(model, new[:k])
truth = elastic_align_pair(model.template, new, t)  # the complete curve, registered (unknown in practice)

f, (a0, a1) = fig(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8))
for c in model.calibration_aligned:
    a0.plot(t, c, color="#6c757d", lw=0.8, alpha=0.35)
a0.fill_between(t, pred["amplitude_lower"], pred["amplitude_upper"], color="#dc3545", alpha=0.18,
                label="80% amplitude band")
a0.plot(t, pred["amplitude_center"], color="#dc3545", lw=2.0, label="predicted aligned curve")
a0.plot(t, truth["f_aligned"], color="#1a1a2e", lw=1.8, ls="--", label="complete curve, aligned")
a0.plot(t[:k], new[:k], color="#e8710a", lw=2.4, label="observed prefix (raw)")
a0.axvline(t[k - 1], color="#495057", lw=1.0, ls=":")
a0.set(title="Amplitude: where the aligned curve will lie", xlabel="t")
a0.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")

for g in pred["phase_accepted"][::6]:
    a1.plot(t, g - t, color="#3f51b5", lw=0.7, alpha=0.35)
a1.fill_between(t, pred["phase_lower"] - t, pred["phase_upper"] - t, color="#3f51b5", alpha=0.15,
                label="envelope of accepted warps")
a1.plot(t, pred["phase_center"] - t, color="#3f51b5", lw=2.0, label="predicted warp")
a1.plot(t, truth["gamma"] - t, color="#1a1a2e", lw=1.8, ls="--", label="warp of the complete curve")
a1.axhline(0, color="#495057", lw=1.0)
a1.set(title="Phase: warps, shown as gamma(t) - t", xlabel="t")
a1.legend(fontsize=8)
print(render(f))
inside = np.mean((truth["f_aligned"] >= pred["amplitude_lower"]) & (truth["f_aligned"] <= pred["amplitude_upper"]))
print(f"<p>observed {pred['n_observed']} of {m} points (up to t = {pred['observed_end']:.2f}); "
      f"{len(model.calibration_indices)} calibration curves; bandwidth {pred['bandwidth']:.3f}; "
      f"aligned complete curve inside the band at {inside:.0%} of grid points; "
      f"its warp in the phase set: {pred['prediction'].phase_set_contains(truth['gamma'])}</p>")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

observed 30 of 51 points (up to t = 0.58); 15 calibration curves; bandwidth 0.112; aligned complete curve inside the band at 98% of grid points; its warp in the phase set: False

FDARS_FENCE_OK

The grey curves are the registered calibration curves. The band covers where the registered complete curve will lie, including the shoulder at \(t \approx 0.8\), which has not been observed yet. The raw prefix (orange) need not lie inside the band, because it has not been aligned. On the right, the phase set is drawn through its accepted members: geodesics on the space of warps from the predicted warp towards each calibration warp, kept when they pass the conformal test. The exact set is available as pred["prediction"].phase_set_contains(gamma). The envelope phase_lower/phase_upper is a pointwise summary for display, not the set itself. In this draw the warp of the complete curve (dashed) stays inside the envelope but is not in the 80% phase set: its Fisher–Rao distance from the predicted warp is too large compared with the calibration residuals. The guarantee allows that about one time in five; the simulation below shows the long-run rate.

docs.title: Checking the coverage
docs.text:
The guarantee is about repeated use, so check it by simulation: draw fresh curves, observe the same prefix, and count how often the band contains the registered complete curve.

import numpy as np
import fdars.conformal as cf
from fdars.alignment import elastic_align_pair

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
m = 51
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
def curve():
    a, s = rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2), rng.uniform(-0.08, 0.08)
    w = t + s * np.sin(np.pi * t)
    return a * np.exp(-0.5 * ((w - 0.5) / 0.12) ** 2) + 0.3 * a * np.exp(-0.5 * ((w - 0.8) / 0.06) ** 2)

X = np.array([curve() for _ in range(30)])
pointwise = cf.partial_conformal_fit(X, t, alpha=0.2, seed=1)
simultaneous = cf.partial_conformal_fit(X, t, alpha=0.2, seed=1, band="simultaneous")

hits_pw, hits_sim, hits_phase, width_pw, width_sim = [], [], [], [], []
for _ in range(60):
    c = curve()
    full = elastic_align_pair(pointwise.template, c, t)
    target = full["f_aligned"]
    p = cf.partial_conformal_predict(pointwise, c[:30])
    hits_phase.append(p["prediction"].phase_set_contains(full["gamma"]))
    s = cf.partial_conformal_predict(simultaneous, c[:30])
    hits_pw.append(np.mean((target >= p["amplitude_lower"]) & (target <= p["amplitude_upper"])))
    hits_sim.append(np.all((target >= s["amplitude_lower"]) & (target <= s["amplitude_upper"])))
    width_pw.append(np.mean(p["amplitude_upper"] - p["amplitude_lower"]))
    width_sim.append(np.mean(s["amplitude_upper"] - s["amplitude_lower"]))
print(f"pointwise band   : average pointwise coverage {np.mean(hits_pw):.2f}   (target >= 0.80), mean width {np.mean(width_pw):.3f}")
print(f"simultaneous band: whole curve inside        {np.mean(hits_sim):.2f}   (target >= 0.80), mean width {np.mean(width_sim):.3f}")
print(f"phase set        : warp inside               {np.mean(hits_phase):.2f}   (target >= 0.80)")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

pointwise band   : average pointwise coverage 0.82   (target >= 0.80), mean width 0.099
simultaneous band: whole curve inside        0.87   (target >= 0.80), mean width 0.325
phase set        : warp inside               0.88   (target >= 0.80)
FDARS_FENCE_OK

All three sets meet their target. They promise different things: the pointwise band covers the curve at each \(t\) separately, while the simultaneous band covers the whole curve at once and is about 3 times wider here. Both models use the same seed, so they share the split and template.

docs.title: Band types
docs.text:
band= Score Guarantee Use when "pointwise" (default) \(\lvert Y_i(t) - \hat Y_i(t)\rvert\) at each \(t\) each \(t\) covered with probability \(\ge 1-\alpha\) you look at the band one time point at a time "simultaneous" \(\sup_t \lvert Y_i(t) - \hat Y_i(t)\rvert / \sigma(t)\) the whole curve inside with probability \(\ge 1-\alpha\) decisions depend on the entire remaining trajectory

For the simultaneous band, band_scale sets the shape \(\sigma(t)\) of the band: "constant" (default, equal width), "training_sd" (the pointwise SD of the aligned training curves, floored at 5% of its maximum, so wider where curves vary more) or a positive array of length \(m\). The result's amplitude_radius is the calibrated multiplier \(R\), and the band is \(\hat c(t) \pm R\,\sigma(t)\).

docs.title: Observation patterns
docs.text:
partial_conformal_predict(model, observed) handles the common case: the curve is observed on a prefix of the grid, observed = values[:k]. partial_conformal_predict_observed also covers the other patterns:

observation= Arguments Meaning "prefix" values, n_observed=None (= len(values)) the first n_observed grid points "fragments" values, fragments (K, 2) inclusive grid-index ranges, increasing and disjoint; values concatenated in fragment order "sparse" values, times values at increasing times inside the domain, not necessarily on the grid

For fragments, the distance between observed parts is a length-weighted sum of per-fragment distances; for sparse times it is the Euclidean distance of the values, with calibration curves interpolated linearly at those times. Each fragment is also located in the template by elastic partial matching (fragment_registrations), for information only: the registration of the observed part (registration) does not enter the conformal sets. The guarantee assumes the observation pattern does not depend on the curve's values.

import numpy as np
import fdars.conformal as cf

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
m = 51
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
def curve():
    a, s = rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2), rng.uniform(-0.08, 0.08)
    w = t + s * np.sin(np.pi * t)
    return a * np.exp(-0.5 * ((w - 0.5) / 0.12) ** 2) + 0.3 * a * np.exp(-0.5 * ((w - 0.8) / 0.06) ** 2)

X = np.array([curve() for _ in range(30)])
new = curve()
model = cf.partial_conformal_fit(X, t, alpha=0.2, seed=1)

frag = np.array([[0, 9], [30, 39]])                       # two windows of 10 grid points
fr = cf.partial_conformal_predict_observed(model, np.r_[new[0:10], new[30:40]],
                                           observation="fragments", fragments=frag)
times = np.array([0.1, 0.3, 0.45, 0.6])                   # four off-grid measurements
sp = cf.partial_conformal_predict_observed(model, np.interp(times, t, new),
                                           observation="sparse", times=times)
for name, r in [("fragments", fr), ("sparse", sp)]:
    print(f"{name:9s}: mean band width {np.mean(r['amplitude_upper'] - r['amplitude_lower']):.3f}, "
          f"phase radius {r['phase_radius']:.3f}")
print("fragment registrations:", len(fr["fragment_registrations"]))
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

fragments: mean band width 0.101, phase radius 0.082
sparse   : mean band width 0.098, phase radius 0.083
fragment registrations: 2
FDARS_FENCE_OK

docs.title: Choosing the bandwidth
docs.text:
The kernel bandwidth decides how many calibration curves contribute to the prediction. Choosing it by minimising band width on the calibration curves themselves would break the coverage guarantee. fdars therefore offers a held-out selector:

  • partial_conformal_fit(..., tuning_fraction=0.3) reserves that share of the calibration curves as a tuning set. Each tuning curve is predicted from the others under the observation pattern of the new curve, and the candidate bandwidth with the smallest mean band width is used. The remaining calibration curves are then exchangeable with the new curve, so coverage stays exact; the cost is fewer calibration curves. bandwidth_candidates overrides the default candidates (quantiles of the pairwise distances).
  • partial_conformal_select_bandwidth(tuning_model, observation=..., n_observed=...) runs the same selector on the calibration curves of tuning_model and returns {bandwidth, candidates, mean_width, n_tuning}. Pass the result as bandwidth= to a model fitted on other curves.
import numpy as np
import fdars.conformal as cf

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
m = 51
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
def curve():
    a, s = rng.uniform(0.8, 1.2), rng.uniform(-0.08, 0.08)
    w = t + s * np.sin(np.pi * t)
    return a * np.exp(-0.5 * ((w - 0.5) / 0.12) ** 2) + 0.3 * a * np.exp(-0.5 * ((w - 0.8) / 0.06) ** 2)

X = np.array([curve() for _ in range(30)])
new = curve()
tuned = cf.partial_conformal_fit(X, t, alpha=0.2, seed=1, tuning_fraction=0.4)
p = cf.partial_conformal_predict(tuned, new[:30])
sel = p["bandwidth_selection"]
print(f"tuning curves: {sel['n_tuning']}, calibration curves left: {len(tuned.calibration_indices)}")
print("candidates :", np.round(sel["candidates"], 3))
print("mean width :", np.round(sel["mean_width"], 3))
print(f"chosen bandwidth {sel['bandwidth']:.3f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

tuning curves: 6, calibration curves left: 9
candidates : [0.053 0.087 0.112 0.136 0.17  0.282]
mean width : [0.186 0.15  0.146 0.145 0.144 0.143]
chosen bandwidth 0.282
FDARS_FENCE_OK

docs.title: Using a known template
docs.text: If a template is available from earlier, independent data, partial_conformal_fit_with_template(calibration, argvals, template, ...) skips the split: every curve passed is used for calibration. The template must not be estimated from those calibration curves, otherwise exchangeability, and with it the guarantee, is lost. band_scale="training_sd" is unavailable here, since there are no training curves.

docs.title: Parameters and results
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning alpha 0.1 miscoverage; can be overridden per prediction (alpha=) cal_fraction, seed 0.5, 42 calibration share and split seed distance "l2" distance between observed parts: "l2", "srsf" (L² between SRSFs, no alignment) or "elastic" (elastic amplitude distance) bandwidth None kernel bandwidth; None = median pairwise distance (or the tuned value) lambda_ 0.0 registration penalty karcher_max_iter, karcher_tol 20, 1e-3 template estimation n_phase_radii 25 radii per geodesic direction when listing accepted warps band, band_scale "pointwise", None see Band types tuning_fraction, bandwidth_candidates None see Choosing the bandwidth

The fitted model exposes template, calibration_indices, training_indices, tuning_indices, calibration_data, calibration_aligned, calibration_gammas and training_sd. A prediction returns amplitude_center/lower/upper, phase_center/lower/upper, phase_radius, phase_accepted, weights (the kernel weights of the calibration curves), registration (partial match of the observed part to the template: start_index, end_index, gamma, distance, domain_fraction), full_registration (only for a fully observed curve), bandwidth, bandwidth_selection and prediction (the handle with phase_set_contains).

What the guarantee does not cover

Coverage is marginal over new curves drawn like the calibration curves, and it is about the registered curve and the warp to this template. It does not cover the raw, unaligned curve, and it does not hold if the new curve comes from a different population (drift) or if its observation pattern depends on its values. With few calibration curves the bands are wide and very small alpha is not attainable.

docs.title: PEER & Wavelet Regression
docs.text:
Scalar-on-function regression estimates a coefficient function \(\beta(t)\) in

\[ y_i = \alpha + \int x_i(t)\,\beta(t)\,dt + \varepsilon_i . \]

FPC regression and P-splines assume \(\beta\) is smooth, or that it lies in the span of the leading principal components. This page covers four estimators in fdars.scalar_on_function for when that assumption is wrong or prior knowledge is available:

Function Idea Best when peer penalised least squares with a structured penalty \(\lambda\,\beta^\top Q\beta\), \(\lambda\) by GCV or REML \(\beta\) is smooth, or you know a plausible shape for it lpeer peer plus a subject random intercept for repeated measures several curves per subject wcr PCR or PLS on the curves' wavelet coefficients \(\beta\) is spatially inhomogeneous (jumps, local bursts) wnet elastic net on the wavelet coefficients, \(\lambda\) by cross-validation \(\beta\) is sparse in a wavelet basis: mostly zero, a few local features

docs.title: PEER: structured penalties
docs.text:
PEER (partially empirical eigenvectors for regression, Randolph, Harezlak & Feng 2012) solves the penalised normal equations

\[ (W_c^\top W_c + \lambda Q)\,\beta = W_c^\top y_c , \]

where \(W_c\) is the centred design with Simpson quadrature weights, so \(\beta\) is on the scale of the integral model above, and \(Q\) is a positive semi-definite penalty matrix. The penalty decides which directions of \(\beta\) are cheap and which are shrunk:

penalty= \(Q\) Effect "difference" (default) \(D_2^\top D_2\), second differences shrinks towards straight lines: a smoothness prior "ridge" \(I\) shrinks every coefficient equally; does not penalise roughness "decree" your decree_q, an (m, m) symmetric PSD matrix encodes prior knowledge: directions in the null space of \(Q\) are not penalised at all

lambda_ is a float (fixed), "gcv" (the default; a 40-point log grid on \([10^{-6}, 10^4]\)) or "reml" (an EM algorithm for the REML criterion). The result holds beta, intercept, fitted_values, effective_df (trace of the hat matrix), the chosen lambda_, lambda_method, gcv (when GCV ran) and model, whose predict(new_data, argvals) scores new curves.

A decree penalty is how PEER uses prior information. If you believe \(\beta\) resembles a shape \(p(t)\), penalise only what \(p\) cannot explain. With \(P = pp^\top / p^\top p\) the projection onto \(p\), the matrix \(Q = (I - P)\, D_2^\top D_2\,(I - P)\) leaves any multiple of \(p\) unpenalised and asks the remainder to be smooth.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
import fdars.scalar_on_function as sof

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n, m = 30, 65
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
k = np.arange(1, 9)
X = (rng.standard_normal((n, 8)) / k) @ np.vstack([np.sin(np.pi * kk * t) for kk in k])
beta = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) * np.exp(-2 * t)                       # true beta(t)
y = 0.5 + np.trapezoid(X * beta, t, axis=1) + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(n)

D2 = np.diff(np.eye(m), 2, axis=0)
prior = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)                                       # prior guess of the shape
P = np.outer(prior, prior) / (prior @ prior)
Q = (np.eye(m) - P) @ D2.T @ D2 @ (np.eye(m) - P)

fits = {
    "difference (default)": sof.peer(X, y, t),
    "ridge": sof.peer(X, y, t, penalty="ridge"),
    "decree: smooth around sin(2 pi t)": sof.peer(X, y, t, penalty="decree", decree_q=Q),
}

f, ax = fig(figsize=(8, 3.6))
ax.plot(t, beta, color="#1a1a2e", lw=2.6, label="true beta(t)")
for (name, r), col in zip(fits.items(), ["#3f51b5", "#e8710a", "#198754"]):
    ax.plot(t, r["beta"], color=col, lw=1.8, label=name)
ax.set(title="PEER estimates under three penalties (lambda by GCV)", xlabel="t")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
print(render(f))
rows = []
for name, r in fits.items():
    err = np.sqrt(np.trapezoid((r["beta"] - beta) ** 2, t))
    rows.append(f"{name}: edf {r['effective_df']:.1f}, L2 error {err:.3f}")
print("<p>" + "; ".join(rows) + "</p>")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

difference (default): edf 5.8, L2 error 0.065; ridge: edf 7.6, L2 error 0.109; decree: smooth around sin(2 pi t): edf 5.8, L2 error 0.047

FDARS_FENCE_OK

The difference penalty recovers the shape but bends towards a straight line near the ends, where the data carry little information. The decree penalty has no cost for the prior shape and gets the lowest error. The ridge estimate zig-zags: ridge does not penalise roughness, and with Simpson weights (alternating 4, 2, 4, ... across the grid) in the design, the least-norm solution alternates between neighbouring grid points. Use ridge only on a coarse grid or after smoothing.

docs.title: Longitudinal PEER
docs.text:
With repeated curves per subject (visits, trials, sessions), responses of the same subject are correlated. lpeer(data, y, argvals, subject_ids, ...) (Kundu, Harezlak & Randolph 2016) fits

\[ y_{ij} = \alpha + \int x_{ij}(t)\,\beta(t)\,dt + u_i + \varepsilon_{ij},\qquad u_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{u}),\ \varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\varepsilon}). \]

It first estimates the variance components by REML on FPC scores, then re-solves for \(\beta\) by penalised generalised least squares with the same PEER penalty. subject_ids may be any non-negative integer labels. The result adds sigma2_subject, sigma2_resid and n_subjects; fitted_values and model.predict are marginal (population-level, without \(u_i\)).

import numpy as np
import fdars.scalar_on_function as sof

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n, m = 30, 65
t = np.linspace(0, 1, m)
k = np.arange(1, 9)
X = (rng.standard_normal((n, 8)) / k) @ np.vstack([np.sin(np.pi * kk * t) for kk in k])
beta = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t) * np.exp(-2 * t)
subject = np.repeat(np.arange(10), 3)                   # 10 subjects x 3 visits
u = rng.normal(0, 0.5, 10)                              # subject random intercepts
y = 0.5 + np.trapezoid(X * beta, t, axis=1) + u[subject] + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(n)

lp = sof.lpeer(X, y, t, subject)
pe = sof.peer(X, y, t)
corr = lambda b: np.corrcoef(b, beta)[0, 1]
print(f"subjects: {lp['n_subjects']}, sigma2_subject={lp['sigma2_subject']:.3f}, "
      f"sigma2_resid={lp['sigma2_resid']:.5f}")
print(f"corr(beta_hat, beta): lpeer {corr(lp['beta']):.3f}   peer ignoring subjects {corr(pe['beta']):.3f}")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")

subjects: 10, sigma2_subject=0.144, sigma2_resid=0.00010
corr(beta_hat, beta): lpeer 0.996   peer ignoring subjects 0.659
FDARS_FENCE_OK

Ignoring the subject effect treats \(u_i\) as noise that happens to be shared by the three visits. peer then partly explains it with \(\beta\) and gets the shape wrong; lpeer assigns it to the random intercept.

docs.title: Wavelet-domain regression
docs.text:
Smoothness penalties and FPC bases spread \(\beta\) over the whole domain, so a coefficient that is zero almost everywhere with a few sharp features is estimated badly. Wavelets localise in both time and scale: a jump or a short burst needs only a few wavelet coefficients. Wavelet regression (Zhao, Ogden & Reiss 2012) therefore works in coefficient space:

  1. each curve is transformed with a discrete wavelet transform (basis.wavelet_decompose_matrix; Daubechies "haar"/"db1" to "db10", "periodic" or "symmetric" boundaries, level=None for the deepest useful level) and its coefficients are concatenated into a row of the design;
  2. a regression is fitted on that design: wcr uses principal-component (method="pcr") or partial-least-squares (method="pls") regression with ncomp components, while wnet fits an elastic net (alpha = L1 share, 1 is the lasso) with \(\lambda\) chosen by n_folds-fold cross-validation (deterministic folds from seed);
  3. the coefficient weights are mapped back to the time domain as beta_t, by the adjoint of the wavelet transform (for the orthogonal periodic transform this is the inverse transform).

Both return intercept, beta_t, fitted_values, residuals, coeff_weights (in wavelet space), the effective level, and model with predict(new_data). wnet also returns selected, the indices of non-zero wavelet coefficients, and the chosen lambda_.

Coefficient scale: per sample, not per unit time

wcr and wnet take no argvals. They model \(y_i = \alpha + \sum_j x_i(t_j)\,\beta_j\) on the sampling index, without quadrature weights. Their beta_t therefore equals \(\beta(t_j)\,\Delta t\) in the integral model. Multiply PEER's beta by \(\Delta t\), or divide beta_t by it, before comparing the two.

Boundary mode: periodic or symmetric

Both modes give a beta_t that is consistent with the fit: beta_t is the adjoint of the wavelet analysis operator applied to coeff_weights, so X @ beta_t + intercept reproduces fitted_values to round-off in either mode. They differ in how the transform treats the ends of the curve:

  • mode="periodic" (default) wraps the curve around, so the last sample is treated as the neighbour of the first. The transform is orthogonal with \(m\) coefficients for a power-of-two \(m\). If \(x(t_1)\) and \(x(t_m)\) differ, the wrap creates an artificial jump that costs fine-scale coefficients near both ends.
  • mode="symmetric" mirrors the curve at each end, so there is no artificial jump; the price is a redundant, non-orthogonal transform with more coefficients than samples (448 instead of 64 for the Haar transform of the 64-point curves below).

Use periodic for periodic data and when the features of \(\beta\) are away from the ends, symmetric when the curves' end values differ and the behaviour of \(\beta\) near the boundaries matters. The example below uses periodic; with symmetric, WNET's estimate is about as good.

The coefficient below is piecewise constant: zero except for a positive block and a narrower negative block. The predictors are rough, Brownian-like curves.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
import fdars.scalar_on_function as sof

rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
n, m = 30, 64
t = np.arange(m) / m
X = np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal((n, m)), axis=1) / np.sqrt(m)     # rough, Brownian-like curves
beta = np.where((t >= 0.3) & (t < 0.4), 1.0, 0.0) - np.where((t >= 0.7) & (t < 0.75), 1.5, 0.0)
y = 1.0 + X @ beta + 0.05 * rng.standard_normal(n)                   # per-sample coefficients

wn = sof.wnet(X, y, wavelet="haar", alpha=0.9, seed=0)
wc = sof.wcr(X, y, wavelet="haar", ncomp=5, method="pls")
pe = sof.peer(X, y, t)                                               # integral scale

f, ax = fig(figsize=(8, 3.6))
ax.step(t, beta, where="post", color="#1a1a2e", lw=2.6, label="true coefficient")
ax.plot(t, wn["beta_t"], color="#3f51b5", lw=1.8, label=f"WNET (haar, {len(wn['selected'])} coefficients)")
ax.plot(t, wc["beta_t"], color="#e8710a", lw=1.6, label="WCR (haar, PLS, 5 components)")
ax.plot(t, pe["beta"] / m, color="#198754", lw=1.6, ls="--", label="PEER difference, x dt")
ax.set(title="A piecewise-constant coefficient", xlabel="t")
ax.legend(fontsize=8.5)
print(render(f))
corr = lambda b: np.corrcoef(b, beta)[0, 1]
print(f"<p>correlation with the truth: WNET {corr(wn['beta_t']):.2f}, WCR {corr(wc['beta_t']):.2f}, "
      f"PEER {corr(pe['beta']):.2f}; WNET kept {len(wn['selected'])} of {wn['coeff_weights'].size} "
      f"wavelet coefficients (lambda={wn['lambda_']:.3g}); "
      f"X @ beta_t + intercept reproduces the fit: {np.allclose(X @ wn['beta_t'] + wn['intercept'], wn['fitted_values'])}</p>")
print("FDARS_FENCE_OK")
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

correlation with the truth: WNET 0.93, WCR 0.70, PEER 0.89; WNET kept 14 of 64 wavelet coefficients (lambda=0.00537); X @ beta_t + intercept reproduces the fit: True

FDARS_FENCE_OK

WNET keeps 14 of the 64 Haar coefficients and recovers both blocks with sharp edges, slightly shrunk in height. The difference-penalised PEER estimate tracks the blocks too, but its smoothness prior rounds the edges and adds ripples in the flat parts. WCR's five PLS components capture the overall pattern without isolating the blocks: PCR/PLS shrink along directions of the predictors, not towards sparsity.

docs.title: Choosing the wavelet and level
docs.text:
• wavelet: "haar" suits piecewise-constant coefficients; smoother Daubechies wavelets ("db4", the default, up to "db10") suit smooth bumps. A longer filter gives a smoother basis but fewer usable levels.
  • level: None uses the deepest level the signal length allows, basis.wavelet_max_level(m, wavelet) \(= \lfloor \log_2(m / (\text{filter length} - 1)) \rfloor\) (\(\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor\) for Haar). Shallower levels leave a larger coarse approximation band.
  • mode: "periodic" (default) or "symmetric", see the note on boundary modes above. With periodic boundaries the grid length should ideally be a power of two; odd lengths are extended by one sample internally.

See Basis Representation for the wavelet transform itself, including thresholding-based denoising.

docs.title: Choosing an estimator
docs.text:
• Smooth \(\beta\), no prior information: peer with the default difference penalty, or the P-spline and FPC estimators of Scalar-on-Function.
  • A plausible shape for \(\beta\) from earlier studies or physics: peer with a decree penalty that leaves that shape unpenalised.
  • Repeated curves per subject: lpeer.
  • \(\beta\) with jumps, bursts or isolated features: wnet (sparse) or wcr (dense, few components).
  • Many more grid points than curves and an interest in where \(\beta\) is non-zero: wnet with alpha close to 1, then read off selected.

docs.title: Regression Diagnostics
docs.text:
A fitted regression summarizes the average relationship between predictor and response, but a handful of unusual observations can dominate that summary. Regression diagnostics identify which observations exert outsized influence on the fit, so you can decide whether they are valuable signal or corrupting noise. In functional regression the same logic applies to the FPC-score design: an observation can be a high-leverage point (unusual predictor shape), a large-residual point (unusual response), or — most dangerously — both, which makes it influential.

After fitting a functional regression model you typically want to answer three questions: are the model assumptions valid, are any observations unduly influential, and how stable are the results? fdars.explain provides a diagnostic toolkit adapted to FPC-based scalar-on-function models to answer them.

Diagnostic Function Question Leverage & Cook's distance influence_diagnostics How influential is each observation? DFBETAS / DFFITS dfbetas_dffits Which coefficient / fit does a point distort? Leave-one-out PRESS loo_cv_press How well does the model generalize? Variance inflation fpc_vif Are the FPC scores collinear? Permutation importance fpc_permutation_importance Which scores drive the prediction? Conditional importance conditional_permutation_importance Same, corrected for correlations Regression depth regression_depth Is the coefficient estimate robust? Explanation stability explanation_stability Does \(\beta(t)\) change across samples?

The influence, DFBETAS/DFFITS and PRESS diagnostics rely on the hat matrix, which is only defined for the linear FPC model. VIF, importance, depth and stability are more general and apply to any model built on FPC scores; stability is model-free because it refits the whole FPCA-plus-regression pipeline on each resample.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.simulation import simulate
from fdars.explain import influence_diagnostics

np.random.seed(0)
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 60)
X = np.asarray(simulate(n=36, argvals=t, n_basis=6, efun_type="fourier", seed=1))
beta_true = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
y = np.trapezoid(X * beta_true, t, axis=1) + 0.3 * np.random.randn(len(X))

# Inject one influential point: unusual response
y[5] += 4.0

diag = influence_diagnostics(X, y, ncomp=3)
lev = np.asarray(diag["leverage"])
cook = np.asarray(diag["cooks_distance"])

f, ax = fig()
ax.scatter(lev, cook, color="#3f51b5", s=36, alpha=0.85)
thr = 4 / len(y)                                  # common Cook's-D cutoff
flag = np.where(cook > thr)[0]
ax.scatter(lev[flag], cook[flag], color="#dc3545", s=70,
           edgecolor="k", zorder=3, label="flagged")
for i in flag:
    ax.annotate(str(i), (lev[i], cook[i]), fontsize=8,
                xytext=(4, 4), textcoords="offset points")
ax.axhline(thr, color="#6c757d", ls="--", lw=1, label=f"4/n = {thr:.3f}")
ax.set(title="Influence plot: Cook's distance vs. leverage",
       xlabel="leverage", ylabel="Cook's distance")
ax.legend()
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The injected point (index 5) jumps out as high Cook's distance — it moves the fit far more than a typical observation.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Write the FPC-score regression in matrix form \(y = Z\beta + \varepsilon\), where \(Z\) stacks the intercept and FPC scores. The hat matrix \(H = Z(Z^\top Z)^{-1}Z^\top\) maps observed to fitted values, \(\hat y = Hy\). Its diagonal \(h_{ii}\) is the leverage of observation \(i\) — how strongly its own response pulls its own fitted value. Leverage depends only on the predictors; a curve with an unusual FPC-score profile has high leverage regardless of its response.

Cook's distance combines leverage and residual size into a single influence measure — how much all fitted values shift when observation \(i\) is deleted:

\[ D_i = \frac{r_i^2}{p\,\hat\sigma^2}\cdot\frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2}, \]

where \(r_i\) is the residual, \(p\) the number of parameters, and \(\hat\sigma^2\) the residual variance. A common rule flags \(D_i > 4/n\). Two finer-grained measures localize the effect: DFFITS measures the change in observation \(i\)'s own fitted value when it is deleted, while DFBETAS measures the change in each coefficient, revealing which direction of the model a point distorts.

docs.title: Leverage and Cook's distance — influence_diagnostics
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from fdars.simulation import simulate
from fdars.explain import influence_diagnostics

np.random.seed(0)
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 60)
X = np.asarray(simulate(n=36, argvals=t, n_basis=6, efun_type="fourier", seed=1))
beta_true = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
y = np.trapezoid(X * beta_true, t, axis=1) + 0.3 * np.random.randn(len(X))

diag = influence_diagnostics(X, y, ncomp=3)
high_lev = np.where(diag["leverage"] > 2 * diag["p"] / len(y))[0]
print(f"high-leverage indices: {high_lev.tolist()}")
Return key Type Description leverage ndarray (n,) Hat-matrix diagonal \(h_{ii}\) cooks_distance ndarray (n,) Cook's distance \(D_i\) p float Number of model parameters (intercept + components) mse float Residual mean squared error

docs.title: DFBETAS and DFFITS — dfbetas_dffits
docs.text:
from fdars.explain import dfbetas_dffits

infl = dfbetas_dffits(X, y, ncomp=3)
print("DFFITS cutoff:  ", round(infl["dffits_cutoff"], 3))
print("DFBETAS cutoff: ", round(infl["dfbetas_cutoff"], 3))
Return key Type Description dfbetas ndarray (n, p) Per-coefficient influence of each observation dffits ndarray (n,) Change in own fitted value when deleted studentized_residuals ndarray (n,) Externally studentized residuals p float Number of parameters dfbetas_cutoff float \(2/\sqrt{n}\) suggested threshold dffits_cutoff float \(2\sqrt{p/n}\) suggested threshold

The studentized residuals against leverage give the second classic diagnostic view. Points in the upper corners — large residual and high leverage — are the ones to scrutinize.

image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Most points sit in the central band between the dotted \(\pm 2\) lines, marking a well-behaved bulk of observations. The red point flagged at high studentized residual is the outlier we injected at index 5 — reading residual against leverage separates a mere large residual (a vertical outlier) from a genuinely influential point that also sits far out in predictor space.

docs.title: Leave-one-out PRESS — loo_cv_press
docs.text:
The PRESS statistic sums the squared leave-one-out residuals, and loo_r_squared rescales it to an out-of-sample \(R^2\). Unlike the training \(R^2\), PRESS penalizes models that fit any single point too tightly — an honest complement to the leverage plot.

from fdars.explain import loo_cv_press

press = loo_cv_press(X, y, ncomp=3)
print(f"PRESS:        {press['press']:.3f}")
print(f"LOO R²:       {press['loo_r_squared']:.3f}")
Return key Type Description loo_residuals ndarray (n,) Leave-one-out residuals press float Predicted residual sum of squares loo_r_squared float Out-of-sample \(R^2\) from LOO residuals leverage ndarray (n,) Hat-matrix diagonal tss float Total sum of squares of the response

docs.title: Variance inflation — fpc_vif
docs.text:
Leverage and Cook's distance ask whether individual observations destabilize the fit; the variance inflation factor asks whether the predictors do. When two FPC scores carry overlapping information, their coefficients trade off against each other and the estimates become numerically fragile. VIF quantifies this per component:

\[ \text{VIF}_k = \frac{1}{1 - R_k^2}, \]

where \(R_k^2\) comes from regressing score \(\xi_k\) on all the others. \(\text{VIF}_k = 1\) means component \(k\) is orthogonal to the rest; \(\text{VIF}_k = 10\) means 90% of its variance is already explained by the other predictors. FPC scores are orthogonal by construction, so in a pure FPCA model every VIF should sit essentially at 1 — a departure signals numerical ill-conditioning or, once scalar covariates are added, real collinearity. A conventional cutoff flags \(\text{VIF} > 5\).

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.simulation import simulate
from fdars.explain import fpc_vif

np.random.seed(0)
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 60)
X = np.asarray(simulate(n=40, argvals=t, n_basis=6, efun_type="fourier", seed=1))
beta_true = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
y = np.trapezoid(X * beta_true, t, axis=1) + 0.3 * np.random.randn(len(X))

vif = fpc_vif(X, y, ncomp=5)
scores = np.asarray(vif["vif"])
labels = [f"PC{k+1}" for k in range(len(scores))]

f, ax = fig()
ax.bar(labels, scores, color="#7b2d8e", alpha=0.8)
ax.axhline(5, color="#dc3545", ls="--", lw=1, label="VIF = 5 threshold")
ax.axhline(1, color="#6c757d", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set(title="Variance inflation factor per FPC component",
       xlabel="component", ylabel="VIF")
ax.legend()
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Every bar rests at 1: the orthogonal FPC scores show no collinearity, exactly as expected (mean_vif ≈ 1). Read this plot alongside the influence diagnostics — it confirms that any instability you do see comes from individual observations, not from the design.

Return key Type Description vif ndarray (K,) Variance inflation factor per component labels list[str] Component labels mean_vif float Mean VIF across components n_moderate int Count with \(5 <\) VIF \(\le 10\) n_severe int Count with VIF \(> 10\)

docs.title: Residual diagnostics
docs.text:
The classic residual plots need only the fitted values and residuals of the linear model, which we reconstruct from the fitted FPC coefficients. Three views expose different assumption failures: a curved residuals-vs-fitted trend flags missing nonlinearity or a funnel shape flags heteroscedasticity; a Q-Q plot checks the Gaussian-error assumption that underpins parametric prediction intervals; and a scale-location plot re-examines variance homogeneity on the \(\sqrt{|e_i|}\) scale, where a flat smoother means constant spread.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.simulation import simulate
from fdars.explain import influence_diagnostics, dfbetas_dffits

np.random.seed(0)
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 60)
X = np.asarray(simulate(n=40, argvals=t, n_basis=6, efun_type="fourier", seed=1))
beta_true = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
y = np.trapezoid(X * beta_true, t, axis=1) + 0.3 * np.random.randn(len(X))

# Reconstruct fitted values and residuals from the FPC linear fit.
diag = influence_diagnostics(X, y, ncomp=5)
lev = np.asarray(diag["leverage"])
infl = dfbetas_dffits(X, y, ncomp=5)
# residual = studentized residual undone via leverage + MSE, but the simplest
# honest route is an ordinary least-squares refit on the same FPC scores:
from fdars.regression import fpca
sc = np.asarray(fpca(X, t, n_comp=5)["scores"])
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), sc])
beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(Z, y, rcond=None)
fitted = Z @ beta_hat
resid = y - fitted

# 1) residuals vs fitted (point size = leverage)
f, ax = fig()
sizes = 20 + 400 * (lev - lev.min()) / (np.ptp(lev) + 1e-12)
ax.scatter(fitted, resid, s=sizes, color="#4a90d9", alpha=0.6)
ax.axhline(0, color="#6c757d", ls="--", lw=1)
order = np.argsort(fitted)
# light loess-style trend via a low-order polynomial
coef = np.polyfit(fitted, resid, 2)
ax.plot(fitted[order], np.polyval(coef, fitted[order]),
        color="#dc3545", lw=1.2, label="quadratic trend")
ax.set(title="Residuals vs fitted (point size = leverage)",
       xlabel="fitted values", ylabel="residual")
ax.legend()
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The trend line hugs zero and the spread is even across the fitted range: no obvious nonlinearity or heteroscedasticity.

image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Points track the diagonal, so the Gaussian-error assumption holds — parametric prediction intervals (see uncertainty quantification) are justified here. Heavy tails would bow the points away from the line at the extremes.

image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The smoother stays flat, confirming roughly constant variance (homoscedasticity).

Residuals are reconstructed, not returned

The fdars.explain diagnostics return leverage, Cook's distance and studentized residuals but not the raw fitted values. The plots above refit the same FPC design with ordinary least squares (fpca scores plus an intercept) to obtain fitted values and residuals — an exact reconstruction of the linear model, done transparently in NumPy.

docs.title: Importance and robustness
docs.text: The final group of diagnostics asks not which observations matter but which parts of the model matter and how much you can trust them. All four operate on the FPC scores, so they apply to both fregre_lm-style and logistic models (stability is model-free).

docs.title: Permutation importance — fpc_permutation_importance
docs.text:
For each FPC score, randomly shuffle its values — severing its link to the response — and measure how much the prediction error grows. A large increase means the model leans heavily on that score:

\[ \text{Imp}_k = \frac{1}{P}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\Big[\text{MSE}\big(\hat y;\,\tilde\xi_k^{(p)}\big) - \text{MSE}(\hat y)\Big], \]

averaged over \(P\) permutation replicates. The measure is model-agnostic and stays non-negative for genuinely useful predictors.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.simulation import simulate
from fdars.explain import fpc_permutation_importance

np.random.seed(0)
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 60)
X = np.asarray(simulate(n=40, argvals=t, n_basis=6, efun_type="fourier", seed=1))
beta_true = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
y = np.trapezoid(X * beta_true, t, axis=1) + 0.3 * np.random.randn(len(X))

imp = fpc_permutation_importance(X, y, ncomp=5, n_perm=50, seed=42)
vals = np.asarray(imp["importance"])
labels = [f"PC{k+1}" for k in range(len(vals))]
order = np.argsort(-vals)

f, ax = fig()
ax.bar([labels[i] for i in order], vals[order], color="#4a90d9", alpha=0.8)
ax.set(title=f"Permutation importance (baseline MSE = {imp['baseline_metric']:.3f})",
       xlabel="component", ylabel="MSE increase when shuffled")
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The bars rank the components by how much shuffling each inflates the error — the tallest is the score the model relies on most.

docs.title: Conditional permutation importance — conditional_permutation_importance
docs.text:
Plain permutation importance can overstate a score when predictors are correlated, because shuffling one score also breaks its correlation with the others. Conditional permutation fixes this by shuffling \(\xi_k\) only within bins of the remaining scores, preserving the conditional distribution \(\xi_k \mid \boldsymbol\xi_{-k}\). Comparing the two versions tells you how much of the apparent importance is real rather than an artifact of correlation. Because FPC scores are orthogonal, the two should agree closely here.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.simulation import simulate
from fdars.explain import conditional_permutation_importance

np.random.seed(0)
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 60)
X = np.asarray(simulate(n=40, argvals=t, n_basis=6, efun_type="fourier", seed=1))
beta_true = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
y = np.trapezoid(X * beta_true, t, axis=1) + 0.3 * np.random.randn(len(X))

cimp = conditional_permutation_importance(X, y, ncomp=5, n_bins=5, n_perm=50, seed=42)
cond = np.asarray(cimp["importance"])
uncond = np.asarray(cimp["unconditional_importance"])
labels = [f"PC{k+1}" for k in range(len(cond))]
x = np.arange(len(labels))

f, ax = fig()
ax.bar(x - 0.2, cond, width=0.4, color="#4a90d9", alpha=0.8, label="conditional")
ax.bar(x + 0.2, uncond, width=0.4, color="#dc3545", alpha=0.8, label="unconditional")
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(labels)
ax.set(title="Conditional vs unconditional permutation importance",
       xlabel="component", ylabel="importance")
ax.legend()
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The two sets of bars line up: with orthogonal scores there is no spurious importance to correct for. A gap would flag a component whose apparent influence rides on correlation with others.

docs.title: Regression depth — regression_depth
docs.text:
Regression depth measures how central the fitted coefficients sit inside a cloud of bootstrap re-estimates. The function bootstraps the fit \(B\) times and reports the depth of \(\hat\beta\): a value near \(0.5\) means the estimate lives in the middle of the cloud (robust), while a value near \(0\) means it sits on the boundary, where a small data perturbation could swing it. It also returns a per-observation score_depths array, so you can see which cases sit deepest in — versus at the edge of — the resampled score distribution.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.simulation import simulate
from fdars.explain import regression_depth

np.random.seed(0)
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 60)
X = np.asarray(simulate(n=40, argvals=t, n_basis=6, efun_type="fourier", seed=1))
beta_true = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
y = np.trapezoid(X * beta_true, t, axis=1) + 0.3 * np.random.randn(len(X))

rd = regression_depth(X, y, ncomp=5, n_boot=50, seed=42)
sd = np.asarray(rd["score_depths"])

f, ax = fig()
ax.hist(sd, bins=12, color="#2e8b57", alpha=0.8)
ax.axvline(rd["mean_score_depth"], color="#dc3545", ls="--", lw=1,
           label=f"mean = {rd['mean_score_depth']:.3f}")
ax.set(title=f"Score depth distribution (beta depth = {rd['beta_depth']:.3f})",
       xlabel="score depth", ylabel="count")
ax.legend()
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

A beta depth of ~0.34 (out of a maximum 0.5) puts the coefficient vector comfortably inside the bootstrap cloud — the fit is robust to resampling. Observations with low score depth are the ones sitting near the edge of the score distribution.

score_depths is per-observation here

The R reference reports one depth per FPC component; the Python binding instead returns one depth per observation (score_depths has length \(n\)). The plot above reflects the Python semantics — a distribution over cases, summarized by mean_score_depth.

docs.title: Explanation stability — explanation_stability
docs.text:
Stability analysis asks: if I had drawn a slightly different sample, how much would \(\beta(t)\) move? It bootstraps the entire pipeline — FPCA plus regression — and reports the pointwise coefficient of variation of \(\hat\beta(t)\):

\[ \text{CV}(t) = \frac{\hat\sigma_{\text{boot}}\big(\hat\beta(t)\big)} {\big|\overline{\hat\beta}(t)\big| + \epsilon}, \]

with a small \(\epsilon\) guarding against division by zero where \(\beta(t)\approx 0\). Low CV marks stable regions; peaks mark stretches of the domain where the coefficient function is unreliable. Because it refits from scratch each time, the function takes the raw data rather than a fitted model.

import numpy as np
from docs_fig import fig, render
from fdars.simulation import simulate
from fdars.explain import explanation_stability

np.random.seed(0)
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 60)
X = np.asarray(simulate(n=40, argvals=t, n_basis=6, efun_type="fourier", seed=1))
beta_true = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
y = np.trapezoid(X * beta_true, t, axis=1) + 0.3 * np.random.randn(len(X))

stab = explanation_stability(X, y, ncomp=5, n_boot=50, seed=42)
cv = np.asarray(stab["beta_t_cv"])

f, ax = fig()
ax.plot(t, cv, color="#c0392b", lw=1.4)
ax.fill_between(t, 0, cv, color="#c0392b", alpha=0.12)
ax.set(title=f"Coefficient of variation of beta(t) (mean CV = {cv.mean():.2f})",
       xlabel="t", ylabel="CV")
print(render(f))
image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The CV spikes near where \(\beta(t) = \sin(2\pi t)\) crosses zero (around \(t\approx 0\), \(0.5\) and \(1\)) — the denominator shrinks in those neighborhoods, so a high CV there is largely an artifact of near-zero coefficients rather than genuine instability. Away from those crossings the coefficient function is estimated consistently across resamples.

Flagging is not deleting

A flagged point is a point to investigate, not automatically remove. High influence may reflect a genuine, informative extreme observation. When influential points are truly contaminating, prefer a principled remedy — robust regression down-weights outliers without hand-deleting data.

Leverage vs. influence

High leverage alone is harmless if the point follows the trend (large \(h_{ii}\), tiny Cook's \(D\)). It only becomes influential when paired with a large residual. Always read the two diagnostic plots together.
